Uniform Title:
Kālottara Main Title: Kālottara Mahātantra Secondary Title: Bṛhatkālottara
Manuscript: NGMPP Reel No. B 29/59, Manuscript No. pra-89. Description:
A version of the *Kālottara* known as the *Bṛhatkālottara* (the Great Kālottara), so named on account of its extensive length. It is referred to as a *Mahātantra* in the colophon.
Notes: Revision 0: February 16, 2013; Part 1 Revision 1: December 16, 2013; Part II added (now complete).
Internet Publisher: Muktabodha.

Kārttikeya said:
Salutations to you, the omniscient; salutations to you, the creator of all.
Salutations to you whose essential nature is undecaying, to you who are pure consciousness alone.
Salutations to you whose essential nature is never lost, who are pure consciousness alone;
salutations to the peaceful radiance whose body transcends all means of valid cognition.

Salutation to Śiva, the Supreme Self, the Lord who is without beginning or end, whose inner nature transcends the six forms of consciousness and the instruments of action, and who is beyond both rejection and acceptance.
Salutation to you who are identical with reality, to the immeasurable self who is beyond all divisions;
salutation indeed to him who is distinct from the knower, the act of knowing, and the object of knowledge.
Salutation to the Brahman of bliss, whose essential nature is pure cognition;
salutation indeed to Him who is distinct from ignorance and whose body is knowledge.
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, Śaṅkara, bestower of grace upon all!
You have indeed related this great Tantra in detail, which removes inauspiciousness.
Yet these mortals are short-lived, possessing little strength and little intelligence.
Seized by the crocodile of ignorance, they are deprived of bliss.
Therefore, O Lord, explain to me that bath like a sacred thread-mantra,
by the mere knowledge of which one may attain union with Śiva.
Tell me the characteristics of mantras, the details of ritual bathing, worship, and so forth;
as well as the procedure for the daily fire offering (nityahoma) and the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Furthermore, tell me now the sixfold injunction regarding the determination of the oblations,
both in general and in detail, as well as their defining characteristics.
Tell me specifically the ritual procedure for initiation (dīkṣā),
as well as the origin of the tantras and their particular descent into this world.
The application of the characteristics and the commitments, as well as the application of the bases;
the characteristics of the mandalas and the application of the weapons.
The ritual procedure for Sarasvatī, the chapter on exposition,
the rules regarding days unfit for study, and the characteristics of the practitioner and the teacher.
The ritual procedure for the bell-thread, likewise the rules for the water-pot,
the rules for expiation, and [the penance] for transgressing prescribed injunctions.
The ritual procedure for overcoming death, the characteristics of the temple,
the consideration of the divisions (aṃśaka), and the very means for attaining spiritual perfection.
Furthermore, the installation of the *liṅga* preceded by the ritual acquisition of the ground (*bhūparigraha*),
as well as the various modes of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) for villages, altars (*piṇḍikā*), and so forth.
O you who possess the characteristics of a bull, please explain with care the ritual for ascending the purifier (pavitrārohaṇa),
the proportions for the great ablution (mahāsnāna), and likewise the procedure for the door of the linga.
The funeral rites, the characteristics of the sectarian marks, as well as the definition of the vows;
likewise, the chapter on flowers, peace, concentration, and their defining characteristics.
"O Lord of Gods, please explain these and other [topics] to me in their proper sequence. Thus ends the first chapter in the *Kālottara-mahātantra*.
Īśvara said: O destroyer of Krauñca, that which is supreme, peaceful, free from disease, and consisting of eternal bliss—
its essential nature should be known in ten ways.
It is indefinable, beginningless, subtle, eternal, and free from affliction;
it is to be known as likewise permanent, the Lord, all-pervading, and auspicious.
Such is the form of the Supreme, beyond the range of the path of speech,
devoid of all means of valid cognition, and the destroyer of even the slightest trace of duality.
I shall describe the very form of the Other as being without another;
it is both with parts and partless, void, yet enriched with creative powers, and adorned by the ether.
The consumption [of smoke] and the inhalation of smoke through the throat and lips are prescribed;
thus, the eightfold method known as *parā* and called *svara* has been described by me.
O Six-faced One, the nature of that deity named Sadāśiva, who is of the form of sound,
should be known in its eightfold aspect for the sake of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Otherwise, how could one attain liberation from the bonds of existence?
Having realized the reality of Sadāśiva, they go to the stainless Śiva.
The practitioner should therefore practice that which is infallible, immutable, peaceful, eternally blissful, free from disease, stainless, and pure— indeed, the totality.
O God, that which consists of the mass of sounds is recited as *sakala* (with parts):

With one foot [standing] in the place called Ujjākhya, the moon is compared to the sun;

Tejaśvin, Śakra, Udadhi, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Siṃha;
two Śaśāṅkas, Viśvarūpin, and Narasiṃha as the last.
These Rudras are fully described as established in their offices of authority;

Having stepped out [from the heart], one should fashion the Universal Form (viśvarūpa) pervaded by the measure of the path;

This [practice] should be performed by men as a bestower of success, granting both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Know the fourth to be the head, named after the Lord (Īśvara). The tuft (śikhā) is to be known as "Uhaṅka," endowed with the universal form (viśvarūpa).
The tenth is considered to have eight eyes;
it is known as Astra, Śaśin, and named Śiva, O Śikhidhvaja.

One should apply the six seed-syllables— namas, svāhā, likewise vauṣaṭ, hūṃ, vaṣaṭ, and phaṭ— in sequence to the heart and the other [limbs]. Mantras ignited by the syllable *oṃ* and joined with these seed-syllables bestow their fruits.

Therefore, I shall now declare the Śiva-mantra known as Prasāda, letter by letter:

By merely bathing once, the destruction of all sins occurs;
he who performs it seven times shall obtain the fruit of all sacred fords.
One who knows the mantras becomes a *snātaka* after reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times; he should repeat it three times at each junction of the day (*trisandhyam*).
By the power of that [act], his fathers, grandfathers, and likewise his renowned great-grandfathers go to the imperishable world of Śiva.
For this purpose, O Mahāsena, he performs that which is praiseworthy for the Śiva-yogins,
wonderful and pure, through the vision of Śiva.
I shall further declare the Pāśupata [rite] for those who are afflicted by Vināyaka.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of the crest (Śikhā) ending with the syllable Phaṭ,

One should not employ the Mahāpāśupata weapon against the body;
this is known as the "Single Practice," which bestows all enjoyment and liberation.
The limbs of Brahmā, as well as Śiva and Mahāpāśupata;
at the time of initiation, one should worship Śiva together with the weapons of the world-protectors.
One should compose the world’s scriptures beginning with the syllable *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*;
one should likewise fashion the *sadyojāta* form-mantra for the sake of grace.
"The complete [form] of *prasāda* has been declared; now the partless (*niṣkala*) is being described.
Thus ends the chapter on the extraction of *prasāda* in the great tantra, the *Kālottara*.
Now, I shall describe the extraction of that which is called Niṣkala;
it is the form of the universe accompanied by its medicinal herb, known as Rudra, and is the solar orb [devoid of the visarga and the bindu].
Then follows the union of the half-moon and the sound (nāda), which is unconscious and curved;
this is the supreme partless mantra, Śiva himself, the manifest Sadāśiva.
The great heart-mantra, accompanied by its five limbs, bestows enjoyment upon men; it is all-pervading, possesses both vowels and consonants, is endowed with the nasal bindu, and is multiform.
Aṃśumān is Viśvarūpa, and together with Īśvara, it is considered the head; by the sixth [syllable] the tuft (śikhā) is to be known, and from there the eighth [syllable] follows.

One should utter the weapon-mantra (*astra*) beginning with *śaśinā viśvarūpaṃ* and ending with *phaṭ*; one should then arrange the limbs of Śiva (*śivāṅga*), beginning with the syllable *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*.
At the time of worship, one should employ the heart-seed syllable as the embodied mantra;
this single enclosure alone accomplishes all desires and aims.
Thus ends the chapter on the Niṣkala-mantras in the Kālottara.
I shall proclaim the *Śūnyoddhara*, which destroys great sins;
by merely remembering it even once, a practitioner in any state whatsoever [is purified].
It dissolves into the body of Śiva like milk merging with milk;
it is formless, yet possesses the universal form, and is immortal, designated as the Void (Śūnya).
Because it is devoid of the limbs of Brahmā, it is proclaimed as "empty" (śūnya).
For the purpose of dispelling obstacles, the Praṇava should be employed in the placement of the form, ending with the syllable Phaṭ.
This supreme secret must not be told to just anyone— not to women who have children or hair, nor to those who are afflicted by disease.
O Śikhidhvaja, emptiness has been taught for both the seekers of enjoyment and the practitioners of yoga;
for those who are detached from the ritualistic section [of the Vedas], there is no confusion among the various streams [of doctrine].

the characteristic of the Void has been declared—always perform its recitation as if it were the vital breath (prāṇa).
Thus ends the chapter on the extraction of the mantra of emptiness in the Kālottara.
I shall describe the characteristics of Kalāḍhya, who follows in due order:
he possesses rays and is situated above the one named Viśvarūpa, who is the source of all.
One should know that which is enriched with the *kalās* as the destroyer of all misdeeds;

The sky is rendered pure by the rays [of the sun] and the syllable ŪH, which pervades above and below;

Now, I shall describe to you in order the Brahma-mantras and the limb-mantras (aṅgas) for this [deity], which have been prepared with mantras beginning with the syllable Om and ending with Namaḥ.

beyond that, one should extract the seventh letter, which is Āśūmānudakaprāṇa.
A lotus stepped upon by Indra, Nandīśa, and Ekapāda—

know that the five-syllabled word which arises from *nidhana* is likewise a foot.

From the two-syllable [mantra], the state of Śiva is attained; from the two-syllable, all states are attained; thereafter, the state of the Supreme Self (Paramātman) is to be known as the four-syllable [mantra] in its condensed form.

In the Tantra, that four-syllable term "all-of-all" (sarvasarva) is to be understood;

it stands beyond Rudra and precedes Brahmā and Viṣṇu.

when repeated twice without an interval, are said to constitute a single eight-syllable word.
Even that which was previously unacquainted, the state established before, remains as it was;
thus, step by step, everything up to the state established before consists of the nature called form.
Thirty-two filaments are to be employed on the seat of the Lord;
for each witness, the four castes are mentioned twice to form a continuous sequence of words.
That which is to be understood is the lotus on the shoulder; its designator is the supreme word.
The word consisting of the syllable *turu* is proclaimed as four-syllabled through its repetition.
One should also [place] the six-syllable *pataṅga* from the subsequent [mantra], as well as the four-syllable one situated before it; and also the two called *piṅga*, which have the word *udita*.
8b) In the same way, the state of gnosis is to be known as the word "knowable," and likewise the word "sound" is the state of sound;
even for the most subtle state, its nature consists of the words of enumeration.
The state of Śiva consists of two syllables, and it is of the nature of an address;
furthermore, there are eight auspicious words beginning with "tu" and ending with "sarva."
O Mahāsena, these are the names of the great-souled guardians of the directions, from Śakra down to Īśa, to be recited in sequence during the performance of the sacrificial rite.
The three-syllable word *sarvada* is traditionally known as the lord of all mantras;

at the end, there is a word consisting of a single syllable situated within the lunar orb for the sake of the Vajra and the others.

while the syllables are said to be three hundred and sixty-eight.
But the worship of the God of gods, who possesses both collective and individual forms,
is not suitable for Vyāsa, as he is the foremost among those characterized by mantras.
Even a single phoneme is proclaimed to be expressive of the Lord;
for all [phonemes] are applicable to the One, since they are the forms of Śiva.
9a) They perform all actions; they accomplish every single purpose;
they assume all forms; they possess the power to fulfill all desires without fail.
All these [practices] arising from the body of Śiva are not to be scrutinized by those of small intellect;
having understood the scripture as authoritative, they should be performed with purity for the sake of liberation.
And for the sake of accomplishment, O Mahāsena, even an impure fruit is sometimes obtained here; how much more so, then, the supreme state of Śiva?
Thus ends the chapter on the extraction of mantras in the *Vyomavyāpin*, known as the *Kṣayamantra*, within the great tantra, the *Kālottara*.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Ṣaṇmukha, to the true characteristics of the throat and the lips;
having extracted the universal form (viśvarūpa), it is situated above in the radiant energy (tejas).
Then one should place Narasiṃha below that, and Kṛtānta below him;
below that, the syllable of Śakra, and below that, one should place Rasa.
Having placed *prāṇa* below that, and again *ūhaka* below that,
[one reaches] *aṃśumān*, which resides in the universal form (*viśvamūrti*) and is proclaimed as being located in the throat and lips.
Preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, it thus becomes four syllables long;
having placed the form of the universe (*viśvarūpa*) within the letter *va*, one should endow it with the digits of the sun.
The first, third, fifth, and seventh [are] Sadyojāta;
the ninth is Sadyodeva; and likewise the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth.
The tenth and the twelfth [syllables], adorned with their respective seed-syllables (jāti), beginning with the heart-mantra;
this supreme mantra of the throat and lips pacifies the suffering of all living beings.
That mantra which pacifies the afflictions caused by poisons, crushes the wicked and harmful,
and pierces through everything, should be known as being like a wish-fulfilling gem.
Thus, this group of eight mantras is renowned in this scripture known as Kāla;
for each one, there resides a seat consisting of seventy million mantras.
Thus ends the chapter on the extraction of the mantra for the throat and lips in the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain purification in brief:
the cleansing of the external limbs with water together with auspicious clay.
Purity through truth is the restraint of the senses by means of *yama* and the other [observances];
it is the purification of the *sattva* by perceiving its equanimity, free from discursive thought.
O Mahāsena, the intellect (buddhi) is also proclaimed to be purified through the practice of yoga;
the vital breaths (prāṇas) are always purified according to the rules by the power of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Purification from meditation has been taught for the Pradhāna, whose nature consists of the Guṇas;
indeed, the Self is purified by the power of consciousness, as stated by the Supreme Lord.
Having taken up a bamboo staff and having covered his head,
the practitioner of mantra should then go outside to a secluded place near water.
In a bean-cake, in a cremation ground, at a triple-way or a quadruple-way,
on a crowded royal road, or likewise in a recitation hall or a grove;
One must avoid [voiding] in a temple of the deities and especially on a cow-path;
one must avoid feces, urine, and so forth, because they cause the destruction of splendor.
Having placed the purifier (pavitra) against his ear, he should always void feces and urine;
by day he should face north, and at night he should face south.
Having thus performed the necessary cleansing, one should wipe the anus with a clod of earth;
one should not look at one's own reflection, nor should one gaze into the sky.
For the purpose of removing odors and stains, one should perform the appropriate purification with pure,
stainless water that has been strained through a cloth.
One should take sand that is praised, free from worms, hair, and the like,
originating from a pleasant region, fragrant, devoid of grass, and pure.
First, having grasped the penis with the left hand,
the wise man should wash it with clay and water, rubbing thoroughly between each finger.
Exactly that many [clods] should be given; afterwards, both hands are washed.
Furthermore, when the voiding of feces has been performed, purification is prescribed.
Seven types of earth should be applied to the feet by the wise man, three to each foot;
then three on the hands, and finally one to both [the hands].
Having offered seven [handfuls of water], O Mahāsena, one should wash with clay and water;
then, having risen, one should slowly wash the waist, the thighs, the shanks, and the feet.
Taking earth with the left hand, one should purify it five times;
one should also cleanse the hands and the wrists with earth and water.
This is the purification for householders; when the sun is in the middle [of the sky], one should diligently practice the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) twice as long as the [usual] middle [period].

Having risen during the morning twilight, one should offer water for honor (arghya) to the Sun while facing the east; and the recitation (japa) should likewise be performed with food obtained by gleaning (uñchita).
Likewise, at the time of midday, one should offer [the water] facing south;
having offered the *arghya* while standing in the evening, one should then sit down and perform the recitation (*japa*).
First, one should perform the Vedic twilight ritual; that itself is the heart-rite of Śiva.
Then, having formed the Mahāmudrās, one should dismiss [the deity] with the words, "Forgive me."
Thus, having first performed the ritual bath, one should carry out the twilight worship (saṃdhyā) there as before.
Thus ends the chapter on twilight worship in the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
One should perform the daily, occasional, and other rites beginning with the ritual bathing;
now, O Six-faced One, listen to that very process in its true order.
In this scripture, the *Kālasūtra*, which grants all desires to men, the entire procedure—
including the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), worship, and so forth— is preceded by the prescribed rite of bathing.
Therefore, the general procedure for bathing shall first be explained:
[it may be performed] in the currents of rivers and streams, in pools, or in lakes.
One should perform the ritual bath in a pond, a long reservoir, or a beautiful and auspicious place known as a *devakhāta*, or in a secluded lotus-pool, or even in one's own home.
For the sake of purification, one should perform a bath by drawing water from a nearby source;
for the successful accomplishment of the rite, one should take up earth as before and bathe.
Having purified the ground with a blade, one should deposit [the remains] in an impure place within the heart;
having formed an añjali from two parts, [one should place it] on the riverbank or in a house.

The first portion is for bathing away impurities; the next is prescribed for ritual bathing. [One should bathe] the two feet, the shanks, the thighs, the waist, the anus, the penis, and the two buttocks.
Having washed his hands according to the rule and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) as before,
he should take up earth with the Astra-mantra and rub it on both his knees.
A wise person should diligently rub [the body] from the head down to the feet;
then, the wiping should be performed for the sake of removing dirt during the bath.
Then, having touched the center of the *uttarācchala* as before,
the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the ancestors who are devoid of initiation (*dīkṣā*) should be performed.
Having first performed the ritual placement (*karanyāsa*), one should carry out the prescribed rite of bathing;
recollecting the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one should carefully collect the earth.
One should divide the three portions separately according to sequence:
the first portion consecrated with the Astra mantra, and the middle one consecrated with the Brahma mantra.
11b) One should consecrate the third [portion] with the mantra recited for Śiva;
one should perform the binding of the directions there with a portion of the mantra recited for the Astra.
Having recited the Śiva-mantra, one should remember the Śiva-tīrtha, which is circular and situated on the outside,
while facing north.
Having restrained the Ganges-water flowing from his mass of matted locks— which destroys all sin—
envelop your body with that portion which has been consecrated by recitation over the limbs of Brahmā.
Having recollected the Śiva-mantra, one should immerse oneself in the midst of the Śiva-tīrtha; performing the act of immersion, one should keep the Śiva-tīrtha in mind.
Endowed with the movement of the wheel and with the *samanvāmalaka* and other [substances],
one should first perform the ritual bath according to the rules, and thereafter [the other].
Then the ritual bath (vidhisnāna) should be performed; having leaped up, one should gaze at the sun, drawing the sacred waters to the bank of the tirtha with the heart-mantra and the akuśa-mudrā.
Having performed such a bath, one should change one's loincloth;
it should be twelve finger-breadths in width and thirty-six finger-breadths in length.
A cord of fifty threads, a loincloth hanging down by three parts,
and two garments that are seamless, well-whitened, and fine, are beneficial for a householder.

The upper garment and the Pavitra belong to the three [twice-born classes], while the Brahmasūtra belongs to all three; however, the upper garment for Śūdras is different from that, and it should be worn accordingly, not otherwise.
One should let the offerings remain until the worship is completed and never hold them above;
the tips, the middles, and the left sides [of the grass blades] are for the gods, the brahmins, and the ancestors, respectively.
12a) "Namaḥ," "svāhā," and "svadhā"—with these, one should perform their libation in due order.
First, one should satisfy the Saṃhitā, as well as the world-protectors and the planets.
To Yama, the King of Dharma, to Death, to the Ender,
to Vaivasvata, to Time, and to the immediate taker of life.
Atri, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, Gālava,
Pulastya, and Cyavana were always gratified and remained bestowers of peace.
After offering to the father and wife, one should again offer to the maternal and paternal ancestors;
then, having brought water from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), the rite should be performed heart-to-heart.
White flowers, white mustard seeds, and likewise sprouts of blue dūrvā grass should be placed upon the head after bathing; a tilaka made with yellow pigment (rocanā) should also be applied.
It burns away intense sin and destroys misfortune;
this, O Six-faced One, is declared to be the ritual bath (vidhisnāna) by way of brief description.
Thus ends the chapter on ritual bathing in the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
Thereafter, the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) should be performed after the water-bath;
however, one who is unable [to perform the water-bath] may perform this destroyer of sins even without the water-bath.
Taking a handful of ashes consecrated with the Saṃhitā mantras,
one should first perform the impurity bath from the head down to the feet.
Thereafter, the ritual bath (vidhisnāna) should be performed with the heart-mantra;
one should then carefully scatter the fivefold ashes over the head while reciting the Īśāna mantra.
In the mouth it is fourfold, in the face eightfold by means of the terrible [face], in the heart likewise;
in the secret region it is threefold, according to the division of the stations of the thirty gods.
Having firmly bound the feet with the Sadya mantra through diligent effort,
one should truly perform the contraction of all the limbs with the Sadyojāta mantra.
Smearing with ashes is prescribed for a twice-born man; for a kṣatriya, it is otherwise ordained:
having smeared all that [except] the face according to the sequence of the limbs.
The Vaiśyas should apply the Tripuṇḍraka on the forehead alone, and the Śūdras likewise; or else, a Tilaka should be made. Now listen to the distinctions regarding the recitation of mantras (japa).

O Six-faced One, having washed his hands and feet thoroughly and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) as before, he should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā-pūjā) and other rites, as well as recitation (japa), meditation (dhyāna), and so forth.
Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the ash-bath in the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
I shall fully explain sacrifice according to its rules and in proper sequence;
it should be understood as being of two kinds, corresponding to the respective qualifications [of the performer].
For ascetics and yogis, external worship is prescribed toward other powers; however, internal sacrifice is ordained for those devoted to the supreme.
Having bathed according to the previously mentioned procedure, the wise practitioner, with his mind dedicated to Śiva,
should perform the *māyā*, *vāk*, and *samaya* [mantras], and indeed avoid any physical contact with others.
The worship hall, situated in the northeastern direction, should be beautiful to behold;
it should measure thirty-two cubits, or alternatively, twenty cubits.
Equipped with couches and pillars, having four doors and arched gateways,
it is well-concealed, secluded, delightful, strewn with flowers, and auspicious.
This [shrine] is well-perfumed with the fragrance of incense, anointed with sandalwood and other unguents,
covered above with a canopy, and adorned with hanging strings of pearls.
Abounding with white cloth banners, with many-colored flags raised high,
sprinkled with saffron water, and grey with powdered camphor.
A dwelling enriched with lamps whose flames are steady and filled with the rays of mirrors is thus recommended for daily worship; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Such being the case, from both existence and non-existence,
one should first prepare a beautiful vessel for the arghya offering with the Praṇava.
Or, in a square or circular area marked with four horns, one should offer the *argha* oblation to the Sun,
using either the Śiva-Gāyatrī mantra, the *praṇava*, or the *hṛdaya* mantra.
One should offer the *argha* oblation to the Sun and worship him daily once,
using *argha*, flowers, perfumes, and preceded by incense and lamps.
One should worship with diligence and dismiss [the deity] saying, "Forgive me.
Then, one should fill the vessel again, provided with scents, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
And at the doorway, one should worship the door-keepers upon the doorposts;
one should worship Nandīśvara on the southern doorpost.
One should worship Mahākāla at the northern branch of the Yamunā-uccāra,
and Sarasvatī and Gaṇeśa at the Śrīrūrcādu-gvara.
O Six-faced One, having worshipped with offerings of flowers, *arghya*, incense, and oblations (*bali*),
one should then cast flowers and various [substances] with the *Pāśupata* weapon. With three snaps of the fingers, one should likewise perform three strikes with the palm and the heel.
Through this, peace is produced for those [disturbances] pertaining to the celestial, the atmospheric, and the terrestrial realms.
Having performed the binding of the directions with the Astra-mantra and the veiling with the Kavaca-mantra,
he should face north and remain seated upon a beautiful seat.
Having purified the hands with the Śiva-weapon mantra, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi);
then, with focused awareness, one should gaze at the tip of the nose while forming the dhvaja-mudrā.
He should hold his neck like a conch shell, with his head slightly bent forward.
Keeping the spinal column erect and the nose straight, one should touch the teeth with the teeth; slightly raising the tip of the tongue, with the eyes not too wide open and the lips [closed].
Having purified [the hands] with the *karavastreṇa* [mantra], one should sequentially assign the Brahma-aṅgas,
beginning from the little finger up to the thumb.
Having placed Īśa and the others [at the fingers], Jyeṣṭha and the others at the heart and other limbs,
and the Astra-mantra on the palms, one should place Śiva on both palms.
Then, having formed the tortoise-mudrā (*kūrmamudrā*), one should fix the self there;
then, for the sake of purifying one's own impure vital breaths, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
Then, one should gradually lead the senses, which are considered to be under the control of the *akṣa*, [into the center];
by means of the self, the purification of the self must be performed within the self in due order.
O child, one should purify the tree of the body, which consists of impurity, māyā, and kalā,
by means of the five *praṇavas* and the five breath-controls (*prāṇāyāmas*).
Having burned [the body] once with the *recaka* breath up to the crown of the head by means of *māyā*,
one should perform the immersion (*plavana*) from that ash, and one should cause that ash to be flooded away quickly.

O Fire-bannered One (Agni), by means of the downward expulsion (*recaka*) from the anus, one should first install the Support-Energy (*ādhāra-śakti*); then, by means of that energy, one should install the lotus.
One should place the self, shining like the stars, within the *recaka* [exhalation];
then the "fist of knowledge" (*vidyāmuṣṭi*) should be performed, wherein Brahman itself becomes the object of one's vision.

One should not conceive of the form of Sadyojāta for the sake of accomplishing all limbs, [but rather] Īśa as the head, Tatpuruṣa as the speech-organ, Aghora as the heart, Vāmadeva as the private parts, and Sadyojāta as the feet.
O God, Sadāśiva is indeed complete and possesses five faces;
likewise, the syllable *oṃ* consists of nectar, resembles a water-pot, and is as pure as a lotus.
In the inhalation of the agitation, by means of that [mantra] ending with *vauṣaṭ* and consisting of the [five] classes [of phonemes],
one should contemplate one's own body as completely filled as soon as it has been filled by that.
Thereafter, having invoked Śiva, who possesses both external and internal aspects and is as radiant as ten thousand suns, with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, [he should proceed].
Having first arranged the limbs of Brahmā by means of pervasion, one should then form the Mahāmudrā; thus one becomes the body of the five-faced one.
Then, the rite of eradication (uccāṭana) should be performed with the palatal [syllable] by means of the Śivāśin;
one should effect the evacuation of the quarters by means of the threatening gesture, the weapon, and the glance.
14b) Having covered the sacrificial ground with armor as if with a cloth,
one should then take up the argha vessel, whether made of gold or of clay.
One should carefully perform the eight-syllable [mantra], which is surrounded by the state of its non-existence;
one should make it consecrated by the *saṃhitā* and rendered nectar-like by the *dhenumudrā*.
One should purify [the site] with the Astra-mantra, [protect it] with the Puri and Varma [mantras], and veil it;
then, with a collection of flowers, one should worship the mantras of the limbs of Śiva-Brahman.
One should worship oneself first, and afterwards perform the purification of the site;
then, the collection of ritual substances should be prepared by consuming [the offerings] once.
There, first, one should worship Gaṇanāyaka on the northwest corner of the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) with water for honor (argha), sandalwood paste, incense, and so forth.
Immediately after that, [one should worship] the gurus, beginning with Śiva, with the mantra: "Oṃ namaḥ śivādibhyaḥ."
He should cause that seat and linga to be removed with the Astra-mantra, even if they are enduring.
One should worship the Liṅga with the six-syllabled mantra;
one should place the garments, flowers, ointments, and other offerings in the northeast direction.
One should bathe [the deity] with a pitcher over which the Śivāstra mantra has been recited for the pacification of obstacles;
one should then arrange that flow emerging from the liṅga and the pedestal.
Having offered the *argha* along with flowers, he should contemplate the pervasion of the *liṅga*;
then, according to the rule, he should perform the placement of the *ādhāra-śakti* with the syllable *praṇava*.
The reality of the stalk-bond is the lotus-stalk extending to the end of time;
likewise, the world is the thorn that threads through the five unreal entities.
15a) The great knot is the principle of Māyā; Vidyā is the lotus of knowledge.
Vāmā and the others are situated upon the filaments, starting from the east and so forth, with the Heart-mantra.

One should worship Dharma and the others within the principle of the intellect (buddhitattva), and one should worship the weapon in the form of a lion at the pericarp of Manonmanī, by conceiving it as half of her form.
One should place the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), dispassion (vairāgya), and sovereignty (aiśvarya) from the fire [element];
white, red, yellow, and black, looking toward one's own back.
One should worship, in sequence, the seed-syllables, the sprouts, and the infinite [deities] such as Dharma and the rest, beneath the seat of the reality of the self in the station of Brahmā.

The lotus consists of the pericarp and petals; Manonmanī is upon the pericarp in the middle of the left [side], while Vidyā resides on the back of the pedestal, within the sphere of the end of the principles (tattva).
Having worshipped with scents, flowers, and other offerings the seat of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), beginning from the foundational power (Ādhāraśakti) up to Manonmanī.
From Īśvara down to Śakti, the form belongs to that which is designated as Rudra;
beyond that, one should invoke the all-pervading [deity] upon the top of the *liṅga*.

Thus it has been stated in brief; understand it in full detail: having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the form that is the essence of the mantra, which is free from fear, according to the distinction between the knowledge-mantra and the self.
With five [arrows], he should fashion the five heads in those locations;
thereafter, with Tatpuruṣa alone, he should contemplate the faces of the Lord.
Pervade the navel, heart, belly, neck, and back in sequence; likewise, the two shoulders and the chest of many forms.
Likewise, the hips, the two sides, the buttocks, the genitals, and the anus, as well as the two thighs and the calves, are situated in their respective order.
Then, one should fashion the two calves and the feet in sequence with the Vāmadeva hymn,
as well as the two hands, the two feet, the pair of arms, and the nose.
One should always fashion the head of the Lord with the Sadyojāta mantra;
thus the deity becomes Sakala (with parts), otherwise he is Śiva Niṣkala (without parts).
He, however, should be considered the Lord, whose form is the universe in its manifold aspects;
established through the power of yoga, he is not afflicted by karma.
This is indeed the blameless form of the Supreme Lord as he sports;
it resembles pure crystal and is radiant with rays of light issuing from his own limbs.
One should meditate upon Maheśvara, the God of gods, who has five heads,
three or five eyes, a serene countenance, five faces, and the ocean as his seat.
He has ten arms and large eyes; at the snake-sacrifice, he wears the sacred thread, and holds a blue lotus, a sword, a rosary, and a bracelet. He is fearsome.
With his five right arms, he holds the trident smeared with [ashes] of Hara,
a citron, a bow, a shield, and the gesture of granting boons (varada) along with a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
On the left side of the God of gods, five arms are proclaimed;
Īśāna has the luster of pure jasmine, while Nara is like saffron from the east.
To the south is the terrible Añjanavat, and Vāmadeva is always to the north; Sadyojāta, resembling the flower of the pomegranate tree, is situated in the western direction.
One should meditate upon Sadāśiva, who has the form of a mass of snow and five faces,
measuring only the size of a thumb-joint, situated above the pericarp.
Having thus fashioned the body of the mantra, one should then instill radiance within it;
thereafter, the ritual application (karaṇa) should be performed according to the instruction from the mouth of the Guru.
Having attained a state of identity with Śakti, Mantra, Ātman, and Śaṅkara, one should,
like the vital breath, abide within the center of the lotus of the heart, which is filled with the splendor of the lunar light.
Returning from the *dvādaśānta* by means of the exhaling breath (*recaka*), one should place [the mantras] in sequence;
having attained the *śāntamudrā*, one should manifest them like a reflection.
One should unite the entire [manifested form] according to one's capacity with the partless, eternal, and supreme [reality].
They say that this is the form of the Self; one should unite it within the form of Vidyā.
Having consecrated that place with a steady mind, one should fashion the supreme form;
first performing the lotus-mudrā, one should prepare the seat for Śiva.
With the *āvāhanī* [mudrā] one performs the invocation; likewise, with the *namaskāra* [mudrā], one performs the salutation.
With the *śaśikarṇī*, one performs the installation; and with the *nirodhinī*, the placement of the harsh [seal].
One should contemplate the expulsion of other obstacles of that nature by means of Kālakarṇī;
likewise,
one should effect the oneness of the embodied and the unembodied through Āvāhanī, like the rays of the sun.
Then, one should place the heart and the other [limbs] according to their indicative marks, names, and proximity.
Having placed the *astra-mantra* upon both hands, one should perform the welcome (*svāgata*) for the Lord;
then water for the feet (*pādya*) should be offered at His feet, and thereafter food for the mouth (*mukheṣṭha*) should be presented.
There, the water of honor (arghya) should be offered facing [the deity], starting from Śiva and proceeding in order down to Sadyojāta;
thereafter, the ritual bath for removing impurities (malasnāna) should be performed with scented oil, myrobalan (āmalaka), and other substances.
Then one should perform a bath with powder of stainless fish-scale (nirmacchaya);
thereafter, one should bathe it with milk, curd, ghee, and honey.
The bath should be performed with the *hṛdaya-mantra* using water for each [deity] in succession;
between the offerings of flowers and incense, all perfumes should be offered last.
One hundred and eight *maḍukas* should be offered in sequence;
meanwhile, the mantra should be recited over the palm of the left hand starting from the top of the *liṅga*.
One should dismiss with the *arghya* offering the flower that was previously placed;
[one should do so] with the root mantra of the *gaḍḍuka*, and with the *patākā*, *nātha*, and *kaṃbu* [mantras].
Water should be offered upon the top of the *liṅga*, and the remainder should be poured onto the altar;
for there, beneath that, are one hundred and eight, along with a half—indeed, O God, those eight.
The water-jars should be offered according to the prescribed rule and in due order:
white, made of gold, fragrant, containing excellent gems and fruit, and adorned with flowers.
One should adorn [the image] with various jewels such as bracelets, armlets, and necklaces;
then, one should bathe it in sequence with all medicinal herbs, clarified butter, and grain using the eight [substances].
In the absence of a physical substance, however, one should visualize her as having a formless nature.
One should not touch the *liṅga* with the left hand, nor should its top be left empty.
One should dismiss [the deity] with that same offering (arghya) as before, accompanied by flowers;
this procedure is the auspicious purification performed with a soft, clean cloth.
One should smear the joints of the moon with sandalwood and saffron;
one should adorn it with bracelets, armlets, necklaces, and so forth, decorated with various jewels.
Then one should perform worship with jewels, gold, and garments;
having fully honored the Supreme Lord with flowers, water for the guest-offering, and fragrant blossoms.

One should offer perfumes, flowers, water for honor (argha), lamps, and so forth with the Sadyojāta mantra; and incense and other such offerings for the Lord should be given devoid of the breath-assignment (prāṇanyāsa) and limb-assignment (aṅganyāsa).
O Vāmadeva, one should not offer garments, ornaments, or betel;
one should offer the recitation of mantras, fire oblations, worship, and so forth, with the third [mudrā].
One should place the food offering (naivedya) in the eastern direction with the Puruṣa-sūkta; in the northeast (īśāna), one should arrange for the Lord an umbrella, a seat, and so forth.
One should perform those rites not explicitly mentioned in various forms;
thus having completed the worship of the All-pervading Lord, one should worship Īśāna located in the northeast corner.
Having meditated upon [the deity] as white as cow’s milk, one should worship with flowers and other offerings;
one should place Puruṣa on the eastern petal, resembling the petals of the Karṇikāra flower.
Aghora is in the south, resembling a split lotus;
Vāmadeva is like the pomegranate flower in the north.
In the west, the seed-syllable is like a conch, jasmine, or the moon;
for the purpose of bathing, the heart [mantra], possessing a luster like a pearl, is to be worshipped.
In the northeast, the head is placed, resembling clear lapis lazuli;
in the southwest direction, however, the crest has a radiance equal to the form of lightning.
One should place the black-colored armor in the northwestern direction;
the eye, possessing the radiance of the moon, sun, and fire, should be placed in front.
One should place the Weapon-mantra (Astra) on the tips of the petals, radiant with the luster of blazing fire;
likewise, one should assign the faces and the limbs to the locations of enjoyment.
Having manifested the forms of the reflected images, one should worship them like the All-pervading Lord;
one should offer water for the feet, water for sipping, and the respectful offering (arghya), or else perform the eightfold flower offering.
He should be worshipped with blue lotuses and the like, with *kunda*, jasmine, and *jāti* flowers, as well as with *kubjaka*, *dhūrtūra*, *vakra*, *karavīra*, and *pāṭala* flowers.
One should devotedly offer various kinds of food offerings (*naivedya*) in diverse vessels, consisting of *kadamba*, *damanaka*, and other unbroken flowers desired by the Lord.
Milk-rice mixed with ghee, fruits, roots, sugar-cane, and curd;
various kinds of sweetmeats made with sugar, as well as mung-bean garlands and boiled rice.
Aśoka-varti, ṣaṣkulyā, apūpikā, and likewise ghr̥tikā;
pure bulbous roots and many kinds of side dishes.
One should cause thick, unctuous, and very cool milk to be offered to the deity;
it may be given separately for each face and limb, or even from a single source if [individual portions] are unavailable.

One should worship Ananta and the others at the tips of the petals; there, one should worship the Vidyeśvaras on the neck of the pedestal, and the Gaṇeśas and the Lokapālas at the base of the pedestal.
Then, in the location of the weapon, one should place the stable foundation upon the *brahmaśilā*;
thus, by means of the distinctions of its own pervasion, one should deposit the enclosure of the All-pervading Lord.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite, he should offer mouth-freshener to the Lord:
namely, betel-leaf with camphor, as well as a hand-towel.
One should offer a garland of lamps to the east, and thereafter incense in due order;
then the ritual of dismissal (nirmārjana) should be performed, followed by the offerings of water for honor (argha), water for the feet (pādya), and so forth, in sequence.
Then, O God, the wise one should perform meditation with a one-pointed mind,
[visualizing] yourself enveloped by the limbs of Brahmā and by the spheres of Ananta and Indra.
By means of the concealment of the vital breath and its fluctuations, one should perform mental recitation;
there is neither a meditator nor an object of meditation, as it is a sphere beyond conceptual construction.
When it has attained a state of fusion, that exists in the ultimate sense;
the mind is to be made mindless, and from that, the striking of the lips ends with speech.
Having taken up an auspicious rosary of one hundred and eight beads known as Rudrākṣa,
he should have it fashioned from fresh, unbroken *kaṇṭaka* seeds provided with stalks.
For the sake of attaining all siddhis, one should [worship] with one face, three faces, especially four faces, six faces, and likewise five faces.
O Six-faced One, the rosary should be fashioned with seven, eight, nine, ten, or eleven beads. Furthermore, the string of the rosary should be prepared accordingly.
Having worshipped the thread with the heart-mantra and having enveloped it with sandalwood paste,
one should twist it between the thumb and the middle finger, or with the index finger.
Then, at the tip of the serpent's hood, one should perform the circumambulation of the Lord of Nagas;
when the recitation of the mantra consisting of that [mantra] has been completed one hundred and eight times, one should leap over it.
One should never perform a recitation that is either innumerable or confused;
rather, the wise person should diligently recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
Placing the right knee upon the ground, one should offer the recitation (japa);
with Śiva on the left, the application of perfumes and so forth is declared to be performed correctly and in due order.
18b) One must not act contrary to this, nor should there be anything deficient or excessive anywhere.
O Six-faced One, one should have it performed exactly as described until the end of the body, with all rites performed evenly.
The initiate, the spiritual son, the teacher, and especially the practitioner must perform this constantly throughout their entire life, by the command of Śiva.
Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the acquisition [of merit], in the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
In the east, one should cause a pit to be made, four-cornered and measuring one cubit;
it should have either three or five ridges, or it may be prepared as a leveled sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
For fire produced from the forest, or from the houses of the twice-born,
or even from a sun-crystal, or likewise that which is struck by a thunderbolt— these are the sources.
Having placed [the materials] in the vessel, Śivā should sprinkle them and encircle them with the *kavaca* mantra;
the practitioner should perform the tracing with the tip of a sacrificial twig using the *astra* mantra.
Having first drawn three lines facing east and one line facing north with the tips of the thumb and ring finger, one should likewise draw the rays.
Likewise, one should perform the striking with the armor-mantra;
then, having strewn the crossroads, one should place the Gāyatrī upon the seat.
Having worshipped Gāyatrī with perfumes, flowers, garlands, and other offerings in his heart,
he should cause Jātavedas to be received in either an earthen vessel or a copper vessel.

19a) Then, with three handfuls [of flowers], one should recite the Brahma-aṅgas with a tenth part of the root mantra. Having offered [the oblation] for the Heart-mantra and the others, one should earnestly pray to Śiva.
Then, having gone to the fire-sanctuary, one should perform the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rule;
having completed the rites for the fire, an offering should be presented outside in the various directions.
Having offered oblations of all kinds of food to Indra and the others in the ten directions,
and having sipped water and touched the limbs, one should perform the ritual placement of the hands (karanyāsa).
Accompanied by those who have entered the mouth of Śiva, one should perform the rites of Śiva,
especially during the offerings of lamps, incense, food, and the *vala* oblation.
The utterance of "svāhā" should be performed, as well as the remaining salutation;
having praised with hymns and prostrated, one should dedicate the ritual action to Him.
Then, having offered the *argha* in reverse order, one should contemplate the form of the Savior (Tāraka);
the dismissal of the fire should be performed there, or else its retention elsewhere.
And one should worship Caṇḍanātha in the northeast with the mantra ending in *hūṃ phaṭ*,
using garments, food, perfumes, drinks, arghya, floral offerings, and sacred purificatory items (*pavitraka*).
Having set aside the arghya vessel and sipped water, one should touch [the limbs];
the ritual placement (nyāsa) should be performed according to one's ability, and the Śivasaṃhitā should be recited.
Having understood the worship of Śiva outside the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to be threefold, one should cause [the deity] to descend by means of the *dhruva* mantra alone;
having cast it like a seed into the womb (yoni), while remembering Śiva abiding in the true void (*sadvyoman*).
One should offer five oblations with the *sadyojāta* mantra beginning from the heart;
this constitutes the placement of the mortal element (*martyadhāman*), after which the placement of the male principle (*puṃsavadhāman*) occurs.
One should scatter a tip of *kuśa* grass with the *vāmadeva* mantra while facing north;
by this, a male child is born, and neither a female nor a neuter.
Having thus performed the *puṃsavana* rite, one should then perform the *sīmantonnayana*;
the fashioning of the five faces should be carried out in their proper sequence.
O son of Kṛttikā, the removal of conceptual construction (kalpanā) is taught in this scripture;
thereafter, the extraction from the body (dehakṛṣṭi) should be performed, consisting of thirty-eight digits (kalās).
One should remember the face, the arms, the eyes, and the ears with a concentrated mind;
likewise, the threefold rite should be performed with the *śikhā* and the *aghora* mantra.
Having fashioned the body and provided the three types of grain in due order—this is called the triad of rites; the *sīmantonnayana* is prescribed for the eighth month.
O son of Kṛttikā, the fashioning, the crafting, the opening,
and the birth-rite of the faces should then be performed by means of the Vaktra and Varman [mantras].
Then, with the *vaktravaktra* mantra, one should perform the removal of the [impure] stalk;
likewise, having sprinkled the fire for the immediate purification of the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*).
For the sake of protection, one should begin the spreading of ashes and *darbha* grass,
starting from the east and south, and likewise in the north and west.
Then the enclosing sticks (paridhis) should be offered, made from the Palāśa tree, quickly;
they should be one cubit in length, or alternatively, a seat (viṣṭara) measuring ten finger-breadths.
20a) One should perform the worship of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and Īśāna seated upon their thrones;
the world-protectors (lokeśas) should be worshipped all around, together with their respective weapons and vehicles.
From the time of conception until birth, one should offer oblations with sesame seeds;
thereafter, the rites known as *jātakarman* (birth-rite) and *nāmakarman* (name-giving) are performed.
Thereafter, one should perform the rite with clarified butter; now the purification of the clarified butter is described.
Having heated the *śruk* and *śruva* ladles, one should touch them with *kuśa* grass whose tips have not been cut, while reciting the *varma* mantra.
One should place the tip with the tip, the middle with the middle, and the root with the root, respectively;
having done this three times with the Śivāstra mantra, one should deposit [the offerings] to the right of one's own directions.
One should heat cow's ghee in a copper vessel over a fire in a pit;
thereafter, the examination should be performed, and then one should cause the person to step upon it.
Taking two blades of darbha grass that have not been touched by impurities,
one should perform the sprinkling there with the thumb and the ring finger.
Facing the three [deities], one should perform the *saṃplava* rite while facing away;
then, taking a blade of darbha grass and whirling it three times, one should cast it downward.
The Nīrājana is declared to be the illumination that dispels all defects; one should now cast that firebrand and cause the fire to be kindled—listen to the procedure for this.
One should throw the firebrand into the midst of the clarified butter three times;
this is called the "circumambulation with fire" (paryagnikaraṇa), which one should perform for everything using the heart-mantra.
Then, having formed the *dhenumudrā*, one should visualize the nectar falling;
and during the application of the *vaktrābhighora* [mantra], one should perform the sprinkling (*kṣepaṇa*) into the mouth.
20b) By means of the application of oblations with one's own mantras, starting from the western direction and ending with the eastern,
that which is called the "Terrible Face" is said to be the supreme illumination of the faces.
The union of Śiva and the individual soul (aṇu) should be conceived by means of two [faces]:
from the Puruṣa and Aghora faces, in the northern and western directions respectively.
One should perform the reconnection there by means of an oblation of one individual offering;
and from two faces, one should cause a single oblation to be offered.
The joining of the mouths is said to be performed by means of the application of the five oblations;
through Īśāna comes the inexhaustible fire-oblation, and through Puruṣa, the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
For severe rites such as expiation, as well as for cruel acts,
and for the fire-oblations of subjugation and attraction, one should perform the oblation with the Vāmadeva mantra.
The procedure for the daily rites is intended to be told in this final chapter;
having understood this, O Mahāsena, one should perform the ritual resolve according to the measurement of the sacrificial pit.
For the act of making one a slave should be performed in this manner and not otherwise;
the primary [deity] of this rite must be offered oblations, while the secondary ones are those whose faces are turned elsewhere.
The naming ceremony should be performed according to reality, [giving him] the name Śivāgni;
subsequently, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) for the sake of perfecting the remaining consecratory rites.
The departure from the womb, the first feeding of solid food, the investiture with the sacred thread,
and everything up to the tonsure and the gift of the cow— this entire cycle of rites was performed by me on the day of the vow with the Pūrṇāhuti.
Alternatively, one should cause the Śiva-fire to be prepared in another manner according to the sequence;
one should cause the threefold full oblation to be offered, consisting of Ātman, Vidyā, and that which is called Śiva.
By that, the fire of Śiva arises, which is devoid of all ritual refinements;
or else, one should generate the fire of knowledge, which bestows perfection in all actions.
21a) Having [visualized] the heart-lotus according to the teaching through the *sauṣumna* [channel],
one should cast [the seed-syllable] into the center of the sacrificial pit, resembling ten thousand suns.
In the obligatory, occasional, and optional rites, one should dismiss the Lord of Vāgīśvarī— who bestows auspiciousness and is the fire of knowledge— by means of the heart-mantra.
Taking up the vessel of clarified butter, one should offer oblations with the *śruva* ladle,
saying "To Sūrya" and "To Soma," joined with the word "svāhā" at the end.
Uttering the words, "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt,
svāhā," one should offer four oblations for the successful completion of the rite.
Then, with the heart-mantra, one should place Śiva’s fire within one's own heart;
afterwards, one should prepare the seat in the middle of the sacrificial pit according to the prescribed rule.
One should fashion the form and faces according to the latent impressions of karma;
one should then install the supreme, peaceful [deity] from the heart-lotus as the object of support.
One should worship here with flowers, water offerings, perfumes, incense, and so forth, even if only once;
then, having formed the Mahāmudrā, one should perform the salutation.
Then one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the root mantra according to one's capacity;
one should always offer oblations for the Brahma-mantras and their limbs with a tenth part [of the root mantra], ending each with "svāhā."
Or with clarified butter, or with milk, or with oils mixed with clarified butter;
or with barley, or with rice, or with guggulu and clarified butter.
The daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) should be performed; now the optional oblation (kāmyahoma) is described:
for the purpose of pacification, one should offer dūrvā grass, clarified butter, ghee, and sacrificial fuel-sticks soaked in honey.
Jāti, campaka, lotus, śrīpatra, and fruits—these are beneficial for the fire-oblation (homa) intended for prosperity and desire; karavīra is likewise beneficial for me.
21b) Likewise, for the subduing [of enemies], one should offer mustard seeds and salt;
for the accomplishment of the ritual, one should offer a *karṣa* measure of sesame seeds and clarified butter.
Then one should seek sesame seeds and offer them, as well as barley and other grains, with the conch-gesture (kambu-mudrā);
rice with the fist-gesture, and flowers and so forth with the breath-retention (kumbhaka).
One should offer milk-rice, condiments, and so forth with a *patāka* [ladle];
one should always offer *guggulu* incense in the measure of a *karkadhūka* fruit.
One should perform a *ghṛtāktagāyasa* oblation with a sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) measuring half a cubit in length;
one should always offer three oblations of cooked rice, each the size of a mouthful.
One should consume only a small amount of condiments according to one's capacity for eating and offering;
the salty portion should be one karṣa, seasoned with hingu, parpaṭa, and lavaṇa.
Parched grain and white mustard seeds should be offered in oblations in the measure of a single handful;
for fruits and flowers, the desired quantity is their own natural size.
O Six-faced One, when bulbous roots and fruits have been thus consecrated,
these very bulbs, roots, and fruits are recommended for both daily and optional rites. For the cure of hemorrhoids, however, one should use parched grain flour in cases of pulmonary consumption.
For the rite of eradication (uccāṭana), one should offer into the fire the three, the skull, hair, and bones.

With sharp oil and fuel-sticks produced from the *vibhītaka* tree, while visualizing the target with all their limbs, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) for the rite of inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*).
The upper portion, however, should be made white by the trees once they have reached their final decision;
it is recommended that it be mixed with the wood of the deceased, cemetery ashes, and blood.
It causes the expulsion of Śukra; there is no need for deliberation here.
Thorny trees with bitter fruits should indeed be understood without hesitation.
22a) For pacification, nourishment, subjugation, and attraction, the milky trees are prescribed;
honey is used for appeasement through oblations, and likewise the sacrificial ladle (śruva) alone is employed in the rite of accomplishment.
Among all four-footed animals, the milk of the ewe is most excellent;
it is sweet, weighing one pala, and always possesses two superior palas.
For the sake of complete nourishment and for the attainment of success, one should offer oblations together with the three sweets;
indeed, an oblation performed in a smokeless fire is praised, and otherwise it is not auspicious.
A fire that blazes with a clockwise curling flame grants success in all aims;
likewise, the appearance of other colors, movements, sounds, and shapes [indicate specific results].
Furthermore, the modifications and the crests must be understood by the practitioner:
that which has the luster of a ruby is excellent, as is that which has the brilliance of lac, milk, or iron.
The fire that has the color of the rising sun brings victory to men;
the fire resembling an *indragopaka* insect is beneficial for enjoyment.
Resembling Indra’s bow or like saffron paste,
the red-colored fire is always auspicious, bestowing all accomplishments.
It is observed to resemble molten gold, a mass like yellow orpiment,
the color of turmeric, lac, a dancer’s skin, or the hue of yellow pigment (rocanā).

For the rite of immobilization (*staṃbhanam*), it should be yellow in color; for the rite of subduing enemies (*rājāvaśīkaraṇa*), red is recommended. A sword that is the color of collyrium or a scale (*tulā*) when struck does not grant success.
Always intent upon this rite of killing, expulsion, and destruction,
[the deity] who possesses a color like that of a conch shell, crystal, jasmine, or the moon, bestows the supreme siddhi.
In rites for pacification and nourishment, one with beautiful eyes is always auspicious;
likewise, one with eyes like those of a cat or with a luster like a parrot's wing is praised.
That which resembles the neck of a peacock, or is like that of a pigeon,
variegated, and which suddenly comes into being— this is called *hayamāna*.
Having understood that it should be in accordance with each individual's specific karma,
one should always adopt actions consistent with that karma or abandon them if they are contrary to it.
O Six-faced One, the fragrance of fragrant substances, the fragrance of ghee, the auspicious fragrance,
the lotus fragrance of longevity, and the fragrance of the *bilva* fruit— these are the six.
In the performance of rites involving fierce odors, the *nala* plant is always praised;
possessing a fragrance equal to that of the blue lotus, it always brings about good fortune.
When the fire, being offered oblations, emits a sound like that of a drum or a cloud,
then one should know that the desired success of the rite is at hand.
The conch, the mṛdaṅga drum, and the jīmūtavallabhī lute produce an exceedingly beautiful sound;
these, when struck immediately, are causes for success, whereas the opposite is the case with others.
A fire shaped like an umbrella, a Bhṛgu, or a lotus, resembling a banner or a chowrie, and equal to the forms of a bull or an elephant, always bestows prosperity.
That which takes the form of celestial chariots, canopies, and palaces,
as well as the shape of swans and peacocks, is highly praised.
When the fire has the form of a lion, it is remembered as immediately bestowing success;
likewise, fires that are dense, glossy, wise, smokeless, and exceedingly brilliant [bring success].
O Bhṛgus, from all directions, for the sake of attaining all things,
there arise a harsh crackling sound as well as a hissing and simmering noise.
For the sake of accomplishing the form-mantra of the donkey, camel, buffalo, and so forth,
it should be glossy, turning clockwise, and also possess a pleasant sound.
It should be understood that [the practice] is for the sake of attaining the goal; otherwise, it would be fruitless.
[The smoke should be] dense, smooth, compact, smokeless, and radiant.
Bhṛgus of such a kind are pacified; there is no doubt in this matter.
One should scrape [the ground] while facing east, and likewise one who faces north or downward, as well as one whose hair-tuft (śikhā) is directed upward.
This is not for the sake of worldly enjoyment or liberation; rather, having performed the *pūrṇāhuti* according to the *Śāstra-kālottara*, one should then recollect the *Saṃhitā*.
One should cast a handful of flowers into the fire and sequentially display the mudrās;
having applied a tilaka from the ashes, one should take the fruit [of the rite] with the saṃhāra-mudrā.
Having performed the *pūraka* breath-retention, one should place [the offering] in the heart and cause it to be presented in the hand of Śiva;
one should worship with supreme devotion using flowers, water offerings (*arghya*), ointments, and so forth.
Having praised Mahādeva with hymns from the concluding portions of the Āgamas that are centered on Śiva,
one should place the right knee upon the ground while holding a handful of flowers to the heart.
Having recited the Saṃhitā with a mind focused solely on Śiva,
whatever merit has been acquired by me through worship, japa, fire-sacrifices, and other such virtuous deeds—
O Supreme Lord, that fruit I have offered to you;
O Maheśvara, you are the goal reached through action, mind, and speech.
Having spoken thus, one should offer [the oblation] with one's own voice to the All-pervading Lord;
then, turning away, one should present the *arghya* water, beginning from Sadyojāta and ending with Śiva.
23b) After the weapon-mantra, at the heart and the periphery with perfumes, incense, garlands, and so forth,
the eight mudrās should be offered in sequence for the dismissal of Śiva from this [rite].
Then one should contemplate the limbs of Brahmā entering into the liṅga;
having addressed Mahādeva with "Forgive me," he should be established upon the pedestal.
This procedure applies to both mobile and immobile [altars], but especially to the *phalaka* (wooden board);
however, that which was previously mentioned as being suitable for the *sthaṇḍila* (earth altar) is preferred when the ritual of bathing is omitted.
Likewise, the dismissal of the preceptor Gaṇeśa should then be performed;
the auspicious fire of Śiva should be withdrawn from that [fire] and carried forth.
Or one may cast [the offering] into the fire; thereafter, one should dismiss the *argha* with offerings of all fragrances in the northeast corner of the sacrificial hall.
One should offer garments, food, perfumes, and sacrificial oblations arising from Śiva,
saying "Obeisance to Caṇḍīśvara," and then dismiss [the deity] into the heart from the heart.
In all rites of worship for the gods, an outer bali offering should be presented with rice cooked in milk, clarified butter, and meat, along with various savory side dishes.
Having sipped water and touched [the sense organs], one should meditate upon the Saṃhitā with the heart.
Thus, O son, the procedure for daily worship has been described by me to you.
Thus ends the chapter on the daily rites in the Kālottara.
The Lord said:

Now, therefore, O son of Kṛttikā, I shall duly explain the characteristics of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), as well as the measurements of their girdles (mekhalā) and the large and small sacrificial ladles (śruk and śruva).
A square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the east brings success in imperial sovereignty;
the one called "womb-shaped" (yoni), located in the southeast corner, is recommended for the installation of enemies.
A half-moon situated in the southern direction is established for the slaying of enemies;
a triangle in the south-western corner increases the diseases of serpents.
In the northwest, there is indeed a hexagon, intended for the agitation of enemies;
in the north, however, is that known as the lotus, which bestows prosperity, intelligence, and nourishment upon men.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that grants all desires is octagonal in the northeast;
it should be one cubit in depth for the fire-oblation, or it may be circular or square.
One should arrange the seats of yoga (yogapīṭhas) in the east or the west;
likewise, for the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma), it should be performed in the northeast.
A composition that is neither deficient nor excessive, free from redundancy, and not censured; which is complete, bestows fruit upon men, and is likewise unblemished—is not despised.
This should be performed by those who know the ritual and non-ritual procedures exactly as taught in their own scripture.
The first [line] should be made one finger-breadth wide, and then the subsequent ones should be three finger-breadths and two finger-breadths respectively.
Its depth should be like that of the mouth in a vessel; the yoni-vardhana is wide open, measuring one finger-breadth in length, resembling the shape of an elephant's lip.
The navel, measured by one finger-breadth, is situated above the girdle;
the yoni should be fashioned according to the shape of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and not otherwise.
"Or else, one should conceive [the fire-pit] within the womb as having the form of a *kuṇḍa*.
Thus, while the *kuṇḍa* is prescribed in the rule for daily rites (*nityavidhi*), it is now described for occasional rites (*naimittika*).
For a homa of one thousand or ten thousand oblations, a space of two cubits is prescribed;
for a homa of one hundred thousand, four cubits; and for ten million, six cubits.
For a *koṭi-homa*, it should be eight cubits; beyond this, it may be greater.
For a pit (*kuṇḍa*) of two cubits here, the girdle (*mekhalā*) shall be six finger-breadths wide.
The middle [line] of the square pit is four finger-breadths, while the final [line] is three finger-breadths;
for the square pit, the eastern rim is eight finger-breadths.
It is praised when made with six medium-sized finger-breadths, and likewise with three very large ones;
among these, the first girdle for a six-cubit [staff] should be ten finger-breadths wide.
Another [part] is eight finger-breadths wide, while the outer rim is six finger-breadths;
one should construct the girdle and other features with half a cubit for a temple measuring eight cubits.
The second and third [lines] of that [altar] should measure ten and eight finger-breadths respectively;
and for all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), the yoni should be as it is in the case of the Vāstika.
An increase of two finger-breadths each is beneficial for the width and length;
listen now to a brief description of the characteristics of the various types of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) and their applications.
The square with its mantras is known by the name "Vedāśra" (the four-cornered);
it is formed by the rotation [of the cord] after discarding one-quarter, using the tip of the cord to mark half of each corner.

One should offer eight hundred oblations into one's own fire-pit (kṣetra) according to the specific requirements of that particular rite; the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is considered the seat of the Hotṛ priest, bestowing the fruit of the oblation when used with the Śakti mantras.
The face of the transformation [mandala] is a quadrangle, excluding two parts of the *puruṣa*;
one should rotate a cord equal to the portion of Manu in the shape of a half-moon.
A semicircular pit is prescribed for the Raudra mantras, as it bestows success;
having constructed a square pit as before, one should lead [the ritual] forward into a hexagon.
One should mark [the center] with that measurement from the fourth point of the fish (the intersection) at half the field;
then, by the laying down of six threads, a distinct hexagon is produced.
For the Vāyavya mantras, the half-hexagon bestows the accomplishment of their specific powers; for the Raudra mantras, the triangle grants all accomplishments.
By moving from corner to corner and sub-corner, one reaches the eight directions;
this circular [method] grants success for all mantras—this word is not false.
O Six-faced One, one should fashion a lotus in the shape of a lotus according to circular measurements;
the petals are on the middle rim, while the pericarp is in the center.
Water bestows prosperity, fame, and health; it is praised in all mantras.
By abandoning the portions of modification, one should mark the tip from the corner.
By extending the thread in the eight directions, the [mandala] is produced;
thus the characteristics of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) have been declared, and the characteristics of the large and small ladles (śruk-śruva) are now considered.
The *śruva* ladle should be made one cubit in length;
it is considered to be fashioned from *śāla*, *candana*, *śāka*, *uchcha*, *śiṃśapā*, *sāra*, or *udumbara* wood.
The *śruk* and *śruva* ladles should indeed be made of *khadira*, *aśvattha*, or *jāmbava* wood;
the altar (*vedikā*) should be eight finger-breadths in height, and its hollowed-out cavity is considered to be three finger-breadths deep.
The neck should be five finger-breadths in width, with a measurement of one thumb-breadth;
at the neck, the altar-platform (vedī) should be three finger-breadths in width, and the lower altar (vaśvāpavedikā) likewise.
Alternatively, its opening should be made seven finger-breadths wide and fitted with a foot;
it is beneficial for the passage of clarified butter to have a circumference equal to that of the little finger.
The staff should be made twelve finger-breadths wide at its base, with a jar-shaped ornament at the root measuring sixteen finger-breadths;
at the tip of the staff, a pedestal should be fashioned measuring either two or four finger-breadths.
The handle should be two finger-breadths wide and six finger-breadths in circumference; one should be a *śruk* and the other a *śruva*.
The *śruk* is made of metal, while the *śruva* has a hollow interior the size of a thumb.
The auspicious staff is shaped like a hollow hoof-print, its bowl filled with cotton-wool,
its base and tip occupied by a small stand, and its shaft having the form of a lotus stalk.
The *avaṭa* [the cavity] resembles the frontal globe of an elephant and is joined with a smooth handle;
the *śruk* and *śruva* ladles have been briefly described in this treatise known as the *Kāla*.
Thus ends the chapter on the preparation of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in the *Kālottara*.
The Lord said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme characteristics of the mudrās,
which are employed in the ritual of worship, in the rite of fire-offering (homa), in the rite of recitation (japa), and in the binding of mantras (vali).
One should always display the lotus gesture (padmamudrā) when visualizing the seat;
the invocation of Śiva should always be performed with the gesture of invocation (āvāhanī).

One should provide the water for the feet, the respectful offering, the water for sipping, and so forth, ending with incense; and one should perform the ritual installation while recollecting the mantra of the head-syllable and the moon-ear (śaśikarṇī).
In the presence [of the deity], one should then place the Mahāmudrā at the first junction (ādisaṃdhyā);
one should diligently bestow the Nirodhī and Niṣṭhurā upon the God of Gods.
One should bind the Kālakarṇī mudrā for the destruction of obstacles;
one should employ the mudrā called Liṅga in the application of the mantras of the kalās.
The mudrā consisting of salutation is beneficial for the veneration of mantras;
thus, one should devoutly display these eight mudrās three times to Śambhu.
Having placed both hands palms-upward at the region of the heart, being composed,
one should press the thumbs together while the other fingers are bent inward at their middle joints.
The *āvāhanī* [mudrā] should be employed in the worship of the God of gods;
one should diligently join the tip of the index finger with the tip of the thumb.
Having turned the hand upward, one should display the "moon-petal" (śaśikarṇikā) mudrā;
then, one should place the back of the right hand upon the wrist of the left.
The Vyāna-mudrā is proclaimed as the joining of the middle finger and the thumb;
or else, in another manner, it is formed by the left thumb and [the right index finger].
Having grasped the left index finger with the right fist, one should place its thumb at the heart; the fingers of the left hand form the banner.
One should recite the Śiva-mantra for all mudrās;
however, one should employ the Padma-mudrā for the seat and the one called Dhvaja for the act of meditation.
One should touch with both hands from the feet upwards as far as the crown of the head, and likewise downwards as far as the feet; that is then known as the Mahāmudrā.
One should always press [the breath] with the thumbs of both hands at the beginning, middle, and end, while it is held in proximity.
One should show both hands with the fingers tucked in and the tips clenched,
exerting effort in the restraint of the Lord for the sake of the entire collection of mantras at all times.
Having raised the thumbs of both hands,
or having turned both palms outward, one should offer the *kālakarṇī* mudrā.
For the purpose of destroying obstacles,
one should diligently form a fist with the right hand, keeping the thumb raised.
The knower of mantras should place [the substances] within the center of the left hand;
likewise, the remaining [substances] should be placed upon the right hand.
The Liṅgamudrā, which possesses great power, is to be employed in the worship of the liṅga;
it is formed by pressing the palms of both hands together at the region of the heart.
One should perform a salutation to the mantras with prostrations and the chanting of mantras; the two hands, palms facing upward, are extended and placed in their respective positions.
The fingers should be spread apart; one should place the two thumbs in the middle.
In the ritual arrangement of Śiva’s seat, one should display the lotus mudrā (padmamudrā).
Thus, the eight mudrās are proclaimed in the Kālottara Tantra,
to be employed likewise in worship, in the fire sacrifice, and in the rites of recitation and meditation.
One should then diligently display the eight mudrās with the heart-mantra;
however, the mudrās should be displayed before Śiva while separated by a cloth.
One should not perform the internal meditation (dhyānāntarya) while covered by a cloth;
however, the concentration (dhāraṇā) on the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and whatever else arises in the mind [may be performed].
Thus ends the chapter on mudrās in the Kālottara.
Now, therefore, [I shall describe] the sequence of the ritual for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) of the materials to be thoroughly cleansed,
as well as the lunar days, asterisms, and yogas, and the implements required for the sacrifice.
A place that is endowed with gods and brahmins, free from atheism, and irreproachable;
such is the instruction regarding the ritual of initiation for those whose minds are focused on the beginning and end of yoga.
In the absence of those two, the rainy season is recommended even otherwise;
likewise for initiation, consecration, and the reception of mantras.
