Upon undertaking a vow, upon its release, during rituals involving the touching of ritual substances,
on the full moon day of Kārttika, on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, and even upon the sighting of Rāhu (an eclipse), [one should perform the rite].
27a) On Mount Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śrīśaila, Himavat,
Pāriyātra, Vindhya, Śuktimat, and Ṛkṣa;
One should cause [the rite] to be performed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā,
in Antarvedī, on the Sarasvatī, at the Dvayadvatī, at the Godāvarī, and at Mayānidhi.
At the Narmadā and Kṛṣṇaveṇī, at the five rivers in the Sindhu,
and near the Tuṅgabhadrā and the Candrabhāgā.
In mountain caves, sacred fords, and at the confluences of rivers;
in delightful regions, in forests, and in groves.
There, one should examine the ground according to the sequence to be described;
having taken possession of the ground, one should draw the supreme mandala.
On the fourth, or the eighth, and likewise on the fourteenth,
as well as on the full moon day of the bright fortnight, those desiring prosperity should always perform [the rite].
Those desiring liberation should perform whatever rite they may during the dark fortnight; the intercalary days and other lunar days (tithis) are also remembered as suitable for this purpose.
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, at the sixty-four openings,
during the conjunctions of planets and lunar mansions, at the equinoxes, and at festivals;
In all solstices, one should perform the sacrifice that grants the fulfillment of all aims;
likewise, the three Uttarās, as well as Kārya, Somya, and Gurudevatam.
When the other planets are situated on the shore favorable to the sacrificer, free from affliction,
positioned in their exaltations or friendly signs, and while the malefic planet is situated in its sign of debilitation;
Having diligently collected all the sacrificial materials without exception,
and having bathed properly according to the previously mentioned procedure while remaining fully self-restrained;
One who knows the reality of the meaning of the four chapters—namely, knowledge, ritual action, yoga, and conduct—is indeed Śiva, Śakti, and the Self; for the bonds are said to be threefold.
He who knows the six categories [of reality] and [the means to] enjoyment and liberation is the teacher who has descended from on high;
his limbs are smeared with white sandalwood paste, and he is adorned with white garlands.
Abounding in very smooth white garments and well-scented with excellent incense,
he was adorned with a variegated crown from which radiant light flashed forth.
Adorned with beautiful pearls, auspicious, with fine roots and joined with gems,
it was a variegated earring suspended from the middle of the neck.
O auspicious one, one should fashion a well-crafted ornament, a sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) of pearls,
and a girdle (*kaṭisūtra*) made from beautiful, circular beads.
O Lord, it was made of variegated lapis lazuli, with a blue luster in the center,
composed of rubies, and marked with auspicious characteristics.
And a beautiful bracelet, inlaid with rows of diamonds, should be worn;
likewise, a finger-ring rich with jewels should be worn on the right hand.
Having worshipped Jvara according to the prescribed rite, one should likewise dispel the obstacles;
there, the binding of the directions (digbandha) should be performed, veiled by the armor-mantra (kavaca).
Then the cremation of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) should be performed, followed by the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa).
Having mentally conceived the Vidyā, one should perform the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa) as previously described.

One should perform the deposition upon the body (*dehanyāsa*), which consists of a form composed of the *kalās*; then follows the process of supreme unification (*paramīkaraṇa*) and thereafter the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*).
Then the binding of the mudrās should be performed, followed by the preparation of the arghya vessel;
thereafter, one should carry out the purification of the site and the purification of the ritual materials.
One should worship Gaṇeśa and the Guru in the northwest, and Śiva and the Ātman [in the northeast];
however, one should worship Vāstupuruṣa in the center with a single utterance.
The ritual of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) should be performed with the collection of mantras:
namely, cow dung, cow urine, curd, milk, and ghee, in that order.
With the Sadyojāta, Vāma, Ghora, Puruṣa, Īśāna,
Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Ātman mantras, and with Śiva himself, one [prepares] the kuśa-water.
Having performed the individual consecration of each,
one should afterwards place them together in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay.
The supreme teacher should always contemplate himself as Śiva, reciting the mantra-conjunction a hundred times repeatedly, yet only once [per day].
Having made the right hand rich with the scent of fragrant perfumes,
one should place therein Śiva, who is accompanied by the limbs of Brahmā.
One should worship the Supreme Lord with perfumes, flowers, purifiers, and other offerings;
having meditated upon that supreme splendor within Him, one should perform all ritual actions.
This is declared to be the Auspicious Hand of Śiva, which destroys the fetters;
by means of this, even those bound souls within the sphere of the fetters are liberated in an instant.
Having emerged, those who have not lost their imperishable nature attain the state of Śiva through the power of mantra,
consisting of the scriptures and the Kālottara.
28b) Having consecrated with the water of Śiva all the materials for initiation up to the end of the five elements—
namely sesame seeds, parched grain, barley, dūrvā grass, white mustard seeds, and so forth—
One should touch with the hand of Śiva the flowers, garments, jewels, and ornaments, as well as the food offerings, drinks, and rich perfumes.
Then these things become purified for the attainment of the fruit;
[the vessel] is filled with clear water and contains gems within.
Clad in auspicious garments and endowed with the prescribed ritual for worship,
one should, according to the rules, touch a beautiful golden pitcher with mantras.
Having worshipped it likewise like Śiva, one should install it in the northeast corner; and with the Śiva-weapon mantra, one should place the chisel to its south.
Thereafter, one should cause a scattering [of offerings] with seeds mixed with white mustard,
reciting the Mahāpāśupata mantra from the eastern direction up to the northeast.
The scattering [of grains] should be performed in one place, sequentially within the domain of Īśāna;
then, starting from the northeast corner, one should lead it clockwise around the entire area.
Without resting and without companions, until they have heard the word of Śaṅkara,
they remain near the water-pot, making a display with their white garments.
One should install the Astra-kalaśa while reciting the excellent Pāśupata mantra;
having performed the worship with scents and flowers for those two, one should then proceed with the Śānti rite.
Having prostrated with great affection and requested the peaceful Śiva, "Be present here," I beheld the Lord, who was free from all impurity.
29a) At the installation of the jar, one should observe the omens;
if divine palaces are seen, that omen is considered auspicious.
When various flowers fall from the sky and Indra’s bow appears to men, there will be a gentle rain, especially for those who are praiseworthy.
During the falling of meteors, earthquakes, thunderclaps, the appearance of comets,
the onset of great winds, and the appearance of smoke and mist;
A rain of dust or ash, the cries of birds in the sky,
and the sweet warbling of peacocks, swans, parrots, and other such birds are considered auspicious.
The conjunction with the rays of the sun, the falling of a meteor,
and the sound of conchs, kettledrums, clouds, and lutes are auspicious.
Beholding teachers, Brahmins, women, and kings is always auspicious on earth; however, one should carefully avoid honey, meat, and similar things.
The sight of lotuses, flowers, and a bull is auspicious; likewise, the sight of horses, elephants, and a forest is praised, as is the sight of teeth, which is highly commended.

Donkeys, camels, buffaloes, predatory beasts, ascetics, the naked, and others of this sort are inauspicious; speech that is censured is always condemned, for a sound witnessed through words is not desired.
Sudden quarreling is undesirable, as is a harsh sound arising from negligence;
likewise, one should avoid the sight of houses, trees, or virtuous people that have been struck by lightning.

The sacrifice consists of goats for auspicious rites; likewise, for inauspicious ones, it is with blood. For the sake of pacification, one hundred oblations of clarified butter should be offered with the Aghora mantra ending in the syllable *phaṭ*.
Therefore, O Lord, the wealth [of the sacrifice] should be prepared as before by those who are free from fear and sorrow:
Ananta, Śaśa, Sūkṣma, and the third, Śivottama.
Ekanetra, Ekarudra, and Trimūrti,
as well as Śrīkaṇṭha and Śikhaṇḍin, are the lords situated to the east, near Īśvara.

Having first worshipped Indra and the others, the Vajra and the rest should then be meditated upon in their proper order by the great-souled ones, according to the colors of the lords of their respective directions.
With forms terrifying and formidable with fangs, you are the leaders;
O great powerful ones, with copper-colored eyes and faces that inspire fear, dissolve this [obstacle].
With tawny eyebrows, tears, and body hair, they were short and born of great power;
they had drooping lips and flat noses, resembling lightning and the young of a peacock.
The lords of the weapons— Svāya, Dhākara, Śiva, and Sarvayamoggaśakti— are to be worshipped constantly with the Pāśupata [mantra].
Having worshipped the weapons according to the rules with food, drink, garlands, and other offerings,
worship performed even without stinginess regarding wealth bestows the fruit of all desires.
The *astrānnā* is for Kālakarṇī; the *mudrā* is the destroyer of obstacles. The *liṅga* is the name for the Vidyēśvaras, and likewise, the *añjali* is for the Lords of the World (*lokeśas*).
Having thus performed all the rites, the preceptor, who is skilled in sacrifice,
should ward off obstacles with the Astra-mantra in the vicinity of the fragrant fire and the sacrificial pit.
Scraping, scattering soil, pounding, sprinkling,
and spreading [the ground], as well as the worship of Vāgīśānī and the laying of the foundation (garbhadhāraṇa).
Thereafter, the Puṃsavana rite should be performed, as well as the Sīmantonnayana;
the Jātakarman must also be performed, along with the heating of the *śruk* and *śruva* ladles.
Then, for the sake of the purification of the body, having offered four oblations in that manner,
one should cause a single full oblation to be offered according to the rules of the purificatory rite.
When this has been done, one should subsequently place the Śiva-fire within one's own self;
having drawn out the fire from the sacrificial pit (agnikuṇḍa), one should maintain it elsewhere.
Having offered the *caru* and the *puroḍāśa* cake to the Fire-god, and not otherwise,
one should thereafter place the seat within the inner sanctum and then install the image.
One should place [the deity] from the region of the heart into the Śiva-fire by means of pervasion,
having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, preceded by the binding of mudrās.
There, one should perform the rite of homa according to the previously stated procedure,
having prepared the sacrificial porridge (caru) in accordance with the rules, together with the limbs of Śiva and the Brahma-mantras.
A sacrificial vessel (caru) made of copper is recommended, or one made of baked clay at its base;
one should wash it with the Astra-mantra and worship it with the Sadyojāta-mantra.
Likewise, one should tie a noose for him around the neck at the region of the throat;
having wiped it with ghee using the left hand, one should then commence the ritual action.
In former times, [the offering] shone with cow's milk and fine śāli rice;
in their absence, it was made with barley, parched grain, ghee, and parched rice flour.
Or else, O Six-faced One, having recited the most formidable armor-mantra, one should slowly cook [the offering] with mild fire using either śyāmāka rice grains or wild nīvāra rice.
The sacrificial oblation should not be poured too loosely, nor should it be poured too profusely;
with equal effort, one should pour the clarified butter over the portions of the victim while it stands steady.
30b) Having removed the sacrificial porridge (caru) from there, one should offer the oblations of the final drops;
then, recollecting the deity with face turned upward, one should slowly wash [the vessel] all around.
The oblations of the final offerings should be given with the *brahma* mantras while tears flow from the eyes;
one should offer them with devotion into a golden vessel, or even into an earthen one, containing clarified butter.
Having properly offered a portion to Śiva, one should indeed conceal and set aside the remainder for the sake of the practitioners' own selves; then, one should cause the disciples to enter.
According to the order of the Brahmins or according to the order of their requests,
[he should choose] those who have been carefully examined, who are endowed with devotion, and who are firm in their heart's vows.

One should not cause the consecration (dīkṣā) to be performed by the self for the sake of purifying the body or for the sake of past karma, since the self is veiled by the impurity of primordial matter (mala).
Its cessation must be effected by means of mantras, like the neutralization of the potency of poison;
initiation alone bestows liberation upon men and brings about the manifestation of consciousness.
That initiation is to be attained through faith and devotion, and not otherwise;
for that which is unreal attains reality only so long as one does not find the Supreme.
When the reality of initiation (dīkṣā) is known, one considers the world to be unreal;
and through initiation on the six paths (ṣaḍadhvadīkṣā), the self attains supreme bliss.
The disciples, having fasted and bathed, pure and endowed with discipline,
[were purified] by the water from Śiva’s hand upon their heads, which was itself as pure as the water of the celestial Ganges.
Having sprinkled [the site] with the *aśiva* weapon-mantra, one should strike it repeatedly with ashes;
then, having placed *darbha* grass over the new entrance, one should perform the consecration (*ālambhana*) with *kuśa* grass.
31a) Facing north while the wise Guru faces east,
the ritual placement of the hands (karanyāsa) must be performed with one's whole being, as previously described.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa with the Brahma-mantras, one should worship the bound soul (paśu) with the heart-mantra,
using perfumes, flowers, and purifiers accompanied by the fragrance of incense.
Afterwards, his worship should be performed, and one should cause that [offering] to be presented to the deity;
having worshipped him, one should then proceed near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Having placed the disciple with his head downward, one should heat him with the *saṃpāta* offerings;
then, all the mantras should cause the *pūrṇāhuti* to be offered into the fire according to the rule.
However, some [teachers] say that, having brought clarified butter near a particular mantra,
three oblations should be offered for each [mantra] in sequence.
At the end of "svāhā," one should cause the full oblation (pūrṇā) to fall with the mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ";
then one should utter the mantra ending in "phaṭ" for the purpose of severing the bonds and granting liberation.
When this has been done, thereafter he should give the five products of the cow, the sacrificial porridge (caru), and the tooth-stick to the disciples in due order.
A wound from the *rājyagrantha* tree is recommended;
it should be made from a milky tree, with a thickness like that of the little finger and a length of twelve finger-breadths.
Having gently rubbed the teeth with the face turned upward and having rinsed the mouth by spitting out a small amount, one should proceed not too far away.

The faces should be directed respectively toward the east, north, northeast, and upward; the accomplishments (siddhis) follow in this order. When the disciples have fallen [into the mandala] according to the divisions of the directions, one should perform the fire oblation (homa).
The homa should be performed with clarified butter, offering one hundred oblations with the Astra mantra.
If the face is turned downward, death is certain; if the face is turned upward, there is always victory.

Facing east, one attains peace; facing the direction of fire (south-east), one experiences distress; facing south, there is fear of death and disease; and facing the direction of Nirṛti (south-west), there is fear of enemies.
In the western face, there is certainly gain and nourishment that arise;
for the purpose of all accomplishments, one should perform eradication in the northwestern and northeastern directions.
If one falls with the face turned upward, one shall attain the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin);
it will also be desired by the preceptor for the increase of his own lineage.
The disciple should enter together with the preceptor into the sacrificial hall,
which is well-kindled, spacious, protected by Nīladaṃbha, and well-perfumed.
Having quickly sprinkled [the disciple] with fragrant perfumes and bright flowers upon the seat,
and having consecrated all his limbs, the preceptor should observe silence.
Then, one should contemplate that sixfold path for the disciples;
having thoroughly purified it from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, one should consider it stainless.
Afterwards, one should recite the Saṃhitā, which is extremely subtle, all-pervading, and the goddess who has caused all principles (tattvas) to descend; then again, the eight mantras of the Vadhūs.
Alternatively, until sleep comes,
one should rise and attend to the necessary duties, bathe, and perform the beautiful [worship] as before.
Having washed their hands and feet, they performed the twilight worship as before;
clad in white garments, well-covered, and having purified themselves, they were seekers of liberation.
32a) Joyful, restrained in speech, purified by bathing, with flowers in their hands and well-prepared in mind,
they should worship the feet of the Guru and sit upon a mat on the ground.
Having bowed their heads to all, and remaining obedient to the words of their preceptor,
they should inquire about the auspicious dream with proper conduct and gentle speech.
Thus ends the chapter on the preliminary consecration for initiation in the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the procedure common to all,
as well as the measure of the oblations as they exist throughout the six paths.
The path of the feet, the path of the worlds, and the path of the principles (tattvas);
beyond that, in sequence, are the path of the phonemes (varṇas) and the path known as the mantras.
On the path of practice, one should perform the worship of the vehicle of Vāgīśī,
as well as the fifteen purificatory rites for the sacrificial animals in their proper sequence.
Sprinkling, striking, cutting, drawing out, seizing, joining together, and the production of the embryo must be performed.
One should perform the severing of the bonds through the specific purification of the channels, by means of the effort, the presiding deity, the enjoyment, as well as the dissolution.
Therein, first, the installation of the principles (tattvas) and so forth should be performed in their proper order;
then the proclamation should be made: "Let there be no further slaughter here."
Fifteen purifications must be performed at each stage for the sake of removing the fetters of bound souls;
otherwise, one shall not attain liberation.
Three times nine padas are to be known, arising from the Pervader of Space (Vyomavyāpin);
the measure of the worlds is considered to be ninety-two.
O Six-faced One, there are thirty-four principles (tattvas) and likewise [thirty-four] phonemes;
there are eight mantras, beginning with Ananta and ending with Kālavidyā.
The offering of oblations is equal for the paths of worlds (bhuvana) and words (pada);
likewise, the fire-sacrifice (homa) for the paths of principles (tattva) and phonemes (varṇa) is equal through the application of the oblation.
O Six-faced One, one should prescribe four times that amount for the entire path of the principles (tattvas), with the measure of oblations being in a row for each individual rite.
One should understand that [the offering] is defective on the path of mantras, but not so on the path of kalās;
at the end of the paths, one should offer eight oblations with Śiva himself.
The number mentioned briefly shall now be stated in detail:
one should offer each individual oblation with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) for every single rite.
At the end of that, one should cause eight oblations to be offered with the Śiva-mantra;
this total number of oblations is declared for the path of the Padas.
There should be three thousand and four hundred;
thus one should offer oblations in sequence within the Bhuvanamālā.
In the ninefold world of Bhuvaneśī, double the number of oblations should be offered;
there shall be an equality of oblations between the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan) and the path of states (padādhvan).
By offering two oblations, one should perform each ritual action;
for whichever caste or principle (tattva) resides on the path within the fivefold ritual procedure.
In the supreme principle of Sadāśiva, within the path of the principles (tattvādhvan), there are four qualities;
in the sound of the principle, it is one thousand mixed with fifty-eight.
Thus has been declared the determination of the oblations on the path of the phonemes (varṇādhvan);
at the end of that, one should cause eight oblations to Śiva to be offered.
The number [of oblations] for the path of the arts (kalādhvan) is said to be in sequence along the great path;
one should offer ten oblations for each and every refinement (saṃskāra).
One should cause eight oblations to be offered with the Śiva-mantra at the end;
two thousand and eight [oblations] are prescribed for the path of mantra.
And in the path of mantra, whatever [rite] becomes defective due to the fire-oblation (homa) in the path of the Sakala,
twenty oblations must be offered for each ritual action.
In the same way, eight oblations should be offered to Śiva;
thus, O son of Kṛttikā, the number [of rites] on the path of the Kalās has been briefly explained.
Thus has the measure of the oblation been declared for the purification of the paths.
Thus ends the chapter on the general oblation in the Kālottara.
The path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) is declared according to the measure of the number of its constituent parts;
the primary lords of these worlds must be purified with diligent effort.
When these [mantras] are purified, those that have become secondary attain purification as well; of this there is no doubt.
In the ritual of offering oblations (homa), the placement of mantras (nyāsa) performed according to the sequence of emanation (sṛṣṭi-nyāsa) bestows the fruit [of the practice].

38a) Īśvara said:
Hereafter, I shall explain initiation (dīkṣā), which bestows the fruit of Śiva;
it is proclaimed to be of two kinds: with seed (sabījā) and without seed (nirbījā).
Is it with seed and eternal? It should be known as such through experience within the mere body;
therein, one should bring the fruit of previously acquired karma to the state of having its seeds burnt away.
Therefore, that which is free from "mine-ness" must be suppressed by him, like the potency of poison;
once that has begun to diminish through experience, he shall go to the state of Śiva.
That is declared to be "with seed" (sabīja), involving the persistence of karma;
"seedless" (nirbīja), through the falling away of the body, one attains full Śiva-hood.
Due to the destruction of his three bonds arising from illusion, innate nature, and karma,
the Guru should empower him for the observances (samayas) that possess seeds.
For those who are like hair or a nest, for the aged, for those who are serpents, and for those whose souls are afflicted by disease—
for them, initiation is without seed and is devoid of ritual observances.
For the poor and the helpless, mental initiation (mānasī dīkṣā) is indeed prescribed;
for those of purified soul, vocal initiation (vācikī) performed with the removal of doubt is recommended.
Or, by touching them with the Hand of Śiva (śivahasta), he should lead those touched to the state of Śiva;
[the initiation] may consist of one principle, three principles, or five principles.
The thirty-six classes of principles, associated with the sixfold paths, exist;
by knowing the supreme Śiva-principle, one becomes the destroyer of the bonds of bound souls.
Otherwise, the bound souls (paśus) are never liberated from the accumulation of fetters (pāśasaṃcaya). Now, that procedure is being stated briefly by way of a summary.
One should carefully provide, in sequence, the ritual acceptance, the five products of the cow, the sacrificial porridge, and the tooth-stick; then, at the end of sleep, one should commence the rite.
Or, one should perform the immediate consecration (sadyodhivāsa) without the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the sacrificial porridge (caru).
Having performed the ritual bath according to the rules, one should then worship the gods and the ancestors.
After worshipping the Lord of the Gate according to the rules, one should enter by the western door.
Then, having sat upon a seat, the binding of the directions (digbandha) should be performed;
thereafter, the cremation of the body (piṇḍadāha) should be carried out, and after that, the dissolution of the elements (tattvavisarjana).

Afterwards, one should perform the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa) and then contemplate the seat (āsana); thereafter, the ritual of hand-placement (karanyāsa) should be performed, followed by the placement upon the body (dehanyāsa).
Afterwards, one should arrange the fires for the various sacrificial vessels;
having concluded the worship of the body, one should then commence the internal sacrifice (antaryāga).
One should arrange two vessels there, one for the *mudrā* and one for the *arghya*;
the former, called "immovable," is placed before Śiva, while the latter, "movable," is for the purification of the bound soul (*paśu*).
Having first performed the purification of the place, and then again the purification of the ritual substances,
one should purify them by sprinkling once with water from the *argha* vessel.
One should perform the worship of Gaṇeśa and the Guru, and worship two water-pots;
thereafter, one should purify the mandala and offer colored powders for the sake of liberation.
Likewise, one should sprinkle other items with the water of Śiva and with the water of the weapon-mantra (astra-vāri).
Having worshipped Śiva residing there, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) as before.
39a) Then, having sprinkled the disciple brought from outside with the Śiva-weapon [mantra],

Therefore, having brought [the deity] inside, one should fashion the form of the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti on the right hand,
from the base (ādhāra) up to Śiva.
One should place the limbs of Brahmā there, as well as flowers, perfumes, and so forth;

Having attained the state of Sadāśiva-Śiva, he was both dependent and independent;

O son, he becomes fit for hearing, studying, and touch only in this way, and not otherwise;

On that day or on the following one, one should cause the binding of the eyes to be performed with a cloth made of silk,

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) specifically for one who is permeated by the essence of power (śakti),

Since the narrative has reached its conclusion through the sequence of the twice-born,
one should touch the tip of a blade of kuśa grass after it has been consecrated in five ways.
One should place the name ending in the dative case within the heart, and there one should install Vāgīśvarī;
thereafter, all the purificatory rites for the disciple must be performed in their proper sequence.
Having first performed fifteen oblations with effort according to the previously stated method,
one should perform [the rites] in the six paths and worship [the deity] together with Kālarudra.
One should cause Kālarudra to hear [this]: "Never shall you be barren here;
strive in that world, for having enjoyed the abode of pleasures, you have gone there."
By the command of Śiva, blindness is again imposed upon him by you;
through this sequential yoga, he is to be purified up to the limit of the *sakala* state.
When the entire reality is purified, one should effect dissolution into the supreme state;
this applies likewise to the Samayin, the Putraka, the Sādhaka, and the Ācārya.
One should effect the dissolution (laya) of all four [elements] without distinction into Śiva;
then, having performed the severing of the crest (śikhāccheda) of Māyā, one should cause the ritual bath (snāna) to be performed.
Thereafter, one should purify the pure path above— namely Vidyeśvara and Sadāśiva— according to the previously mentioned rule by means of the previously described application of oblations.
Their dissolution into the supreme Śiva should be performed by means of the equinox (viṣuva);
through the application of the equinox, the Guru should liberate the bound souls (paśus).
But having attained the equinox of yoga, who could not be said to be liberated from bondage?
Having established the state of consciousness within the disciple's self, the signified (vācya) as well as the signifier (vācaka) should be explained.
"One should contemplate everything as having a single form through the possessor of power (śaktimant).
Thus, the *Ghoṣaṇikā* should be performed in the temple of the bliss of the flow of consciousness (*citsyanda*).
One should contemplate their respective spheres of authority within the individual principles; the initiate, established in his office, is the enjoyer within the profound mystery.
40a) However, for a spiritual son (*putraka*) who has deviated from the conduct of the observance (*samaya*) within the principle of Śiva,
the initiation of the observance (*samayadīkṣā*) must be performed for him in due order at the appropriate time.
Or else, by virtue of his capacity, he should protect [the world], remaining eternally established in Śiva;
for the practitioner, there is absorption into Śiva, while for him who enjoys [the fruits], there is the state of the Lord.
The dissolution of the teacher occurs in Śiva, while his enjoyment resides in Sadāśiva;
having understood this, the Guru should indeed unite [the disciple] with each respective principle (tattva) in due order.
O Śivā, everything should indeed be given by Śiva to Pūrṇa;
however, one who is engaged elsewhere should avoid it, and thereafter [bestow] the authority in due order.
One bestows immediate nirvāṇa, while another is considered to do so at the end of the body;
and the second is likewise established as twofold through the distinction between being with seed (*savīja*) and without seed (*avīja*).
Those who are without seed (nirbīja) are not at all endowed with the rules (asamaya); those with seed (sabīja) are likewise not [endowed with them].
In the second [initiation], that of the teacher (ācāryatva), one should worship Śiva in the nirbīja [rite].
The seedless initiation is called the state of the inauspicious (aśiva), while the seeded initiation possesses the nature of light;
thus is this initiation attained, and thereafter one should cause [the initiate] to hear the rules (samaya).
Initiation alone bestows liberation upon men and cuts away impurities from their very roots;
therefore, one should perform the worship of Gaṇeśa, the Guru, and Viśveśvara.
Through the practice of meditation and concentration, those [powers] become eternal in their knowledge;
indeed, they arise for a person through initiation alone in his final birth.
Thus ends the chapter on initiation in the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
But for the initiate (samayin) and the spiritual son (putraka), and especially for the practitioner (sādhaka),
it has been taught by the command of Śiva as a lifelong daily practice.
Bathing, worship, recitation, meditation, and fifthly, fire-offering—one should always perform these daily; thus they are further declared to be the obligatory rites.
On the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights,
on the fifteenth day at the end of the day, during a solar transit, and during the southern solstice.
In the case of an intercalary month, when a day is omitted, at the commencement of the six aśītimukha periods,
and during solar and lunar eclipses, the period of impurity is double that of the Ajapāda and other rites.

Thus, the obligatory (nitya) limb has been explained; now the occasional (naimittika) is being described. Initiation (dīkṣā) and consecration (pratiṣṭhā) are to be known as the two types of the occasional.
The daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites—these three must be performed by the teacher;
likewise, O son, the three must also be performed by the preceptor, except for the rite of installation (sthāpana).
The triad beginning with the daily rite (nitya) must be performed as an exposition by the teacher;
however, O Six-faced One, the daily and optional rites for the practitioner are those prescribed in his own scripture.
It is proclaimed that for both the initiate (samayin) and the spiritual son (putraka),
one should always perform what is taught in one's own scripture and avoid the scriptures of others.
A son-like disciple who abides by the commitments must always perform service to the guru and his brothers; however, this should not be done for a mere practitioner (sādhaka).
In times of illness, with medicines, and likewise during fear of a powerful king,
as well as during birth-impurity (sūtaka), one should diligently perform worship after purification through contact.
The Guru or the practitioner must always perform the obligatory rite;
one should not perform rites for specific desires, but should practice atonement according to the injunctions.
The Guru is to be worshipped like Śiva, yet one should not employ him in ritual acts—
whether they be obligatory, optional, or rites of expiation, such as recitation and worship.
One should not, even in thought, remember anyone other than the worshipful Mahādeva; one should behave toward the wives and sons of one's guru as one would toward the guru himself.
One should not look upon a naked woman; one should always honor a maiden. One should not engage in jesting in the presence of the guru, the gods, or the sacred fire.
One should avoid excrement, urine, and spittle, as well as the water from the nose;
one should carefully avoid the impurity of those devoted to the Left-hand Path (vāmācāra).

One should diligently avoid laughing at those with missing limbs or extra limbs, as well as those who are superior in birth, learning, or scriptural knowledge, and likewise avoid making idle chatter about them.
A woman who is an ascetic should never be enjoyed, especially one with fragile limbs;
likewise, one should not enjoy the wife of a hero, nor one who is menstruating.
He should approach his wife during the period favorable for conception, but he must avoid her on the sacred festival days (parvan).
Śiva alone is to be worshipped; nothing else whatsoever is to be worshipped.
One must never create any sense of duality regarding Śiva, the Supreme Self;
one must not commit the eternal loss [of merit], and one should avoid the omission of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā).
Mental derangement, negligence, lust, anger,
recklessness, doubt, supreme fortitude, deceit, and likewise crookedness.
One who lacks diligence, lacks enthusiasm, is an atheist, or is agitated;
one who is an atheist, violates the bounds of conduct, or reviles the scripture of Śiva.
One should never engage in conversation with those defiled by the great sins (mahāpātaka);
one should avoid greed, pride, delusion, and worldly pursuits.
One should not perform worship even mentally with the left hand;
one should never touch the *liṅga* with the left hand.
One should not practice the left-hand path (*vāmācāra*), for what is "left" does not bestow fruit.
A practitioner of mantra should not disturb a woman, and he should abandon all laughter.
One should avoid whatever vows, worship, and so forth are mentioned by others;
rather, one should perform that which is prescribed in one's own scripture, ensuring that the ritual section remains unimpaired.
One should avoid exertion as well as phlegm, and instead accomplish [the practice];
one should not criticize the Lord as the cause, nor the scripture spoken by Śiva.
Slander should be avoided with effort; one should not step over a *liṅga*.
However, during her menstrual period, she should avoid cooked food that has been turned six times [on the fire].
One should not touch a bed, a couch, a pestle, a threshold, a broom, a mortar, a grinding stone, or a hearth.
One should not touch twice-born men, living beings, or elephants with one's foot; nor should one step over the remains of offerings (nirmālya) from the gods, nor should one step over their names.
One should not employ the property of the gods or the property of the guru for one's own use;
rather, even if it is neglected or stolen, it must be protected with great effort.
One should not perform acts contrary to the service of the guru, the gods, or the sacred fire; nor should one apply rituals such as worship and fire-offerings to oneself.
As long as Śaṅkara has not been worshipped, one should not perform any other [rite];
for those who abide in the principle of Śiva (Śivatattva), O Śiva, they should be served by the wise.
Those who desire auspiciousness should regard [beings] as being in various states;
they must be protected with great effort from fear, poverty, and passion.
She who is dependent on others and has fallen from her status should not be allowed to go out; nor indeed should she be made to do so. Men, however, should not go outside at night.
One should avoid taking up residence there in a cremation ground, a temple, on the bank of a river or a well, in a royal palace, or likewise in a forest.
One should not cut down a tree that has various spreading branches and a sturdy trunk;
one should not cause a wound at the navel, nor speak of the mark of the navel as being like a conch.
One should always contemplate the Truth before the city of the teacher, the Son; with [offerings of] food, water, lotuses, and garlands, at the proper time... [text fragment].
One should separately prepare auspicious garments, bedding, and seats according to the appropriate measurements.
One should avoid association with those who possess false knowledge and with those who follow the "shining" (dīpya) sūtras;
one should completely avoid those who are cruel.
One should always perform salutations to the gods and to Brāhmaṇas;
one must not seize the property of Brāhmaṇas, nor should one establish oneself upon the property of kings.
One should avoid attachment to one's own self and [worldly] objects;
one should avoid lack of fortitude, the relishing of "mine-ness," and suffering within sufferings.
One should avoid those [actions] that are performed for the sake of one's mother or wife;
one should also avoid causing the departure [of others], acting as a maker of exits, and the harming of living beings.
One should not practice the animal-sacrifice scriptures, the attainment of power through injury, or the doctrine of elemental spirits;
one must not act with shamelessness, nor should one subsist upon all forms of worldly yoga.
One should avoid playing with weapons such as poison, snakes, swords,
and the like; likewise, one should protect oneself according to one's own scriptures.
Protecting himself constantly in this way, he should avoid the practices of others;
he should shun from afar those who are thieves, kings, and those previously associated with them.
One should avoid frivolity, recklessness, and likewise living as one who bears another's sectarian mark; one should also avoid fear regarding those who bear other marks.
One should not risk even one's own life for that [initiation], nor should one ever doubt it;
at the time of worship, one must avoid contact with one who is uninitiated.
One should indeed perform one's reclining [only at the proper time] and avoid sleeping during the day.
At the time of bathing and eating, one should maintain silence and ward off impurity. One should always avoid [the performance of] installation and the recitation of praises for Dākṣāyaṇī.
"Having entered the fourth stage of life, you have adopted the doctrine of those two [the Jains]:
that the wife belongs equally to both the husband and the one who performs the ritual."
One should always perform the favor of both [the teacher and the disciple] through exposition and formal installation;
one should protect these and other such duties as prescribed by me, O Atri.
One should diligently avoid harming living beings with the mind; one should not even cause others to act in a manner that is hostile toward living beings.
This alone is the destruction of one's enemies; this alone is the supreme austerity:
one should never depart after seeing a linga with its top exposed.
Thus ends the chapter on the pledges (*samaya-paṭala*) in the *Kālottara*.
The Lord said:

At the conclusion of the initiation, at the conclusion of the consecration, and at the conclusion of the purificatory rite, one should perform the yoga of Caṇḍeśvara; listen, O Six-faced One, to this according to its true nature.
One should divide a square field measuring five cubits into twelve parts;
one should then discard one part from each of its two sides.
One should rotate the thread from the center; thus the city of the moon arises. In its middle, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus measuring one cubit.
One should fashion a single-pronged [vajra] made of white goat-skin, beneficial for the arms;
it is yellowish-green, shaped like a half-moon, four-cornered, and has the luster of the sky.
One should fashion the door joined with vermilion and the pericarp with the luster of gold;
one should conceive of the pedestal of the moon by means of the very term "yogapīṭha."
Alternatively, one should mentally recite the six-syllable mantra while being focused on the Savior (Tāraka);
having diligently worshipped Caṇḍeśa with the previously mentioned mantra.
Having worshipped him with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as with various kinds of food and ornaments,
one should satisfy him one hundred and eight times with the remainder of the clarified butter.
One should satisfy the heart and the other limbs in sequence by means of twenty oblations;
whatever has been offered to the God of gods, that one should assign to Caṇḍa.
One should diligently avoid iron, as well as bipeds and quadrupeds; O Lord, the collection of gems and one's own property are also declared [to be avoided].
The remainder should be given to a Caṇḍāla, as well as whatever else has been prepared for Śiva;
one should not mentally transgress the dust-line situated at a distance from oneself.
43b) Whatever has been offered to Caṇḍeśa should be cast into deep water;
or it may be reduced to ashes and scattered, but one must never consume it.
Therefore, for those who act otherwise and violate the command of Śiva, Caṇḍeśvara is the punisher; he is the lord even over those who have been initiated.
There is no fear anywhere from the efforts of Caṇḍeśvara;
therefore, those who have taken refuge in the path of Śiva are indeed his worshippers.
One should meditate on him who is white as a trident and an axe, holding a *kaḍamaḍa* lute and a rosary,
possessing long arms and a broad chest, resembling crushed collyrium.
Thus, one should visualize the face with three eyes, holding a *ṭaṅka* axe and granting fearlessness,
whether in a manifest or unmanifest *liṅga*, in a mandala, on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), or in a fire-pit (*nala*).
Likewise, in a mobile or stationary image, in a gem, in one adorned with various jewels,
in a liṅga made of fragrant substances or food, or in one fashioned from horn, stone, or wood;
Likewise, when the worship of Caṇḍa is performed with a liṅga made of flowers,
then, upon the completion of the sacrifice, on a ground marked with a svastika, [the ritual continues].
One should perform the avabhṛtha bath for oneself and for the initiated person;
the earth should be made auspicious with the sound of musical instruments, and the recitation of benedictions (svastivācana) should be performed.
One should recite many hymns and mantras that resound with praise for the Self,
using the water-pot presided over by Śiva, which wards off all suffering.
Having bathed, he should thereafter worship the preceptor (deśika) and likewise the guru;
he should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor according to his ability, such as an elephant and so forth.
Or is it the reverse? From village to village, or from field to field;
for the teachers it is double that distance, and for the practitioners it is half of that.
But for the sons [of the teacher], one should always feed them, according to one's ability, with a quarter [of the portion] or even among others;
they should be initiated, honored, and made to recite the Vyāhṛtis, and [the teacher] should always feed them as if they were sacrificial animals (paśus).
One should not, even in one's mind, perceive any difference between the fire of the *liṅga* and the Guru;
in this way, the direct worship of the Guru alone must be performed—thus have I declared.
Or, in the absence of the preceptor, worship should be performed preceded by mantras;
as well as the sprinkling of elephants, horsemen, chariot-warriors, and weapons with water.
One must perform the pacification of obstacles, which is the cause of victory in battle.
Thus ends the chapter on the Caṇḍa-sacrifice in the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
One should not fashion a navel for the purpose of the Master’s consecration, nor for any of the optional rites; indeed, a navel does not bestow fruit in those cases.
The worship of Parameṣṭhin should be performed in the northeastern direction and other quarters;
it is skillful regarding the four categories and uniquely cognizant of the six categories.
Likewise, one who has completed the observances of knowledge (vidyāvrata) should consecrate with the Guru-mantra a heroic man who is courageous and devoted to the welfare of all beings.

First, in a temple of Śiva, the limbs [of the mantra] beginning with "Śivam" and "Brahmāṇi" should be recited by one who is pure for one year while residing in a monastery, having restrained the collection of the senses.
Constantly subsisting on alms and sleeping upon a bed of kuśa grass,
he was intent on worship and fire-offerings, his mind purified through spiritual cultivation.

Regarding the "fragment of knowledge" (*vidyālavasta*): when the mandala is completed with one hundred thousand [recitations], the Guru—having thus fashioned nine lotuses—should perform the sacrifice as before.
Therefore, one becomes fit for initiation; otherwise, it never occurs anywhere.
Because of his capacity for both cursing and bestowing grace, the Guru is thus praised.
This supreme and meritorious vow shall also lead to spiritual perfection;
it is now being prescribed for the sake of the practitioner's own accomplishment.
When the Mūla, Arka, Yāga, and Indu nakṣatras are together with Śravaṇa,
during the bright fortnight on an auspicious lunar day, in a favorable yoga, and during the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa).
On the eighth or the fourteenth day, the consecration is recommended;
for the purpose of bathing, a comfortable throne should be placed in the northern direction of the mandala.
It should be placed on the back of a two-cubit altar, eight finger-breadths in height,
covered above with a canopy and adorned with hanging garlands of flowers.
The sacrificial pavilion was adorned with victory banners on all sides and provided with heaps of flowers,
unbroken rice, sesame seeds, parched grain, and offerings for the attainment of success.
One should fashion a pedestal there, measuring thirty-six finger-breadths, beautifully adorned with various auspicious garlands such as the svastika and other designs.
That [mandala] should be made four-cornered, adorned with four feet and one hundred eyes;
it is praised when elevated by one-fourth, and likewise its width at the foot [is the same].
One should carve a lotus in the center, joined with leafy creepers;
it is recommended that the wood be from a milky tree, or arising from the *kāyavāsa* or *utsa* trees.
One should determine the [dimensions] for the practitioner and others by decreasing them by four finger-breadths;
[this is done] with jars filled with water, having thorns made from *śruk* and *mūtra*.
Having worshipped with ten beautiful vessels containing jewels, shaped like conchs, svastikas, and lotuses, and having placed the Śiva-weapon in the center;
One who knows the ritual procedure should diligently place the eight [syllables] beginning with *ana* and ending with *ya* in sequence upon the eight [parts];
he should worship the mandala and offer oblations to Śiva.
Having bathed [the deity] according to the rite with the services of the mantra-cakra-cycle,
[he should offer] a white cloth as an upper garment and all ornaments that are free from blemish.
Adorned with a crown, necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments,
he was endowed with beautiful earrings and radiant, auspicious rings.
With the resounding noise of conchs and drums, the sounds of musical instruments being played, and the cries of "Victory! from bards and panegyrists;
One should place an auspicious throne to the west of the mandala,
upon which a single flower and unbroken rice grains— having attained the status of the mantra-throne— are placed to the north.
One should not cause him to sit upon that seat of authority;
having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa according to the rules, one should fashion the "hand of Śiva."
Having worshipped according to the prescribed ritual with garments, garlands, perfumes, incense, and so forth,
one should present the meditation belt, the rosary, and a manuscript of the Saṃhitā.
A pair of scissors eight finger-breadths long should be given, as well as a measuring cord;
a needle with a thimble should be provided, along with an umbrella and auspicious sandals.
With a fan, a chowrie, and a beautiful vehicle according to his preference,
one should thus honor the disciple who has been invested with authority.
Then the Guru, the teacher, having caused the disciple to enter the mandala and having taken his place at the southern image, should cause the disciple to pay homage.
From this day forward, [this] should be performed for those who possess devotion to the knowledge of Śiva,
who are pure-minded, humble, and whose minds are dedicated solely to Śiva.
Thus, for those of bold intellect who are disciplined and whose minds are solely intent upon Śiva,
favor is shown toward those seekers of liberation who are devoted to such virtues.
This must be performed without hesitation by you, who follow the command of Śiva;
from this day forward, the authority has been transferred by me unto you.
You must perform this until it has been transferred elsewhere;
having prostrated before the Lord, proceed as previously instructed.
Thereafter, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa), which is a ritual of the highest order.
The *pūrṇāhuti* should be offered by the preceptor; he should then perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the Brahma-mantras and their limbs.
Thereafter, the offering of three oblations must be performed by the Guru.
Then he should effect a dissolution into Śiva, [who possesses] the office of Sadāśiva;
when that office has been entrusted to him, his state becomes that of one who has set out on the great journey (vānaprastha).
Or one should offer a thousand oblations with the Śiva-mantra;
then authority is granted once more by Śiva, the Supreme Self.
Furthermore, you may exercise this authority as you wish;
it should be performed until the end of the body, or as you desire.
Having undertaken the vow of the teacher, one should practice it, for it is the highest of all vows.
Thus ends the chapter on the initiation of the preceptor in the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
For the initiate and the spiritual sons, there is consecration at the end of initiation;
one should perform the preliminary rites, such as the sacrifice, according to the previously stated procedure.
First, the fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed on the path of the steps as previously described;
one should then perform the fire sacrifice of the limbs of Śiva and effect their dissolution into the reality-level (tattva).
Listen again to the qualification for the two [levels] according to the previously stated rule:
one is a *samayin* in the principle of *māyā*, while a *putraka* is in the principle of *śiva*.
The practitioner (sādhaka) [should act] within the principle of Īśvara, while the teacher (deśika), however, [acts] within Sadāśiva;
one should cause those who have been initiated to perform this very office (adhikāra).
One should offer oblations numbering fifty, one hundred, one hundred and fifty, and two hundred;
then, having filled the *śruva* ladle with clarified butter, one should cause the *pūrṇāhuti* (final full oblation) to be offered.
When this has been performed, the qualification for the worship of Śiva arises;
through the initiate (samayin) and the worshipper (pūjaka), one becomes an aspirant (sādhaka) in the accomplishment of mantras.
"May this accomplishment of the worship be free from obstacles today.
Afterward, one should cause the disciples to receive their own commands and then confer the consecrations in due order.
The teachers in this treatise known as Kāla are proclaimed in successive order.
Thus ends the chapter on the initiation of the Samayin, Putraka, and Sādhaka in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
One should ascertain the transmission of the ten Tantras exactly as it exists, through the lineage descending from the peaceful Śivatattva, which is beyond the lower [principles].
46b) That which is produced by desire and that which is born of sacrifice; that which is not won through the cause of the *nāda* and the *ciṃtāṃkāra*;
that which is radiant and subtle, accompanied by exertion, and likewise possessing the luster of the rays of the sun.
The collection of tantras that emerged from the *Urdhvavaktra* consists of ten parts;
it is proclaimed as the division of Śiva—retain this very distinction.
O Six-faced One, the measure of each one is thirty *nakṣatras*;
the Śāntyatīta [level] is called Kāmika, while the Śānti [level] belongs to the Lord of Yoga.
Know that which is beyond thought to be the cause of the foundation arising from knowledge;
"Nivṛtti" and "Ajita" are indeed the faces of Śiva.
The blazing Heart of Śiva, as well as the head known as Sūkṣma;
the thousand-fold Śikhyā, Śambhava, Bhārabhūti, and Āśumān as the armor.
The eye should be known as Suprabha, joined with the moon, sun, and fire;
now I shall describe the Aratārakas in their proper order according to the lineage of the gurus.
The power called *kāmika* belongs to the one named *praṇava*; that born of yoga belongs to the one named *sudhā*.
From the two [powers] called *dīptā*, there arises the inconceivable; and the causal power belongs to the one named *kāraṇa*.
And that which is manifested is the radiant speech of the Lord known as Śiva;
it is revealed by the one called Sahasra, who is more subtle than the subtlest of time.
That [tantra] of the one named Aṃśumat, who is the light of the entire [universe], was well-proclaimed;
within those [tantras], the Tantras were truly taught by Sadāśiva.
Thus has the first sequence of the Guru’s lineage been declared;
furthermore, from the *Trikala* was obtained the *Kāmika*, and from the *Trikala* came the *Hara*.
From that, the Lord [attains] the pure *tantra* born of sacrifice, known as *bhasma*;
from Dīptarudra it is inconceivable, and from Gopati it belongs to Ambikā.
From cause to cause, Prajāpati was thus attained;
from him, the unconquered Suśiva was attained; and from him, Acyuta was attained by Umā.
From the radiant Īśa, Trimūrti was obtained; from him, Hutāśana;
from Sūkṣmasūkṣma, Bhava was obtained; and from him, Prabhañcana was obtained.
From Kālasaṃjña comes Sahasrārddha; from there, Bhīma and Vāyu;
from Daśeśa, Suprabha; and from there, Vigrahīśa and Śaśin.
Aṃśumān and Aṃśu-saṃjña were then seized by Ravi;
thus, these ten divisions of Śiva have been fully described.
And here I shall state the sūtras, numbering ten, which constitute the summary of the ritual activities concerning the reality of mantras;
now, therefore, follows the definition of the summary of the ritual activities concerning the reality of mantras.
This initial sūtra has been shown in brief by Īśāna in the Ādi-tantra;
it is revealed in this tantra known as the Kāmika.
There are thirty-two hundred thousand mantras of immeasurable power,
as well as the thirty-six principles and the rites that are both regular and occasional.
And the distinction between what is essential and what is non-essential is demonstrated in that treatise. || 1 ||
Now, therefore, the true nature of the person (puruṣa) is being declared.
Bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men, and adorned with mudrās and maṇḍalas—
thus has this Yoga-sūtra been proclaimed by the Supreme Lord.
Wherein there exists the discernment of the principles and of the Puruṣa,
O Mahādeva, that is the true nature [of the self], adorned with mudrās and maṇḍalas.
And thirty-two thousand mudrās in the form of mandalas have been proclaimed in the Yogaja-sūtra as bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men.
Then, scorched by the fierce mantra and finding their malevolent illusions thwarted elsewhere,
they [acted] through the power of Śiva’s energy, preceded by the propitiation of the mantra.
This sūtra, preceded by mantras, has been taught as inconceivable;
they call it "Ugra" and "Aghora," and through its recitation, one destroys the accumulation of sins.
From the dissolution of ignorance, consciousness is born;
and thus, the mere hundred thousand [recitations] of the mudrās and mantras have been demonstrated.
In the inconceivable Great Tantra, the Sūtra itself is revealed;
furthermore, for those who are devoted to the left, one should bestow [the result] below by means of the left power (vāma-śakti).
One should produce discernment by which yoga proceeds;
this cause was indeed previously stated by Śaṅkara in the Sūtra.
For those devoted to the left-hand path (vāmācāra), Vāmadeva is the restrainer;
through the ripening of time, they shall again attain the supreme state through discernment.
In this tantra, which has the causal nature as its essence, ten lakhs of mantras for accomplishing siddhis have been taught, along with their mudrās, maṇḍalas, and classes.
Now, the reality of Śiva (śivatattva) is revealed for those devoted to virtuous rites,
preceded by the worship of the maṇḍala together with the collection of mantras and mudrās.

48a) This initial sūtra has been proclaimed in the tantra known as the Ajita for those who are engaged in meditative absorption and dhyāna, and whose souls delight in worship and fire-offerings (homa).
For those who are dispassionate toward the injury of living beings, the knowledge of reality arises;
once that has arisen, ignorance is never again obstructed by anything.
One million [recitations] of the mudrās, maṇḍalas, and mantras have been demonstrated;
this tantra named Ajita has been proclaimed therein with great effort.
Now, the reality of the Self is demonstrated here in its entirety;
know that supreme reality of the Lord to arise from yoga.
This should be known as the *Ādisūtra*, the leader of the tantra called *Dīpta*,
wherein the discernment of the self of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is taught in its entirety.
By means of which the discernment characterized by reality is manifested for men,
through that very concentration (dhāraṇā), the supreme pervasion of the object of focus is produced.
One hundred thousand dhāraṇīs have been shown here in brief,
as well as those of the mantras, the deities, and likewise the ritual instruments.
The explanation of the first sūtra which was shown by Dīptākṣa [is concluded]. || 6 ||
Now, the yoga of the universal self, which bestows everything, is described by me.
Always and in every respect, indeed, you must practice truth with diligent effort;
this should be known as the primary aphorism in the *Tantrāloka*, the leader of tantras, which is called the Subtle (*sūkṣma*).
Having reflected upon this with one's whole being, as it is now being told by me,
one should apply oneself with effort to that [instruction] for the sake of realizing its true nature.
By the very word "kuru kuru," there is the grasping of the head-mantra (śiromantra),
which is the causal essence of mantras, mandalas, and mudrās.
Two hundred thousand [verses] are proclaimed in this most excellent tantra called Sūkṣma;
now, therefore, from the knowledge of Śiva, the Supreme Self, [arises] Jvālinī.
O son of Kṛttikā, this is the first sūtra therein, concerning the collection of mantras and mandalas, [attained] through two hundred thousand recitations of the dhāraṇīs.
Jvālinī is the supreme power (parā-śakti) of Śiva, the remover of inauspiciousness;
she is of unimpaired nature through the yoga of concentration and meditation.
Liberation, which is imperishable and free from all afflictions, is attained through the sequence of mudrās,
and especially through the retention of mudrās, maṇḍalas, mantras, and dhāraṇīs.
Each one is declared to consist of one hundred thousand [verses], while that known as the *Tantra* consists of a thousand.
Then, having meditated upon the body of the omniscient Lord according to its true nature—
Becoming absorbed in that and merged within it, one enters specifically into the state of its true nature;
know this to be the primordial sūtra in the system known as the Aṃśumat-ananta-tantra.
The one God is without a second; He alone is the one who hears all and is the one for all.
The one God shines through the activity of differentiation, like the moon appearing in various forms within a mirror.
By the word "body" (tanu), [is meant] the armor of primordial nature, the cage of delusion.
The self-knowledge that consists of the investigation of that [reality] is proclaimed by the name "Ray."
Now, therefore, listen to that which is to be known as all that is considered luminous, whether it be of the nature of the ten eternal forms or otherwise.
This should be known as the opening sūtra in the Tantra named Suprabha:
"The entire world, both stationary and moving, consists of the nature of the moon and the sun."
49a) The continuum of consciousness and non-consciousness is clearly composed of knowledge and ignorance; therein, the teacher must understand what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted.
The partless knowledge has been declared in the *Suprabha*, which is known as a Tantra;
thus, these ten Tantras were produced for the sake of Śiva’s work.
The five Brahmans are the limbs that abide in Śambhu;
their very Sūtras have been shown by me out of affection for you.
"I shall demonstrate this at the time of exposition for disciples of steady intellect.
Thus ends the chapter on the divisions of Śiva in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
Listen, O Six-faced One, to the enumeration by way of eighteen measures:
each stands at thirty-three hundred thousand in number.
Vijaya, Pārameśa, Nisvāsa situated beyond, then Prodgīta, that which is called Vimva, Siddha, and the one named Santya.
Likewise, the Nārasiṃha is proclaimed, and after that the Candrahāsa;
then follows the Vīrabhadra, and thereafter the Svayambhuvana-mantara.
Visara, the one called Rauva, Mākoṭa, the one named Kiraṇa,
Lalita, Nala, and Parā is remembered as the last.
These are known as the divisions of Rudra, which serve as the means for practitioners to attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
From the head [of Śiva] arose Vijaya, and from the forehead, Pārameśvara.
In the past, the triple-sectioned Nisvāsa emerged from his eyes,
and then the two-sectioned [text] for the sake of enjoyment and liberation issued forth as a song from his two ears.
The thirty-fold variety of the upper face and its reflection should be understood;
likewise, the three-tiered [structure] is established as arising from the neck and the shoulders.
The *saṃtāna* has two sections emerging from the region of the armpits,
while the *nārasiṃha* has a single division emerging from the region of the chest.
From the two breasts of the Lord, that which is called Candrahāsa emerged in two divisions;
from the heart and the neck, they declare that which is called Vīrabhadra to be likewise twofold.
The fire-element (āgneya) is the command of the Athula [tradition], which pierces through the single opening of the belly;
it has spread forth from the central abode of Svāyambhuva by means of a single piercing.
Visara is situated at the sides, Vibheda within the body of Śiva,
and Raurava is established by a single division in the region of the back.
O Śāṅkarī, Mākoṭa is born from the waist and has three divisions;
its single division, however, is the radiance that has issued forth from the generative organ.

The *kuvaya* stone is indeed charming and brings success; it arises from that [stone] and is of two types. There are five varieties of *saurabha*, and those of *parameṣṭhin* are produced by the knees.
These eighteen should be known as the primary leaders;
they are designated by those very names and are the illuminators of the two types of knowledge.
Together with the cognitions, they arise in that manner as eighteen-fold in number;
however, their mutual designations should be understood to be like those of the Rudras.
Indeed, many sub-varieties are described by me in brief:
Vijaya, Vṛṣabha, Raudra, Mohana, and Padmasaṃkuka.
Vijaya is declared to be fivefold, and Pārameśvara sevenfold;
[the others are] Pauṣkara, Haṃsa, Mātaṅga, Yakṣiṇī, and Vāmadevaka.
Dadhīci is to be known as the seventh; the Pratiṣṭhā belongs to the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvara).
The breathless state (niḥsvāsa) is of three kinds, and it is prescribed as having three sections (trikāṇḍa).
Niḥśvāsakārika is indeed remembered as the triad of the north;
the first tantra is Udgīta, and immediately after that is Prodgīta.
The orb of the face is established as undivided from the thirty-six principles;
that orb of the face is Hayagrīva, the formidable mass of primordial wisdom.
Arṇara, known as Mohacūrṇa, Vimala, Bhāsura,
Patahruka, Naṃguhya, and Vavanateyaka.
Then [he taught] the Atiguhya, the Tatotsāha, the Viśvarūpa,
the Vibhāvasu, the Dhūlibheda, the Mahocchvāsa, the one called Saṃtāna, and likewise the Amṛta.
The *keśara*, *tilaka*, and that which is named *kambu-koṭi*—
these varieties of the mental [mark] on the orb of the face have been described by me to you.
The Siddha, Vāsuki, and that which is called Caṇḍa emerged as Siddhas;
the lineage is of two kinds, namely the Rudra-lineage and the [ordinary] lineage.
O Śikhidhvaja, the Nārasiṃha [mantra] should always be known as having a single division;
the Sūryabheda and Candrahāsa [mantras] arise from two divisions each.
Mahākāla and Vīrabhadra are of two types, while Vīrabhadraka is of one type; likewise, that which is known as Āgneya and Vāthulāhuṃ is also of one type.
Likewise, the Svāyambhuva [Tantra] is to be known as established through differentiation;
it is considered twofold: the Viśara, which includes Keśarāhu, and the Visara.
Raurava has one division, while Mākoṭa arises from three divisions;
Mākoṭa, the seat of Brahman (Brahmapīṭha), and likewise that known as Nirvāṇa.
The single division is known as *kiraṇa*, while the two divisions are considered to be *lalita*.
Furthermore, *lalita* is called *vana*, and this *lalita* exists in two divisions.
But at the time of exposition, the teachers should reveal the two types known as *parā*— namely, the *saura-bheda-parā* and the one simply called *parā*.
Otherwise, however, the validity of created things arises;
in that regard, they become illuminators of knowledge, born from the body of Śiva.
Arising together with the primordial cognitions, they explain [the teachings] in successive order:
the Lord Sun, who is beginningless, is the illuminator of victory.
Śrīrūpa is the ten-syllabled mantra of the Supreme Lord’s exhalation;
that called Rudra belongs to the upward breath, while Praśama resides in the reflection of the face.
In the lineage of the Siddha Bindudhyāyin, there is one named Śiva;
in that of Nārasiṃha, there is the gentle one named Ananta; and in that of Candra, there is likewise one named Ananta.
The all-pervading self of Vīrabhadra emerged from the sky;
it is known as the fiery expansion of the self-born Nidhana, the essence of splendor.
Raurava belongs to Brahma, while that called Makuṭa belongs to Īśvara; Lalita was completed by Vidyālaya, and Bhairava by Samāpta;
the sage Saṃvartaka received Kiraṇa from his father.
O Lord, that Dharma which fell upon Saurabheyī was obtained by the gods;
it is the source of the knowledge of the eighteen Tantras.
The teachers must certainly be mentioned at the commencement of every exposition;
these [teachers], numbering fifty-four, are to be honored by the wise through their explanations. (1)
O Six-faced One, listen now in due order to the primary aphorisms of the eighteen tantras,
which are the diligent retention of the meaning of those tantras.
The six categories are indeed presented in the Sūtra and the Tantra;

This is proclaimed as the opening sūtra in the *Vijaya-tantra*;
here, by the word "infinite" (*anaṃta*), the entire section is encompassed.

it is grasped by the term "Lord of All Yogas," for that is the cause of the tantra.

likewise, by the word *śāśvata*, the eternal state (*pada*) is grasped.
The nature of the Lord, Śiva-tattva, has been shown by this aphorism:
"Now, therefore, [is taught] that which is the source of all knowledge and the refuge of the Pramathas."
I shall proclaim the great tantra honored by the lords of yoga;
this is the primordial sūtra expounded in the Nisvāsa Tantra.
Through the mention of the "birth of consciousness," there is the inclusion of the reality of knowledge (*vidyātattva*);
and through the words "Pramatha" and "Ugra," there is the inclusion of the term "Yogapīṭha."
Everything consists of knowledge and ignorance; through knowledge one may attain the nectar of immortality.
By means of the very term "Yogapīṭha," she is established in the seat of blissful enjoyment.
Now, therefore, having prostrated before the self-existent Lord, the impeller and ordainer of all mantras, the god who brings about the end of death;
This opening sūtra was proclaimed when the tantra was fully sung;
by the word "end of the finale" (nidhanāntaka), the reality of time (kālatattva) is encompassed.
The phrase "for the sake of the finality of the state" (padasya nidhanāya) signifies the inclusion of the finality;
by this sūtra, the Omniscient One and the Immediate Creator are proclaimed. (4)
Thus, for thirty kalpas, the yogi Maheśvara remained engaged in yoga together with Umā—
tranquil and worshipped by the hosts of gods and asuras.
This initial sūtra is established within the mouth of the Tantra;
herein, through the connection with the ritual manual (kalpa), there is the appropriation of the reality of the self (ātmatattva).
And likewise, the relationship between the word "yogi" and the word "yoga" is eternal;
thus it is stated in the Sūtra regarding the face known as the Bimba. (5)
Now, therefore, I shall proclaim the Sūtra born of Śiva, which is the inner refuge;
it bestows liberation upon the illustrious practitioner who, through his own self, bears all powers.
This is declared as the opening sūtra in the Tantra *Mahodayasiddha*.
Here too, by the expression of the word "Śiva," the Śiva-tattva is encompassed.
And by the utterance of the practitioner, "O Śiva, granter of liberation," one who is joined with the principles (tattvas) shall attain a body whose form is space, pervading the sky.
Now, therefore, for the sake of the welfare of all, I shall proclaim the Great Knowledge, which is auspicious in nature, characterized by universal excellence, and whose form is liberation.
This opening sūtra has been clearly elucidated within the tantra’s continuum;
by means of the expression "Sarvatobhadra," there is the inclusion of the reality of illusion (māyātattva).
And thus, by the expression of the word "Śiva," the Yoga-pīṭha is encompassed;
for Māyā, consisting of the three guṇas, is proclaimed as avidyā.
By the very word "Śiva," through the knowledge thereof, one shall attain dissolution.
Now, therefore, follows the instruction on ritual action, which is the cause for the sake of universal liberation;
it brings about the arising of knowledge, the great attainment, and removes the name of "animal" (paśu) from one, bestowing Śiva-hood.
This opening sūtra has been revealed in the *Nārasiṃha-tantra*.
One should perform its ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in sequence by means of the term "karmavijñapti."
The arising of knowledge is born as the cause for universal liberation;
it is the reality proclaimed by Sadāśiva, wherein action is quelled through ritual practice.
And this state of all yoga is subsumed within that of Śiva.
Now, I shall proclaim the Lord whose body is fire, who consists of all knowledge,
who is the speaker, the upholder of the Tantra, and the bestower of the power of liberation through Yoga.
This opening sūtra was revealed in the Vīrabhadra Tantra;
therein, the reality of Sadāśiva is described by way of his fiery form.
Through the description of yoga, liberation, and sovereign power, there is the attainment of the state that pervades space.
Now, therefore, follows the demonstration of the conceptualization of the seed of all consciousness,
which has as its basis the time of the junction between the yugas and the manvantaras.
This primordial sūtra was revealed in the Candrahāsa Tantra;
therein, too, it is through the grasping of the seed of knowledge regarding the reality of time.
That very state is called "departure" (niryāṇa), because of the vision of all-knowledge. || 10 ||
Now, that impurity which was previously bound by one's own [karma] is released again through initiation;
it should be understood as being of three states: the pure (kevala), the mixed (sakala), and the impure (mala).
Having grasped that supreme state there, the other person, though veiled by ignorance,
is released from the three bonds upon the striking of the lotus.
The Self is said to be fourfold, beginning with the Supreme Self (paramātman) due to its appropriation [of the others].
Now I shall describe the incomparable face called Śiva, which is the great Śiva seated upon the lotus of mantras with nine naves, and which is the support of the subsequent [section].
This is the opening sūtra in the extensive tantra called *Viraja*.
In this [tantra], by the term "Śiva," the Śiva-tattva is encompassed.
And likewise, by the word "mantra," there is [the inclusion] of the term "vyomavyāpī."
Now, therefore, for those who have conquered their selves by overcoming the bonds of the individual soul (paśu-pāśa), which has neither beginning, middle, nor end, [is taught] this supreme,
most excellent sword of great Śaiva knowledge for the purpose of severing them.
This initial sūtra was proclaimed in the Raurava Tantra;
here too, by the expression of the word "pāśa," the three bonds (pāśatraya) are encompassed.
And the self is threefold: the bound [self] is designated by the word "paśu" (animal);
the state of being without beginning is proclaimed by the word "pada," which signifies the grasping of a state. || 13 ||
Now I shall proclaim this supreme knowledge, called the Peaceful Separation (Śānti-viyoga), which bestows both spiritual perfection and liberation, as it was sung from the mouth of Śiva.
This is the opening sūtra in the tantra called Mākoṭa-mukuṭī;
herein, through the discourse on the lower and the higher, the apprehension of reality is established.
And likewise, liberation has been described; however, [the meaning] of the term "meditative absorption as sustenance" remains to be explained.

It establishes the investigation into the knowledge of the Lord of Beasts (Paśupati), his fetters (pāśa), and those bound by them (paśu); it is fully endowed with ritual action (kriyā) and conduct (caryā), and it brings forth the stages of yoga (yogabhūmi).
This initial sūtra has been proclaimed in the tantra named Kirana;
it consists of four quarters, contains six categories, and reveals the nature of the Self.
But by the indirect expression of the word "yoga," the supreme state is grasped.

it is the essence of Śiva, the Great Knowledge, which is the highest of all knowledges.

therein, for the sake of the meaning of the flame (jvālā), the reality (tattva) of Sadāśiva is proclaimed.
Thus, by the statement that it consists of all things, it is proclaimed to be all-pervading.
That which is called Nāda is the supreme seed-syllable, abiding within all beings;
it is the supreme, divine bestower of liberation and the granter of all accomplishments.
53b) This is the opening sūtra in the tantra called the Āgneyavāthula;
herein, by the word "sound" (nāda), the Lord's state of being the source of all is indicated.
By the very word "liberation" (mukti), Sadāśiva is known as the agent;
this alone is the first aphorism in this treatise, which is uniquely designated as "Time. (17)
Then, one should contemplate the Great Linga, which transcends the individual soul, which expresses the ineffable,
which is knowledge identical with Śiva, subtle, and the cause of all cognition.
This should be known as the opening sūtra in the Saurabheya system called Panāhvaya.
Now, the unmanifest (avyakta) is declared to be the Great Liṅga, whose nature consists of the principles (tattva) and the qualities (guṇa).
Likewise, by the statement that it is of the nature of Śiva, the state is remembered as Śiva alone;
those mantras which denote that day are of the nature of Śakti.

Thus, O Six-faced One, these eighteen sūtras called Rudra-sūtras are to be demonstrated at the time of exposition to disciples of purified soul.
Thus, this body of Śiva exists in eighteen ways.

The Lord said:
I shall proclaim the state of the true essence of Śiva, which is peaceful and illuminating;
the single-syllabled Brahman "Om," characterized by mantra, tantra, and so forth.

The imperishable state, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa), pervades all; by means of its constituent measures (mātrās), the entire world is intensely woven through and through.
