since that Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, pervades it, he is so named.
Therefore, Sadāśiva is all-pervasive by means of the multitude of his power-rays;
the Lord, the imperishable Master, assumes that very form.
Because he is endowed with that nature, he is called "of the form of space.
To that great Śiva, the all-pervading, the Great Self—
Salutation to the all-pervading one, whose form is space, the supreme source;
that which is called the space of the supreme-non-supreme is entirely without remainder.
Because it is stretched out by the Blessed One and is all-pervasive, it is therefore "bhava";

He is proclaimed as infinite because he is immeasurable, and as unborn because he is unproduced;

57a) Here, the words beginning with "namaḥ" are yours, while the others are [the names] of the faces;
the fourth, "sadyojātam," is declared to be the word for action (karma).
I take refuge in the fourfold state which consists of the essence of ritual action;

in the meritorious field measuring three cubits, which is divided equally on all sides by the constellations.

One should arrange four-petaled lotuses there, eight in number;
outside the path and the cloth-strip, the doors, however, are two squares.
This very [measurement] applies to the lotus, as well as to the skull-mantras;
likewise for the side-doors, the corner-bindings, and the double-pattika.
One should fill nine white lotuses, with pericarpes possessing the luster of gold and variegated filaments,
with red saffron.
The space between the sky-lines is black; the doors should be made according to the measurement of Indra (the unit). The central lotus is always to be worshipped by the name Sarasvatī.
Vāgeśvarī is in the eastern lotus, Hṛllekhā in the fire-lotus;
Citravāgeśvarī is in the southern [lotus], and Gāyatrī in the southwestern lotus.
One should place Viśvarūpā, belonging to Varuṇa, in the west; Śāṅkarī in the northwest; and [the goddesses] named Mani, Vyamā, Modakamalā, and Dhṛti in the north.
Sāvitrī should be recited over all skull-bowls for the purpose of perfecting speech;
it consists of the seed-syllables of Sarasvatī and others, joined with their respective names and the syllable *na*.
In the same way, the deities are to be meditated upon in four ways for the accomplishment of speech;
and in the fire-oblation, it should be performed with the ghee of Kapila using a tenth part [of the total].
He composes both Sanskrit and Prākṛt in a graceful and lucid manner;
being adorned with poetic figures, he becomes a knower of all scriptures through his great literary works.
This supreme secret must not be given to just anyone;
it should be imparted to disciples for the sake of attaining mastery of speech, O son, and not otherwise.
Thus ends the chapter on the worship of Vāgīśvarī in the Kālottara Mahātantra.
Īśvara said:
O Śikhidhvaja, I shall describe to you the eight mandalas of Śiva:
first that known as Sarvatobhadra, and after that the Naranābha.
Known as the Great Maṇḍala, the five-syllabled mantra grants all desires;
it is called the Destroyer of Obstacles and the Slayer of Death.

One should perform the removal of impurities (aghonirmācana), the water-rite (ambu), the rite with two supports (dvayādhāra), and likewise the eighth; having first purified the ground, one should cause the striking with a mirror (darpaṇāhati) to be performed.
One should determine the eastern direction by means of a gnomon, using the desired shadow of Viṣṇu,
or alternatively, by means of a sight-line within the center of a marked circle.
Having stretched a thread extending from east to west, one should mark the center;
then, from that middle point, one should burn [the marks] toward the south and north at both ends.
Two fish-figures should be drawn, extending from south to north;
one should bring them to meet at the corners with a measurement equal to half the dimension of the maṇḍala-field.
Thus, O Sūtra, by the expansion of the fourth [line], the square is produced; therein one should construct the auspicious, beautiful, and virtuous Veda-square.
65b) When divided by eight, one part is considered the lotus, and two parts are the pedestal;
the pathway there is one part, and a door of two parts is beneficial.
That should be made according to the measurement of a lotus and adorned with a cheek;
then one should fashion a corner-binding there, consisting of two squares.
One should then draw a white lotus with one ear [petal] having the luster of gold, with variegated filaments, and its base resembling the twilight.
One should complete the gates in accordance with the [presiding] world-protectors.
The space within the lines of the sky should resemble vaidūrya;
the binding of the corners is reddish, while yellow and white are beneficial for the destruction [of obstacles].
Thus has Bhadra been fully described as the Lord who is the support of Śiva;
it should be performed for both daily and occasional rites for the sake of the attainment of auspiciousness.
Now, the arrangement of the lotus is described by me in brief:
the lotus is of two kinds, namely, the unattached and the attached.
O son of Pārvatī, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men; it is always beneficial when unattached, and eternally beneficial when attached for those seeking liberation.
Each of these should be known as threefold by the Guru who understands ritual action;
by name, they are the child, the youth, and the old, which bestow the accomplishment of results.
Having reflected thus, one should then draw out the lotus in successive order;
one should cast the threads upon the lotus-field in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
The five kalpas are circular and equal in extent to the Padma-kṣetra;
in the first of these, there is a pericarp endowed with nine lotuses.
In the second [circle], there are twenty-four filaments;
in the third, however, the joints between the petals always take the form of elephant frontal globes.
In the fourth [circle], however, are the tips of the petals; in the fifth, they are of a dark-green (śyāma) form.
At its end is the line of space (vyomarekhā), which is beneficial when it is neither too thick nor too thin.
The lotus that is joined together is thus described; now the unjoined is being told:
the unjoined [lotus] has its petals extended toward the cardinal directions, and one should abandon the width [of the center].
By abandoning two parts, one should rotate the petal by its own eighth part;
using a thread for the expansion of the joint, one should cut the petal according to that measure.
Then, by the sequence of right and left, there should be an old lotus;
or else, from the middle of the joint, one should pierce it there like a half-moon.
Then the lotus should become resonant with the fierce thread of the two joints;
one should rotate it from behind according to the measurement of the limbs of the joint-thread.

A sharp-pointed [lotus] is for a youth; by means of that, a lotus bestows both enjoyment and liberation. An old [lotus] is for liberation. One should worship it at the appropriate time in the two directions.
Enough with effort; all ritual action is brought to rest.
One should perform the four-fold stage, firmly established and devoid of the sky.
One should, however, rotate the sky-line here at the tip of each petal;
thus, by way of brief indication, the eight-petaled lotus has been demonstrated.
It should be known that [this] is common to all, except for the mandala of Vighneśa.
Listen now as the mandala known as the "Nine Naves" is being described:
the original field is eight cubits, or ten cubits for the sake of prosperity.
Furthermore, one should rotate it all around with divisions consisting of the number of directions;
however, in the center, there shall be a lotus surrounded by sixty parts.
A path one quarter [of the width] should be made; the gates are lotus-faced, provided with necks and sub-necks, and the neck-encircling [part] consists of six and three [units].
This central lotus, provided with paths and gates, has been described by you in brief; outside of that, a path is prescribed.
That [line] measures five parts, while the one surrounding it on all sides measures ten parts;
then, O son of Kṛttikā, the work should be performed in the cardinal and intermediate directions as previously described.
One should construct eight lotuses according to the prescribed rule, including the gateway lotus and the pathways;
outside of that, there is a five-pada pathway adorned with petals.
The Gārakathinṭu should be like a lotus, with a *padika* [unit] for the surrounding wall;
a skull (*kapāla*) should be made as one *padika*, and three gates should be clearly established in the directions.
The binding of the corners should be with three bands or two bands, and it should be like a vajra.
In the center is a white lotus; in the eastern direction is Māyītā;
in the southeast is the red-colored one; and in the south stands Nīlākṣa.
In the southwest, it is yellow-black; in the direction of Varuṇa (the west), it is white;
in the northwest corner, it is smoke-colored; and likewise in the north, it is red-yellow.
In the northeast, [one should worship] that which resembles a pearl, white, or born from nine or six [syllables],
or else pale-yellow like a lotus, or even pale-red.
The Vyomavyāpin mantra belongs to Śiva alone and is not prescribed for the performance of sacrificial rites;
it is known as the nine-navelled [mantra], or it is called the Prasāda of Śiva.
Having worshipped Śiva in the central lotus and the Lokanāthas in the others,
one should diligently worship the weapons in the outer path with devotion.
He who worships the Supreme Lord within this mandala gains the merit of thousands of horse sacrifices and hundreds of rājasūya sacrifices.
He is not smeared by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water;
for the sake of enjoyment and liberation, one should perform the obligatory, occasional, and optional rites.
I shall describe the great maṇḍala that bestows all accomplishments;
one should first divide the eight-cubit field into twenty parts.
In the center, one should fashion a two-petaled lotus with a path-like border; then, in the cardinal and intermediate directions, one should draw eight petals colored blue.
Equal in size to the central lotus and possessing twenty petals,
they are devoid of petal-joints and are as blue as indīvara lotuses.
Behind that is a path of one square; above that are eight svastikas, each consisting of two squares, arranged in the form of a cross.
There, one should draw svastikas according to the injunctions of the guru's command;
outside, as before, there should be pathways, gateways, and likewise lotuses.
It should have a border joined at the corners with a binding frame and a fillet;
at midday it should indeed have the luster of a lotus, with a pericarp and yellow filaments.
The petals are praised as being unattached, like the sky, and the space [within] is a conceptualization of the sky;
the corners are of a crimson hue, and the walkways have the luster of gold.
The utpala lotuses are dark blue in color; the pericarp is shaped like a pericarp;
the svastikas are the color of molten gold; and the pathways are formed with leaf-patterns.
Having filled the various doors with dust,
one should establish the great maṇḍala known as the Heart of Śiva, which is dear to him.
Those who are indeed purified by the *haṇeśa* mantra, especially during the initiation (*dīkṣā*),
obtain all their desires through the worship of the Great Maṇḍala.
I shall now fully declare the five-syllable mantra for the dedication of vows,
and it must be employed for the removal of the *liṅga* and for the attainment of the supernatural powers (*siddhis*) such as *aṇimā*.
In a square field measuring five cubits on each side, divided everywhere into squares by lines,
there is a lotus of two squares in the center, and then a path of one square.
One should rotate the four [squares] of two *padās* each like the center;
behind that is a path (*vīthī*) of one *padā*, while the doors are two *padās* each.
It is endowed with necks and sub-necks, with a variegated junction of corners;
the central lotus is always white, with a yellow pericarp and filaments.
The eastern lotus is yellow, the southern has the luster of lapis lazuli,
the northern is like crystal, and the western lotus is like a kunda flower.
The first path has a radiance like red gold, and the other is like the form attained by Lokeśvara; such are the gates, O Śikhivāhana.
O you of excellent vows, this mandala of the five eyes has been described to you.
I shall describe the mandala that grants all desires and bestows every wish:
it has four corners with openings for the transformations, and it measures ten cubits on all sides.
Outside, the pathways shall be one *pada* wide, while the doors shall be two *padas*;
they should be constructed according to the measurement of the lotus, and one should fashion their necks accordingly.
The wise one should fill the unattached corner-bands with red;
therein, one should fill the doors with yellow, black, white, and red.
The leafy creeper is adorned like a golden vine,
while the lotus is white in color and endowed with manifold splendors.
The city of all desires is praised for the high-souled one who possesses serene faith;
indeed, through the worship of serene faith, one obtains all desires.
It bestows all desires upon men and is highly honored for every ritual action.
In this matter, it is recommended that my mandala be one that destroys obstacles;
however, on the pathway, there should be svastikas which have the nature of destroying misfortune.

Because it destroys misfortunes, it is called "Ariṣṭadhvaṃsana" (the Destroyer of Misfortunes), since it possesses the nature of destroying misfortunes. Therefore, it is indeed the Destroyer of Misfortunes.
It was spoken by Śiva, the God of gods, the Supreme Self.
Having first made it four cubits in length and two cubits in circumference, the pathway shall be one cubit wide,
and the door-frame shall consist of one cubit.
The circle of the previously described circle should be sixteen finger-breadths [in diameter],
and likewise there should be circles in the cardinal directions accompanied by lotuses.
Five white lotuses are beneficial, with a dark circular interior;
the corners have the luster of fire, and the pathways have the radiance of gold.

One should then cause the various doors to be fashioned by the World-Protectors (Lokapālas). In the center, the partless (niṣkala) [deity] is to be worshipped; the heart-mantra and the others are to be worshipped starting from the east.
The [remaining] eight [deities] should be placed in the intermediate directions, excluding Brahmā and Śiva from the [central] eye;
however, Śiva is to be worshipped with five limbs as before, omitting the doors and so forth.
In this mandala, one should worship that supreme Śiva known as the Partless (niṣkala);
in the case of the Supreme Lord who is partless, one should not designate any other as his support.
The state of all desires for men is not attained without merit, nor is it honored without merit;
having seen the removal of demerit, one is immediately liberated from evil.
Thousands of horse-sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of the *kalā*.
Therefore, I shall describe the foundation of the Buddhas; when the city has been divided into a hundred parts, one should fashion a lotus there, extending across all sides for fifteen parts.
Outside of that, one should sequentially arrange eight lingas in the cardinal directions;
it is beneficial to have a neck joined with a pair of girdles and measuring two padas in height.
With three bays (pada), it should be auspicious, consisting of corner elephants and creepers;
it may be devoid of walkways and doors, or in some cases, provided with walkways and doors.
In some cases, it is considered that creepers, moon-shaped pavilions, and creeper-pillars may be employed;
or one should conceive of a creeper-pavilion-liṅga as a support for the intellect.
Relying upon the intellect of the Teacher, it has assumed manifold forms; that which is supported by the intellect should be known as the bestower of the fruits of all desires.
And for all mantras, it is conceived as the sacred seat (pīṭha);
thus has the description of the mandala been told to you in brief.
Thus ends the chapter on mantras in the *Kālottara-mahātantra*.
I shall clearly explain the procedure for the ten weapons;
however, when not divided, the lotus is considered to be within the four-cornered [mandala] along with its transformations.
On its back, sides, and front, one should fashion two pairs of crescent moons by means of four circular rotations, from the middle of one half-pada to the end of the next pada.
One should draw that [central part] raised by three parts and twice as high in one part;
thus, having fashioned the two horns with very sharp tips by means of a circular rotation of fire.
The base of the middle prong should be half a *pada* in width;
its middle portion should be made one *pada*, and its tip should be free from sharpness.
In this manner, the middle prong should be fashioned like the petal of a blue lotus;
by this procedure, O child, the four-faced [liṅga] must be made.
The remaining lines should be erased; [the moon] has the luster of snow with its central digit, its horns are black in color, and its center has a reddish glow.
The four-faced great vajra, the weapon of Indra, has been revealed;
now listen as I describe the fire-weapon known as the Śakti.
One should cause the city to be made square and divided equally into four parts on all sides;
by the abandonment of three parts, the field of Śakti is produced.
In the same manner, one should divide its upper portion on all sides in front;
then, from the center of that, one should draw a circle, excluding the two front portions.
By means of which a very clear crescent-moon shape is produced,
one should fashion another sharp-edged revolving [blade] within that space.
In the space between those, a square with four sides should be made, resembling the moon;
a triangular peak should be fashioned, O Śikhidhvaja, with its apex pointing toward the center.
69b) At the base of each of those four steps is a pedestal adorned with lotuses;
it extends by one part, and below that is the arrangement of the shaft (daṇḍa).
The three prongs of the trident are black; their center has the brilliance of fire;
the shaft is the color of a yellow lotus, resembling the hue of coral.
The fire-weapon known as Śakti has been described by me only in brief.
Now listen as I describe the *samāstra* and the *kaṅkāla*:
divide a square into four parts and rotate three of those parts.
One should rotate the *yama* syllables there and write the words according to their respective portions:
the forehead, nose, chin, ears, eyes, mouth, and eyebrows.
One should depict him with a beard, hair like flames, prominent fangs, and a terrifying face;
below that foot, a staff of golden luster should be made.
And I have described the Yamāstra, which is slightly black and formidable.

I shall now describe the characteristics of the sword (khaḍga): on a four-sided figure divided according to the Vedas (four parts), one should make thirteen divisions by reducing three, for the sake of achieving the sword-mantra.
That field is divided into four parts; one should divide that root [area] accordingly.
One should draw the upper portion from half [the width], and from the square, one should draw the pedestal (talikā).
The *pragraha* should be made with one and a half parts, shaped like a barley grain;
one should draw it downward with a quarter-part, and the *talikā* there is considered to be elongated.
One should divide its root portion into four parts;
then, having made two parts equal to a barley-corn (yavaka), one should place it with that part.

Above that, one should fashion a half-moon; from its center, one should rotate [the design]. Thus, one should arrange the first part beginning with *ka* and so forth; its width should be determined as four parts of a foot.
The width at the top is the same as that [measurement], and the pinnacle (cūlikā) is of that same extent.
In the center of the *pragraha*, however, one should draw a golden lotus with a radiant luster;
above that, one should write the syllable *laṃ* upon the tip of the stalk.
One should always fill the belly with a half-moon of golden luster;
above that is the sword-weapon, shining like dark illusion, worshipped by the Rākṣasas.
O son of Kṛttikā, the Varuṇa weapon known as the Pāśa is now described:
it should be one cubit in length, four-cornered in shape, and in width it should be like the sun.
One should fashion the components of the noose with half that height;
one should divide the center of the solar portion into three for the navel.
The lamp called *ucchraya* is the life-force (*jīva*); half of the base is the origin of the limbs.
From that, the circumference is by one part, and from that, another by one part.
Above that, three circles are considered to be formed by successive divisions;
just as there are three upper joints, so too there are three root joints.
Having rotated the three circles, one should then examine them with one's own intellect;
the lower part should be made straight, and the exit [of the line] should arise from the curvature.
From one's own field, the face—endowed with eyes, brows, and nose—is located above the feet;
he who would not cause it to revolve otherwise, [should do so] as on the right, so on the other.
The face of that [figure] should be made with that [same] cord, like a wick or a pippala leaf;
the two eyes are on the first cord, while the tail below should be double [the length].
And that effect, like an earring, arises sequentially;
[it is] the eye on the chest, the face, the black-limbed body marked by a mandala.
I have described the great hero Vāruṇa weapon, known as the noose.
Now, understand briefly the Vāyavya weapon and the Akuśa weapon;
the Vedāsra weapon, the Vasu weapon... [omitted] ...the eighth is Saṃjña; likewise, Sūrya and Candra are in the north, each lacking one quarter.
One should describe its lower impure essence as being half the size of the light.
At its base is a water-pot (*kalaśa*), and its handle (*daṇḍa*) should be like a thumb;
it is blackish in color, shaped like a goad (*aṅkuśa*), and marked with [the syllable] *maṇḍi*. Alternatively, the handle may be reddish, shining like gold, or possessing the luster of refined gold.
The Vāyavya weapon is fully described by the name Aṅkuśa.

In a square divided into four parts, by omitting three parts, one should divide [the remaining part] as follows: having enjoyed [the portion] in the root-section again with the [remaining] parts, one should turn toward liberation.
One should divide the half-moon by a fourth part; by that, one should fashion its circular corners. From the width, the height should be taken in sequence as one square and three squares.
The shape of her belly should be fashioned, and below that one should draw a circle;
with half a part, one should round off the center like a half-moon.
The mace (gadā), however, is half the size of the two-footed [lotus]; one should fashion the Tāṭaṅka there.
From the middle of that, one should fashion upwards the auspicious form of Khaṇḍacaṇḍā.
The mace (gadā) should be made with nine joints and resplendent with various jewels;
the weapon of Kubera is named the mace, and it is considered superior even to that of Śaṅkara.
71a) When one has taken that faithful [measure], one should divide it extensively by means of numbers;
having likewise done so for the top and bottom, one should divide each portion on both sides.
One part below that is declared to be the number of Puras;
the extent of the hells is half the number of Manus.
But the bimba-portion, divided [from the base], rises upward from the root;
two parts each, extending from the corners of Vāyu and Nairṛta, constitute the five-fold enclosure.
The destruction of the mantras should be performed by these two through circling above the three steps;
then, from the center, one should divide [the space] into eight parts like a half-moon.
Then, a second square of one unit should be made facing inward;
however, having traversed nine units, it should continue until the end of three units.
This fourth life-force, located at the tip of the crescent moon, revolves externally as the Śāla-peak; beyond that, there is another within.
Just as one would fashion one side-horn, so too should one fashion the other;
having turned back the two side-horns, one should fashion the foot-turnings.
The middle peak should be half the length of the base and equal in width;
the pedestal, situated in the center of the circle, should be two pādas in height and equal in length to the pāda.
A four-petaled lotus should be drawn there along with its pathways;
the upper line of the pathways, however, should terminate within two circles.
The staff should be three or two times the measurement of the handle's width;
it should be twice as wide at its base, which is where the root-ornamentation begins.
Having given a portion by that side, one should then place a thread in front;
thus, one should fashion a triangle with equal sides as the base of the trident.
Around the base and the tip, two lines should be drawn forming a crescent;
at the tip of the trident-wheel, however, it should be marked with two crescents.
The three prongs are always black; the Varuṇa situated between them is beneficial;
the crescent moon is white and auspicious, and the altar has the luster of gold.
The lotus has the luster of jasmine and the moon; the staff has the brilliance of black collyrium;
and the trident is like fire—this is what I have described as the Rudra-weapon.
The Brahmāstra is to be known as the lotus; its characteristics have been proclaimed.
Now I shall describe Viṣṇu’s weapon, known by the name Sudarśana;
first, one should fashion the lotus-field in ten directions in a circular form.
In the first [mandala], the pericarp (karṇikā), the filaments (keśara), and the petals (dala) should be made;
the joints between the petals and the tips of the petals should be provided with lines for the sky (vyomarekhā).
The lotus, resembling a pure jasmine flower or the moon, consists of five parts;
the mouth and the navel occupy one part each, while the outer rim occupies one part.
The functions of the spokes and the hub of the wheel are threefold in sequence;
one should draw each wheel of twelve spokes divided into nine parts.
One should draw a twelve-spoked wheel, devoid of [the central] square on all sides;
one should then draw the field situated within the spokes, beginning from the three-peaked [corner].
But for one who is not colored [by passion], that which is the throat is beneficial all around as a double-footed [measure];
outside of that is the half-moon, situated facing inward due to its circular motion.
In width, it should be one square (pada), and in height, it is considered to be one square;
then, an "half-moon" (ardhacandra) should be made in the middle of the lower and upper [sections].
The mouth-guard (vaktrāraka) should likewise be shaped like a battle-axe (paraśvadha);
it should be made with alternating half-sections, ending in a clockwise curve.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing the work of people, one should fashion a wheel with its spokes diminished;
it should be sharpened at the edge, with a hub increased in gold in the center,
and the spokes of the wheel should always be filled with a counter-clockwise rotation.
The discus of Viṣṇu is said to be that which is completely cut by the edges of its rim.
Thus ends the chapter on the drawing of the *mātrā* in the *Kālottara-mahātantra*.
The Lord said:
The Astra-yāga, which bestows success in all rites, must first be performed;
it grants Śiva-hood and must be performed at the beginning of all the bonds (pāśas).
The original field is four cubits on all sides, established according to the Vedas;
from the second life-line, by means of two parts, it is rotated around the Brahma-thread.
O Indra among fields, the moon indeed arises through rotation;
it is produced there through the conjunction of its upper and lower parts.

The lotus should be considered four times the width of the door-jamb, while the neck of the door should be half of that; it should be constructed according to this measurement, so pay close attention to these specific details.
One should indicate the throat and the cheek with half a part;
the lotus should be white in color, and the crescent moon should have the luster of collyrium.
One should worship the yellow door and the pericarp, as well as that which is called the *ṭaṅka*, within this;
having thus produced the seat (*pīṭha*), one should place the destroyer (*nāśana*) within the *praṇava*.
In the center, one should worship the weapon of Śiva; then, in order, the Vajra and the others starting from the east;
the face on the petal in the south-west, and the lotus on the petal in the north-east.
Worship should be performed with effort using flowers, incense, water for offerings (argha), lamps, and so forth, with the name preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and ending in the dative case.
Having indeed diligently bound the *mudrā* known as Kālakarṇī,
one should perform the meditation on the Vajra and the other [deities] in sequence, beginning from the east.
Now, listen to this Vyāna [section] which is but a fragment of the Pāśupata [tradition]:
[it concerns] the one with five faces, most terrible, ten-armed, and three-eyed.
Deformed, radiant, and fierce, with tawny eyebrows, a beard, and hair standing erect;
[holding] a sword, a shield, an iron arrow, a bow, a thread, and a water-pot.
Holding a spear, a trident, and an axe, as well as the staff of Brahmā in his hands;
standing on one foot, two feet, or with both feet even, he blazes brilliantly.
The best of practitioners should meditate upon Him who is endowed with all limbs and arms, who wears a sacred thread of serpents, and who destroys the suffering of those who bow before Him.
When a lapse in ritual action has occurred, or when fear or strife arises,
the removal of all obstacles is accomplished by means of the consecration following the weapon-sacrifice (astrayāga).
Thus ends the chapter on the weapon-sacrifice in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
In the circle of the planets, worship should be performed within a four-cubit space;
on ground previously consecrated by offerings to the spirits, there should be a lotus marked with a single square.
Having left two finger-breadths in the middle of the lotuses,
one should fashion nine lotuses as the doors, just like the original lotus.
Having divided the door-section into two parts and provided it with the arrangement of the neck and so forth,
the most excellent gurus should fill the lotuses with the forms of the planets.
A reddish lotus is beneficial for the son of the Earth (Mars);
a white one for the Moon (Mercury) and the son of Bhṛgu (Venus); and a yellow one for the son of the Moon (Saturn).
Likewise, for the preceptor of the gods (Bṛhaspati), a black luster is auspicious;
for Saucya, a red one; for Devaśa, a dark-blue one; and for Kenavehita, a smoke-colored luster.

One should offer arghya, perfumes, and so forth, as well as flowers and food offerings, according to their respective colors: the Sun in the center, the Moon in the east, the Son of the Earth (Mars) in the southeast, and Fire in the south.
Budha is in the southern direction, while Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu, is in the south-west;
Kavi is in the region of the western quarter, and Śani should be in the domain of Vāyu.
With only its head remaining in the north, the comet is in the domain of Īśāna;
it causes distress in the center, so one should worship the Sun in that location.
One should perform a hundred oblations for each of the offerings with cow's milk;
through the worship of the planets, all eleven [deities] become present.
At the commencement of a journey, O Viṣṇudeva, one should cause a horse covered with golden garments and grain to be given to the preceptor; this bestows auspiciousness even amidst all portents.
When there is an affliction caused by the planets, a pacification of the planets must be performed;
thus has this planetary yoga been described to you in brief.
Thus ends the chapter on the sacrifice to the planets in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
Next, I shall describe the pacification of weapons (astra-śānti) according to the prescribed sequence,
specifically for portents of celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial origin.
It should be employed for the pacification of planetary afflictions and the like, for the warding off of fever and epilepsy,
for fear of foreign armies, and for the provocation of great diseases.
One should diligently perform pacification rites with offerings made to Vināyaka;
having first recited the Aghora-weapon mantra one hundred thousand times, O observer of noble vows.
One should employ the Vasu, Āditya, Graha, and other mantras as the ground for the wrathful deities;
by reciting them one hundred thousand times, it brings about the destruction of divine portents.
By performing a homa of sesame seeds and clarified butter that many times,
one shall destroy Śikhidhvaja and those born from the sky.
O Śikhidhvaja, by means of a hundred thousand oblations of clarified butter alone,
one shall destroy portents through that *lakṣapāda* fire-sacrifice.
By an oblation of ghee and gugulu, one may destroy false speech;
by an oblation of earth, amṛtā, and ghee, one shall cut away all diseases.
O son of Pārvatī, my child, by reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times,
or by performing oblations with ghee one thousand times, one shall destroy bad dreams.
One removes the afflictions caused by malefic planets by offering ten thousand oblations of barley mixed with ghee;
likewise, one removes the distress caused by Vināyaka and the affliction of Sāman by ten thousand oblations of ghee.
For the rising of a vetāla, one should perform a propitiatory rite with twenty thousand oblations of cow's ghee;
likewise in the case of the breaking of a great tree, and especially in the case of the breaking of a banner.

In the event of conflict with one's own kinsmen, or when a house is inhabited by predatory beasts and crows, or upon entering a forest, or when one dwells in a house frequented by vultures, hawks, and the like;
O Śikhidhvaja, by performing thirty thousand oblations of dūrvā grass, amṛta, and clarified butter,
one should predict peace even during a violent earthquake or the falling of meteors.
By performing ten thousand oblations with ghee, there shall be pacification;
however, if blood flows from the leaves of trees and other objects associated with empty deities, [it portends misfortune].
If they cry out, or dance, or laugh here at the beautiful-toothed one,
then within ten thousand finger-breadths there will be no peace, nor shall it be otherwise.
During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one should perform a pacifying rite (śāntika) by means of two thousand oblations of ghee, specifically through the particularity of the reflected image.
Or, upon seeing birds bearing fruit and flowers out of season,
peace is brought about there by performing ten thousand oblations of *amṛtā*.
When the fear of a thunderbolt has arisen, by performing twenty thousand oblations with ghee from a broken [vessel], pacification is brought about therein.
If a kingdom is destroyed by a hundred thousand [demons], a pacifying rite with sesame and clarified butter shall not suffice;
for there, pestilence arises among the people, the enemy kingdom, and the four-footed animals.
By performing thirty thousand oblations of ghee, pacification (śāntika) occurs therein;
[otherwise], the plague of foot-disease among bipeds or famine may arise.
With fifty thousand oblations of ghee, one should perform the Mahāśānti rite;
likewise, one should arrange the fire-offering for the purpose of pacifying the plague of elephants.
But upon the growth of an elephant's tusk, or when a female elephant is not seen,
or upon seeing a headless torso at night, one should perform a fire sacrifice as prescribed previously.
In this scripture known as Kāla, peace shall quickly come from ten thousand [offerings];
however, for untimely fractures, miscarriages, or travel, pacification is achieved through oblations of ghee.
Wherever there may be an abundance of daughters among one's offspring, there a rite for pacification (śāntika) should be performed;
by performing ten thousand oblations of guggulu resin, [the result] is achieved.
For those who suffer loss of wealth, or whose wife does not conceive,
or who gives birth to a eunuch, or where a child born dies;
Peaceful rites (*śāntika*) will not be accomplished otherwise than by an oblation (*homa*) of milk, nectar, and clarified butter;
wherever deformed beings are born, or where anything obstructed occurs at any time.
Various species, including those with the forms of beasts, were driven away;
there, one should perform the *śāntika* rite with ten thousand oblations of ghee, together with the *Amṛtasahā*.
Where there is fear of a great disease or where there may be a great pestilence,
one should perform a propitiatory rite (*śāntika*) there with ghee, parched grain, and other such items for the sake of all purposes.
O Six-faced One, if there is a lapse in ritual duties among the castes or due to conflict with one's own kin,
peace shall be attained therein through a sacrifice of clarified butter performed according to the ancient rites.
At the time of the journey, the oblation should consist of Kapila cow's ghee;
for the sake of accomplishing the highest siddhi, one should perform the homa with sesame seeds and clarified butter.
In the middling [rite], one should perform half of that; in the inferior ones, a quarter of that.
One should arrange the fire-oblation according to the birth [of the child] during the pacification of weapons.
For those who have taken refuge in the Aghora-weapon, obstacles flee to the ten directions;
indeed, the Aghora-weapon is to be known as the great weapon of Pāśupata.
Therefore, with every effort, one should practice the Aghora weapon-mantra;
it should first be performed with the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa), according to the divisions beginning with the heart.
One should diligently assign the heart, the head, the crest-lock, the armor, and the weapon, in sequence, beginning with one and increasing by one.
One should perform the application of the *jāti* and then place the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), consisting of syllables numbering twenty-four (the Vedas and eyes),
together with the essence of the faces of Śiva.
75a) Having first performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), the best of practitioners should recite [the mantra];
he should meditate upon [the deity] who has five heads, ten arms, and great splendor.
The god was clothed in a garment of tiger-skin, with tawny beard and hair,
adorned with a serpent for a nose-ornament, and wearing a snake as a sacred thread.
The god had teeth like snow, jasmine, and the moon; he was extremely terrifying with deep-set eyes, and he bore a sword and shield, as well as a bow and arrows.
I bow to the God who holds the axe, mace, thunderbolt, and trident ready for grasping,
who wields the staff and goad, and who destroys the suffering of those who prostrate before him.
Such a one should always be meditated upon and diligently worshipped;
one should recite [the mantra] with supreme devotion and perform fire-offerings day and night.
As long as there may be abundant peace, or as long as there is the accomplishment of spiritual attainment,
so long must recitation, worship, and fire-offerings be performed by one desiring success.
Wherever one who recites the Astra-mantra may be, there peace shall always prevail;
the pacification of all afflictions arises in every such place.
One who constantly recites the mantra of the weapon is always worthy of worship, just like the Blessed Lord Śiva himself.
Thus ends the chapter on missiles in the *Kālottara-mahātantra*.
Now, I shall explain in brief how one should perform the rite of pacification (śāntika) by means of the Pāśupata weapon; listen attentively to this concise summary.
O Six-faced One, Śikhidhvaja, one may destroy celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial portents by means of a hundred thousand recitations as well as by burnt offerings (homa).

In the previously mentioned teaching on portents, fire-oblations and recitations are prescribed; however, at that time, the prevention of the portent must be performed with five times the usual number of repetitions.
O Lord Mahāpāśupata, one should always perform [the rite] starting from the foot;
that which consists of one hundred and eight [verses] is established in the lake Hradaharuṇi.
Furthermore, by means of a single oblation, one may cut through all the stages;
for that purpose, I shall fully explain the garland of mantras as it exists.

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Lord of Animals (Pāśupati), who possesses incomparable strength, heroism, and prowess; who has fifteen eyes; who assumes various forms; who brandishes various weapons;
whose every limb and face is like a mass of crushed collyrium; who is fond of the vetāla of the Śāsana; and who destroys all obstacles.
To the one worthy of worship, the bestower of all accomplishments, who causes the devotees to tremble;
to the one with countless faces, arms, and feet; to the one for whom success is attained through mere recitation, the one who mocks the Vetālas;
to the one who agitates the Sākinīs and is the cause of the subduing of diseases; to the devourer of sins, [the embodiment of] the Moon, Sun, and Fire.

To the one with eyes, to the armor of Viṣṇu, to the one with Indra’s thunderbolt in hand, to the staff of Yama, to the noose of Varuṇa, to the trident of Rudra, to the one with a flaming tongue, to the dispeller of all diseases, to the cause of the subduing of the planets, and to the destroyer of wicked serpents.

Oṃ, to the dark-brown one, phaṭ! To the cruel one, phaṭ! To the one with the vajra in hand, phaṭ! To Indra, phaṭ! To the spear, phaṭ! To Agni, phaṭ! To the staff, phaṭ! To Yama, phaṭ! To the sword, phaṭ!
To Nairṛta, phaṭ! To Varuṇa, phaṭ! To the noose, phaṭ! To the banner, phaṭ!
To the goad, phaṭ! To the northwest, phaṭ! To the mace, phaṭ! To Kubera, phaṭ! To the trident, phaṭ!
To Īśāna, phaṭ! To the mallet, phaṭ! To the discus, phaṭ! To the lotus, phaṭ! To the serpent-weapon, phaṭ!

Phaṭ! To the weapon of the Eaters, phaṭ! To the weapon of the Headless Ones, phaṭ! To the Skeleton, phaṭ! To the weapon of Īśāna, phaṭ! To the weapon of the Peacock-feathered One, phaṭ! To the weapon of the Razor, phaṭ! To the weapon of Mātṛ, phaṭ! To the weapon of Brahmā, phaṭ! To the weapon of Śakti, phaṭ! To the weapon of Gaṇa, phaṭ! To the weapon of the Siddhas, phaṭ!

Phaṭ! To the Pilipicchā weapon, phaṭ! To the Gandharva weapon, phaṭ! To the eastern weapon, phaṭ! To the southern weapon, phaṭ! To the western weapon, phaṭ! To the northern weapon, phaṭ! To the Mātr weapon, phaṭ! To the Sākiṇī weapon, phaṭ! To the Yoginī weapon, phaṭ! To the Ḍākinī weapon, phaṭ!

Phaṭ! To the weapon of Ḍāmarikā, phaṭ! To the weapon of Loma, phaṭ! To the weapon of Śiva, phaṭ! To the weapon of Īśāna, phaṭ! To the weapon of Tatpuruṣa, phaṭ! To the weapon of Aghora, phaṭ! To the weapon of Vāma, phaṭ! To the weapon of Sadyojāta, phaṭ!
To the weapon of the Heart, phaṭ! To the weapon of the Head, phaṭ! To the weapon of the Crest, phaṭ! To the weapon of the Armor, phaṭ!
Phaṭ! Phaṭ to the weapon of the eye! Phaṭ to the great weapon! Phaṭ to the Garuḍa weapon! Phaṭ to the Puruṣa weapon!
Phaṭ to the Rākṣasa weapon! Phaṭ to the Dānava weapon! Phaṭ to the Graha weapon! Haḥ! Phaṭ to the weapon!

76b) *kṣaḥ*! To the weapon of Narasiṃha, *phaṭ*! To the weapon of Vārāha, *phaṭ*! To all weapons, *phaṭ*! *vaḥ*! *phaṭ*! *la*! *phaṭ*! *yaḥ*! *phaṭ*! *maḥ*! *phaṭ*! *triṃ*! *phaṭ*! *proṃ*! *phaṭ*! *prīṃ*! *phaṭ*! *bhūḥ*! *phaṭ*! *bhuvaḥ*! *phaṭ*! *svaḥ*! *phaṭ*! *mahaḥ*! *phaṭ*! *janaḥ*! *phaṭ*! *tapaḥ*! *phaṭ*!

Satyaloka phaṭ! All manifestations phaṭ! All principles and all vital breaths phaṭ! All channels phaṭ! All causes phaṭ! All deities phaṭ! Hrīṃ phaṭ! Hūṃ phaṭ! Krauṃ phaṭ! Laṃ phaṭ! To the weapon of Bhairava phaṭ! To the weapon of Māyā phaṭ! To the weapon of Kāma phaṭ!

Kāyāstrāya phaṭ! Kṣetrāpālāstrāya phaṭ! Krūrāstrāya phaṭ! Bhāskarāstrāyai phaṭ! Candrāstrāya phaṭ! Vighneśvarāstrāya phaṭ! Khāṃ khauṃ phaṭ! Kṣāṃ kṣīṃ phaṭ! Bhrāmaya bhrāmaya phaṭ! Saṃtāpaya 2 phaṭ! Chedya 2 phaṭ!

Uproot [them] twice, phaṭ! Terrify [them] twice, phaṭ! Revive [them] twice, phaṭ! Disperse [them] twice, phaṭ! Destroy all misfortune twice, phaṭ! By this constant recitation, all obstacles shall be destroyed. Through this great weapon, great peace arises; of this there is no doubt. To Kūṣmāṇḍa, the Eye!
And for those Vināyakas who dwell in the intermediate meditations (dhyāna) and in the Udumbara tree, peace is attained through one hundred recitations;

it cannot be otherwise. Defects such as fever and consumption, as well as the evil influence of others' digging and water, are pacified by seven recitations, just as [darkness is dispelled] by the sun and other luminaries.
One who desires accomplishment (siddhi) among the highest and lowest attainments should recite [the mantra];
by reciting half a hundred thousand times, a person becomes equal to Rudra.
O son, one who is capable of both punishment and favor may succeed, but not otherwise;
for in all recitations involving weapons, the desire for the fire-oblation is like that of the mantra-recitation.
At that time, the practitioner becomes incapable of accomplishing spiritual attainments and of subduing celestial,
atmospheric, and terrestrial portents.
One shall destroy [the obstacle] without any doubt, just as at the rising of the sun,
by means of a thousand oblations of guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter.
By the power of this king of weapons, one shall destroy all evils;
he who recites this daily is never again afflicted by obstacles.
Thus ends the chapter on the Pāśupata weapon in the Kālottara Mahātantra.

Salutation, Svāhā, Vaṣaṭ, Vauṣaṭ, Hūṃ, Phaṭ to the one whose body consists of fifty letters, whose fangs are the moon and the sun, who has ten arms, to the weapon, to the one whose necklace is the serpent of Yama, to the heart of Rudra, to the head of Brahmā,

Strike down, strike down, *phaṭ*! One hundred and eight times! Those who create obstacles for one reciting this—whether they be *nāgas*, *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, *piśācas*, *pretas*, *bhūtas*, *ḍākinīs*, *sākinīs*, *siddhas*, or *vidyādharas* who have transgressed their commitments—may the power of their mantras, the power of their meditations, the power of their substances, and the power of their *svāhā*-invocations be reduced to ashes! *Svāhā!*

To the weapon of the peacock-feathered arrow (hetraupicchikāstra), which possesses unimpeded intellect, vigor, and prowess, *phaṭ*; to the non-terrible weapon (*aghorāstra*), *phaṭ*. 50.
*Oṃ ślīṃ paśūṃ jñaṃ phaṭ hāḥ* (twenty times), *haṃ* (twenty times); to the great devouring weapon (*mahāsvādakāstra*), *phaṭ*.
*Oṃ kṣāṃ kṣauṃ dakṣaḥ svauṃ* to the Garuḍa weapon (*garuḍāstra*), *phaṭ*. 20. *Oṃ varga* (twice).
To the Great Wheel King of Excellent Vision (*Sudarśana-mahācakrarāja*), sever the enemies!

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, perfected by recitation, to the Great Pāśupata Weapon; homage, homage!

To the Brahmā-weapon, the Chagala-weapon, the Rūpa-weapon—to you who strike down all the wicked, cause them to fall! Cause the embryos of gods, asuras, and mortals established in their vows to fall! Reduce them to ashes! Reduce them to ashes!
Phaṭ phaṭ!
O Six-faced One, he who recites this daily at the three junctions of the day in the presence of Śiva attains all desires without obstacle;
it is the destroyer of celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial portents.
In all calamities, this mantra is the supreme destroyer;
having abandoned all other undertakings, one should commence the recitation of the weapon-mantra (astra-jāpa).
Thus ends the chapter on the discourse of the Great Weapon in the *Kālottara-mahātantra*.
O Destroyer of Krauñca, I shall explain in brief the propitiation of Śiva for all divine portents, especially those born from the sky.
In all falls from the earth, even when there is a terrible omen,
[one should reside] in a beautiful city of four cubits, adorned with four lotuses.
O Lord of Gods, one should worship there in the pitcher as well as in the mandala;
one should install Īśāna in the pericarp together with the Brahma-aṅgas.
One should worship Puruṣa on the eastern petals, Aghora on the southern petal,
and Vāma on the northern petal, together with Śiva accompanied by the Brahma-aṅgas.
Sadyojāta is in the western direction; the [mantras] beginning with the Heart are located in the corners up to the Weapon;
the Eye is in every direction, providing protection in all quarters.
One should worship the mantras of the *candranetra* and *indukalikā* with thread,
and one should perform half a thousand oblations (*āhuti*) for each of them.
With ghee and guggulu, for the sake of pacifying calamities arising from the heavens;
and with half that amount, for the destruction of misfortunes arising from the intermediate space.
By means of an oblation of *amṛta* and ghee, or with ghee alone, in the *bhūta-patra*;
or half of that amount for those born of sacrificial fire, using sesame seeds mixed with ghee.
O child, peace arises even from the affliction of planetary influences;
for those tormented by Vināyaka, the conception of peace is like that of the sky.
Upon the breaking of a great tree, or by the breaking of banners, or by the entry of wild animals into the village, and when vipers and other such creatures appear on the left side.
One should perform ten thousand oblations with sesame and clarified butter;
during the "falling of the elephant" (hastipāta), one should carry out a great pacification (mahāśānti) just as in the case of a celestial portent.
In the case of eruptions caused by spiders or donkeys, one should recite ten thousand times while offering oblations soaked in the three sweets (trimadhu).
This should be done whenever crows, owls, bats, or similar creatures enter the house at any time.
Through twenty thousand oblations of ghee and rice, there is pacification;
likewise during the falling of meteors, a thunderclap, or an eclipse of the moon or sun.
O Mahāsena, [these omens are inauspicious] upon seeing a terrestrial limb, as well as in the sight of a city of Gandharvas,
and especially when there is the breaking of a banner.
When great trees are shattered, when tumultuous sounds are heard,
when there is a rain of blood, a rain of fat, and a most terrible fall of thunderbolts;
Where bears are born, as well as pairs of monstrosities and birds;
where daughters are born by the hundreds, and not even a single male or eunuch.
Where neither bipeds nor quadrupeds are born,
where pestilence arises, or where there is fear among the *rākṣasas*.
Then, one who desires success should perform the rite of Śiva-śānti there;
for the divine [beings], peace is achieved through a hundred thousand oblations, and likewise by reciting the mantra.
For those born of space (ākāśaja), it is by half that [number] through recitation (japa) and oblation (havana);
for those born of fire (haumaja), it is half of that again; and in the case of fierce rites, it may even be equal to that.

For celestial beings, the propitiatory rite is performed with sesame seeds and ghee; for those born of the sky, with guggulu resin and ghee; and for those born of the earth, with dūrvā grass soaked in honey.
But the fifth is the slender one, O glorious one; therein, [it is used] for pacification (*śāntika*).
Hoṃ, to Īśāna... Oṃ Hoṃ, to the face of Īśāna, to Tatpuruṣa...
to the face of Īśāna, to Vāmadeva... Oṃ Phoṃ, to Sadyojāta of the face of Īśāna... Thus, by this very [mantra], [one worships] the Brahmās of Īśāna.
Likewise for the limbs:

one should fashion the Brahma-mantras as the limbs of all [deities] according to their respective colors. The seat is formed with the *praṇava* alone, and the form (*mūrti*) is likewise twofold by that very same [mantra].
The offerings, preceded by water for the feet and water for sipping, should be presented by the bearer;
having understood this, O Mahāsena, one should commence the rite of Śiva-śānti.
Thus ends the chapter on the propitiation of Śiva in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim this most wonderful secret, which has not been told to anyone; that very thing is being declared now.
O Destroyer of Krauñca, I shall now briefly explain the procedure for the King of Mantras—
the great mantra that brings about the destruction of all sins.
Seven crores of mantras reside and abide within it— mantras that bring an end to existence, remove suffering, bestow great fortune, and grant auspiciousness.
It is the supreme destroyer of obstacles— whether superior, inferior, or middling—
the pacifier of various calamities, and the eradicator of all diseases.
The King of Mantras himself is capable of removing all sins and destroying all evil deeds among all forms of expiation.
The god who swallows the planets, who cuts through the embryos of the nāgas,
and who strikes fear into the piśācas, brahmavetālas, and ḍākinīs.
The god who crushes wicked enemies, destroys malevolent spells and evil cries,
grants all desires, and annihilates all calamities.
It bestows enjoyment upon those desiring enjoyment and liberation upon those desiring liberation;
what more need be said here? For men, it is the wish-fulfilling gem of mantras.
The ritual procedure for that God, who bestows good fortune upon the unfortunate, wards off misfortune, and removes all calamities, is now being declared.
The thirty-two syllable mantra, which was previously told to you, should be understood as being enriched with the Tāraka [syllable]; it is the sole hero that bestows auspiciousness.
Having once performed the placement upon the hands for the god Aghora— who is devoid of the Brahma-aṅga and is the destroyer of the terrible— the karanyāsa is then accomplished.
Having placed [the mantra] once from the feet up to the crown of the head, one becomes pure;
one should then place it once upon the body from the head down to the feet.
After the ritual placement of the body (dehanyāsa) has been performed, one should then commence the internal sacrifice (antaryāga);
likewise, the external worship, recitation, and so forth, as well as the fire offering (havana), must be performed.
One should meditate upon the five-headed [deity] garlanded with ten crescent moons;
his meditation is performed according to the disposition of the practitioner, and not otherwise.

For rites of pacification (śāntika) and nourishment (pauṣṭika), white is recommended; for subjugation (vaśya), red is praised. For paralyzing (stambhana), yellow color is used, while smoky grey is beneficial for eradication (uccāṭana).
For killing, [the color] is black; for attracting, reddish-brown (kapila) is beneficial; for subduing, O Lord, it should be likewise.
Having understood the ritual action, one should deliberate accordingly.
Having uttered the Praṇava with the intellect once, one should perform the infusion with the flower,
extending from the limit of incapacity to the limit of capacity through pervasive penetration.
Beyond that, one should not conceive of a supreme form consisting of thirty-two syllables;
rather, from Īśvara up to Śakti, it possesses the body of the principles (kalā) and time (kāla).
Then, one should cause it to blaze intensely with the king of mantras a hundred times;
having invoked [the deity] according to the previous procedure and likewise worshipped with devotion.
First, the preliminary rite of the mantra must be performed;
then, one hundred thousand recitations of the Aghora syllables should be chanted by the practitioner.

O Six-faced One, having resorted to the southern form, one should perform the oblation; it is said that ten [oblations] should be made with guggulu and indeed with the clarified butter of Kapila cows.
Likewise, one who has attained mastery over mantras accomplishes the desired aim of birth;
whether it be superior, inferior, or middling, he shall achieve it, for his word is never false.
One should accomplish the siddhis through a formidable form according to one's own desire;
whatever desires one may long for, those very desires one shall obtain.
By reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times, one will certainly achieve the supreme accomplishments;
likewise, by performing a fire-offering of guggulu resin half that number, the middling accomplishments are easily attained.
Through recitation and fire-offerings, one shall accomplish the attainments of the *lakṣapādātṛ* and other scriptures; there is no doubt in this—this is the truth, the truth, O great ascetic.
In this very same way, one should perform the pacification of the threefold portents;
O Consort of Śaṅkara, there is no other protector for the pacification of all calamities.
81b) No mantra other than Aghora is seen for expiations;
no mantra other than Aghora will bring about success in the face [of obstacles].
There is no mantra other than Aghora that bestows success upon reaching the Kali age;
Aghora is the mantra of attainment, and there is no room for doubt or alternative conception in this matter.
Therefore, with every effort, one should always practice the Aghora [mantra],
whether standing, waking, reciting, walking, eating, or engaged in sexual union.
He whose mind is offered to Aghorā partakes of liberation, and not otherwise;
even one who is not a celibate becomes a celibate, and one who has not bathed becomes a consecrated graduate.
By merely remembering [this] once, the destruction of all sins shall occur;
by reciting it five times, one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
One who recites it seven times attains the fruit of all sacrifices; by reciting it twenty-one times at the conclusion of the worship with a composed mind, one gains the same.
One shall obtain the entire fruit of worship as declared in the scriptures;
having abandoned all other doctrines, one should practice the mantra-doctrine.
Discourses have mantras as their root; therefore, one should be devoted to mantra.
Even in that regard, the contemplator of mantra should perform the recitation of the Aghora mantra.
The investigation of obstacles arising from the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms,
as well as the warding off of all calamities, must be performed with the Aghora weapon.
These two mantra-kings are eternally established within the sun:
the terrible thirty-two-syllable [mantra] and especially the Aghora-weapon.
Therefore, one should practice the two mantras with every effort;
indeed, the preliminary rite for these two mantras must first be performed with diligence.
Then, at the proper time, Śiva himself shall burn away all obstacles;
the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) exists in three forms: whispered, mental, and spoken.
O son of Pārvatī, know that mental recitation is the supreme and the best among those characterized by sattva; know that whispered recitation is middling and characterized by rajas.
The discourse on the Adhamantra is proclaimed by him as being of the nature of darkness (tāmasa),
for it serves as the means for accomplishing the lowest, middling, and highest siddhis.
This should be performed with great effort, preceded by the Aghora weapon-mantra;
one should previously contemplate this most excellent mantra with diligent exertion.
Having first completed the preliminary service, one should then accomplish the siddhis;
his rites will succeed, O destroyer of Krauñca, and not otherwise.
Within the reality of knowledge (vidyā-tattva), that which is the highest portion is desired as accomplishment (siddhi);
the middle portion is known as movement, while the lowest consists of collyrium and sandals.
By the power of this king of mantras, one shall accomplish even the lowest of the low siddhis— subjugation, attraction, and delusion— of this there is no doubt.
He who attempts to accomplish the siddhis without knowing the King of Mantras is like one who,
driven by hunger, tries to grasp the sky with his fist or thresh chaff for grain.
Therefore, with every effort, one should always practice the Aghora [mantra];
by means of it, even those gods, gandharvas, and dānavas who have attained perfection in mantra [are subdued].
All those mantra-adepts remained under the control of that formidable Siddha;
yet, after some time, they eventually fell into poverty.
For those who have attained perfection through the Aghora mantra, whose splendor is immeasurable and inexhaustible,
their heroic power is never thwarted and all their left-handed (vāma) powers are unfailing.
The foremost of practitioners indeed become possessed of unfailing power in all respects;
for him who is always devoted to worship, the mantras are accomplished.
Successes are achieved in those [places] where those who are always devoted to worship find success;
successes are constantly achieved in those [places] where there are those who recite mantras.
Mantras indeed grant fruits to those whose minds are intent upon their oblation;
therefore, one should practice this triad: worship, fire-offering, and recitation.
But having known the supreme form of the Great-Souled Aghora,
the yogi attains knowledge and abandons the portion of the knowable.
From that which is peaceful, Brahman consists of pure consciousness; it is free from conceptual construction, formless, devoid of all means of valid cognition, self-evident, and inexpressible.

Through faith, austerity, devotion, recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth, one attains the excellence of association with great beings; this comes from knowledge, not from bathing at sacred fords.
Through instruction, as well as through practice, observances, and vows, that supreme form— which is devoid of falsehood— is attained.
Neither non-duality, nor likewise duality, neither substance, nor likewise quality—
Brahmā and the other gods do not constantly worship that [which is such].
For that purpose, one should inform living beings; they offer libations day and night, yet they sink into great delusion, being born and dying again and again.
Therefore, with every effort, one should worship the partless [reality],
by the mere recollection of which one shall not undergo birth again.
One who is not Aghora should not worship Aghora, nor shall one who is not Aghora attain liberation;
however, he who remembers Aghora at all times, in every way, and in all circumstances, [attains his goal].
The supreme state is attained, characterized by no returning again.
Thus ends the chapter on pacification within the Aghora-kalpa of the Kālottara Mahātantra.
The Lord said:
Then, let a great propitiation (mahāśānti) be performed with effort through the Rudra-śānti;
herein, O Mahāsena, the sacrifice has been described to you in brief.
A protective rite for the destruction of misfortune should be performed, consisting of a mandala presided over by the Purohita,
measuring five cubits, four cubits, or even eight cubits.
O son of Kṛttikā, the worship of Rudra should be performed in reverse order;
one should effect the pacification of Rudra through the Rudras numbering eight and three.
One should place these five— Rudra, Vṛkṣa, Avimukta, Asambhava, and Puruṣa— in the north according to the ritual procedure.
On the northern petal, however, one should gradually dissolve the five [deities] starting from Rūpānta:
namely Viśvākhya, Mahāviśva, Karāla, and likewise Vikṛta.
Or at the end, that which is called the "deformed" (vikṛta); these five reside in the person (puruṣa). || 5 ||
There are four [beings] known as Piṅgala who fall from the wind-sustained leaves:
one is white, another is black, and the fourth is named Madhu.
Ananta, Tathādri, Śuṣka, and the host of Avapara—
these mighty Rudras are stationed in the west within the principle of Time (Kālatattva).
Karāla and Vikarālā are in the southwestern petal within Māyā;
four thousand [deities] are established in the southern petal within Vidyā.

That which is called the head, that known as the mouth, that called the hand, and the fourth, which is endowed with the feet and consists of the linga— these should not be meditated upon by one who knows the reality.
Furthermore, the Rudras ending with Ekajaṭā, Dvijarā, and Trijaṭā reside in Vahniśvara;
then there are the triad of Svāhā, Svadhā, and Vaṣaṭkāra, who are the Hotṛ-Rudras.
These six classes [of mantras] belong to the former; in the *sakala* sound, there are the Rudras, the *bhūtatantra*, the *mahābhūta*, the *paśu*, and therein the Lord of Umā (*Umāpati*).
O Śikhivāhana, all beings, at the appropriate time, should worship these six.
Umāmaheśvara, whose essence is the reality of Śiva, is to be worshipped in the center.
Having worshipped the Rudras according to the prescribed rite with cool, fragrant flowers and ointments rich in sandalwood, and with milk-rice and clarified butter;
Then one should worship Tatveśvara, Sikhāṇḍin, and the others in reverse order; thereafter, one should worship Śiva ending with Ananta in the center. Now hear of the nine principles (tattvas).
From the Praṇava to the Pole Star (Dhruva), the seat of Śiva’s feet, the Great Earth (Mahābhū) is in the center. || 1 ||
The seat ending with Tatpuruṣa is Śāśvata, located in the east as Sadāśiva;
the seat of Īśvara is Aghora, situated in the southeast, extending as far as Jyotīrūpa and blazing like fire.
The seat of the science of light (Jyotirvidyāpīṭha), beginning with Parameśa, is situated in that sky;
the formless seat of Māyā (Māyāpīṭha) extends to the end of the earth, abiding in the night-wanderer (the moon). || 5 ||
The seat of Niyati, consisting of the letters from *svaḥ* to *devān*, is situated in the clouds;
it is established in the wind and the quarters, and by its true nature, it culminates in bliss.
Having meditated upon it, one should likewise correctly establish the seat (pīṭha) and the side (pārśva) in a state of perfect tranquility. || 8 ||
From Jñāna to Muktipada, the Pīṭha situated in Prakṛti is located in the northern direction. || 9 ||
Thus, this great sacrifice of the words is to be fully honored by mere placement (nyāsa);
through the division of each individual word, the auspicious goddesses reside within the vessels of nectar.
They are enumerated as being encompassed by the circle of the *sarvajyaṅkāra*;

they are illuminated by the *praṇava*. Having ascended upon you, the son of the final end (*sarvāvasānatanaya*), they are situated and established in the eastern foot of the pedestal (*pūrvapīṭhapāda*). They are to be worshipped with the word *anaccita* and praised with a prostrate body.
All the Rudras have been struck down in succession as before.

Clarified butter, milk, curd, honey, fruits and the like, grains, and animals that have not been bathed; the group of foodstuffs made from sugar-candy, milk, and the aforementioned category of grains— that is the *caru*, and that is the *puroḍāśa*, as demonstrated by their respective divisions.
The classification of the numerical praise, as well as the characteristics of the substances and the oblations, are explained there;
in the first section it is told, and in the second the hymn of praise is recited.
This third section of the mantra of the Blessed Lady consists of three hundred verses;
however, the first two sections are in verse, while the mantra is not expressed in prose.
Following the section on division, the section on praise is now declared.
I shall proclaim the propitiatory rite for Rudra, which is auspicious and the means for accomplishing all goals;
it has been conceived in union with Rudra for the benefit of human beings.
Upon hearing this sin-destroying [text], all obstacles perish,
as do bad dreams, diseases, and the planetary influences from the ten directions.
Salutations to the one of many forms, to the all-pervading one, and to the one whose form is the universe;
salutations to the one who dwells with Pārvatī, and to the Lord of Nandī.
I pay homage to Rudraśānti, the destroyer of vetālas,
who dwells in the temples of the gods for those afflicted by mountain-spirits.
For those in whom no conception occurs and whose lineage suffers decline; those who, once born, perish or become eunuchs.
Wherever Mārīca arises, and where the planets are constantly present in the house,
the fetus falls prematurely, or it is born with its limbs constricted.
They are afflicted by famine itself, and the kingdom suffers from terrible calamities;
where the guilds are in conflict and there are numerous plunderers as well.
Likewise, when a house is afflicted by a *kandala* (fungus), the father and mother see a monkey in their dreams; [it is said that] the seed grows in the field.
Furthermore, if cattle, servants,
or laborers residing in the house become rebellious, one should perform a rite of pacification there.
Where a well roars, the backbone breaks, and trees, though unburnt by fire, exude much blood; [there is danger].
"O King,
out of season the trees have blossomed and have likewise borne fruit in great numbers."
Meteors fall and terrible earthquakes occur; due to these inauspicious omens, another fire constantly spreads.
I shall relate, according to the truth, the narrative concerning the origin of the Rudra-śānti.
On the summit of the king of mountains, there is a place named Girisañjanaka;
there resides Rudra, the Supreme, who is devoted to that [state] and intent upon the sixfold [path].
It was surrounded by numerous yakṣas, rākṣasas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and bhūtas.
Then all the hosts of gods,
together with Brahmā and the entire assembly, went to Maheśvara.
How was he praised? Having praised the blue-throated one who has the bull as his banner, together with Umā, by means of Soma-libations, hymns, purificatory rites, and boon-granting prayers.
The Lord of Gods understood that the human progeny was suffering.
"Grant her peace, you who liberate from all seizing spirits.
Having heard the words of the gods, Hara, the three-eyed Lord of the Forest, [responded].
Agni and Vāyu, and especially the Blessed World-Protectors.
And all the Vaijapālas and the invincible Rāṣṭrapālas,
as well as the goddesses, hosts of bhūtas, yakṣas, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas.
The Kūṣmāṇḍas, Ādārvas, Aghoras, and Guhyakas who wield bows;
the guardians of the temples of the gods, the hosts of bhūtas, and the night-stalkers (niśācaras).
Kālakarṇī and Mahākālā, as well as other Himaka spirits, and likewise the Ahasmā and other such seizing spirits (*grahas*).
Diseases of the heart and chest, diseases of the abdomen, diseases of the mouth, fevers, and consumption;
diseases of the head, diseases of the limbs, and most terrible primary ailments.
These and other diseases, which are invoked by the gods, have been fully described;
those grahas, together with their respective hosts, were brought into the presence of Hara.
Having prostrated themselves again and again, they addressed the Lord of Gods:
"O Great God, we are unable even to endure this splendor, let alone behold it; what, then, shall we do by your command? O Lord of Fierce Penance, [tell us] what must be done.
Mahādeva, his eyes bloodshot with anger, spoke thus.
"By what cause and through whose fault are human beings now afflicted with suffering?
To them, Maheśvara spoke in the presence of the Lord of the World:
86a) This is our way of life here: Brahmadatta has seized the excellent horse;
those men in this world who are evil-doers are swallowed up by darkness.
And those grahas who are exceedingly desirous of killing, desirous of offerings,
joyful, or even distressed, [affect] men who are ruined, fallen, or lost.
"O Lord, you have described these rites performed with various anxieties while watching for a flaw; O Blessed One, be gracious unto me."
"Command us, O best of gods; what further remains to be done?
Thus addressed, the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, spoke to his attendants.
The boon-granting Lord, whose vehicle is the spirits (Bhūtas), proclaimed this Rudra-śānti;
having heard this Vidyā-mantra, one indeed never returns from the state of non-return.
His head shall split into seven pieces and he shall be struck by the rod of Rudra;
for seven thousand births, that planet-shaman shall be cooked in the Caurava hell.
Furthermore, he who would transgress this most terrible knowledge—
thus addressed, the Blessed One stood before the planets.
Having caused the pledges to be heard,
the Lord proclaimed this vidyā after having praised Mahādeva, Bhavānī, and Brahmā in the past.
Homage and auspiciousness to the immeasurable, the invincible, the supreme refuge!
Oṃkāra, Vaṣaṭkāra, Brahman, Svāhā, and likewise Svadhā.
Sāvitrī, Bhūtasāvitrī, and Rudrasāvitrī;
likewise Rudrāṇī, Brahmasāvitrī, and the divine Sarasvatī.
Umā, Kṛṣṇā, and Śivā— who are eternally established in the heart— are present among gods, asuras, and humans, and among all things both stationary and moving.
Having thus offered praise in his presence, the gods departed for their own worlds;
and while the hymn has been told, the sections of mantras are now being recited.
In worship, one should employ the word "namas"; in the oblation (havana), that which ends in "svāhā" is beneficial;
in nourishing (āpyāyana), one should employ "vaṣaṭ"; and in the eight [rites], one should apply "vauṣaṭ".
One should apply the conjunction of the *jāti* vowels in the place of the two *ṭha* letters;
thus is the symbolic location proclaimed, since it is beneficial according to its name.
Oṃ, obeisance to Rudra. Oṃ, obeisance to Vṛṣabha.
Oṃ, obeisance to Avimukta. Oṃ, obeisance to Asambhava.
This is the Rudrapañcaka.
Oṃ, homage to Viśvarūpa. Oṃ, homage to Mahāviśvarūpa;
homage to Vikṛtarūpa. Oṃ, homage to Avikṛtarūpa.
Oṃ, homage to Ekapiṅgala. Oṃ, homage to Śvetapiṅgala.
Oṃ, homage to Madhupiṅgala. Oṃ, to Niyatī in Vāyupatra;
oṃ, homage to Ananta. Oṃ, homage to Ādra.
Oṃ, homage to Śuṣka. Oṃ, homage to Payogaṇa.

Oṃ, obeisance to Karāla; Oṃ, obeisance to Vikarāla; Oṃ, obeisance to Sahasraśīrṣa (the Thousand-headed One); Oṃ, obeisance to Sahasravaktra (the Thousand-faced One), obeisance to Sahasraliṅga (the Thousand-linga One). These are the four thousand names within the principle of Vidyā.
On the southern petal.
Oṃ, obeisance to Ekajaṭā. Oṃ, obeisance to Dvijaṭā.
Obeisance... [to] Vahnipatra.
The six Rudras are established in the reality-principle (tattva) of Īśvara.
Oṃ, obeisance to the Lord of Beings; Oṃ, obeisance to the Lord of the Great Elements;
Oṃ, obeisance to the Sovereign of Time. [These are] in the six eastern petals within the principle (tattva) of Sadāśiva.

Oṃ, homage to Umā, who assumes a single form. Oṃ, Kuru 2! Ruṇḍini 2! You are Rudra among the gods; O Viśākha, god of gods, slay, slay! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! Grind, grind! Act, act! Muru 2! Remember the peace of Rudra! O Kṛṣṇapiṅgala, [homage] to the sovereign lord of the untimely Piśācas.
Salutation to Viśveśvara; thus [are] Umā and Maheśvara in the pericarp, within the Śiva-tattva.
Oṃ, to Vyomavyāpin, whose form is space, the all-pervading Śiva, the infinite, the lordless, the non-dependent, the eternal— these are the nine words in the principle of Śiva (Śivatattva).
Oṃ, salutation to Śiva, who is eternal, established upon the seat of yoga, the perpetual yogin whose food is meditation;
to the source of all, whose head is Īśāna, whose face is Tatpuruṣa, and who resides on the eastern petal as Sādākhya.
To the one whose heart is non-terrible (aghora), whose secret is Vāmadeva, whose form is Sadyojāta— Oṃ, salutations again and again!
To the protector who is more secret than the secret, who is imperishable, who is unaltered by all yogas, whose nature is light, in the principle of Īśvara, on the fire-petal.

O Supreme Lord, O Supreme One, you who are the unconscious space of consciousness, all-pervading, formless, primordial, the splendor of splendors, the light of lights, and the master of the principle of knowledge, reside in the petal of the western direction.

Formless, without fire, without smoke, without ash, distinct from all else, neither one nor many, *dhū dhū dhū*, *oṃ bhūḥ*, *oṃ bhuvaḥ*, in the reality of faith, in the petal of non-selfhood (*nairātmya*).
Oṃ svaḥ! O you who arise from the non-ending, the ending, and the source of endings; O Śiva, the Supreme Self of all; O Maheśvara, Mahādeva, in the principle of Time, on the petal of Varuṇa!

O Lord of Existence, of Great Splendor, Sovereign of Yoga! Release, release! Subdue, subdue! All, all! Existence, existence! O Source of Existence, Bestower of Happiness upon all Beings, in the principle of Niyati, at the tip of the arrow of destruction! Muñca 2 pramatha 2 sarva 2 bhava 2 bhavodbhava sarvabhūtasukhaprada vyayavyadale niyati tattve.

O Brahmā who is present in all, O Viṣṇu and Rudra, supreme one, unworshipped, unworshipped, unsatisfied, stationed there and there before; witness, witness! Turu, turu! Pataṅga, pataṅga! Piṅga, piṅga! In the northern petal, in the principle of Puruṣa.
Jñāna 2, Śabda 2, Sūkṣma 2, Śivasarvada Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya. Oṃ namo namaḥ śivāya namo namaḥ oṃ; the principle of Prakṛti (Prakṛtitattva) is on the petal of Īśāna.
O Six-faced One, by the constant recitation of the Rudra-śānti, one is liberated from all sins amidst all calamities and all portents.
One is liberated from this, there is no doubt; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Śikhidhvaja!
For the wise one who begins with initiation, including the rites of installation, worship, and so forth.

Afterwards, one does not perform [the rite] directly; one is separated from the desired merit and the purification [resulting] from disease, the attainment of the cause for prosperity, the pacification of the region, and [the performance of] ritual acts.
One should constantly perform [the ritual] in cremation grounds, as in the case of Māriyā;
likewise for pacification (*śānti*), destruction (*naṣṭa*), attraction (*karṣaṇa*), subjugation (*vaśya*), expulsion (*uccāṭana*), and killing (*māraṇa*).
Is it not to be perceived because of time? No, nor is it eternal.
Thus ends the chapter on the propitiation of Rudra in the *Kālottara-mahātantra*.
The period of Śivāvāra is declared for those who have been initiated in due order.
Now, what is to be avoided and what is to be performed by those established on the path of Śiva?
On the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights,
as well as during all *vyatīpāta* yogas, on days of lunar increase, and at the waning of the day;

And at the transition [of the sun] to another sign, as well as on the six solstices, worship and fire-offerings should be doubled; one should remain awake, and there is no need for [ordinary] conduct.
Protection for those who are afraid, compassion for ascetics,
and kindness toward all beings, along with patience, truthfulness, and freedom from envy.
Lying for the sake of one's guru or deity is not considered a fault;
likewise, there is no punishment for one who is without support, nor is there any [restriction on] eating or sleeping at any time.
A bracelet known as Rudrākṣa should be made, either uneven or even and firm;
one should wear it with one, three, or five faces for the sake of attaining prosperity.
A [spear] with two, four, or six points is praised, provided it is without blemishes and has sharp thorns;
likewise, one that is scarred, worm-eaten, excessively large, or devoid of its rings is not recommended.
One should never wear a Rudrākṣa that is worn out at its base or rubbed smooth;
