however, one may wear two on the crest-lock of the right arm, provided they are deficient by four beads.
One who is not a practitioner of celibacy becomes a practitioner of celibacy; one who has not bathed becomes a bath-graduate (snātaka).
By the mere remembrance of the rudrākṣa, one is indeed glorified in the world of Rudra.
It burns away the sins of speech, mind, and body, acting as a binding fire;
therefore, with every effort, one should always wear that which is called Rudra.
Because it is not worn, great effort is required and its accomplishments remain far away;
therefore, the rudrākṣa should indeed be worn by both those who have been initiated and those who have not.
A golden ring should always be worn on the right hand;
it should be set with a ruby, an emerald, or a sapphire.
The two earrings, adorned with various radiant gems and endowed with the brilliance of the sun, should be worn;
and from the preceptor onwards, there should not be seventeen and a half [units] for the three-fold ura (chest-ornament).
That thread, consisting of three strands, tripled, round, rubbed smooth, and well-twisted,
should be fastened by the monkey-demon and led up to the very limit of the head.
Therefore, one should make it double that length;
by twisting its knot, the sacred thread (upavīta) for kings and others should consist of three, two, or one strand respectively.
Only that much of the worship should be maintained, and not its further retention;
the name "Śiva" belongs to the twice-born alone, while the one called "Kavaca" belongs to the king.
The designation "deities" is for the Vaiśyas, and for the Mudrās it is within the group;
the designation follows the falling of the flower, and that [designation] is beneficial according to its measure.
One should not abandon one who is without wealth, the weak, the frightened, or those situated in a difficult place;
one should assist cows in rising up when they have sunk into mud and the like.
This [treatise] is intended as a teacher for the blind among all four castes;
indeed, among all castes, the twice-born is considered the one who bestows favor.
A Kṣatriya [should avoid] three, a Vaiśya two, and a Śūdra those born of his own womb; however, one should completely avoid the touch of artisans and the like, as well as the *hotṛ* priest.
In this manner, assistance should be rendered by all four types of instructors;
the duty of the twice-born toward the stages of life (āśrama) has thus been proclaimed in its fourfold form.
The student and the householder proceed in succession to the forest-dwelling stage;
however, the duty of the householder’s stage of life does not belong to the Kṣatriyas, nor any other.

Or rather, fear is prescribed for them [only] regarding their celibate life (*brahmacarya*). There is indeed a distinction between the stages of life (*āśrama*), but no difference in their ultimate goal (*niṣṭhā*) is found.
One enjoys two fruits, while liberation is common to both.
The religious student (brahmacārī) is said to be of two kinds: the temporary (bhautika) and the lifelong (naiṣṭhika).
The material [initiate] is to be known as threefold; it is stated concisely as follows:
first, the one who has completed his studies (vidyā-snātaka), and another, the one who has completed his vows (vrata-snātaka).
There is yet another, the *ubhayasnātaka* (one who has bathed in both), as well as the *bhautika*; thus, there are indeed three kinds.
It is declared that his status as a householder occurs upon the completion of his studies and the performance of the *snāna* ceremony.
The second is declared to be the *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong student); his conduct lasts until the end of the body.
Wearing a fine girdle, with matted hair, carrying a staff, or shaven-headed, he is pure and subsists on alms.
Constant residence in the teacher’s household, self-restraint, speaking the truth,
bathing at the three times of day, and the subduing of anger— these constitute the practice of celibacy for a student.
The renunciation of a lifelong celibate occurs after ten thousand recitations of the Aghora mantra;
having performed the Vrateśvara Yoga, there shall then be liberation from the vow.
Bathing, worship of the gods, fire-offerings, giving gifts, and libations to the ancestors must be performed; likewise, one's own wife must be protected, and love must be eternal.
O son of Pārvatī, the householder should be understood to be of four kinds.
In the forest, performing oblations into the fire of the nose, subsisting on pure roots and fruits,
sleeping on the ground, conquering the sense of possession, and avoiding the acceptance of gifts.
Bathing three times a day, performing fire oblations, worship and meditation day and night,
and the restraint of all the senses— this is the mode of life for one who has not yet attained stability.
The renunciation of all activities, dwelling in the forest clad in bark garments,
and the state of viewing everything with equanimity toward pleasure, pain, and the like.
Internal purity with the utterance of "svāhā," constant meditation in the forest,
and the renunciation of the pleasant and unpleasant— this is declared to be the conduct of an ascetic.
This tetrad has been described; each one, moreover, is fourfold.
Thus ends the chapter on the Āśrama in the *Kālottara Mahātantra*.
Īśvara said:
I shall further explain the fourfold sphere of Śiva:
Śiva, Śikhā, Jyotis, and Sāvitrī are the spheres.

The family (kula) should be known as the field of activity (gocara); by that, one who has been initiated is to be known. Those who possess its signs are the Śaivas; the rest are considered to be the Maṇḍins.
One should conceive of the body of Śiva as being fourfold within the sphere of perception:
the family of Śiva denoted by mantra, the resonance (nāda), the digit of the moon (candrakalā), and the crest (śikhā).
Then, one should know the state of the senses (gocara-sthiti) as extending from Bindu, Arddhacandra, Jyotis, Sāvitrī, and Īśvara, up to Āśiva and Īśvara.
When the consciousness of the Śiva-enclosure is only as much as the navel, then,
according to the Śiva-āgama, it is joined with the seed-syllable of the self-knowledge of Vāgvīra.
That family known as Śiva should be understood as eternal, blissful, and of the nature of the Self.
From that arises the power of Nāda, which is the supreme state of Brahman.

Or else, [one should contemplate] the Mother [of the alphabet], threaded upon the needle of the *śikhā* (the top-knot), which is the machine of the *kalās*, consisting of mantra-pearls, pierced by the sun of *nāda*, and extending from the *ānā* up to the *daśānta*.
Then the crest (śikhā) is to be known as the family (kula), by virtue of its support in the reality of Sound (nāda);
whereas the station (saṃsthāna) is in the reality of the Drop (bindu), which consists of the attainment of the state (pada-sāda) that is Śiva-natured.
In the *virāma* known as *jyotis*, there is the *vastra* [tantra] through the power of *paśu* and *pāśa*;
in the one known as *sāvitrī* within the *kula*, the *tantra* of all is mixed.
Śiva and Śakti are the totality, and that which exists below is of the nature of Īśvara;
for wherever there is an enjoyer, that indeed is his lineage.
Śiva, Śikhā, as well as Jyotis, Sāvitrika, and Kula—each of these is fourfold; this is known as the various types of bali offerings.
Prājāpatya, Mahīpāla, Kapota, and likewise Granthika.
These divisions have been fully described within the sphere known as Śiva;
they are the Kuṭilas, the Vetālas, the Padma, the Ahaṃ, and that Śikhākula.
The Dhṛtarāṣṭras, Vakas, Kākas, Gopālas, those known as Jyotis, the Kuṭilas, Māṭharas, and others who carry staffs and medicinal pills.
Sāvitrī has declared this mode of conduct for those within her range; listen now to that.
Non-violence, service to the teacher, study of the Vedas, purity, self-restraint,
truthfulness, and non-stealing— this indeed is the beneficial doctrine of Prajāpati.
Because they protect the earth through rites for destruction and nourishment, as well as through acts of enmity, pacification, and so forth,
the rulers of the earth are indeed practitioners (*sādhaka*).
Those who, like pigeons, gather the grains that have fallen upon the ground,
and whose life is sustained by that sustenance— they are indeed accomplished practitioners (sādhakas).
Those who, having prepared a large collection, abandon it all at once for the sake of the deity, are considered *granthikas* practitioners; they are eaters of what is left over.
Those who remain with their families in the vicinity of rivers and oceans,
yet are crooked, should be known as practitioners intent on the worship of Śiva.
Those who are unable to visit sacred fords, yet live by their bows together with their wives,
and are endowed with great courage, are indeed *sādhakas* known as *vetālas*.
Self-restrained, lotus-like, and capable, they accomplish the goals of sovereignty and desire;
those practitioners are known as Padmas, always devoted to the practice of begging for alms.
Those who are endowed with the yoga of knowledge and remain free from the enemies that are the Daityas are known as Haṃsas; they are practitioners whose consciousness has arisen spontaneously.
O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, by means of celibacy and truth, as well as by what has been thus obtained, the entire world has indeed been conquered; this is your considered view.
Those who always practice knowledge or even the dharma of vows,
being intent solely on their own self-interest, are considered practitioners (*sādhaka*) who have reached the goal of a single destination.
Resorting to bodies of water and remaining there for the sake of supreme accomplishment,
they are the *visas*, *ṣaṭkas*, *hāras*, and the *vaikaṅkas* who are practitioners (*sādhakas*).
Those who wander here together with the cows and dwell in the cow-pens are the cowherds; indeed, they are the practitioners (sādhakas) for the attainment of the fifth seat.
Those who emaciate their own bodies through the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other such penances,
eating only a single *tuṭi* at a time, are considered *sādhakas* known as *tuṭilas*.
Having made roots, tubers, and fruits their food, and a wife of *kuśa* grass through their wisdom,
those pure practitioners of the Māṭhara school, devoted to the practice of begging, are indeed true seekers.
Furthermore, those practitioners who are well-restrained by eight pills, each equal in size to a single mouthful and consisting of bulbs,
roots, and fruits, [attain success].

Engaged in the discipline of their own bodies and devoted to the heroic posture (vīrāsana) at night—these are called the staff-bearing practitioners (daṇḍin-sādhakas); all this has been declared to you.
Whether they be commoners or established in specific [ascetic] vows, whether they be practitioners of the vow or even householders.
Thus ends the chapter on the sphere of activity in the *Kālottara-mahātantra*.
Īśvara said:
The religious student and the householder are each of two kinds;
I shall tell you everything regarding what is to be avoided by them, or what is to be given up entirely.
One should avoid meat, salt, excellent horses, and the drinking of turmeric;
likewise, one should avoid the adornment of women's limbs, singing, instrumental music, and dancing.
Except for that which pertains to Śiva, singing, instrumental music, and dancing are forbidden;
eating at improper times and giving gifts should be avoided by those observing vows. This is beneficial.
One should avoid garlands, ornaments, and perfumes, as well as the avoidance of ritual sacrifices;
one does not incur fault when consuming honey in times of distress, nor in the case of pride, weapons, and the like, which are trivial matters.
One who delights in the celibate life (brahmacarya) and is pure is considered a *vratī* and a *snātaka*;
even those others should likewise acquire the aforementioned object.
That preceptor was also told in the Tantra:
"The vow of the lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) is arduous, and it is indeed forbidden for one who is merely a worldly seeker (bhautika)."
Approaching the teacher’s wife, theft, sexual intercourse during auspicious times,
shaving, and the consumption of ghee and similar items are considered things to be avoided by a householder.
Whether rich in flowers, ornaments, and perfumes, or even by its own nature, food is not defiled by the scent of disease; rather, it is the digestive power that is the determining factor. 91b)
The mandala for the preceptor, intended for his daily meal, should be one cubit in size, four-cornered, and marked with four lines.
For the practitioners and others, it is proclaimed that each successive stage is characterized by the reduction of one line [of hair];
the wearing of hair is recommended, or alternatively, shaving may be done according to one's preference.
The husbands, however, wear matted hair and have their bodies smeared with ashes;
they should wrap their matted locks but must not wrap their shaven heads.
For the body of those [beads] should be circular, or else uniquely oval;
those known as "golden" should be circular, while the wise should fashion them with matted (jaṭā) shapes.
The [first] sixteen [verses], consisting of nine, six, one, and sixteen, have the appearance of the coils of a serpent in uneven [arrangement];
the others, however, are according to the path of the *pathyā* meter, and their arrangement follows the established rules of the śāstra.
Having fashioned the field with well-proportioned dimensions, its colors, parts, knowledge, positions, and so forth, Kūṭila was born from that former one.
The bases for the ashes should be made either firm and high or even;
they are recommended to be one span (vitasti) in length and one finger-breadth (aṅgula) in height according to the measurement of the thread.
One should raise the upper garment to a height of twelve finger-breadths;
it should be four finger-breadths wide, and in its center, a well-fastened cord should be placed.
Alternatively, a gourd vessel sixteen finger-breadths in length should be prepared;
one must carefully avoid using ashes that have originated from a funeral pyre.
The staff should be made equal in length to one's own body, thick like a thumb, or otherwise one cubit long; it should be made of banyan, khadira, or śiṃśapā wood.
The alms-bowl should be made twelve finger-breadths in width and eight finger-breadths deep; it may be made of copper or fashioned from a leaf.
One should avoid the palāśa, madhūka, kadamba, āmra, and campaka leaves; one should also avoid the vaṭa and aśvattha trees, as well as the piśāca, arka, and other such [plants], O Lord.

One should avoid those of the four castes who have committed offenses, those under training, and those accused of crimes; likewise, one should avoid food obtained from outcasts when performing the act of begging for alms according to the rule.
Remembering Śiva, one should place the staff, the weapon, and the heart within the vessel.
One should eat the food that has fallen into the vessel, but should discard what has fallen upon the ground.
One should not remain for long; rather, one should turn back, indeed turn back.
One should diligently maintain silence, or else [speak] only as much as is required to fill the alms-bowl.
Alternatively, one should subsist on gleaned grains or food obtained from many households;
having placed the almsfood in a cool and tranquil spot, it should simply be brought back.
Having washed his hands, feet, and so forth, the wise one should recite the mantra as before;
he should then offer water for sprinkling with the *hṛdaya* mantra to Śiva and again to the Guru.
92b) Food should be prepared by others and consecrated with the three-syllable mantra;
it then quickly becomes nectar, and through its renown, death would be destroyed.
One should eat while observing silence, and not after the night has passed;
thus is described the general characteristic of wandering for alms.
There is no merit equal to alms-giving; there is no austerity equal to alms-giving.
Whatever merit exists in all sacred fords and whatever fruit exists in all sacrifices [is attained thereby].
Whatever fruit is obtained from all types of giving, as well as from practices such as the Cāndrāyaṇa penance,
a man who subsists on alms shall obtain that same fruit multiplied ten millionfold.
When the cooking has been completed and the guest turns his face away,
all the gods and ancestors turn their faces away from him.
When the time has arrived, it should be given with careful deliberation and effort;
for he indeed uplifts ten generations of ancestors and ten generations of descendants.
Of all worthy recipients, the guest is indeed the supreme recipient;
whether he be deficient in limb or complete in limb, neither his vow nor his birth [is the determining factor].
He who is worthy of worship without hesitation shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice;
he who, when the time has arrived, avoids begging from afar.
That lunar day departs taking with it all the fruit of his merit,
when he makes a request without reflection while the cooking is not yet finished.
He is called a slayer of Brahman, yet he is pure through hundreds of various forms;
knowing this, one should always diligently undertake the wandering for alms.
The perfections of one who subsists on alms and has conquered his senses are truly accomplished;
O Śikhidhvaja, all other forms of receiving gifts are said to be excluded for such a person, with the exception of alms.
Thus ends the chapter on the pledges in the *Kālottara Mahātantra*.
Kārtikeya said:
Two types of gurus have been declared for the two [classes of disciples], namely the *bhautika* and the *naiṣṭhika*, respectively;
yet, in truth, I do not possess knowledge regarding the classification of those to be favored.
The Lord said:
Listen, O Six-faced One, to the reality of liberation and enjoyment as they truly exist:
the teacher is considered to be of two kinds, namely the celibate student and the householder.
Both of these are eligible for initiation (dīkṣā) and consecration (pratiṣṭhā);
however, they are intended for those whose minds are solely intent on liberation and whose natures are averse to worldly power.
The student (brahmacārī) is to be known as the teacher for those seeking the two [goals],
and likewise the householder for those of the previous castes and stages of life who abide in their respective duties.
Liberation is traditionally held to be common to those who have realized reality and possess that knowledge;
however, the status of being a husband is likewise honored by householders in the case of husbands.
The householder alone is honored by those seeking the fruits of sacrifice;
for others besides the householder, there is no entitlement to enjoy such rewards.
Therefore, a householder should be accepted as a guru by those seeking both worldly enjoyment and liberation from fear;
indeed, by merely bowing to such a person, one obtains the fruit of a hundred thousand [prostrations].
One attains the fruit of a thousand cows by prostrating at the feet of one's own guru;
yet he would not obtain even a sixteenth part of that merit which is gained by [prostrating] before one who bears a Śivaliṅga.
When he was satisfied, the entire world, including all things moving and stationary, became satisfied;
when he was contented, O Lord, Sadāśiva himself became contented.
Therefore, with every effort, one should worship the Śivaliṅga,
even among the Buddhists, Vaiṣṇavas, Pañcārthikas, Śauras, Kālamukhas, and others.
A Śaiva may hold authority over all, but one who is not a Śaiva can never [do so] by any means;
in that regard, the latent impressions (vāsanā) must be understood through their distinctions, for here [in this world] there are indeed bound souls (paśu).
I shall explain the classification of the transgressions arising from those who have been initiated.
The householder and the student are considered the two types of the initiated;
in the absence of the father, O Śikhidhvaja, the sons shall provide the sacrificial fee.
Repeat pages 94 and 95.
94a) From the chest, by an equal portion, likewise from the specific parts of the maiden;
thus the eldest is most excellent, and the others are born in equal measure.
The father shall take the estate of one who has no son, and in his absence, the mother;
in her absence, the paternal uncles, and likewise others who offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
Regarding those born from the paternal side: when some are born from one's own lineage, they are [the heirs];
in the absence of the paternal side, those born from the maternal side are the recipients.

In the absence of those [heirs], the king shall take the property, excluding the two sides [of paternal and maternal kin]. In this manner, the rights of the maternal grandfather and others are declared to be forfeited in favor of the grandson and his descendants.
A married woman, having lost her husband’s family,
must strive diligently to seek refuge from those born of her father’s side.
In brief, wealth arising from one's own lordship alone should be accepted;
this applies both to common folk and to those whose inner selves are capable.
If they have offspring, however, a sixth part by measure should be taken from them;
when the materials required for the rite are available, the king shall receive his share, and no one else.
One should offer to the king things that are of great value and delicious;
however, wealth from a Brahmin who has been excluded from the four castes must not be accepted.
One should take [substances] such as those from fishermen, which arise from contact with water;
or else, one should bring forth that which arises from immersion, or what is carried by the waves of a garment-drenching stream.
Thus, one should discern the eighteen-fold *ṛk* through the intellect of the treatise,
distinguishing between its internal and external applications.
The sins of those who take food from one who gives alms are incurred through that very act and not otherwise;
the penance for a householder has been declared, and now that pertaining to a student is being stated.
From Brahmacāryudbhava came Ṛkṣa and Ṛkṣiṇas, who were born of his own lineage.
Because there is no continuity of their own lineage and because their inheritance belongs to another lineage, such persons are said to be "severed"; one should avoid those who bear their emblems.
Furthermore, because of the absence of his own lineage, or likewise because of the supreme lineage, the king indeed destroys the mind; he does not thereby become a debtor.
A written document, witnesses, and possession—these are the threefold means of proof for debtors.
Possession is not valid without a means of proof, nor is a means of proof valid without witnesses.
Wealth derived from women, children, or the king, as well as the sky and the army, is lost;
indeed, where there is no enjoyment, it is not beneficial for thirty years.
Having been proclaimed according to the rules of documentation in the presence of the king, and having again taken it to heart,
one should carefully examine the witnesses when there is mutual consent between both parties.
In cases of verbal assault, physical assault, theft, and combat, witnesses are not to be examined;
rather, in a legal proceeding, one should investigate the plaint as the essential core.
One devoid of her is as good as slain, while one who has seen her shall be victorious;
one should examine legal disputes with those who are skilled in the meaning of the Dharmaśāstras.
O Six-faced One, I shall explain his investigation once again.
But for those who assist in the ritual procedures of the knowledge of Śiva,
a celibate student (brahmacārī), having stood upon his station and having accepted a gift, [attains the goal].
O child, having acquired wealth, land, and so forth, one enters the stage of the householder; for them, the distribution of shares should be arranged according to the rules for householders.
Thereafter, one should determine the division of property among the mother, sons, brothers, and others,
by means of the three kinds of evidence, beginning with witnesses and using equitable measures.
And here one should examine legal procedure according to the eighteen points;
thus has this investigation been presented in brief.
Furthermore, one who is younger but endowed with learning, age, and noble birth,
or one who was previously initiated with effort in the absence [of others] there, should be honored like a guru.
96b) One should wait upon the eldest and greet him like a guru;
he should be honored with supreme devotion day after day, just like one's own teacher.
In his absence, however, his wives should be worshipped with great effort.
A woman can never be a Guru; therefore, one should not cause her to initiate disciples.
A woman who has taken a vow should be honored equally; one should never act toward her as if she were a mere ascetic.
One should never bow down to her, nor look at her when she is naked, nor gaze at her with force.
The eldest brother is always to be honored; thereafter, he should be instructed in the scriptures.
Alternatively, another scripture should be heard from someone else for the sake of accomplishing one's duties.
One should always worship [the teacher] as a guru and avoid treating him as anything else;
for he is the speaker, the awakener, and the third is the giver of liberation.
One should worship everything as Śiva, because He is the bestower of liberation to human beings;
He who impels all living creatures toward Śiva, the supreme cause.

They say that the one who impels is the *codaka*, while the foremost and most excellent is the *guruddhaureya*. The *dīkṣā-guru* is the bestower of liberation, whereas the *bodhaka* is the one who reveals the scriptures.
Indeed, the teacher who awakens one must always be honored with diligent effort;
thus has this brief summary of the discipline established by the Guru been told.
Thus ends the chapter on the investigation of the Guru in the Kālottara Mahātantra.
97a) Īśvara said:
I shall fully explain the *aṃśaka* (astrological division) which bestows fruit upon practitioners;
indeed, the analysis of mantras must be performed according to the *aṃśaka*.
Without their respective portions, mantras are seedless and devoid of fruit;
just as a tree without seeds is never seen to bear fruit out of season.
Just as a seed sown in saline soil is devoid of fruit,
so too one should never recite a mantra that is deprived of its constituent parts.
Therefore, I shall describe the three types of *aśakas*; having understood them, one becomes worthy of success (*siddhi*).
Having written the *mātṛkā* on the ground, excluding the six *kūṭas*:
One should separate the syllables of the mantra and lead each one individually to the *anusvāra*;
the separation should be performed according to whatever name the practitioner possesses.
One should place the letters of the practitioner at the beginning and likewise at the end of the mantra;
then, one should count them in order according to their designations as *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari*.
If a mantra is auspicious in its initial portion and likewise at its end, it shall grant success;
and if it is successful at the beginning and successful at the end, it becomes effective in that very instant.
One should consider everything from the *susiddha* category up to the *susiddhānta* as being like the *siddha* [category];
however, one should avoid from afar the names of enemies at both the beginning and the end.
The *siddha*, the *susiddha*, the *ari*, and likewise the *sādhya* share a single purpose;
for at the beginning of the mantra it is situated as the *siddha*, and at its end it is exactly the same.
Know that those who are well-established at the beginning will likewise be so at the end;
for them, there are indeed no thousands of enemies in the middle.
The *siddha* [letter] removes doubt; the second, the *udāsīna*, does the same;
the *susiddha* bestows fruit quickly and certainly destroys enemies.
One should avoid [a planet] that is occupied by an enemy at both its beginning and end, as well as by the teeth of Death;
likewise, one should avoid those that are well-established at the beginning and end, or those that were previously enemies at the end.
Having thus understood that portion, O Six-faced One, one should offer the mantra to the disciple with the *prasāda* and *praṇava* mantras of the first syllable.
One should conceive of Nāśaka as being [manifested] from Navātman and Ghoradeva;
for these are considered to be the sovereign lords of the kings of mantras, bestowers of grace upon all.
They are capable in all undertakings; one should not assign a fractional share to them.
Alternatively, the wise man may assign a fractional share in another manner.
Indeed, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Śakra, as well as Yakṣas, Gandharvas,
Rākṣasas, Daityas, and Vidyādharas— the base ones among them— should be known as pure, being portions of that [pure essence].
A twice-born man who bathes at dawn, is capable, pure in all respects, self-controlled, and compassionate;
who is united with the Self through the knowledge of Brahman—he is to be known as a portion of Brahman.
One who is illusory, endowed with courage, a hero, fond of women, envious, yet firm,
and always skilled in the means for accomplishing tasks— such a person should be known as possessing a portion of Viṣṇu.

O wise one, that man who is enriched by devotion to Rudra, who is heroic, who frequents the abodes of Piśācas, and who is fond of the great vow (mahāvrata), should be known as a partial incarnation of Rudra.
One who is intent on singing, dancing, and holding a parasol, devoted to the sight of elephants,
and capable of narrating stories of divine power should be known as one possessing the portion of Indra (Paurandara).
A man who subsists on milk, lives by the wind (or is a wanderer), delights in gardens, and is fond of molasses, sugar-candy, and boiled rice;
who is stiff-limbed and desirous of a Naga maiden—such a person should be known as one with a Naga portion (nāgāṃśaka).
Adorned with bracelets, armlets, necklaces, and various ornaments,
and possessing limbs endowed with the quality of sattva, he is to be known as one who possesses a portion of the Lord of Yakṣas.
Delighting in song and dance, adorned with garlands, fine garments, and beautiful perfumes,
he who aspires to that sovereignty is the most excellent among the Gandharvas.
He has the smell of raw flesh, his gaze is piercing, and he is fond of excellent flavors; he should be known as having a portion of a Rākṣasa, with a name terrifying due to the knitting of his brows.
A man who possesses a mind fixed upon the hollows of the earth— deep, vast, and unshakeable— who speaks of great battles and discourses, should be known as one who has a portion of a Daitya.
One who desires the accomplishment of the thirty-fold sciences, who is devoted to his mother and wife,
whose mind is firm, and who seeks self-exaltation, should be known as a partial incarnation of a Vidyadhara.
Overcome by wretchedness, fear, and impurity, fond of foul odors and meat, and experiencing intense suffering due to base actions— he is called a portion of a *piśāca*.
The pure portions have been fully described; now the mixed portions are explained again:
[the face] adorned with a halo of radiance from the tips of its well-red nails and locks of hair.
Furthermore, his feet have toes with hidden joints like the shell of a tortoise;
his shanks are well-rounded, and his thighs are as beautiful as the trunk of a plantain tree.
Broad at the slopes of its hips and curved with the undulations of the three folds,
it is a vast abode for the goddess Kamalā, extending as far as the end of its slender waist.
With a neck like a conch shell, lips like the bimba fruit, and a cage-like pair of long arms;
with a prominent and well-formed tip of the nose, and eyes that are tremulous and flickering.
His face was pure with its own inner radiance, marked by the form of a bow;
his forehead was as broad as that [bow], and he was beautifully adorned with a parasol upon his head.
With the tips of great peacock feathers and blue-black hair upon his face,
he is overcome by the strength of the intellect of a being, endowed with patience and joy.
Endowed with enthusiasm and joy, devoted to Rudra,
and possessing a mixed portion, such a person is fortunate in all undertakings and achieves all successes.
The new moon and full moon days of the practice, as well as the beginning of the entire [cycle], are established in two ways;
they reside within the throat and the lips, once in the middle of the two fortnights together with the Mothers.
Having understood this, one should bestow a portion [of the teaching] and a mantra that is beneficial for him;
a mantra is said to range from a single syllable up to six syllables.
The Vidyā may consist of seven syllables up to fifteen kinds;
Bālā consists of seven syllables up to twelve syllables.
Above that, however, the vowels [should be placed] from the letter *va* up to the end of the thirty-two consonants;
above those, the nasal stops (*niroja*) are to be known, extending as far as three hundred letters.
Up to three hundred [syllables] it is a Kumārī; up to four hundred, a Śatā;
thereafter, up to one thousand syllables, they are proclaimed as Vṛddhavidyās.
Beyond one thousand recitations, it is proclaimed that the knowledge assumes the form of a staff (daṇḍa).
Know that at two thousand recitations it becomes a hymn (stava); when chanted with devotion, it brings success.
The morning twilight is beneficial for children during recitation, fire-oblation, and worship;
at sunrise it is for young maidens, and during the [first] watch of the day for those established in youth.
The worship of the Madhyāhna-sthaviras is performed at midday; that of the Vṛddhas in the afternoon; that of the Daṇḍakas at twilight; and for the remaining [groups], the worship is at night.
For mantras, recitation, fire-oblations, and so forth are beneficial when performed in the forenoon;
however, he who performs them otherwise is overcome by all obstacles.
Whatever one desires to accomplish does not succeed for one who ends with the word "manas";
furthermore, the food offering for all [deities] consists of milk-rice with ghee and curd.
Various modakas and many kinds of candied sweets, when prepared with effort at the proper time, grant success; this word is not false.
The fifty [letters] beginning with *ka* and ending with *ha* are, in sequence, the two wings;
however, O child, it is said that the first wing is devoid of *ṛ*, *ḷ*, and *ṇ*.
In this way, know the ten vowels, excluding the neuter ones;
one should place them in three ways, together with the *anusvāra* and *visarga*, as well as the nasalized (*vināma*) vowel.
The short days are prescribed as white, while the long days are indeed black in three ways; one should calculate the lunar dates (tithis) there, beginning with the first day (pratipad).
Childhood, youth, maidenhood, old age, and likewise the bringer of death—
these five lunar days (tithis) are to be known as existing threefold within each fortnight.
Birth, waning, and destruction—each of these occurs in groups of five in succession;
likewise, there are the rising, the setting, the twilight, the revolving, and the dissolution.

At sunrise, one should perform rites such as pacification (śāntika) and so forth; likewise, at the time of laughter, one should employ subjugation (vaśya), attraction (ākarṣaṇa), and immobilization (stambhana) during the twilight hours.
The son of Pārvatī has declared that [the mantra] rotated is excellent for the eradication of enemies;
when the sun has set, it is excellent at sunset—knowing the proper time, one attains success.
For each individual period, the six [asterisms] beginning with Kṛttikā should be known;
therein also, the internal time should be understood as existing in a threefold manner.
Rites such as pacification (śāntika) and others grant success through the movement of the iḍā;
subjugation, attraction, and delusion are accomplished through the piṅgalā.
One should practice killing, expulsion, and so forth while situated at the equinox;
each one should be known as fivefold through diligent attention to the movement of the channels.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—
because it touches below and flows forth, it is known by the name Pṛthivī (the Earth).
The fire-element flows upward from those two, and between them the fluid element is considered to be;
on the side of the cavity flows the wind, pervading all and flowing through the Lord.
Stambhana (paralysis) is effective on the path of Pārthiva; Śāntika (pacification) is beneficial on the path of Vāruṇa;
and Vaśya (subjugation), Ākarṣaṇa (attraction), Mohana (delusion), and so forth, are accomplished by means of Tejas, without a doubt.
The wandering by way of the path of the wind and the battle by way of the void—
thus has this measurement of time been briefly described by me.
But without this, my son, nothing at all is accomplished;
therefore, one should practice the knowledge of time with every effort.
Thus ends the chapter on the characteristics of the divisions of time in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the supreme essence of Gaurī, which has not been told to anyone; out of affection for you, O Six-faced One.
It bestows incomparable all-encompassing good fortune, prosperity, intelligence, beauty, and sons;
it always increases longevity and nourishment for those who desire worldly success.
Mantra-meditation, the maṇḍala, and the accomplishment of mudrās—
these five types of ritual procedures (kalpa) I shall now briefly explain.
Having firmly grasped from beyond that sovereign deity— who is Citrabhānu, Śiva, Kāla, endowed with great power (Mahāśakti), and enriched by the syllable U— the officiant [should proceed].
Overcome by the two stars (the letter *u*), it is joined with the word *gaurī*;
it should be made to end in the dative case, signifying "to Gaurī" as the expression for gold.
101a) Therein, for the three wealthy [classes], one should not utter the six limbs endowed with the birth-mantra;
rather, one should recite the seat with the *praṇava* alone, ending with the sixteenfold vidyā.
From Īśvara down to Śakti, the form [of the deity] is [visualized] with one's own heart-mantra;
the Gaurī mantra has thus been fully explained, and now the Śiva mantra is being stated.
And likewise, at the appropriate time, one should extract the seed-syllable of Śiva;
the vital breath (praṇava) conjoined with the long vowel and the letter 'Ś', together with the six limbs and the [six] classes.
Here, one should perform the placement of the seat (*āsana-nyāsa*) once with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) using the sixfold method;
likewise, one should perform the placement of the form (*mūrti-nyāsa*) at the heart with the heart-mantra, as well as the offering of incense, lamps, and so forth.
The *Yāmala* has been told, O child; now hear the *Ekavīra*.
It is all-pervasive, joined with emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), and follows the sequence of fire, *māyā*, and the earth-syllable.

The seed-syllable consisting of Śiva and Śakti, beginning with the heart-mantra and free from ritual constraints, bestows all desires; O child, they know this seed-syllable to be the supreme among seeds.
I shall proclaim the meditation mantra correctly and in due order,
beginning from two finger-breadths up to the limit of twelve finger-breadths.

In the home, however, it should be made with care according to the proportions of a temple of Fire; it may be made of gold or silver, or prescribed as being made of brass, honey-wood, or other timber.
White sandalwood, *śrīvāsa*, *devadāru*, and auspicious *apāmārga*—these five lumps (*pañcapiṇḍī*), accompanied by *śiva*, should be prepared with effort so as not to be manifest [to others]. 101b)
In the corners there are five circles, and above them should be the fifth;
[these represent] Lalitā, Śubhagā, Gaurī, Kṣobhaṇī, and Śakti herself.
The directions of Agni, Rakṣas, Vāyu, and Īśāna should be circular;
one should assign the powers of Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Kriyā, and Jñānā to the directions starting from the east.
He is joined by the seats and enclosures, with Śiva situated on his left side;
one should represent Śiva as unmanifest, devoid of the lines of the *lakṣma*.
This is proclaimed as the unmanifest form of Śiva and Śivā; it should be known as bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, especially for women.
Therefore, I shall describe the manifest form of the auspicious Śivā, which is common to all:
she may have two eyes or three eyes, and she may be either pure alone or accompanied by Śaṅkara.
She stands with her feet level upon a lotus, possessing two or four arms;
she may be seated upon two lotus-thrones, or likewise seated upon a lion and the Dharma-wheel.

Gaurī should be installed in her proper place; there, the first [form] is the two-armed Satī, holding a sacrificial ladle (*śruk*), a rosary (*akṣasūtra*), a bud (*kalikā*), a small stick (*salākā*), and a ball of clay (*palapiṇḍikā*).
In his right hand he holds a sword or another weapon,
and in his left a book, a betel-leaf case, a staff, the gesture of granting fearlessness, and a water-pot.
102a) One should offer the *gaṇeśa*, mirror, and *iṣṭā* one by one in sequence,
as each of the eight *sadyahasta* [positions] is established in its respective place.
Through the variations of the modulations (mūrchanās) as fangs, there would be sixty-four types of knowledge;
for each of the two aforementioned groups of eight, there are two on each side.
But she who bears four hands, through the division of the eight mountains,
has twenty-eight pairs for each group of eight, according to the number five and eight.
When they are mutually unconscious, the previously mentioned number proceeds;
whether visible or invisible in the mouth, one should clearly determine the path.
She should be understood as possessing the characteristics of the *liṅga*, consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest;
she should make Śiva manifest through her unmanifest form and splendor.
One should fashion either the Unmanifest as Śiva, or Speech as the Supreme Goddess;
or else, both in manifest form should be fashioned, endowed with their characteristic marks.
Gaurī should be eight tālas in height, while Śiva should be nine tālas;
she may be made with a short seat, emaciated, or even deformed, yet she bestows auspiciousness.
Alternatively, the Ardhanārīśvara form should be fashioned according to the correct proportions. Thus the visualization has been fully described; now I shall indeed explain the mudrās.
One should visualize the previously described lotus gesture (*padmamudrā*) on the seat;
the *liṅgamudrā* is prescribed for Śiva, while the *vāhanīmudrā* is for both.
The Śakti-mudrā belongs indeed to Gaurī, while that which is known as the Yoni-mudrā is formed by the interlocking of the fingers,
placing the two thumbs upon the middle fingers.
O Six-faced One, when both the tarjanī and ucchata mudrās are joined together, they form the Śakti-mudrā,
which bestows auspiciousness and agitates all sentient beings when preceded by the mantra.
I shall now duly describe the mandala in its proper sequence:
it is square, four cubits in measure, and divided on all sides into eight parts.
In the middle four squares, one should fashion a three-petaled [lotus];
then, in sequence, a triangle, a half-moon, a full moon, and a square, each doubling in size.
The two-pada section for the child should be doubled at the vicinity;
in this manner, the fourfold gateway should be constructed with great care.
The corner region from the two doors is considered to be two squares like a thunderbolt;
on its sides, there is half a door-measure, excluding one and a half squares for the neck.
In the center of the triangle is an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp, possessing the luster of pure jasmine or the moon; the triangle itself has a red radiance.
Above that is a half-moon, yellow with the luster of refined gold;
the doors are yellow and black, and the corners have the brilliance of diamond-ointment.
103a) Having thus turned back [the obstacles], one should fashion a mandala that increases fortune;
or else, one should arrange the Sarvatobhadra mandala.
One should worship there according to the rules, either on a beautiful sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or elsewhere;
one should perform the invocation (āvāhana), as well as the installation (sthāpana) and the binding (rodhana).
One should perform the rite of *sannidhāna* (bringing the deity near) and then the rite of *saṃmukhīkaraṇa* (making the deity present);
this should be performed day after day with great care upon a consecrated mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
One should remember the Earth-tattva up to the seat [of the deity] just once;
thereafter, from Īśvara down to Śakti, one performs the mental visualization of the forms.
One should invoke the supreme, the parasapara, the principle of power (śaktitattva) within the umbrella;
thus the practitioner should perform this invocation in the images and other such objects.
For the sake of attaining fortune, the best of practitioners— whether a man or a woman—
should smear [the image] with the five nectars and so forth, and anoint it with saffron and other substances.
Red garments should be given, especially flowers—
whether fragrant white ones or others endowed with scent.
Incense made from black agallochum (kṛṣṇāguru) should be offered, or camphor combined with musk;
various types of sweetmeats and many sacred offerings should also be presented.
One should cause him to drink milk mixed with sugar-candy;
furthermore, he may eat bulbs, roots, fruits, and so forth, according to his own inclination.
One should offer betel-leaf combined with camphor and various enjoyments;
facing north, one should worship the Supreme Goddess.
Having worshipped with supreme devotion, O son, he should diligently perform the recitation (japa) every day, either one thousand and eight times or one hundred times.
O Śāṅkarī, in the case of the ancillary rites (aṅgas), the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed one-tenth of that [number],
while the recitation (japa) for Śiva should be performed according to one's own capacity.
Sacrifice is recommended in a lotus-shaped or a quadrangular pit;
in the absence of those, it should be one cubit in measure, level, and provided with three girdles.
One should sprinkle the sacrificial pit with water from the *argha* vessel;
likewise, the *śruk* and *śruva* ladles and the oblation materials grant success [only when thus purified], and not otherwise.
One should conceive the fire of knowledge situated there within the lotus of the heart;
having worshipped it according to the prescribed rite through the path of the suṣumnā, one should offer [oblations] to another.
Having visualized Gaurī in her form for two hundred [breaths], one should afterwards cause the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) to be offered;
O God, she shall become present in the daily, occasional, and other rites.
O son, one obtains all desires by making oblations into the fire of knowledge.
Day after day, one should perform the fire oblation with jasmine flowers,
or with campaka, palāśa, or karavīra flowers, saturated with clarified butter.
With lotuses or blue lilies, or with *śrīphala*, *madana*, betel nuts,
*jātī* fruits, oblations, saffron, or filaments.
It should be performed with camphor, especially with sandalwood;
likewise, there should be an oblation of ghee from a tawny cow combined with guggulu resin.
Likewise, an oblation of dūrvā grass is praised, and an oblation of parched grain (lāja) is especially recommended;
an oblation with bulbous flowers is beneficial, and one with jasmine (jātī) flowers is particularly so.
One should always avoid the oblation of *sumanā* flowers;
however, an oblation of *dūrvā*, *amṛtā*, and clarified butter, accompanied by the three sweets (*trimadhu*), is further recommended.
Likewise, oblations should be made with white mustard seeds and the flower-buds of the Brahma-tree (Butea monosperma),
along with its tender leaves and from its tender branches.
One seeking subjugation should perform a fire sacrifice with salt, while one skilled in the rite of homa should likewise perform the oblation for attraction using the tongue and oil.
For the purpose of immobilization (stambhana), a fire-oblation (homa) with powdered nāgakeśara is desired;
for nourishment (āpyāyana), white-colored [substances] are recommended, while red ones are praised for subduing (avaśya).

For the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*), it should be yellow in color; for cruel rites (*krūrakarman*), it should indeed be black. Afterward, one should apply the full [mark] and then fashion the *tripuṇḍra*.
Having offered the oblation to the Goddess and having prostrated again and again,
one should perform the reverse *argha* offering, beginning from the weapon (*astra*) and ending with the earth (*bhū*).
One should perform [the rite] with an image, but never the dismissal (visarjana) therein. One should arrange the dismissal upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), in fire, or within a mandala fire.
Afterwards, the bali offering should be given to the spirits in the field, as well as outside;
having sipped water and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should meditate upon the imperishable Śakti.
One should diligently offer libations to the preceptor and others seven times;
one should always worship a maiden with care, five, seven, or eight times.
O Śikhidhvaja, women who are united with their husbands should be honored with great effort;
furthermore, whatever has been given by the Goddess should be bestowed upon young maidens.
Or one should give it to those devoted to Śiva, or one may consume it oneself on some occasion;
thus has this secret, the sacrifice of the Subhagā, been described.
One seeking victory obtains victory; one seeking sons obtains sons;
one seeking a daughter obtains a daughter; and one desiring wealth shall obtain wealth.
One shall attain auspiciousness free from fear, and even unimpaired fortune;
by reciting [this], a king obtains undiminished majesty.
Would he not bestow the entire earth with its nine divisions and the oceans?
When seven hundred thousand recitations have been performed, perfection arises.
105a) "Even Indra and the other gods do not have power over her; what need is there to mention humans and the like?
Thus, the practitioner must first perform this service for her.
Having performed the initiation for women or men, one should cause [the gift] to be given;
O child, in this supreme mantra, one should not assign any portion (nāṃśaka).

One should perform the initiation with five *kalpas* and a hundred oblations in due order; five *kalpas* are to be offered as oblations for each, and when there is capacity, the application of the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) is performed.

O Śikhidhvaja, the conjunction of all— namely the initiates (samayin), the spiritual sons (putraka), the practitioners (sādhaka), and the masters (ācārya)— must be performed within the principle of Śakti.
In the principle of Māyā one is a Samayin; in the principle of Śakti, a Putraka;
in Īśvara, a Sādhaka; [the state of] Bhoga; and in Sakala, one is established as an Ācārya.
Having understood this, one should diligently arrange the two parts of dissolution;
for if a teacher performs initiation without knowing the two parts of dissolution, [the rite is fruitless].
An ācārya together with his disciples shall be cooked in the Raurava hell;
therefore, having ascertained [the disciple's fitness] with effort, the teacher should perform the initiation.
At the conclusion of the initiation, the rules (samayas) must be proclaimed to the female practitioners and those of lower status;
[the same applies] to women of the ritual manual, to gods, to Brahmins, and especially to gurus.
One should carefully avoid disparaging the teacher, the sacrificial fire, the practitioner, and so forth;
one must never engage in mockery or show contempt at any time.
One should mentally avoid the theft of property, enmity,
fickleness, as well as greed and the transgression of the teacher's command.
One should not cause a woman to receive initiation; the vow is excluded for women. One should always, with great effort, cause [a man] to receive the perfected mantra from every source.
Furthermore, there is no restriction regarding time here, nor should one assign a specific portion [of the ritual];
red garments should be worn, as well as collyrium and fire.
Her eyes should always be adorned with collyrium, her feet dyed with lac,
and her head diligently decorated with fragrant flowers.
The mouth should be provided with betel-leaf; the neck should be endowed with a necklace;
both hands should wear a multitude of bracelets, as well as earrings and finger-rings.
One should always wear fragrant scents and red garments;
likewise, sexual union should always be avoided during the day and on the sacred festival days (parvan).
One who is menstruating should diligently perform the internal sacrifice (antaryāga);
she should not eat the remnants of another's food, yet if she eats them, she incurs no fault.
One should avoid using the teacher’s bed, seat, drink, and sandals;
upon seeing the teacher, one should diligently move away from the ground, like a cow.
106a) Worship should be performed at the three times of day, or even at a single time;
as long as Gaurī has not been worshipped, eating is not beneficial.
Having honored her with betel, garments, and abundant perfumes, one should wear [the marks];
at the time of dawn, one should always worship Bhavānī with devotion.
One must never perform any ritual mantra over the image while it is being used for various purposes,
such as a grinding stone, a mortar, a broom, or a threshold.
One should not touch with one's foot a maiden, a woman, a child, a sword, a weapon, fire, a twice-born man, a teacher, an elderly person, a water-pot, a jewel, or a garment.
O Śikhidhvaja, worship with the left hand must be avoided;
O child, oil, meat, and the like should be shunned on every sacred festival day.
Especially on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, on the full moon, during the sun’s passage into a new sign, during eclipses, and at the beginnings of the sixty-year cycles.
A special worship should be performed; one should always honor the Ācārya. On the third day, the *gara* (poison-remedy) rite should be done, and likewise, worship on the fourth day.
One should cause the food offering (naivedya) taken by the Goddess to be given to young maidens;
one should avoid performing worship in the presence of those who have not received initiation.
She should be surrounded by maidens, or in their absence, by women who are deeply devoted and fortunate; the application of *tilaka* and sprinkling [with water] is beneficial.
White flowers for the sake of accomplishment, as well as sprouts of blue dūrvā grass,
should be placed daily upon the head, adorned with the mantra of the Goddess.
One should always hold a mirror; one should not touch a funeral pyre or a corpse, nor should one touch a moving flower or withered flowers, O son.
A woman deprived of her husband should not touch gold or silver, nor one who is dull-witted,
lame, crippled, one-eyed, or of wicked intent;
nor one who subsists by the emblem [of a sect], nor a dyer, nor one born from the ashes of a funeral pyre.

Those who perform the *sūdaliṅga* rite of the three ears, those who steal, those who are devoid of ritual action, those who follow mere logic (*haituka*), those who are known as such, and those who delight in reviling Śiva— these are synonyms for atheists; they should never be honored even in thought.
One should diligently avoid liquor and meat;
one should carefully offer sweets and foods that are fit to be licked.
Food that has not stood overnight should be offered with great care;
however, one must diligently avoid food cooked in oil and long, fibrous vegetables.
Red wicks should be offered, and red flowers with effort;
likewise, fragrant white lotuses and *maru* flowers.
One should worship with red Aśoka flowers and Karavīra flowers;
as for the sweetmeats, they should be cooked so that they do not become stale.
One should offer milk that is thickened and cooled, as well as curd;
one should cause water mixed with camphor and strained through a cloth to be given.
One should indeed perform that which arises from the Veda, for it is pure; one should not perform anything else that is harmful.
One must carry out the commands of the Lord through action, mind, and speech.
Having abandoned worship, vows, and the like, one should honor the husband with one's head; for there is no one equal to the husband, O child, as he is indeed the savior-guru of women.

O wise one, who indeed is the master regarding dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa? Know that the husband is the master; for through the husband's knowledge, dharma arises, and through his protection, artha is attained. One should protect [the wife] by means of the husband's knowledge.
Desire is fulfilled through the husband, and liberation arises from serving the husband;
knowing this, one should with great effort never transgress the command of the husband.
By worshipping her, good fortune is produced;
and by observing the commitments (samayas), one shall obtain whatever is desired by the mind.
By transgressing the commitments (samaya), one encounters misfortune,
poverty, the torment of suffering, and separation from one's kinsmen.
Therefore, with every effort, one should always protect the pledge;
for transgression of the boundary is like falsehood, while its observance is like truth multiplied a thousandfold.
107a) One should avoid dejection, cowardice, and laughter, as well as sleeping in empty houses,
and [sleeping] by ponds, wells, large trees, or in the temples of deities.
Sleeping, weeping, and especially eating—
worship at night is not recommended, nor is eating, particularly so.
One should not utter a loud laugh, nor should one harbor malice toward others even in the mind;
one should not commit violence against living beings, nor should one point out the faults of others.
One should avoid association with those who are procrastinating and have similar dispositions; one should always give to ascetics and to devotees of Śiva, and not otherwise.

One should not study the scriptures of the materialists (paśu-śāstra), and one should avoid the doctrine of elemental spirits (bhūta-vāda). One must always practice compassion toward all beings, as well as grant them fearlessness.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a merit greater than fearlessness;
indeed, the gift of fearlessness is the true gift, whereas the Cāndrāyaṇa and other such rites are not.
O Nāmana, that bath which consists of not harming and avoiding the service of snakes is the supreme knowledge for the wise: non-violence toward all living beings.
All sacrifices, sacred fords, austerities, observances,
vows, gifts, worship, fire-offerings, and the like do not equal even a sixteenth part of this.
O son of the Kṛttikās, there is indeed no ornament greater than the granting of fearlessness;
therefore, living beings must not be harmed in this scripture, the Kālasūtra.
This ritual procedure for Gaurī has been told to you in brief;
it must never be given to those who have not received initiation, nor to those who are not devoted.
Thus ends the chapter on the Gaurī-yāga in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
I shall explain the Mṛtyuñjaya [mantra] according to the prescribed ritual sequence:
having formed a triangle with half the area of a square, one should reduce it by three units from the square.
One should have the pitcher made circular, provided with a mouth and filled with fragrant substances;
one should cause the western door to face it, for its opening indeed faces the west.
The pedestal should be fashioned facing the east, prepared with the syllable *jyaṃ*;
then, one should project the form upon the pericarp using the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*).
One should establish the supreme reality by means of the three-syllabled mantra *oṃ juṃ sa*;
then, with the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should display the water-pot mudrā (*kumbhamudrā*).
O son, by this oblation, the subduing of obstacles arises;
it conquers death for all those who are constantly endowed with devotion.
Alternatively, O son of Kṛttikā, the sacrifice should be performed upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
the preceptor constitutes one form, and the reciter of the weapon-mantra is the third.
All [the practitioners] should wear white garments and perform worship to the deities of the sacrifice;
they should properly recite the mantra ten thousand times and likewise commence the fire-oblation (homa).
One should offer oblations of milk, dūrvā grass, clarified butter, amṛtā, punarnavā, milk-rice, sacrificial cakes, and fuel-sticks made from milky trees.
Four-faced and four-armed, situated in the center of a lunar disc,
holding a vase with two hands and adorned with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Having meditated with effort on [the deity] whose entire body is like camphor powder and whose form is perfumed by flower garlands, one should then display the mudrās.
Placing the beautiful fist of the right hand upon the palm of the left hand is known as the Kumbha mudrā; its efficacy is equal to a hundred recitations of the Koṣṭha mantra.
Thus, one should recite this mantra day after day to the God who removes death;
for him, there shall be health, nourishment, sovereignty, prosperity, long life, and sons.
The medicinal herb used at the beginning of a sacrifice is supreme in the procedure for elixirs (rasāyana);
it is celebrated as "Mṛtyuñjaya" (the Conqueror of Death), the foremost destroyer of death and disease.
Thus ends the chapter on Mṛtyuñjaya in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
The five Lords of Vows (Vrateśvaras) are traditionally known; for them, a five-day period is supreme.
That mandala, which increases prosperity, has been described in detail.
I have previously described the faces beginning with Īśāna,
which constitute the limbs of the Sakala form as well as those of the one enriched by Kalās.
The Brahmans have briefly declared that for one who has mastered the mantras and is intent on the destruction of suffering, the lips are indeed like a vessel.
And among these very [deities], one should perform the fivefold worship with devotion;
up until the limit of Śuddhavidyā, one should place the seat upon the Praṇava (Om).
Their worship, however, should be performed according to the previous sequence;
[one should meditate on] Īśāna, three-eyed and with the luster of a pure kunda flower, in the central lotus.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Lord, the destroyer of the suffering of those who bow to him, holding a water-pot and honoring with his hand a rosary of beads.
One should place a man, red as saffron, upon a lotus in the east;
he holds a trident and the gesture of fearlessness in his hands, bestowing fearlessness upon all living beings.
He has one face and three eyes, is formidable and black in luster,
adorned with a garland of skulls, and bearing a sword and a shield.
On the southern lotus, one should worship Aghora, the destroyer of terrors,
who resembles the flower of the pomegranate and possesses the luster of hibiscus and vermilion.
One should place the god Vāmadeva, who holds a blue lotus and is honored by a citron in his hand,
upon a lotus in the northern direction.
The Lord is white as a snowy cloud, three-eyed, all-pervading, and two-armed;
he holds a spear and a bow, is gentle and serene, and possesses beautiful eyes.
Meditating upon Sadyojāta, who has the luster of a jasmine flower, situated on the lotus of Varuṇa;
they have two arms, one face, three eyes, and are seated in the midst of a lotus.
The lord of practitioners should meditate upon them, situated in the directions with their respective colors;
he should then recollect them as having three, five, or ten eyes, and twelve arms.
One should fashion their faces according to their respective castes;
thus the Lords of Vows (Vrateśvaras) have been described, and they are to be worshipped as before.
For each individual face, one should perform a hundred-fold recitation;
likewise, one should satisfy [the deity] with an offering of sesame seeds a hundred times eight hundred times.
Having gratified and prostrated before Śiva, one should offer them the vow;
the offering of matted locks (jaṭā) to Īśāna must be performed with great care.
One should present the staff and the loincloth to Puruṣa;
the receptacle for ashes to Aghora; and the alms-bowl always to Uttara.
One should diligently enter the Brahmadaṇḍa through the Sadyojāta [face];
and having offered the vow, there is dismissal by means of each respective [mantra].
One should cast away that which was done for the removal of matted locks at the sacred bathing place;
one should display the eight mudrās in their proper sequence upon each face.
Having bestowed the mudrās in due order, their dismissal should likewise be performed step by step;
thus has been described the sequential dismissal of the Lords of the Vows.
Having performed this, one should then carry out the mounting and other rites as approved for the specific species.
Thus ends the chapter on Vrateśvara in the Kālottara Mahātantra.
The Lord said:
The abode of the Guru for the accomplishment of spiritual attainments.
At the time of the wedding procession, upon seeing an evil or bad dream,
one should likewise perform the mantra-ritual with those [deities] obtained in the dream.
The *yogapīṭha* (seat of yoga), measuring thirty-six finger-breadths, should be placed in front;
having mentally conceived the food upon it, one should diligently worship the form with incense, perfumes, and other offerings using the *hṛdayamantra*.
Having recited the Śiva-mantra one hundred and eight times, one should likewise perform the fire sacrifice (homa),
after meditating upon the Guru and prostrating before him again and again.
And with hands placed upon the village, he should say again after the initiation:
"O God, I perform this mandala before you for the sake of Parameṣṭhin."
O Lord, by your grace, may I obtain that through which this ritual procedure has been accomplished;
it has been taught by you, O Guru, in the supreme Śiva doctrine.
Then, whether the Guru is present or not, one should worship him as before;
having diligently obtained his permission, one should then commence the ritual action.
Thus ends the chapter on the Guru-yāga in the Kālottara Mahātantra.
The Lord said:
O Destroyer of Krauñca, I shall declare in brief the occasions when study is forbidden:
the full moon, the new moon, the eighth day, the fourteenth day, the sixth day, and both the first days of the lunar fortnights.
During the Vyatīpāta yoga, at the sun's passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti), as well as during the three Aṣṭakā festivals,
and especially when there is thunder at twilight, a lightning strike, or a preternatural glow in the quarters of the sky.
When a sage has died, when a perfected being (siddha) has died, when a great king has died,
when drinking [the water] of the Tārakolkā [comet], and when there is the appearance of a smoke-bannered fire (dhūmaketu);
In the case of mist, a strong wind, or unseasonable rain,
as well as when a *hakala*, a branch, a *māṇḍūka* frog, or a cat intervenes [between the moon and the observer].
During an *anadhyāya* (period when study is forbidden), one should perform the offering and worship for three nights;
likewise during an eclipse of the moon or sun, and similarly when there is a thunderbolt strike or an earthquake.
In the rite of ascending the purifier (pavitrārohaṇa), there are seven acts to be performed, namely giving gifts and worship.
Now I shall describe other characteristics; understand them in brief.
In the crush of ascetics, in the destruction born of yoga,
in the presence of a wicked or cruel king, and likewise upon seeing those who are deformed or one-eyed.
He [is used] in the sense of "distant," "welcome," "desired," and in reference to cattle, kings, and garments.
In the Kṣaṇika, Aṅga, Gīta, Vāṃti, and likewise in the Uttara [Tantras], all [periods] are to be known as non-study; worship should be understood to be of two kinds.
Thus ends the chapter on non-study in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
111a) Īśvara said:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme Pavitrārohaṇa,
which is established as a limb of initiation (dīkṣā), and is eternal, consisting of the threefold nature.
For men, that which is deficient in substance, mantra, and ritual action is fruitless;
therefore, they say that the *pavitrārohaṇa* is indeed an obligatory constituent part [of the rite].
It has indeed been stated that the purificatory rite (*pavitraka*) performed by one who is exceedingly fierce is most excellent;
therefore, it should be performed at the proper time as previously taught by the Supreme Lord (*Parameṣṭhin*).
By that, the year-long worship clearly becomes complete for one who worships the Supreme Lord with devotion for even a single day.
O Śikhidhvaja, I am unable to describe the fruit of its merit;
it was in the past worshipped even by the mind of the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Upendra.
Having propitiated that supreme state, who then would not worship it? [End of the Previous Chapter; here, however, 111b] * * * * * * * * * *
One should fashion them with effort;
the knots of the *liṅgas* must be made according to the distinction of the principles (*tattva*), for otherwise they are not beneficial.
I shall now explain the attainment of whichever reality belongs to whom,
whether by means of the principles (tattva), phonemes (varṇa), digits (kalā), mantras, words (pada), or likewise by worlds (bhuvana).
One should fashion knots for the purifiers according to that same number;
from one finger-breadth up to the end of the hand, they should extend according to the sequence of pervasion.

One should prescribe the deposition of the principles (tattva-nyāsa), beginning from the earth up to primordial nature (prakṛti). In this manner, for the hand-liṅgas, [the deposition extends] from the Puruṣa up to Śiva.
The *tattvanyāsa* has been fully explained; its application is prescribed for the installation.
Having determined the dimensions according to the size of the *liṅga*, one should likewise prepare the sacred thread and the sacrificial altar (*sthaṇḍila*).
In the case of a variegated image or a linga made of fragrant substances, it is beneficial to apply that [ointment] as a wick;
or one should fashion it to the size of a cubit within a water-pot, in water, or in fire.
The third [liṅga] among the liṅgas is designated as Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman;
its circumference at the top of the liṅga is exactly like that of the Ātman.
The width of that which consists of knowledge is likewise [determined], excluding two parts;
therefore, the sacred thread called Śiva is deficient by those two parts.
From the top of the head down to the pedestal, the area for all the deities of the fourth [layer] should be divided by one hundred and eight, or by half of that, or again by half of that.
112a) Three [recitations] should be offered at the head for all, granting all accomplishments;
or else, a triad should be performed daily with one hundred and eight [recitations].
Three [types of] works should be performed with wealth acquired by one's own effort, using either half or a quarter [of that income].
Thus, for those possessing manifest signs (vyaktaliṅga), it is beneficial exactly as it is made manifest.

The increase for the threads shall be ten or twelve [per cubit] from a length of ten cubits; the shadow at the end of the clearly defined thread is determined by the measure of five, four, and four [cubits].
Just as there is a purifier for the unmanifest, so too is there one beneficial for the manifest and unmanifest;
the fourth purifier extends from the head down to the knees.
The fourth [element] extends as far as the pedestal (pīṭha) from Śiva down to the domain of Kālāgni;
one should arrange three, two, or five [of these elements] within the manifest (vyakta).
From this [thread], one should take a single portion, and immediately thereafter a large portion;
then two necks of thread, or two, or one, joined with nine strands.
Likewise, one [should offer] to one's own form, to the host of the Guru’s brothers,
and to Caṇḍīśa and Kṣetrapāla, together with the nine Lokapālas and Vasus.
Likewise, for the bell and the rosary, the purificatory thread (pavitra) should be four finger-breadths long;
one should always cause the vessels and other items to be wrapped with three strands.
The fire for the household emblems should be placed; there should be the abandonment of those things made of clay.
With the *śruk* and *śruva* ladles, there is the application of the *yatra*; on the cloth mat, there are the two yoga-bands.
The abandonment of canopies and water-vessels is prescribed;
however, having wrapped them with a thread, they should be taken to one's own home or to a temple of Śiva.
Thus, having performed the preparatory rites, one should commence the daily rituals;
therein, at the outset, one should worship the Sun according to the prescribed rule as a daily rite.
Having offered the fragrant purifier (gandhapavitra) therein, one should indeed cause [the deity] to enter the chest;
having worshipped the lords of the doors, one should then drive away the obstacles within the womb (garbha) in due order.
One should cast the flower with the *śivāśinī* mantra like an iron arrow into the center of the house;
one must enter through the western door and not by any other.
Following the sequence of the *tālāpārṣṇi* footstep, while recollecting the weapon-mantra,
one should place the weapon-mantra in the directions and perform the veiling with the armor-mantra.

First, one should perform the purification of the elements through meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās), as well as the ritual of making oneself complete (sakalīkaraṇa); then the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) and the external sacrifice, followed by the preparation of the offering water (argha) with mantras.

One should prepare the eightfold vessel for the arghya offering and perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana) and other rites; the demarcation of the ground should be performed by binding it according to the method seen in the scriptures.
The purification of substances by means of burning and sprinkling with nectar should be performed;
furthermore, the sprinkling of the materials should be done with the water from the arghya vessel.
Having performed the striking with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra), sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is beneficial;
one should perform the nourishing rite (āpyāyana) and display the cow-mudrā (dhenumudrā).
113a) One should worship all the Gaṇeśas in due order in the northwest;
and having worshipped the Guru in the northeast with excrement, flowers, and so forth, in sequence.
Then, one should worship the Pāśupatas in the northeast corner;
afterwards, one should cause the scattering of parched grain, white mustard seeds, and other such items.
Having worshipped the pitcher in the northeast according to the sequence from the rakshasa to the monkey in the ten directions, one should place the setting sun situated in front of it.
Having worshipped with flowers, perfumes, unbroken rice, food offerings, and confectionery preparations, and having paid obeisance while forming the mudrās as before;
One should place the world-protectors within the jars according to the sequence starting from the east;
having diligently worshipped them with devotion using perfumes, lamps, and other offerings.
One should place Vitkrama in the southwest and Kamalodbhava in the north;
then, one should provide an uninterrupted stream [of water] into the jars until the end.
Having covered the Śiva-kumbha behind the Śastra-kumbha,
the Guru should, by the command of Śiva, instruct the world-protectors.
For the sake of protecting the sacrifice and for the destruction of obstacles,
you must remain armored upon your respective mounts and with your weapons ready for the welfare of Śiva.
Then, one should place a water-pot (karkarī) upon the back of the scattered [grains];
one should then construct a perimeter wall using ashes, white mustard seeds, and darbha grass.
After performing the extensive rites of worship,
one should display the mudrās; thereafter, one should bathe the liṅga.
Everything should be performed according to the previously stated method, exactly as it has been described.
Therein, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with the mantras both individually and collectively;
the suppression (nirodha), however, should be performed right there with the Niṣṭhuramudrā.
Having paid homage to the remaining fire situated in the pit, one should dismiss it;
thereafter, the scraping of the pit must be performed day after day.
One should avoid generating the Śiva-fire; one should deposit there whatever has been consecrated within the belly in that temple of Śiva.
One should perform the ritual dismissal (visarjana), or else one should cause a fast (laṅghana) to be undertaken;
furthermore, a single mandala should be prepared on the outside using the dung of a tawny cow (kapilā).
One should cause [the disciple] to consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and having sipped water for purification, one should touch him;
[he should eat] millet prepared with milk and drenched in ghee and sugar-candy.
Having offered the sacrificial porridge (caru) accompanied by the two libations (āghāra),
one who is pure should then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and subsequently prepare the tooth-stick (daṇḍakāṣṭha).
Having sipped water, touched [the body], and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) as before,
one should ascend a bed of kuśa grass with the head directed toward the northeast.
At night, one should keep a vigil with various dances, such as the *toṭya* and others;
then, having risen at dawn and performed the ritual bath as before, [one should proceed].
One should constantly perform [the rite] according to the ritual actions seen in the ancient scriptures;
special worship must be performed, and the libation to the fire must be offered.
One should place the Sūtras of Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman, as well as the Fourth (Turya), into the pitcher; then, with the Astra-mantra, one should offer them into the Karkarī vessel after the Lord.

Having recited the mantra one hundred and eight times over the sacred thread, which is joined with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings and consecrated by Śiva, one should place it upon the head of Śiva.
It should be given by way of emanation, resembling a wave of nectar;
that which consists of the Vidyā is half of that, while the Pavitraka known as the "quarter" is a quarter of that.
Those seeking liberation should perform the Cāturmāsya rite in reverse order, wherein the practice consists of the Self-knowledge that is Śiva, and the vow likewise consists of the nature of Śiva.
Or else, according to one's own capacity, material beings should perform this supreme vow for two months,
or for a fortnight, or even for seven days.
Having removed the *pavitraka*, one should place it in a clean location;
then, at the conclusion of the worship, one should place the *liṅga* upon one's head.
Having diligently applied the purifying thread day after day,
all rites such as worship and fire-offerings should be performed twice at the conclusion of the vow.
To rectify any deficiency or excess, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with a sword;
