then one should offer the vow to Śambhu, saying: "O Lord, let that which resides in my heart [be fulfilled]."
One who desires liberation should offer [the ritual] to Śiva without personal desire;
thereafter, the preceptor, the practitioners, and others should perform the worship properly.
One should worship other devotees of Śiva, as well as one's own family circle,
with gold, land, goods, and vehicles, according to one's capacity.
Artisans, slaves, laborers, and female servants who subsist by their work—
these lords of men should be honored with effort by a wise person.
"May Sadāśiva be gracious; may all rites be fulfilled.
At the conclusion of the Pavitrārohaṇa, one should perform the Caṇḍayāga.

Having worshipped according to the previously mentioned procedure within the city endowed with the Vedas, one should perform the rites beginning with the preparation, taking recourse to the northeast direction.
Having worshipped him with devotion as if he were Śiva, one should thereafter perform the avabhṛtha rite;
that merit which exists in all sacrifices and that fruit which is found in all sacred fords [is obtained thereby].
Whatever merit is found in all acts of giving, and whatever fruit is found in all forms of austerity—
that fruit is obtained multiplied ten millionfold through the consecration.
All obstacles perish, as do planetary afflictions and diseases,
as well as the harms caused by Vināyakas, Kṛtyās, Khākhodakas, and the like.
All those [sins] go to ashes through the power of this bath;
and one should honor the preceptor and the gods with offerings according to one's ability.
Having paid homage to the most excellent gurus with the sound of musical instruments and drums,
one then attains the desired fruit through the rite of the sacred thread investiture (*pavitrārohaṇa*).
Thus ends the chapter on the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrārohaṇa*) in the *Kālottara-mahātantra*.
The Lord said:
Practitioners and others established on the path who have abandoned right conduct fall to a lower state;
therefore, one must observe the conduct spoken by Śiva.
Whatever fault has arisen through fate, negligence, or delusion—
[one should remedy it] by means of ritual bathing, the Jaya-fast, burnt offerings, and water-pots (gaḍḍukas).
O Mahāsena, having understood the strength and weakness of karma through self-restraint, one should offer the gift of the five products of the cow, which destroys impurity and misdeeds.
When the body is in extreme pain, likewise during fear of thieves or kings,
during the danger of fire or water, and furthermore during the period of birth-impurity (sūtaka).
In the case of the guru, the deity, and the fire-ritual, a constant omission does not entail fault;
for Śiva has declared that this applies eternally to both the initiate (samayin) and the spiritual son (putraka).
Whether his own or another’s, the practitioner should perform the three daily rites (nitya, etc. for both himself and the Guru, while remaining established in the stream [of consciousness].
The guru is to be worshipped with devotion, but one should not employ him in ritual action;
likewise, if one's own guru has been engaged in a rite of expiation or a daily rite.
In that case, an expiation must be performed consisting of one hundred thousand oblations to the Dakṣiṇāgni fire.
Therefore, with every effort, one should not employ one's own guru [for such a rite].
One who is the brother of one's own guru, and especially the son of the guru.
By granting them permission, however, they are purified by the Lakṣapāda rite;
likewise, the Pavitrārohaṇa should be performed at the conclusion of the initiation itself.
If one abandons an unworthy son of the guru and appoints another,
his initiation is indeed fruitless, and he goes downward for a great kalpa.
One should never, even in one's mind, ascend a high seat belonging to the guru;
nor should one use his bed, sandals, or couch for sleeping.
One is purified from speaking unvirtuous words, from charcoal-like [deeds], as well as from deception such as guile,
and from being childless, by means of a formidable recitation and likewise by eating only at night.
Having transgressed the command of the Guru, one is not purified otherwise than by [reciting] twenty thousand [mantras];
therefore, one should diligently worship the Guru with prostrations and the scattering of flowers.
By prostrating at the feet of the Guru, one obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows;
such a Guru is of noble birth, engaged in his own duties, and devoted to the study of the scriptures.
Free from egoism, avoiding the wives of others,
solely intent upon the pure path, and endowed with both gentleness and courtesy.
Free from censuring others, devoted to sentient beings, firm in his vows,
having crossed over the observances of knowledge, he is bathed and intent upon the accomplishment of siddhi.
Fearless, pure in soul, and affectionate toward the devotees of Śiva—
a teacher of such a nature is to be sought; one who is the opposite is inauspicious.
The Guru is declared to be like a father; the preceptor (deśika) and others are to be propitiated.
Likewise, the teacher (ācārya), the elder brother, and the spiritual practitioner (sādhaka) are to be propitiated.
A fellow initiate is said to be a kinsman, and one who is beneficial is like a brother;
one should conceive of each subsequent person as being progressively higher than the preceding one.
The householder and the celibate student are established in two ways regarding expiation;
I shall explain that for the materialist, and especially for the lifelong student.

Each [type of purification] is twofold, distinguished by being either with desire (sakāma) or free from desire (niṣkāma). However, the purification for one who is free from desire is considered to be twice that for one who acts with desire.
That purification which has been proclaimed for desire pertaining to the elements was also declared by Kapardin as the purification for one who is established in freedom from desire.

But for one who desires [results], she should be worshipped twice as often by following the sequence of daily rites and so forth; Maheśvarī should be worshipped either once a day or three times a day.
At the time of morning, at midday, and during the eighth watch, when the sun has set,
worship should never be performed.
Just as with the planets, it is likewise for practitioners:
if the one-day worship is omitted, one should recite the mantra a thousand times while offering the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
If a collision occurs due to negligence, the expiation for unintentional action should be performed;
for intentional action, it should be doubled, and the worship [should likewise] be doubled.
From divine affliction, as well as from delusion, from disease, and likewise from fear of kings.
Due to these defects, it is unintentional; however, the remainder of what is to be known is intentional.
[The duration] is from one day up to a limit of seven days.
Therefore, one should increase the offerings, fire-oblations, and other rites by three hundred each,
from the eleventh day onwards until the rite is completed on the twelfth.

For that long, the knower of mantras should destroy the three southern limits; for the sake of the upright and the virtuous, he should perform the recitation of the Aghora mantra for a year, ten thousand, or a million times, or until the end of ten months, performing the ritual transformation.
If the *homa* is omitted, one should prescribe an expiation in exactly this same manner. The worship performed on the eighth day and subsequent days is proclaimed to be twofold [in merit].
If that [pavitrārohaṇa] is omitted, the expiation must always be fourfold;
furthermore, the pavitrārohaṇa performed during the three months beginning with Āṣāḍha [is essential].
118b) Two hundred thousand [recitations] for Aghora; likewise, one becomes pure through the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One should always avoid worship, the twilight prayers, recitation, fire-offerings, and indigestion.
He who performs [the rite] out of negligence should recite the *dakṣiṇa* [mantra] a thousand times;
he who is distressed by the arrival of [adversity] should recite the *dakṣiṇa* joined with ten thousand [times].
But during the twilight dalliance, one becomes pure by reciting the Sadyojāta mantra once for every hundred [acts].
It is declared that for an act committed unintentionally, the penance is as described; for an intentional act, one should perform double.
That which is prescribed for a student (bhautika) is doubled for one who has taken the final vows (naiṣṭhika).
A fourfold [penance] is prescribed for one who has attained steadfastness in desire;
where one recites the *japa* a thousand times with two,
three, or more repetitions, that expiation which he is capable of performing himself is difficult to accomplish.
Furthermore, brothers, kinsmen, and friends must perform double the penance;
however, the penance arising from a preceptor must be performed by the preceptor or his son.
O Mahāsena, one should not perform [the ritual] oneself, but rather have it performed by others;
likewise, one should consume fruits, roots, flowers, and food, or cause them to be gathered.
At the beginning of each [rite], the Guru should first bestow [the protection] and afterwards apply it to himself;
this is for the sake of general protection against the sword [of obstacles], and furthermore, for the purpose of expiation and other such rites.
O son of Pārvatī, one's own mantra must not be employed for all purposes indiscriminately.
One should not perform the rites of the Gāruḍa or Bhūta-karma out of greed or delusion;
however, he who performs them through negligence, being pure and joined with the face of Dakṣa, [is purified].
Those who revile the guru among the initiates, spiritual sons, and others,
should depart far from that place and recite the Sadyojāta mantra a hundred times.
One should not commit adultery through action, mind, or speech;
if one should act out of delusion, purification comes through half a lakh of recitations.
O Six-faced One, for a maiden, the penance must be double; likewise among other castes, if someone eats [forbidden food] unknowingly and it is discovered afterwards.
Food and other items touched by intoxicating liquors such as *madirā* and *āsava*, or those originating from semen, urine, or feces, or those pecked at or licked by crows and dogs;
One should likewise avoid a crow, as well as contact with jackals, monkeys, and cocks;
one should also abandon food that has been touched by such beings or defiled by the remnants of the food of Śūdras and others.
But having eaten the food of those whose food should not be eaten, or having had intercourse with another's wife,
one should bathe, fast for a day and night, and then perform the rite of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One who practices the thirty-two syllables one thousand times at each twilight,
eating only at night for three days, bathing three times a day, and remaining intent on meditation;
Alternatively, on the fourth day, one should perform a thousand oblations of that which is to be given.
Having given food as before, he is then purified by eating only at night;
thus is the rule prescribed for the king who has his mind focused solely on Śiva.
The bath for a Vaiśya is declared to be threefold, while that for a Śūdra is proclaimed to be once;
for all of them, it is ordained that if done intentionally, the rite should be performed twice.

Having bathed, one should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), each prepared in a hundredfold measure, for three nights; meanwhile, one should practice the recitation of the thirty-two-syllable mantra.
The accumulation of his great sins—
such as theft, sexual union with another's wife, the drinking of liquor, and so forth— is utterly destroyed.
Having intentionally killed Brahmins, one should recite the Aghora mantra while standing in the midst of cows;
this [purifies] for two years, provided one is well-restrained.
Eating only what is offered, bathing three times a day, and always performing the ritual placement (nyāsa),
he should then go to a sacred field of Śiva at the end of two years.
Therein, one should perform a vow according to one's capacity, such as the Kṛcchra or Cāndrāyaṇa at times;
at the conclusion of the vow, initiation (dīkṣā) should be received as before, and the worship of the five lotuses (pañcābja) should be performed as before.
One should give all one's possessions to the guru, as well as to the deśika and the ācārya;
however, having drunk liquor, one must perform a special act of vomiting.
For three days, one should drink hot water mixed with ghee while performing the *ghora* recitation;
having reached a temple of Śiva, one should recite it thirty thousand times for each of the three [days].
Or, having intentionally committed theft of gold, silver, or the like,
one should remain in a secluded place with a concentrated mind, reciting [the mantra] fifty thousand times.
One should recite the mantra of Bahurūpa thirty thousand times; otherwise, one is not pure.
Purity in worship and in the fire-sacrifice is attained by subsisting on milk, roots, and fruits.
One should renounce this wealth again at will and perform it;
in its absence, one should perform twice as much of the previously mentioned recitation (japa).
There is no atonement for approaching the wife of a guru,
nor for [approaching] a preceptor or a practitioner who observes the Śiva-vow.
However, for those [offenses], purification occurs through the recitation of one hundred thousand times as previously stated,
provided that no blood is seen upon the striking with a staff or similar punishment.
The practitioner of mantra is purified by half of that [penance];
thereafter, he should request [forgiveness] and perform the heating rite (tāpana), even if he has unintentionally eaten food touched by a woman in her menses.
One is purified by recitation accompanied by fasting; it is not otherwise.
For an intentional act, purification comes through bathing and performing oblations, which must be performed twice as much.
If one should eat anything oneself without first giving it to the Supreme Lord,
or to the Guru, through negligence, one should likewise recite the *tryaṣṭa-śata* (one hundred and twenty-four) [mantras].
Whether during a death-impurity or a birth-impurity, or if one has eaten during such impurity,
one should intentionally recite the terrible weapon-mantra a thousand times.
The food of a group, the food of a courtesan, and likewise that of those who have fallen [from their caste];
and furthermore, at the parting of the hair ceremony, the eye-opening ceremony, and the naming ceremony.
At the time of the first feeding of solid food (annaprāsana), one should eat and recite five hundred [mantras];
likewise for one who is about to pass away, after having eaten [the funeral meal] and so forth.
Starting from the immediate *śrāddha*, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times on the right side;
whether done intentionally or unintentionally, if it concerns a *śūdra*, it is fourfold.
At a tree, a grove, a large pond, a well, a lotus-pool, or a temple of Śiva;
and during a marriage, the rite of releasing a bull, or the gift of cows—one should recite [the mantra] one hundred times.
When one eats meat or other such things out of ignorance or through favor,
one shall attain purification by reciting the Aghora mantra ten thousand times.
Due to the failure to observe the rules regarding sexual intercourse, food, and drink,
one is purified by half of the penance prescribed for the three acts of anointing the body, bathing, and wearing clothes.

Purification for the loss of food, drink, or enjoyments shall be performed with five hundred [repetitions]; for one who breaks the vow of sleeping on the ground, he should recite the Astra-mantra one hundred times.
But when the affliction caused by planets, spirits, piśācas, and the like has been severed,
one who is pure from various impurities should recite the Aghora mantra three hundred times.

121a) Having performed rites for pacification and nourishment, one becomes pure after three hundred [days] due to confinement or the death of a relative; however, in the case of birth-impurity, one is purified without the performance of worship.
The expiation for those established in the Śiva-dharma has been declared;
as has that for those established in the worldly dharma (loka-dharma) when a death-impurity occurs or when worship is performed.
The internal sacrifice (antaryāga) should likewise be performed by those who know it;
having performed rites such as eradication (uccāṭana), one should remain pure through the Aghora mantra.
A practitioner of mantras should never perform the killing of anyone by means of a mantra;
rather, having performed the consecration of deities and initiation in the three types of sacred sites and so forth, [he should proceed].
Purification from the Aghora [mantra] occurs after ten thousand recitations; one becomes pure by fasting.
For the sake of the *paṭṭakāpyā*, there should be a binding of silk, wool, or *muñja* grass, reaching up to the head.
Wherever a gift of leather has been accepted,
one must especially recite three hundred [mantras] of the Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Milk, curd, and ghee, as well as honey, meat, and the like; salt, oil, pungent substances, and various fragrances.
Then, by reciting three hundred [times] of this very [mantra], one is purified;
likewise, silver, gems, gold, coral, and pearls [are purified].
A bull among cows, an elephant, a woman, or a horse— the best of these is the one who is beautiful,
resides in a temple of Śiva, possesses many forms, is endowed with all qualities, and is pure.
O Six-faced One, even when there is a mixture of many sins, one should perform a recitation of at least half a lakh [of mantras] for the acceptance of a monastery.
Then, by reciting the thirty-two-syllable mantra,
one shall attain purification from the fault of mixing food as well as from the mixing of vessels.

One becomes pure by reciting the *Maghara* mantra three hundred times for [stealing] wood, a *pala* of grass, and so forth; for ten thousand [repetitions], one is purified from the confusion of wombs.

In the case of killing a living being by means of sweating, or even when it is killed unintentionally, one should recite the mantra one hundred times for each creature; however, if done without desire [for the result], half of that number is required.
For killing a rat, [the penance is] one hundred [times]; for a cat, it is one thousand;
for killing a female jackal, it is likewise; and for a monkey or a cock, it is double.
For killing snakes or birds, as well as insects such as worms;
for killing lions and other wild beasts, or goats and other livestock; [one must perform penance].
Likewise, if one is bitten out of negligence by a sister, a jackal, or the like, or by a serpent, one should indeed recite the Catuḥśatāstra of Bahurūpa.
Having bathed with white water, one should also recite the Astra and Aghora mantras;
[one may then dwell] together with one's own people, Mlecchas, Cāṇḍālas, Buddhists, and Kāpālikas.
If one touches a tree from a cremation ground with the heart-mantra of Vāk-kasa-syasadya,
one should perform a bath with one's clothes on and recite [the mantra] one hundred times over the right [hand].
When there is throbbing on the left side, as well as upon seeing a bad dream,
upon thinking of something undesirable, and upon the sound of untruth being proclaimed; 121a)
Through action, mind, and speech, one should mutter the *hṛdaya* mantra a thousand times.
If semen or the like is emitted while one is sleeping unintentionally,
one should bathe along with one's clothes and then recite the Astra-mantra one hundred times.
In the case of an abortion due to desire, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times on the third day;
by giving a cow as a gift, however, one is purified by half a lakh [recitations].
A pure person reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times should give a hundred cows;
however, if he eats in the row of a Śūdra even once intentionally, he becomes pure by reciting it ten thousand times.
If one causes distress to practitioners and others through action, mind, or speech,
one should act in such a way that some degree of remorse arises.
Having previously observed a three-night fast and being purified, he who, endowed with the thirty-two syllables,
should void excrement or urine in a temple;

In a temple of the gods, in Rāma’s presence, and especially in a sacred field of Śiva, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred times; for a specific desire, it should be recited twice as many times, whereby one becomes pure.
Having intentionally or unintentionally killed a woman, a Śūdra, or a child,
one is purified by reciting the Ghoramantra twenty thousand times or eighty thousand times.
For a twice-born man, there shall be no eligibility for performing rites for ten days;
for a king (Kṣatriya), it is twelve days, and likewise fifteen for a Vaiśya.
A Śūdra who has undergone the initiation for Nirvāṇa should diligently suspend his recitation and meditation for one month;
however, for those who have received the initiation for Nirvāṇa, no birth-impurity (sūtaka) exists at all.
For them, there exists the birth-impurity (sūtaka) according to the worldly initiation;
where there is no cutting of the top-knot (śikhā), that initiation is considered merely worldly.
The internal sacrifice (antaryāga) must be performed even by worldly initiates;
recitations, circumambulations, and other rites should be performed with diligent effort.
Furthermore, if one belonging to one's own caste consumes the leavings of one who has been initiated, due to the mixture of impure remnants,
one should bathe and recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having eaten at the house of an artisan or similar person, or when establishing a pond or a garden,
as well as having eaten with other ascetics (liṅgins), one should recite the Dakṣiṇa [mantra] a thousand times.
The student (brahmacārī) and the householder (gṛhastha) are those whose food may be eaten; the other two [the forest-dweller and the ascetic] are never [to be so] anywhere.
However, for the forest-dweller and the ascetic, one should recite the mantra as before while facing south.
But for a twice-born man who has broken his vow of fasting while engaged in such recitation, he is most sinful; by the loss of yoga, he has set himself upon the path of his gurus.
Another wicked-souled person may give [the gift], yet both of them shall go to hell;
this applies to all types of mixed marriages for the sake of mental purification.
The non-terrible mantra (aghoramantra) should be recited until the mind becomes serene;
after the recitation, through the practice of visiting sacred sites and the yoga of worshiping Śiva.
By the offering of water-pots, by the oblation of sesame seeds and clarified butter,
by the presence of the preceptor, and by the recitation of the Saṃhitā;
By serving the gods, cows, and the twice-born, one leads away hundreds of sins;
like the sun freed from clouds, one thus shines resplendent in the world.
Therefore, for the sake of removing the mass of sins, one should perform expiation;
Lokeśvara remains established for the sake of fame and peace at all times.
Thus ends the chapter on expiation in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
Therefore, I shall describe the penance for the linga, known as Śikhidhvaja;
for the linga is said to be of three kinds: the manifest (vyakta), the fearful (bhaya), and the artificial (kṛti).
No distinction should be made regarding gender with respect to the rules for expiation;
the reality is the same for all three, as established by the preceptor.
Regarding the cause for expiation, however, there is no distinction between the types of lingas;
know that the Lord of Sacrifice (Yāgeśvara) is the mobile one, and the second is the immobile one.
One should indicate that the linga is of two kinds: that which is established as pre-existent, and likewise that which is to be established;
the former is that which has been previously endowed with its beginning, while the latter exists without it.
Likewise, non-duality and the mark of duality are of two kinds;
the former is the uncommon [mark], while the other, excluding that, is the common [mark].
122b) When the transgression occurs through one's own eightfold signs, purification is for the offender; however, when the transgression is caused by another, purification is prescribed therein.
And for both one’s own chosen *liṅga* and the practitioner, there is purification here.

Offense is to be known as twofold: that committed by oneself and that committed by others. Each of these two types is further to be known as twofold, according to the distinction between intentional and unintentional.
That [initiate] is also to be known as twofold: the worldly (bhautika) and likewise the ultimate (naiṣṭhika).
The worldly is to be known as twofold: the preceptor (deśika) who is a Samayin and so forth.
The purification for those who have committed offenses against the *liṅga* is now described again:
if the *liṅga* is to be reinstalled after being moved, the purification must be twice as great as that for one that was merely fixed in place.
If the previously established [deity] is mobile, one should prescribe purification twice over;
if it is stable, purification is fourfold. One should prescribe purification for that which was previously established.
Likewise, when the offense is common, purification is declared to be twofold;
however, for that which is designated as both dual and non-dual, one should prescribe purification that is twice as much.

However, that purification which is considered double for each successive stage in the case of common [offenses] applies when one's own chosen *liṅga* has been violated or when it has been defiled by another.
They declare that for the sake of purification through expiation, the penance for one who acts with desire should be double that which was performed by oneself;
however, for one who is free from desire, it may be performed either by oneself or by another.
123a) O Śikhidhvaja, having understood [the fault] again and again, one must perform the expiation;
for the teacher, the purification is considered to be double that of the practitioners.
For those who have become materialists, however, purification is beneficial when performed twice;
for those of the castes and those outside the castes, if they are corrupt, there must be purification of the emblem.
Likewise, when the *liṅga* has been touched, listen now to the purification that precedes it:
the groups consist of the four castes, with the *naṭaka* and the supreme *vartaka*.

Purification occurs through sipping water (upasparśa) for the first group; the second group is considered to require bathing. The third group consists of crows and the like, for whom purification arises through a full bath.
The fourth, however, is the outcaste (svapaca) and others; he should enter the water with his clothes on.
O Mahāsena, by such contact, the fourfold aim of life is proclaimed [to be attained].
Furthermore, the measure of those defects residing in the *liṅga* is now stated,
upon the mere occurrence of which a man becomes liable to perform penance.
The first grave offense (pātaka) is declared to be stepping over the shadow of the Liṅga;
purification from this occurs by reciting the Aghora mantra three hundred times.
When the *liṅga* has been turned over, one becomes pure after a thousand [repetitions] from the *ghora* [mantra];
when the *liṅga* has rolled three or four times upon the surface of the earth.
Purification occurs after twenty thousand [years] when there is no rain; one becomes pure after one hundred thousand [years] when there is no falling of clouds.
But when a calamity has occurred, one should declare purification after two hundred thousand [years].
If it is not far off, purification shall occur through ten thousand (abhighāta);
upon touching with the foot or crossing over, one should declare purification after thirty thousand.
Likewise, Kapardin has stated that purification occurs upon contact with the dust of one's feet;
however, if the water is defiled, it requires thirty thousand recitations, whereas for two thousand recitations, it is purified by that water itself.

One becomes pure even without bathing a hundred thousand times by means of the *sūtra* and *sutrodaka* alone; however, purification from contact with blood, semen, or menstrual flow is declared to require bathing a hundred thousand times.
By touching water sprinkled from that [vessel], one becomes pure after two hundred thousand [steps] marked by the foot;
however, upon contact with feces, one becomes pure here by washing the foot with water after two hundred thousand [steps].
One should declare purification from falling into a pit for discarded flower offerings after one hundred thousand [repetitions];
and from falling into a pit of excrement, one is considered pure after one hundred and fifty thousand.

Purification occurs through uprooting for a stable [image], and through re-installation for one made of lac; however, for one residing in a human [temple], it occurs through the removal of the eager [defilement] when that which is devoid of eagerness has been abandoned.
If the *liṅga* is eager to fall from the hand, it is [the result of] ten thousand [repetitions];
if it falls by itself from the hand, it is one-sixteenth more than that.
But if [the image] is dropped from the hand while one is eager [to offer it], and the auspicious [liṅga] falls,
one becomes pure by measuring a cubit from the previously mentioned [distance], doubled.
If, after ten thousand [recitations], the luster does not diminish due to fire,
then when it has become devoid of luster, one should perform purification by discarding it after a hundred thousand [recitations].
Even when one is maimed, or has lost their luster, or falls into a river, a pit, or the like;
or when killed, destroyed, or fallen into a great abyss through negligence.
If the *liṅga* has been struck by one's own kinsmen, or carried off by vultures and crows,
or sprinkled by those slain by the king, by thieves, or by outcastes;
If [the thread] is touched by two opposing groups, its removal is prescribed;
however, one should carefully burn a hundred thousand [times] and then re-establish it in that same form.
Then the practitioner, having burnt away his sins, attains purity;
otherwise, he will certainly not be liberated, due to the possibility of deficiency in the ritual procedure.
In this very manner, one should undertake the expiation for the rosary;
however, for the *liṅga* and so forth, one should prescribe purification by means of half [the prescribed penance].
If the bell is struck with the foot during transgressions,
the preceptor who is conversant with the Tantra must prescribe an expiation equal to that for the Linga.
When the four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, who have not received Śiva-initiation,
touch their own chosen liṅga, they should perform an expiation.
Purification is declared to be achieved by one, two, three, four, or up to a hundred [repetitions].
If one's own chosen *liṅga* is seen by groups of fishermen through negligence,
the practitioner attains purification by [reciting] ten thousand [times]; otherwise, he is not pure.
If touched by a crow or similar bird, a man is purified by bathing together with a woman.
Purification from the sin of ten thousand Veda-recitations occurs when [the Linga] is defiled by Svapakas and the like;
likewise, when a Linga is touched [by such persons], it becomes pure through double that amount [of recitation].
If a *liṅga* is touched by those initiated in their own stream (*svaśrota*), one incurs no fault therein;
however, if the *liṅga* is touched through negligence by those following the Vāma or Dakṣiṇa paths, [there is a fault].
The mantra-practitioner is purified by ten thousand [repetitions] through the great bath (mahāsnāna), and not otherwise;
one should avoid contact with those who follow either the left-hand or right-hand path.
One becomes pure by bathing after touching one hundred [such persons], and by touching two hundred [who have committed] minor offenses;
however, one should avoid even the sight of those who are guilty of the five great sins (pātaka).
From ten thousand repetitions of conversation and the like, one becomes pure; from twenty thousand, one is purified by touch;
from a hundred thousand, there is purification from sharing a bed; and from a million, one is pure even through eating together.
From contact with Buddhists and Cārvākas, from censuring Śiva before others, and especially from corrupting the scriptures and associating with those who have fallen— these [are causes of loss].
One should avoid contact through effort, for one becomes pure by avoiding such contact; indeed, one should completely shun the company of Kaulikas and Apālikas.
124a) One should never engage in dispute with those who hold the five objects and the faces of time; likewise, one should avoid conversation and physical contact from afar.

Likewise, one should never engage in dispute with the teachers of the Sāṃkhya doctrine who maintain the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda), nor with those who are greedy for sacrificial victims.
One should completely avoid contact with Digambaras and Śvetāmbaras;
likewise, one should not even engage in conversation with Bhāgavatas.
But the deluded soul who forms an association with those who have abandoned [the path] undergoes fruitless exertion; he shall not attain that state of Śiva.
One should never harbor hatred nor ever engage in dispute;
for he who is gentle-natured shall attain purity through his union [with the truth].
One should recite the mantra fifty thousand times for the liṅga and perform the great ablution (mahāsnāna);
when one's own chosen deity has been worshipped, a great worship (mahāpūjā) consisting of twenty thousand [recitations] must be performed.
Where there is indeed a hundred-thousand-fold recitation (*lakṣajāpa*), there should be an offering of two thousand and eight hundred portions of milk, curd, ghee, and so forth, upon the ground.
The great bath (mahāsnāna) with fruits such as the *palā* and others is equal to that [of the previous offerings],
as is the bath with two thousand *jātī* and *pūga* fruits.
Likewise, it consists of *kakkola*, nutmeg (*jātī*), *punnāga*, and *śrīphala*;
joined with *raktāvartī*, it is endowed with a divine fragrance.
In that very same manner, one should fashion a large wick in front of Śiva.
The "Great Bathing" (mahāsnāna) is fully described; the "Great Worship" (mahāpūjā) is half of that.
For ten thousand [repetitions], one should prescribe a fast for each individual case.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with one-tenth of the recitation (japa), and the offering of water-pots (gaḍukā) with one-twentieth;
[one must observe] truthfulness, vows, celibacy, sleeping on the ground, and eating only at night.
Abandoning the anointing with oil, speaking the truth, and being intent on bathing—
these must indeed be performed by those skilled in the scriptures until the conclusion of the recitation.
Upon the completion of the expiation (prāyaścitta), one should worship the preceptors (deśikas) in due order;
then, one should satisfy them according to one's ability with land, gold, clothing, food, and other gifts.
When someone is unable to perform an expiation at any time,
it should be performed by others through prayer, and moreover, it must be done with double the prescribed effort.
A teacher who knows the mantras should neither be entreated nor need do anything at all;
rather, one should worship one's own teacher in the Śiva-scripture as if he were Śiva himself.
For children, the ignorant, the elderly, those who enjoy pleasures, those afflicted by disease,
women, and artisans and the like, no expiation is prescribed.
Therefore, among them, only the seedless initiation (nirbījikā-dīkṣā) should be performed, and no other;
for initiation alone, when devoid of conventional observances (samayācāra), is traditionally held to bestow liberation.
But that initiation is independent, whereas that which is dependent is conjoined with a seed-syllable.

When he is devoted to the worship of the Liṅga— whether out of devotion toward women and children, or even toward those who are very capable devotees, such as seed-givers and preceptors— then [he attains success].
When a transgression has occurred, one should cause the penance to be administered;
their purification by means of that penance is as previously stated for one-quarter [of the offense].
Special worship and gifts must be given; otherwise, one is not pure. However, if the fire-oblation (*homa*) is omitted, as it is with the *liṅga*, one should perform the penance.
If one fails to perform the *pavitraka* rite before the end of three months,
O Ghorā, one should recite [the mantra] two hundred thousand times and undergo purification by means of the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
O King, when the body is extremely afflicted, or likewise during fear of thieves or during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka), one need not perform worship; there is no great fault in this.

However, what is the mental task here? A practitioner (samayin) or a spiritual son (putraka) should worship with the voidnesses (śūnyatās), which accomplish all goals, using the appropriate [mantras].
That which is established in one's own stream is to be worshipped, not that belonging to the left or right;
one's own guru must not be appointed for rites such as worship and recitation.
The Guru is to be worshipped like Śiva, and the Preceptor (Deśika) again like a father;
the practitioners (Sādhakas) say they are always like sons, and [the disciples] like brothers.
Those who abide by their commitments like friends should be regarded as such by one desiring auspiciousness;
they should be employed for the sake of the truth, especially in the rite of consecration.
And in the practice of accomplishment, the practitioner should be applied in that manner according to their desired state;
whether one's own or another's, they may be employed in the worship of Śiva.
Neither the initiate nor the spiritual son should eat without having performed worship;
therefore, O God, after this point, one must perform worship when a corpse is present.
A housewife becomes *sūtakī* (impure due to childbirth) through connection with the birth; it is not otherwise.
One who eats another's food should stay far away at that time, but one who is fit for worship may enter.
O Knower of the Vedas, if one becomes impure due to birth-impurity (sūtaka) either from contact or otherwise,
even then one should perform the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) during that period of impurity.
The supreme Śiva is to be propitiated with prostrations, hymns of praise, and other such offerings,
once the purification of Māyā has been performed and the cutting of the topknot (śikhā) is completed.
For them, birth-impurity (sūtaka) and death-impurity (mṛtaka) do not apply regarding worship;
however, at the time of worshipping the Deity, droplets may fall upon their limbs.
O Six-faced One, the expiation should then be prescribed in due order:
from the feet up to the knees, the Sadyojāta mantra is recited seven times.
Then, by performing this according to the ritual rules, that practitioner becomes a pure man within cyclic existence.
(126a) If drops [of saliva] should fall from the knees down to the secret place, they must be wiped away.
Or by reciting it twenty-one times, one becomes pure through mere remembrance.
One should contemplate the thread of many forms emerging from the heart;
one should perform the ritual at the locations [of the body], such as the head, starting from the heart.
What is the expiation for this transgression? By reciting that [mantra], one is purified; not otherwise.
If one should intentionally or unintentionally cross over a flower garland belonging to a Bhautika, [this is the rule].
Purification for that [offense] occurs through ten thousand repetitions; for the remaining three cases, it is as previously stated.
Indeed, having unintentionally caused the loss of a deity, a teacher, or sacred substances, [one must perform this].
A bhautika [offering] is purified by a hundred thousand steps; the remainder is as before.
Whatever has been touched by the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings), that should not be consumed by a person.
In that case, purification shall consist of three-quarters [of the penance] for touching, stepping over, or eating [forbidden things];
likewise for sandalwood and other items that have entered among meat by mistake.
In that regard, purification by foot refers to the cleansing of discarded flower offerings (nirmālya) from pure liṅgas and the like,
as well as the property of the deity, the property of the guru, the property of Caṇḍeśvara, and the property of the dog.
A man becomes liable for expiation by eating [forbidden food] as well as by giving it;
in giving and in transgressing, the penalty is equal, while in neglecting it, it is half of that.
O Gurudeva, one should diligently avoid half of that [portion] and substances belonging to other castes;
for he who worships non-duality (advaita) may, through negligence regarding the linga, fall into duality (dvaita).
126b) But for those who are unwilling, there are one hundred thousand [recitations] for the third [category] as well, as before.
Thus, indeed, in the mantra of Dvaita, one should avoid it in the Nirācāra [rite].
If the vessel for the *argha* offering is not released, or if it breaks and water begins to flow,
one becomes pure by reciting two hundred and then a thousand [verses] respectively through five [stages].

O son of Kṛttikā, one who is constantly pure in the perception of what is to be known— whether it be worms, meat, and so forth, or even when the wind-enemy element arises in a general way— is [liberated].
For one who has been seized by a king, enemies, water, or hunger, or from the presence of a thief,
the Aghora mantra should be recited two hundred times there for the pacification of terrible calamities.
Having ascertained the place, the time, and the strength [of the offender], one should cause the expiation to be administered by three,
five, seven, or ten preceptors who have mastered the scriptures.

One should not cause an expiation to be administered by fools, nor by those who procrastinate, nor by atheists, nor by those who rely on mere logic, nor by those habitually devoted to the study of their own [non-Vedic] scriptures.
However, it must be exactly as taught in the scriptures, neither deficient nor excessive in any respect;
by giving less or more, the preceptor becomes a partaker of sin.
Therefore, with every effort, one should practice the conduct prescribed by the scriptures.
Thus ends the chapter on expiation in the *Kālottara-mahātantra*.
127a) Īśvara said:
Now listen as the procedure for the rosary is being told:
that which consists of one hundred and eight beads is proclaimed as the best.
Half of that size is praised as the medium [bead], and half of that again is beneficial for the small [bead].
That which is made of Rudrākṣa is for great servants; it grants liberation and is supremely auspicious.
The downward-facing [mandala] should be made with one face, three faces, four faces, five faces, or six faces; therefore, one should avoid those that are mixed.
One should join face to face, avoiding the face at the base;
this indeed applies to all gems, whether they are produced from trees or from water.
The *putraja* [bead] is for the sake of obtaining sons; the *padmaja* is for the attainment of the powers such as *aṇimā*;
the *indrākṣa* thread bestows sovereignty; and the *cakrākṣa* thread is likewise.
This leader of sūtras, who brings about the pacification of misfortune and is free from harm,
was fashioned from gold and silver, and further adorned with the remaining metals.
For killing, one should employ trapu (tin), sīsā (lead), and iron, along with a large conch shell;
for nourishment, a conch-shell thread and pearls increase one's progeny.
Crystal is for bestowing prosperity upon men; coral is used for subjugation;
in its absence, one may use clay; and rājavartana is for eradication.
This sūtra is like a beneficial jewel-necklace that grants all desires to men;
one made of gems leads to enjoyment and liberation, while one made of grain leads to an increase in harvests.
Alternatively, it is taught that one who has emerged from samādhi should perform the recitation of the mantra;
or else, it should be performed by all people while remaining bound [in restraint].
The thread-material for the accomplishment of the arcane yakṣa-mothers and the guhyakas has been declared by me; now their dimensions shall be described again.
That which is the size of an *āmalaka* fruit is declared to be the best;
that which is the size of a partridge egg is middling, and that which is the size of a chickpea is the lowest.
It is taught that the auspicious knotting should be performed as before using a cord of nine or three strands;
this applies to the Nāgapāśa, the Sāvitra, or the Rudrākṣa.
One should perform the rite called Mevā for half the length of the book and must not exceed it;
one should wash with the deity Sadyojāta and rub with the deity Vāmadeva.
One should fumigate with *bahurūpa* incense and smear with *puruṣa* ointment;
one should consecrate each [of these] one hundred times with the fifth mantra.
And one should not likewise recite the *Meru* mantra with the *Aghora* mantra during the fifth [rite];
rather, the eight mudrās should be displayed and each should be worshipped in sequence.
Having worshipped Meru with five [offerings] as before, according to the Śiva-rite,
one should perform mental recitation (japa) using the ring finger and thumb in reverse order.
By performing [this] exactly one hundred and eight times, the fruit becomes ten millionfold.
One should perform the recitation in a whisper, moving either the middle finger or the thumb.
From a hundred recitations, that fruit which [otherwise] amounts to one hundred thousand arises for him;
while performing the recitation, he should cause it to be spoken while pressing the ring finger and the thumb together.
One who recites the succession of syllables neither too fast nor too slow shall obtain a thousandfold fruit; this word is not false.
For the sake of enjoyment, one should draw [the breath] along the path of creation like a rosary;
for the sake of liberation, one should draw it slowly upward along the path of dissolution.
The mantra-practitioner must not overstep Meru; by overstepping it, he becomes a partaker of fault.
One thousand recitations of the Bahurūpa mantra must be performed; by that, he is purified.
If one falls to the ground through negligence, two hundred [repetitions] should be recited;
if one falls on both feet, then one thousand should be recited.
If that [impurity] falls upon a garment, it attains purification by a single hundred-fold [ablution];
likewise, the priest shall prescribe for him an expiation according to the specific mark [of the offense].
However, it must be fashioned with the foot [of the wood]; otherwise, one will not attain success. Or, an akṣamālā lacking the [central] Meru bead should be made with great effort.
The merit of that [act] is a hundredfold when one uses a rosary;
there is no fault in bypassing it, for it is like Mount Meru.
And likewise, in the case of falling [from the staff] and other such incidents, the expiation is as prescribed in the Sūtras.
Thus ends the chapter on the rosary of beads in the *Kālottara-mahātantra*.
The Lord said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme characteristics of the bell,
by whose sound all obstacles flee in the ten directions.
All diseases, malignant planetary influences, as well as fierce Vināyakas, evil dreams, wicked Rākṣasas, Vetālas, Bhairavas, and Śivās.
The ḍākinīs, spirits, and serpents such as Karkoṭaka and others;
some desire offerings, while others desire passion and pleasure.
By hearing the sound of the bell, they become possessed of heroic vigor;
therefore, one should always ring it with every effort at the time of worship.
I shall now describe its measurement and its foundation:
having made the square threefold, one should divide each side into eight parts.
The ravakṣetra is in the lower portion, and the grahakṣetra is said to be in the middle portion;
one should fashion the trident or the bull according to the scriptures.
129a) One should extend the half-moon upwards from the center within the solar field; having added [the width] on both sides by an eighth part, its face and its base are likewise [extended].
But when asked in reverse, O Candralekhā, one should turn it back;
the lolling [of the tongue] is eight parts, and the emergence of the weapon is from the eighth part.
Having completed the central field, one should then cause the *pragraha* (the supporting beam) to be made;
a *sāraka* of two units is recommended, and its width should be four units.
It should be smooth and equal in height; above that is the *alasāraka*.
Its width is four units, and its height is two units.
Above that, one should cause a trident to be made, or else the excellent Pāśupata [linga],
or a bull should be fashioned, or a very beautiful lotus.
In this manner, the bell should be fashioned from the five metals;
it should be made from metal produced in the region of Rava, or from silver, or even from gold.
A sharp lancet made of steel and adorned with various jewels is recommended;
having thus fashioned it with care, one should wash it with water and ashes.
Having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should bathe it with fragrant water;
having worshipped it with the Aghora mantra using an abundance of flowers, incense, and water offerings (argha).
One should recite the mantra of Bahurūpa one thousand and eight times;
it shall always produce terror in all wicked beings.
One should satisfy all mantras and move the weapon with the weapon-mantra.
When offering incense, it should be moved at the sound of that [mantra], without delay;
at the conclusion of the worship, it should be carefully placed so that no breakage occurs.
In the case of a major transgression such as jumping over [the image], the expiation is like that for the linga;
however, when [the image] has been installed, it must be performed with one-eighth [of the prescribed penance], and not otherwise.
A bell that has been consecrated is not merely a crusher of the wicked;
rather, it is the supreme dispeller of obstacles in the form of door-bolts.
When it falls to the ground, for what reason? Then one should recite the hundred-fold *ghora* mantra. But when it is broken, having recited the *sahasra*, one should then have another one made.
In the midst of that, having performed worship with nothing else, one should cause [the rite] to be done;
by the ringing of the bell, one attains all desires.
Thus ends the chapter on the characteristics of the bell in the *Kālottara-mahātantra*.
The Lord said:
I shall now proclaim the chapter on flowers in due order as before,
for the benefit of practitioners and for the attainment of the fruits of all desires.

And likewise, one should play the auspicious hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) upon the self consisting of the dyads and so forth; similarly, one should designate the offerings, beginning with the filling and purifying of the *ālaya*.
Śiva, the granter of all desires, should always be worshipped with fresh flowers that are unblemished and free from dust, such as the *vakapuṣpa*.
Nor with *merupatra* leaves, nor with fruits, nor with saffron filaments, nor even with fragrant flowers— especially with *brahmapadma* lotuses— should one worship with such effort.
Thus, Maheśvara is to be worshipped with flowers offered with supreme effort;
for them, the state of being stale persists for the duration of a year.
Red and white lotuses, water lilies, blue lotuses,
white lotuses, yellow lotuses, as well as *punnāga* and *vilva* leaves.
Thus, the primary flowers have been proclaimed as the middling ones;
regarding these, one should entertain no suspicion of them being stale after five days have passed.
Kunda, kubjaka, drākṣā, mallikā,
agastya, kiṃśuka, arka, dhuttūra, bhṛṅga, and likewise the surabhidrumavikā.
The *tilaka*, *aśoka*, *jātī*, *mālatī*, *jāti*, and *campaka* trees; as well as the *mandāra*, *maruva*, *varddharīka*, and *kāṣṭacampaka*.
Madana, damana, two types of droṇa-flower, two types of pāṭala, yūthikā, pārava, tamāla, and karṇikāraka.
Āḍharūpa, samī, kuśā, and indeed saṃkhapuṣpikā;
likewise, the two kinds of kadambapatra, sumanā, and keśara.
Jayaṃtī, Valāmoḍhā, and likewise the fourth, Vijayī;
the land-lotus is praised, as is the lotus of another land.
Gairika, brahmapuṣpas, tagarika, and vinākila should be offered,
as well as govindapuṣpa and karpūrapatrikā.
Gopālasūrya, O Sūrya, what is this dream of yours? One should always cause Kāśāya, Karkaṭīpuṣpa, and Kerala to be given as the middle [offering].
One should avoid the ketakī flower, the pumpkin, that which originates from the nimba tree, the piśāca flower, that produced from the śālmalī tree, and that originating from the girikarṇikā.
Thus, O Six-faced One, fresh flowers should be offered—
leaves, flowers, and fruits of divine medicinal plants.
Kuśa grass and flowers endowed with beauty and fragrance should be offered with great effort and diligence. They must be presented with careful attention.
O Six-faced One, the forms and smells previously mentioned are excluded along with the breaths; they have been carefully avoided because they are not well-established.
Fragrant flowers are for enjoyment, while those endowed with beauty are for liberation;
therefore, the practitioner seeking accomplishment should take whichever one among those mentioned is available.
Thus ends the chapter on flowers in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
131a) Īśvara said:
O Six-faced One, listen now to the procedure for the eight flowers according to the truth:
eight flowers are to be offered to Śiva, the Supreme Lord.
By the offering of these eight flowers, Śiva becomes worshipped:
non-violence is the first flower, and the restraint of the senses is the second.
The flower of patience, the flower of compassion, and the flower of supreme knowledge are considered the [first] three;
the flower of austerity, the flower of wisdom, the flower of intention, and likewise the eighth, the flower of being.
The "Eight Flowers" (Aṣṭapuṣpikā) has been declared for ascetics established in the highest state;
by the mere knowledge of this, one attains liberation while living (jīvanmukti).
The procedure for the Muṣṭapuṣpī rite is now explained once more:
water belonging to Varuṇa, flowers, Soma, ghee, milk, and curd.
The *prājāpatya* consists of food and the like; the *āgneya* consists of incense and lamps;
and the *vānaspatya*, the fifth, consists of fruits, flowers, and so forth.
The terrestrial [flowers] are the bulbous roots and so forth; the aerial are the fragrant sandalwood;
and the one called "half" is the *śivapuṣpa*—thus is the "eight-flower offering" described.
For those whose minds are always established in equanimity, the first [of the three watches] is always recommended.
131b) I shall further explain the eight flowers as they truly are:
first, a flower should be offered upon the seat with a pure mind.
The gift of the image should be performed with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), or alternatively with another [mantra] such as Puṣpa;
by the offering of five [mantras], one should fashion the five limbs.
Furthermore, the "eight-flower offering" (aṣṭapuṣpikā) is not prescribed for Śiva on the eighth lunar day;
alternatively, the "five-flower offering" (pañcapuṣpaka) should be presented to him with the [five] Brahma-aṅgas.
One should extend the Īśāna [face] with the Netra-mantra, and that [Puruṣa face] with the Puruṣa-mantra;
the Aghora [face] is joined with the Śikhā [mantra], or endowed with the Śiras-mantra.
The *sadyojāta* mantra is considered the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*), while the fifth is indeed the flower (*puṣpa*).
The remainder are known as the seat (*āsana*) and the form (*mūrti*), and then again this supreme one.
The root flowers are the lotus and others; these, excluding the face and limbs of the Lord, are the eight flowers common to all.
They bestow all accomplishments, are suitable for all stages of life,
and are common to all castes alike.
One should worship Śiva once, twice, or thrice a day—
at the time of dawn, at midday, and likewise when the sun has set.
One should worship with supreme devotion according to the rite of the eight flowers (aṣṭapuṣpa-vidhāna),
[offering] to the poor, the helpless, children, women, and the ignorant.
For those who enjoy pleasures, for those who are physically robust, and likewise for those whose souls are absorbed in meditation, [disease arises].
The "Eight Flowers" (Aṣṭapuṣpikā) has been taught for those devoted to the Śiva scriptures, who are intent on various spiritual accomplishments, and who are both attached and detached.
Thus ends the chapter on the Eight Flowers in the Kālottara Mahātantra.
Īśvara said:
Now, therefore, I shall duly proclaim the vows in their proper sequence:
on the eighth and the fourteenth days of both fortnights.
Having fasted and become self-restrained, with his inner self purified according to the threefold rule, he should then, on the following day, being pure, worship Śiva with special rites.
One should perform recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth according to the previously stated procedure;
one should worship the Guru or the practitioner and others with supreme devotion.
Then, one should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in mouthfuls; having sipped water and touched [the sense organs], one should subsist on sacrificial food (haviṣyānna).
By this method, one should diligently observe the vow for as long as life lasts,
[honoring] the father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather.
By the power of this vow, one shall dwell in the world of Śiva;
this vow named the Śiva-vrata is the most excellent among all vows.
But for those who are incapable, the vow of eating only at night is the supreme remover of sin.
One observing a vow should not practice celibacy, sleep on the ground, bathe, avoid oils and such things, eat sacrificial food, or speak untruth.
O child, this is the supreme vow, always beneficial for ascetics,
[to be observed] on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, and at the beginnings of the six Aṣṭamīs.
A householder should observe the night-fast according to the very same rules as Yama;
furthermore, I shall now proclaim the supreme vow among all vows.
This practice, which causes the destruction of great sins and leads to union with Śiva, must be performed with supreme devotion; therefore, one should carry it out with diligent effort.
Having fasted diligently on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, and having completed the daily obligatory rites, one should carefully perform the auspicious ceremony.
In the center of the pavilion, upon a dais adorned with canopies and banners,
provided with victory-pennants and decorated with various garlands and heaps of flowers.
There, one should worship the Lord of Gods with extensive offerings according to one's means,
having first extracted the three groups of eight syllables along with the *tāraka*.
"Śivāya sa namo'stu"— this nine-syllable mantra;
with this, one should worship Śiva, the supreme cause, there.
One should worship the Lord of Characteristics with ten thousand *kunda* flowers,
or otherwise, one may worship Him with *kunda* flowers as they are available.
One should offer agallochum, sandalwood from Malaya, moon-fragrance, saffron, and liquid; one should also present a hundred lamps with four large wicks.
One should cause various kinds of food offerings, abundant fruits and roots,
ginger, and milk to be presented before Śiva.
O Six-faced One, the prescribed mantra should be recited one thousand times;
likewise, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with guggulu resin and clarified butter.
A vigil should be kept at night with various musical instruments;
then, at the time of dawn, having performed the daily obligatory rites, one should thereafter rise.

Having worshipped Śiva situated there according to the previously mentioned sequence, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed as before; thereafter, the rite for Kāma should proceed in front of Śiva.
One should offer the portion of the tantra spoken by Brahmā to Śiva;
likewise, one should cause it to be given to the preceptor in a vessel of food and gold.
Gold, livestock, cattle, and land should be given to him in due order;
he should then devoutly offer his vow to Śiva with self-restraint.
Having dismissed the Supreme Lord who has been duly worshipped with water offerings,
one should then perform the dismissal at night, or otherwise at another time.
One should subsist on the remnants of the Brahmakūrca mixed with sacrificial food (haviṣyānna).
This vow is proclaimed to bestow long life, prosperity, fame, and sons;
at the end of the body, one rejoices in the world of Śiva together with one's ancestors.
Having fasted on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should observe the vow;
and one should perform the Sarvabhadra rite in the sacrificial pavilion previously described.
The special ablution (viśeṣasnāpana) should be performed immediately after the daily rites;
it must especially be carried out by the practitioner for Śiva.
There, at Kumbhauṣṭaka, the practitioner must perform the consecration in due order, according to the sequence of the yoga.
In the first [case], there should be a water-pot (kalaśa) joined with Devabhūta, Jaṭā, Śatāvarī, and Abhayā.
The practitioner should bathe with that [substance] consecrated by the Sadyojāta mantra, combined with white sandalwood; this is the consecration by means of the Vāma mantra.
After a hundred recitations, one should perform a bath with a jar of saffron water, as well as with mercury, musk, white mustard,
and gorocanā.
The fifth [consecration] is the sprinkling mixed with the moon (the letter *sa*), performed with the fifth [mantra];
and the sixth is performed with the fruit-vessel (*phalakumbha*) by means of the heart-mantra—these two should indeed be carried out by the wise one.
Having thus performed the bathing ritual with the head [anointed] with *hemagarbha* and the topknot with *vajrodaka*, one should commence the sacrifice of desire (*kāmāyāga*).
O Lord,
O Six-faced One, one should commence the great consecration with a thousand fruits, or with one hundred and eight fruits.
Having bathed [the image] in succession with milk, curd, ghee, honey,
and scented water, and then with the fruit of *rocanā*;
Having anointed [the image] with half a pala of camphor, along with fruit, flowers, and water,
one should then, out of devotion, cover it with beautiful garments.
Lamps, garlands, food offerings, and drinks should be presented before him;
thereafter, Śiva, the supreme cause, is to be worshipped with *damanaka* flowers.
One should offer black agalloch (kṛṣṇāguru) as incense, along with camphor, saffron, and keśara; or one may combine vānara and vānameru as the incense in the direction of the wind.
Having done this, one whose self is purified should perform a recitation (japa) of one thousand times;
likewise, one should arrange an oblation (homa) with guggulu resin using the root mantra.
Having performed the fire sacrifice according to the rule, one should offer it to Śiva,
as well as to the preceptors, the practitioners and others, and likewise to the initiates and spiritual sons.
One should worship with supreme devotion, beginning with garments and gold;
a vigil should be kept at night, and the ritual seating (āsana) therein is now described.
One should offer cow's milk, unbroken, and mixed with ghee.
This is known as the "Supreme Vow"; hear now the fruit of merit therein.
O Mahāsena, thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices are not worth even a sixteenth part of this vow.
Because he uplifts ten generations before him and ten generations after him, he rescues his families.
The vow should be performed in the month of Vaiśākha exactly as prescribed;
however, one should worship the Supreme Lord with *dhuttūra* flowers.
By the merit of this vow, one shall become an attendant of Śiva;
on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, one should arrange the chariot procession.
Likewise, in the months of Phālguna, Caitra, or Kārtika, it grants all perfections;
or on the eighth or fourteenth day of the bright fortnight.
During the bright fortnight of the mothers, as well as during the planets of the Nāgas and Daityas,
on the seventh and thirteenth lunar days, one should perform the rite for increasing the power of the earrings.
One should cause a large, variegated banner to be carried around the entire city,
equipped with strings of tinkling bells and adorned with beautiful arrangements.
One should cause the hundred-fold recitation of the terrible mantra of the Gurus to be performed;
having established it before the door, the performance of instrumental music and dance should take place.
135a) Likewise, one should have another large cloth-painting made for the outer area,
depicting ancient narratives and the life of Sītā and others.
When this has been done, on the second day, having performed worship especially with distinction,
it should be worshipped with effort by both the householder and the ascetic in due order.
The teachers, the lords of practitioners, the initiates, the spiritual sons, and the others [should be honored];
at the conclusion of that, the chariot procession must indeed be performed by the practitioner.
It was beautifully fashioned with various cloths, adorned with banners and flags,
equipped with small bells and chowries, and provided with garlands of bulls and fine fabrics.
One should have the gatekeepers depicted at the gates upon the cloth,
and likewise fashion the weapons, such as the vajra and others, in their anthropomorphic forms.
Whether it is endowed with five sanctuaries or not even a single sanctuary,
one should construct a single sanctuary adorned with the foremost bull.
One should draw the chariot using bulls, stallions, or even elephants;
meanwhile, dancing and singing should be performed before it, and various kinds of incense should be offered.
Having been entreated by the patron (yajamāna), the chariot was paraded through the city;
at the conclusion of the chariot procession, the Supreme Lord seated within the chariot—
Having lifted up the auspicious pedestal, one should place it before Śiva;
then, having worshipped it with effort in due order using flowers, incense, and other offerings ending with those items.
One should offer the fruit of the chariot procession to Śambhu, who holds the spear in his hand.
O Destroyer of Krauñca, one should keep vigil at night with songs, instrumental music, and dances,
and with stories derived from the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
On the third day, a special worship must be performed with diligence,
having worshipped [the deity] with supreme devotion by means of the preceptors and Śiva-yogins.
One should diligently prepare a mandala of offerings (valimaṇḍala) before the deity and worship it with various kinds of food, following the sequential order beginning with Rudra.
One should fashion rice grains there with various cooked fires and through the mental visualization of flour, assigning them colors such as white, yellow, and so forth.
Having offered a circle of oblations (valimaṇḍala) to Śiva with supreme devotion,
one should utter the sounds of the *nāndī* arising from the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
The ancestors rejoice at his sound of celebration (*nāndī-ghoṣa*), and not otherwise;
one should diligently offer the sound of celebration for the sake of Śiva.
One shall deliver one’s fathers, grandfathers, and likewise great-grandfathers, as well as sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons; what could be greater than this?
136a) If she has lost her offspring, or if at that time some [child] has been killed,
or has been cast away, or even cremated, one should perform the Nandīghoṣa rite.
One should diligently cause him distress by means of clothing, footwear, perfumes, as well as wealth,
and various kinds of drinks.
Especially on the fourteenth and eighth days of the month of Āṣāḍha,
one should bathe the Supreme Lord with an abundant quantity of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having anointed [the image] with sandalwood paste,
one should offer guggulu incense and present milk-rice mixed with ghee to Śiva.
Having worshipped with supreme devotion by means of ten thousand lotuses,
or a thousand, or half of that, or according to what is available;
The fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed diligently with lotuses soaked in clarified butter;
one should then offer the vow (vrata) consisting of lotuses into the left hand of Śambhu.
One should place the knee on the ground with the left leg and arrange flowers;
having recited the Saṃhitā once, one should offer it to the deity.
One should worship the teachers and the devotees of Śiva with garments, land, and other offerings;
one should not perform the offering of a seat with cow’s ghee, but rather with three handfuls of water.
The vow named Sarvakāmaprada is known as the Brahmātman.
Especially on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
one should bathe Śiva with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) with supreme devotion.
One should smear it with saffron and then cover it with garments;
one should then offer a hundred lamps along with four large wicks.
One hundred and one kalpas [are required] for each [deity]; the garments should be red.
One should provide various kinds of sweets and fruits and roots as offerings.
One should offer thick, cooked milk cooled with moon-pearls;
he should then be worshipped diligently with ten thousand blue lotuses.
Or, having worshipped according to what is available, the recitation should be performed with its corresponding splendor;
a true fire-oblation should be performed with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter.
Thereafter, one should formally announce the vow to Śiva according to the prescribed ritual:
"May Sadāśiva be pleased with me by means of this preeminent vow."
Then, one should worship the preceptor and others according to one's ability;
by one desiring success, the ritual seat (āsana) should be prepared with *kaliṅga* and *pīlāja*.
Those desiring prosperity, those desiring sons, and those desiring joy should have this performed;
by following the sprinkling of this vow, one attains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
In this manner, one should perform the month of Bhādrapada, offering worship with *kanavīra* flowers;
likewise, there should be bathing, worship as before, ritual adoration, and the offering of a seat.
One who always desires joy shall attain the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
One should worship Meru with Vakapuṣpa flowers in the month of Āśvayuja;
[the ritual consists of] bathing with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), followed by sprinkling and anointing.
One should worship with jasmine flowers when the *sumanā* is available, O charioteer;
one desiring a son should perform the offering of curd there.
By the power of this vow, one attains the fruit of the horse sacrifice when the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight arrives in the month of Kārttika.
Having observed the fast while remaining in a state of impurity, one should worship the Supreme Lord;
a great ablution (mahāsnāna) should be performed with one thousand measures of water.
And likewise having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with milk, curd, ghee, honey, and likewise with scented water;
Having worshipped with bilva leaves, saffron, and filaments,
a garland of lamps should be offered, O Mālāvati, in four rows.
Black agallochum incense should be offered, along with camphor and saffron;
various kinds of foods, as well as vegetables, roots, and fruits, should also be presented there.
These should be given with great effort; one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times. Likewise, a fire offering (homa) should be performed with guggulu resin and clarified butter.
In that regard, the teachers are indeed to be honored— ten, twelve, or five—
with gold, jewels, and garments, and especially with lands and vehicles.
One should keep a vigil at night and likewise perform worship in the morning;
thereafter, one should offer the vow to Śiva, the Supreme Soul.
One should consume the *brahmakūrca*; its sequential application is now described:
cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass.

One should indeed diligently take up the Kapila [cow dung], consecrated with the five Brahmans; and the cow's urine, the measure of which is equal to a cow's hoof-print, consecrated with the Vāmadeva mantra.
One should place half a *karṣa* of cow dung, consecrated with the *Sadyojāta* mantra,
into a *pala* measure of clarified butter, reciting the *Ghorarudra* mantra eight times.
A person should consecrate three palas of curd with effort using the Īśāna mantra; likewise, one should consecrate eight palas of milk with the same mantra.
O Auspicious One, having recited the Śatāvartī mantra over two palas of kuśa-water,
one should place it around the sacrificial pit (homakuṇḍa), depositing it one by one in due order.
One should not consecrate all one hundred and eight [offerings] there;
having set aside one-third of them, one should present that to Śiva.

In the same manner, one should offer [the gift] into a golden vessel for the preceptor. Having observed the vow, he should then offer land, an excellent horse accompanied by gold, and a portion of his wealth consecrated with the Brahma-mantra at the conclusion of the worship.
Having passed the evening twilight and having taken up the *brahmakūrca*—
so called because it was fashioned by the Brahmas and dispels even the sin of killing a Brahmin— [one should perform the rite].
Therefore, this is known as the Brahmakūrca, which has been practiced by Brahmā and others;
one is liberated from the five sins accumulated in this life and previous births.
One should perform [the rite] at the conclusion of the initiation (dīkṣā), at the conclusion of the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), and at the conclusion of the purificatory thread ceremony (pavitra);
or in the months of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, Caitra, Māgha, or Phālguna.
Whoever drinks it with devotion while purified shall attain union with Śiva.
Thus ends the ritual for the Brahmakūrca in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
O Six-faced One, especially on the fourteenth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
one should perform the ritual bathing according to the previously mentioned procedure, without regard for wealth or expense.
Having worshipped with fragrant flowers, especially with *caṃpaka* blossoms,
one should perform the previously mentioned rites such as recitation (*japa*) and fire-offerings (*homa*).
One should diligently give a cow as the sacrificial fee to the preceptor;
O son, the *brahmakūrca* rite should be performed as before.
Having worshipped Śiva with *arka* flowers a hundred thousand times during the month of Pauṣa,
one should likewise perform the ceremonial bath, the offering of food, and the giving of gifts during the month of Kārttika.
Whoever performs this with such effort shall become a lord of the reality of the Vidyā.
O son, this should be performed throughout one's life, or at least every year.
One who desires imperishable liberation should hand over that vow;
the vows and observances arising from the scriptures should be performed.
In this [system], those things such as the dependent nature (paratantra) and so forth must be diligently avoided.
Thus ends the chapter on the Vow-Pilgrimage in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
Especially toward those who are poor, helpless, or incapable;
toward children, the elderly, the sick, and toward women or fools.
O Six-faced One, I shall describe the ritual procedure for them so that they may be liberated;
one should perform it on the full moon day of Phālguna immediately after the daily duties.
At night, there should be a special worship provided with a great ceremonial bath;
furthermore, two great lamps and one hundred and eight [smaller] lamps should be offered.
He should worship Śiva Paśupati with ghee, guggulu incense,
and various kinds of sweetmeats and diverse foods.
Having purified eight soft pieces of clay and having worshipped Śiva, the Supreme Lord and the ultimate cause, many times with offerings of cooked rice;
O son, these three types of Brahmins who are devotees of Śiva should be honored before Śiva with devotion according to one's capacity, without any stinginess regarding wealth.
One should keep a vigil at night and worship Śiva before the image of Śiva;
having thus honored this excellent vow of Śambhu, one should conclude it with worship in the morning.
Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer, and Śiva is this entire world;
Śiva performs sacrifice everywhere, as does he who is Śiva and even delusion itself.

Whatever evil has been committed by me through action, mind, or speech— whether deficient or excessive, O Mahādeva, and whatever is perceived as being of the nature of ritual action— [may it all be purified].
O Supreme Lord, O Parameśvara, accept all of that— whatever has been performed by me, whether it be obligatory, occasional, or for the sake of specific desires— O Śiva.
All that, O Supreme Lord, has been offered by me unto you;
O God, you abide as the soul of time, perceived by consciousness yet inconceivable.
O Lord, Master of the World, perform this act— whether it be afflicted or unafflicted— with equanimity toward all beings, and do so with compassion.
I have never performed any vow, such as giving or the like;
yet by this preeminent vow, everything has been accomplished by me.
O Śambhu, by your grace and at your command, this excellent vow— consisting of the observance of vows, gifts, and so forth—
is now offered by me to you, O Lord.
By ascetics and yogis, both healthy and afflicted; by children, the ignorant, and the elderly; and by women, men, and those tormented by disease.
In the month of Phālguna, one should diligently perform a vigil before Śiva;
for those who do not especially worship Him on that day of spirits (the fourteenth), [they incur great fault].
The Teacher is the lord of the spirits, yet he is even surpassed by them;
therefore, in the month of Phālguna, one should conquer the mind of the spirits.
On the eighth and the fourteenth days, the vows have been prescribed as before;
all those vows have indeed been performed by you.
Thus ends the chapter on the vow of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Phalguna in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
Īśvara said:
Alternatively, it is said that for the sake of the vow, one should begin from the bright fortnight of Caitra;
having fasted on the sixth day while remaining pure, O Six-faced One, one should especially worship [the deity].
Having fashioned a clay image, one should likewise fashion it on a cloth; this is the distinction.
It has six faces and twelve arms, like a child, with a golden luster.
The god whose vehicle is a peacock, filled with all-encompassing beauty,
adorned with a spear, a bell, a banner, an axe, a noose, and a cock.
