Having worshipped with supreme devotion by means of white flowers, [the deity] who holds a staff, the gesture of fearlessness, and the boon-granting mudrā, and who is resplendent with a garland of skulls and snakes.
One should cause white offerings of food, perfumes, garments, and so forth to be presented;
likewise, one should take the juice of *brāhmī* and a *pala* of *kāpila* ghee.
With one thousand and eight recitations of the mantra over ghee and *aśvattha* wood,
one should worship the preceptor with devotion by means of garments, gold, food, and vehicles.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should consume *brāhmī* juice mixed with ghee that has not been struck by a pestle;
this should be performed month after month until the end of the year.
If one should practice the eightfold [vow] with pure celibacy,
he shall indeed become a great poet on earth, like Vācaspati himself.
He grasps the scriptures at a single glance and stands upon the heads of disputants;
for him, the Rākṣasas, Vināyakas, and various kinds of planetary spirits [have no power].
The ḍākinīs and ḍāmarikas never harm them;
nor do the most terrible Skanda-grahas, nor the Pasmāra and other evil spirits.
By the power of this vow, O Mahāsena, they do not cause harm;
this most excellent of vows, which increases prosperity, should be performed.
The six-faced one, the son of Pārvatī, Skanda, Guhya, Kumāraka,
Kārttikeya, Bāla, and likewise the other, Krauñcasūdana.
And there is the one named Tārakārāti, as well as another, the son of Kṛttikā.
One should worship both Vaiśākha and Viśākha month after month;
[one should worship] Sūrya, joined with the digits of the sun and adorned upon his head by the moon.
O Śikhidhvaja, the mantras of the twelve [deities] are to be understood in their proper sequence.
Thus ends the vow of the youth.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should perform the Mātṛvratam;
sixty-four Mothers, together with Bhairava, should be worshipped.
By means of abundant, well-prepared, and auspicious offerings of garlands, perfumes, garments, and food,
even a maiden obtains a bridegroom who shall have many sons.
A king attains victory and enjoys his kingdom without thorns;
so too do Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and others of the Shudra caste.
One attains victory everywhere and is even freed from fear;
the Mothers should likewise be worshipped with effort according to one's capacity.
In front of that [liṅga], he should honor the devotees of Śiva according to their specific vows and conduct;
by performing it in this manner according to the injunctions, one attains the fruit of recitation everywhere.
Brahmāṇī, Māheśī, Kaumārī,
Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Aindrī, Cāmuṇḍā, Yogeśī, Gaurī, and Ambikā.
The Āgneyī, the Vāruṇī, the Vāyavyā, the one known as Vyoma, as well as Bhuruṇṭhā, Rātri, and Suptarātri.
Lam is Padāgajavaktrā and Gāruḍī; one should conquer Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and likewise the other, Parājitā.
One should likewise worship Siddhāraktā, Śuklā, and Utpalā;
and likewise Bhuruṇṭhā, Rātri, and again Sukharātri.
Kālarātri, Mahākālī, Mṛtyudūtī especially,
Śivadūtī, Varṣakarṇā, and Vighnaghaṭodarī are to be worshipped.
Galagarjā is to be worshipped, as well as Ulkāmukhī;
likewise Haṃsavaktrā, Vaktrā, and Siṃhavyāghramukhī.
The goddesses are Jīmūtāmukhī, Mārjārī, Ṛkṣavānarī,
Uṣṭramukhī, Navamukhī, Gomukhī, and likewise Sumukhī.
Bhairavī is to be worshipped, as well as Kṛṣṇaraivatī,
she known as Śuṣkaraivatī, and likewise Saṅku-raivatī.
Laṅkeśvarī, Bhadrakālī, Śrīghoṇā, Siddhi,
Ghaṇṭākarṇī, and Nidrā are proclaimed as the Mothers (Mātṛs).
Whoever worships on the ninth day when the month of Āśvayuja occurs, their powers shall become unimpaired; of this there is no doubt.
141b) Whoever remembers [the deity] with devotion day after day, through worship and service,
will not be afflicted by the evils of the planets, especially by the magical spells of others.
Bad dreams, diseases, malevolent spirits, and obstructing demons (vināyakas);
Skanda-grahas, pūtanās, and likewise ḍākinīs and ḍāmarikās.
By remembering him, pestilence, famine, and defilement are destroyed; moreover, there arises great honor from even those who are reviled by crows and owls.
Thus ends the observance dedicated to the Mothers.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should paint Ananta upon a cloth;
he should be the size of a single joint of blue dūrvā grass.
Between the lines for *rati* and *prīti*, one should place the arrow of the Goddess, holding a noose;
it should be positioned at the intersection, equal on all sides but not exactly in the center.

Having worshipped with various flowers, garments, food offerings, and lamps, as well as with various kinds of incense and the sound of diverse musical instruments played from the heart, [one should proceed].
One should worship [the deity] in a delightful grove in the center of a flower mandala;
the preceptor should be worshipped with effort according to the prescribed method and one's capacity.
If a person offers food made of gold and wealth according to their capacity and with devotion,
they attain the fulfillment of their desires and becomes beloved by everyone.
A woman shall obtain good fortune both in this world and in the next;
or else, she should worship month by month according to the sequence of the ritual order.
One should worship [the deity] for one year for each disputant.
Having worshipped Madana, Citta-bhū, Kāma, Manmatha, Rati-priya, Anagna, Kandarpa, and Makaradhvaja;
Likewise, one should worship him known as Kusumāyudha, as well as Pūjyamāna Bhava,
Viṣamabāṇa, and the twelfth, Ratipriya.
In the month of Bhādrapada, one should always worship [the deity] with effort while remaining unclothed;
by means of this very observance, one should perform the Kāmavrata.
Thus ends the vow of desire.
I shall now describe the Gaurī-vrata, which increases the good fortune of women;
one should perform the Gaurī-vrata on the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra.
Having fasted with great effort, one should perform this ritual procedure,
having put on excellent red garments and being free from anger and greed.
On the sacrificial ground, a fragrant maṇḍala one cubit in size should be prepared;
with very cool saffron and water, one should draw a circle.
In the center there, an image made of metal should be worshipped;
in the absence of one born from honey, it may be fashioned from the wood of the *surāṅka* tree, O Lord.
It should be made from red sandalwood or Jāva wood according to the prescribed measurements;
or else, having worshipped it with fivefold oblations, it should be honored according to the ritual rules during the month of Caitra.
Having worshipped with red flowers, combined with jasmine and campaka,
as well as with pāṭala, karavīra, and red lotuses, in whatever manner appropriate.
It was abundantly adorned with *pārita*, *mallikā*, and *kukṣa* flowers, as well as red lotuses,
land-lotuses (*sthalapadma*), *kiṃśuka*, *sumana*, and *utpalakaṇṭaka*.
In this manner, she should be worshipped with effort using flowers and other offerings;
furthermore, she should be repeatedly anointed with camphor and saffron.
One should cause various kinds of jewels to be given— diadems, bracelets, earrings, ornaments, and the like, including their settings.
One should carefully offer edible foods combined with ghee and sugar-candy,
as well as cool thick milk and *śikhariṇī*.
Then one should cause him to offer a beverage and water along with the moon;
furthermore, red garments, as well as food and drink, should be given.
And at the conclusion of the worship, one should diligently honor the teacher with gold,
garments, food, and drink, O son, provided there is no deceitfulness of mind.
I shall declare the names of the goddesses in their proper order, month by month.
Speaking in due order:
Gaurī, Umā, Lalitā, Subhagā, and Bhagamālinī.
Manonmanī, Bhavānī, Kāmadā, and Bhogavardhinī.
One should worship Ambikā, Kṛṣṇā, and Ruḍhālī in sequence. These are for the bright fortnight; now hear likewise regarding the dark fortnight.
Rati, prīti, dhṛti, vṛddhi, mati, and ṛṣṭi are proclaimed;
likewise prajñā, medhā, caryā, śrī, rakṣā, and kīrti.
One should diligently observe the vow during both the bright and dark fortnights;
however, due to incapacity or the absence of necessary materials, it is more beneficial to perform it during the bright fortnight.
This should be performed month by month, or, in its absence, beneficially once every year;
therein, the installation [of the deity] should be carried out according to the path prescribed in the scriptures.
I shall explain, month by month, in due order during the bright fortnight:
milk, curd, ghee, cow urine, and water infused with *kuśa* grass.
Likewise, water with bilva leaves, as well as another with sandalwood water,
and also water with sesame seeds and lotus filaments.
O Six-faced One, Nāgakeśara, Lavanga, and Śaśin are said to belong to the bright fortnight, beginning from Caitra.
Now listen to how the consumption [of substances] is performed during the dark fortnight:
one should consume *valā*, *kakkolaka*, and *śatāvarī*.
It is endowed with the fragrance of śirīṣa flowers, and likewise red pearls.
The twelfth fast, the Tārodaka, has been described to you;
thus is proclaimed the Gaurī-vrata, which bestows good fortune upon women and grants sons.
For women in this world and the next, longevity and health are attained by abandoning this [other] vow; among women, no other vow is as beneficial as this one.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the vow of Gaurī;
likewise, one should offer worship, red garments, betel-leaf, and saffron.
A mirror, a fan, an umbrella, a seat, excellent drink,
and all household utensils made either of gold or of copper.
And one should diligently give as many [garments] to the preceptor,
as well as clothes and ornaments for women and young girls.
These should be given with great effort if one desires prosperity for oneself;
thus has this entire Kumārī-vrata been described.
Thus ends the Gaurī-vrata.
Now hear from me regarding the sacrifice of the lunar mansions and lunar days, as well as the conjunctions of the planets:
on the eighth and the fourteenth day of both fortnights.
When Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Maghā, Svātī,
Śravaṇa, and Revatī likewise constitute the six lunar mansions, it is called Ṣaṇmukha.
If Bhāskara, Candra, Āditya, Kavi, Soma-suta, Guru,
and the Nakṣatras should occur in their proper sequence starting from the lunar day (tithi), O son, [then it is auspicious].
If the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight falls on a Sunday coinciding with the Śraviṣṭhā nakṣatra,
one should especially perform a ritual bath for Śiva, the Supreme Self.
One should worship with red flowers, beginning with the *aṅgarāga* of *rocanā*;
likewise, one should offer cow’s ghee and milk as the food offering (*naivedya*).
One should offer a garland of lamps fueled by ghee or sesame oil,
and present incense of guggulu smeared with ghee before Śiva.
One should offer a gift of gold to a Brahmin who is a devotee of Śiva;
however, the practitioner must not provide a seat made of saffron.
This Sūryavrata should be performed with devotion by those whose wealth is diminished for the sake of obtaining sons;
thus, sons endowed with all auspicious marks are born to him.
Thus ends the Surya-vrata.
If Rohiṇī should coincide with the eighth lunar day of the moon, one should then perform the Candra-vrata;
having worshipped Śiva according to the rules with baths consisting of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and other offerings.
One should worship the Supreme Lord with anointment of moon-bright sandalwood paste, as well as with white garments and flowers.
The food offering (naivedya) should consist of jars of milk combined with white sugar;
the seat should be made of sandalwood, and it is beneficial to remain awake during the night.
Those who desire long life should always perform this; it is beneficial for the accomplishment of fame and prosperity.
Thus, by the gift of a golden vessel, the vow known as the Candra-vrata is accomplished.
This concludes the Soma-vrata.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, when the lunar day coincides with the Sun,
one should worship according to the previous rite while observing a fast, but not as a bearer of sectarian marks (liṅgin).
One should worship with saffron for body-unguents and with fragrant flowers;
milk-rice mixed with ghee, measuring one *prastha*, should be offered to Śiva.
One should diligently bestow a gift of land upon a devotee of Śiva;
by means of this foremost of vows, one shall attain sovereignty over the earth.
This is called the Bhūmivrata; indeed, the protector of the earth should cause it to be performed.
Thus ends the vow of the earth.
When the conjunction of Jupiter and Maghā occurs on the fourteenth lunar day,
one should fast and worship Maheśvara, the God of gods, on that day.
With the performance of the great ablution preceded by great wicks,
one should worship with sandalwood unguent and white flowers.
One should offer incense equal in measure to the moon [one pala] in a light vessel;
furthermore, one should cause cool garments and a horse to be presented to the preceptor.
145a) Dates and fruits, as well as sitting and staying awake at night, are beneficial.
This very observance is called the *Vrata*, which increases longevity, prosperity, and fame.
Thus [ends the section on] Devavrata.
When the yoga consisting of Budha and Svāti arises on the eighth lunar day,
one should perform a great ablution preceded by the prescribed rite of fasting.
One should worship Virūpākṣa with body-unguents consisting of the four equal ingredients;
two large wicks should be offered, and one hundred and eight lamps should be presented.
One should worship with light saffron incense and white flowers;
one should offer various kinds of sweetmeats as the food offering (naivedya).
One should offer the crown and other ornaments to the preceptor in the presence of Śiva;
likewise, the girdle, the earrings, the bracelets, and the two rings.
The vehicle is the Vēgadaṇḍa; in its absence, either of the two excellent ones may be used. Having worshipped it with supreme devotion, one should offer food mixed with sugar and ghee.
One shall attain the status of a Rājarājeśvara equal in number to the hairs on one's body;
therefore, this vow has been proclaimed as the "Rājarājeśvara."
The vow of the Lord of the Kings of Kings.
O child, when the conjunction of Śukra and Śravaṇa occurs on the eighth or the fourteenth lunar day, one should then perform the vow.
Having observed the fast according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the great ablution (mahāsnāna).
One should apply unguents to the body with sandalwood, yellow orpiment, and saffron.
The four great lamps and incense—black agalloch—is beneficial.
One should offer before Śiva various enjoyments as an oblation consisting primarily of ghee, accompanied by fire.
Having honored the preceptor with garments, gold, food, and ornaments,
one should present a fresh elephant to him in the presence of Śiva.
Each of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharvan [Vedas] is indeed likewise;
this which has been proclaimed by me to you is called the Mahāvrata.
Having illuminated the entire earth with its seven islands and oceans,
one should perform a night vigil endowed with great magnificence.
The fruit that belongs to the world of Śiva for one's fathers, grandfathers, and likewise great-grandfathers, as well as for sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons— [that fruit is obtained].
This, known as the Great Vow (Mahāvrata), must be performed by the lords of the earth.
Thus ends the Mahāvrata.
O Mahāsena, listen now to this vow which should be observed when the eighth lunar day of the bright fortnight coincides with the Raivatī-Candra yoga, or on the fourteenth day (Bhūtā).
The great ablution (mahāsnāna) should be performed immediately after the daily rites;
O limb, one should apply body-unguent with camphor and arrange the worship with jewels.
White flowers should be offered, along with many ornaments;
one should burn camphor incense, and the food offering should consist of milk-rice and ghee.
One should offer a young, gentle white horse to Śiva;
one should cause eight horses and an elephant to be given to the preceptor.
Seeking a kingdom, one obtains a kingdom— whether it be the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, or Atharva Vedas, or likewise a horse or an elephant— as far as the earth extends, by means of that boat.
One desiring sons obtains sons, and one of the Vasu lineage [obtains them] in succession;
one desiring enjoyments obtains enjoyments, and in the principle of knowledge (vidyā-tattva), eternal ones.
Whatever desire the practitioner of mantra may wish for, he shall obtain those infinite desires;
therefore, this vow is declared to be the Universal Form (Viśvarūpa).
One should offer water with kusa grass as a libation, and thereafter keep a vigil at night.
Thus ends the Viśvarūpa-vrata.
Based on the conjunction of constellations and lunar days, and through the association of lunar days with planets,
I shall once again explain the vows exactly as they are established.
When the conjunction of Rohiṇī and the eighth lunar day truly occurs,
a special worship must be performed with great effort by those desiring sons.
When the conjunction with Jupiter occurs on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa,
or through its conjunction with the Moon, Śaṅkara should be especially worshipped.
One should offer milk-rice mixed with ghee to Śiva;
one should worship Śiva as before with incense, lamps, offerings, and so forth.
Clarified butter should be used for the offering; this is the vow for all desires.
When the conjunction of Āditya and Raivatī occurs on the fourteenth day, [this rite should be performed].
On the eighth lunar day, when it is conjoined with the Maghā constellation, one should worship Śiva as before;
the Bilva fruit is prescribed for the seat, and this is declared to be the Ādityavrata.
Health arises for him, along with his sons and circle of kinsmen,
when the conjunction of Rohiṇī and the Moon occurs on the fourteenth lunar day.
On the eighth lunar day, when it coincides with the asterism Mṛgaśīrṣa, one should then observe the Candra-vrata,
having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed method as previously described.
If one offers curd and milk as the food offering (naivedya) and likewise milk for the seat (āsana), one shall obtain fame, health, and sovereignty; this word is not false.
When there is a conjunction of Aśvinī and Mars on the fourteenth lunar day,
or a conjunction of Bharaṇī and Mars on the eighth, one should then perform the Somavrata.
Having worshipped Śiva with supreme devotion through the five-fold offerings (pañcopacāra),
O son, one shall obtain a kingdom by means of a red lotus seat.
O Mahāsena, when the conjunction of Rohiṇī with Mercury occurs on the fourteenth day or the eighth day, one should perform the Budha-vrata.
Having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rite, preceded by the great ablution (mahāsnāna).
One who desires a son should offer a seat, milk-rice, and ghee, accompanied by a large wick; otherwise, his wife and cattle will increase.
When the fourteenth lunar day (caturdaśī) occurs in conjunction with the constellation Raivata and Jupiter,
one should then perform the Guru-vrata due to the conjunction on that eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī).
By consuming the fat of a tawny cow mixed with the juice of *brāhmī*,
one attains mastery over speech through the power of this vow.
O Bhārgava, know that when the Śravaṇa nakṣatra coincides with the fourteenth day, it is the Śukra-vrata; and again, when it coincides with the eighth day.
Having worshipped the Supreme Lord with extensive offerings according to one's means,
and having partaken of the seat and the honey there, one shall attain the Great Knowledge.
When the Bharaṇī-Śani yoga occurs on the fourteenth lunar day,
or likewise when this same yoga occurs on the eighth, then one should observe this vow.
Having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rites and spoken words that are entirely appropriate, Saturn,
situated in the eleventh house, indeed bestows auspicious results.
O child, that which is adverse is auspicious; for that purpose, one should observe a vow.
Gold, silver, coral, topaz, and pearl—these indeed [are the offerings].
O child, one should carefully cause a conch shell, a silver star, and iron to be given to the preceptor in sequence, with diligence and according to what is available.
Thus ends the chapter on the observance of the planets in the *Kālottara-mahātantra*.
Kārttikeya said:
O Lord, O child, please describe in detail the vows for every month,
and indeed for the entire year, for all living beings here on earth.
Īśvara said:
When one observes the fast by eating only at night on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa,
one should worship Rudra, known as Saṃkara, together with Bhavānī.
Having brought the Goddess and the Great Śaṅkara here with the *bindu*,
one should perform the worship of their respective mantras with special care.
By drinking a handful of cow urine and consuming sacrificial food (haviṣya), one obtains a hundredfold the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
O Śikhidhvaja, having nourished and worshipped Saṃbhurudra and all others as before,
one should then worship the devotees of Śiva on the eighth day of the dark fortnight.
Having completed the worship of the preceptor, one should drink three palas of cow’s ghee;
then, having eaten sacrificial food (haviṣyānna), one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one should worship the deity named Māghamāseśvara,
together with Ambikā, accompanied by the mantras as previously described.
Without having worshipped the Śaiva preceptors, one should consume three palas of milk.
One shall obtain the merit of a hundred horse-sacrifices; of this there is no doubt.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna, one should worship Mahādeva.
Immediately after the daily rites, the Mālinī [mantra] accompanied by a thousand [recitations] should be given to a devotee of Śiva; one should cause him to consume a pala of sesame seeds.
Śivayogins obtain the fruit equal to that of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
In the month of Caitra, one should worship Sthāṇu and Indrāṇī on the eighth day of the dark fortnight;
one should especially worship a devotee of Śiva on every eighth day.
Then, regarding gold, clothing, land, and so forth, there is no deceit concerning wealth.
Having cast off the bondage of the Lord’s vision, one obtains the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha).
One should worship the one named Śiva during Vaiśākha according to one's capacity;
following the previously mentioned procedure, one should always worship a devotee of Śiva.
By drinking water infused with kusha grass, one obtains the fruit of a human sacrifice.
O son, having performed the daily rites there, you must always worship the eldest Paśupati together with Pārvatī according to the prescribed ritual.
By pouring water from a cow's horn, one obtains the fruit of a cow-sacrifice.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, one should worship Ugrarudra together with Manonmanī with great reverence;
by drinking water infused with *kuśa* grass, one shall obtain the fruit of royal splendor.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship the Great One named Sarvanāman with the left-hand power (vāmaśakti);
having offered a lotus-seed rosary, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
On the eighth day of the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship the deity named Tryambaka,
joined with the power of Jyeṣṭhā, according to the procedure previously described.
Having offered the leaf after the worship of the Guru, one has thereby performed a hundred perfect sacrifices; it is not otherwise.
In the month of Āśvina, having offered a jewel-encrusted water-vessel together with a beautiful consort to the Lord who is worshipped by many, one shall obtain the merit of a Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice.
In the month of Kārttika, one should worship the Great One named Rudra with Manonmanī;
having worshipped the Guru according to the prescribed rite, one should consume cow's curd.
O Six-faced One, by that [act], ten thousand Agniṣṭoma sacrifices have been performed;
at the end of the year, one should feed Brahmins who are devoted to Śiva.
One should worship with supreme devotion that person who is the preceptor of vows, by offering land, elephants, vehicles, and an abundance of jewels and wealth.
O son, one shall not obtain that fruit through stinginess regarding wealth or by laughing at oneself when the month of Pauṣa has arrived, during both fortnights.
On the fourteenth, the eighth, or even on the full moon day,
having always performed the obligatory rites according to the rule, one should then perform the optional rite.
A special worship should be performed right there with a pure mind;
the food offering should consist of one prastha of refined sugar, milk, and other such items prepared with fire.
One should feed and honor Brahmins numbering eleven (the number of Rudras);
the image should be one span in height and fashioned from eight barley grains.
One should have her adorned with horns, a wooden frame, and anklets;
then that tawny cow (kapilā) should be offered to Śiva and subsequently given to the preceptor.
Listen now to the merit of the vow associated with all the vehicles:
[one travels] in celestial chariots that fulfill all desires and shine like ten million suns.
It was crowded with throngs of Rudras, surrounded by Rudra-maidens,
joined by the sounds of bellowing bulls, and filled with the resonance of various songs.
Whomever he conquers there with his arrows, along with their three times seven lineages,
as well as those born in the families whose number is equal to the count of his body hairs— [all these he destroys].
For that many thousands of yugas he is honored in the world of Rudra;
having attained proximity, he then proceeds to the [highest] state.
O Śivā, by this rite, having offered a sword made of flour as an illusion according to the prescribed rule,
one shall attain the status of a universal monarch.
In the month of Phālguna, by offering a discus, one obtains the station of Indra;
and in Caitra, by offering a ladle made of flour before Śiva.
It is declared that one shall attain the world of Śiva by offering a staff-weapon before Śiva in the month of Vaiśākha at Brahmahastī.
One should prepare a cake the height of a forearm and offer it at the conclusion of the worship;
one is liberated from the five sins and is glorified in the world of Rudra.
One should offer this wheel made of elder and youngest [parched grain] to Śiva;
by doing so, one is liberated from the consequences of past actions and goes to the world of Rudra.

In the month of Āṣāḍha, one should offer a noose made of flour to Śiva; by this, one is liberated from the misdeeds accumulated during previous festivals, as well as those gathered in this life and others.
He who offers a banner made of flour before Śiva according to the prescribed rite in the month of Śrāvaṇa shall attain liberation, which grants final release.
He who, in the month of Bhādrapada, offers a mace made of flour,
having attained lordship over treasures, is glorified in the world of Śiva.
In the month of Āśvayuja, one should offer a trident made of flour measuring half a hasta before Śiva; this removes the sin of killing an embryo.
When one offers a discus before Śiva during the month of Kārttika,
it burns away the sins committed in seven lifetimes, just as fire consumes fuel.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, having offered a lotus made of flour to Śiva in this manner, one shall attain universal sovereignty.
For all nocturnal vows indeed, it has been proclaimed by me that after performing the obligatory worship, one should perform the optional worship.
O Guru, worship should be performed every month, indeed at every change of the moon;
however, a great worship (mahāpūjā) must be performed according to the prescribed rite at the end of the year.
The preceptors should be honored with gold, garments, food, and vehicles;
then, O son of Kṛttikā, one shall obtain the full fruit as described.
O Mahāsena, through deceit regarding wealth, one is separated from the desired form;
likewise, he who gives a horse made of flour in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa [attains the same].
Having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rite, one is glorified in the world of the Sun for a thousand divine years; at the end of that period, one shall become a lord of the earth.
One should offer two tooth-sticks made of *pauṣya* flour before Śiva.
Endowed with his three-times-seven generations of kin, he is glorified in the world of Śiva for a thousand divine years; at the end of that time, he shall become a lord of the earth.
The great hero, a universal monarch endowed with all sovereignty,
who offers a horse-chariot of the color of a māgha flower to Śiva,
shall indeed deliver his parents from the Raurava hell and other such realms.
He dwells in the world of Śiva for thirty thousand divine years;
at the end of that time, he shall become the lord of the entire earth divided into nine regions.
In the month of Phālguna, one should offer eleven groups of bulls made of flour;
by placing this offering before the head [of the deity], one shall become the sovereign of the three worlds.
For a thousand divine years he shall remain so, and at its conclusion, he shall become a lord of the earth;
in the month of Caitra, he shall possess a house made of sugarcane, provided with male and female servants.
Equipped with household utensils and adorned with various [ornaments],
one should, at the conclusion of the worship, offer it to Śiva with supreme devotion.
For eight hundred divine years he is glorified in the world of Rudra;
at the end of that time, remembering his past births, he shall attain the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
In the month known as Vaiśākha, one should offer seven bowls of rice for the sake of Śiva at the conclusion of the worship, with a heart full of joy.
A wise man who burns two hundred palas of guggulu resin, accompanied by the recitation of the *randhra-mantras*, shall attain union with Śiva.

O Lord of the Earth, in the month of Jyeṣṭha, at the conclusion of the worship before Śiva, one endowed with devotion shall dwell in the world of Śiva together with twenty-one generations of their lineage.
At the end of that [period], he enjoys the earth with its nine divisions and its oceans;
in the month of Āṣāḍha, the circular path of the Trident-bearer should be prepared.
The bali-maṇḍala should be fashioned with various kinds of food offerings, adorned with various small vessels, and strewn with various colorful ornaments.
Having worshipped the Supreme Lord, he should then offer [the oblation] to Him,
as well as to his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather.
O lord of the earth, accompanied by his sons and grandsons, he shall dwell in the world of Śiva for thousands of divine years; at the end of that time, he becomes a sovereign of the earth.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, at the conclusion of the worship, a celestial chariot made of flowers and filled with various beautiful arrangements should be offered to the Lord.
O Lord of the Earth, for a duration of ten thousand years in the world of Rudra,
he becomes a lord of yogis, at the end of which time he shall attain liberation.
In the month of Bhādrapada, whenever one performs the worship of Rudra,
one should first burn guggulu incense and then burn suradāru.
The marrow of the bilva fruit mixed with ghee, as well as various other types of ghee,
and fifthly, agallochum (aguru) should be offered with all one's heart as incense to the Lord.
O Six-faced One, he who burns [the forest] continuously for one month,
O Śambhu, let him be joined with his children, cattle, and kinsmen in the state of Yāti.
But he who, with devotion, fills a single vessel with milk and ghee for Śambhu every day without interruption throughout the month of Āśvayuja;
O Six-faced One, I am unable to describe the fruit of his merit;
as for those born into his lineage who are again struck by the blows of misfortune, [their fate is likewise beyond measure].
They go to Mount Mahāmeru in the world of Rudra and dwell there at their pleasure for more than ten million years; at the end of that time, they become lords of men.
Those who have attained the initiation of Śiva become devotees of Śiva, wise, and freed from sin;
having reached that initiation, they go to the supreme goal.
Whoever should cause a cup of sugarcane juice placed in a cloth to be offered before Śiva continuously for the duration of one month at the conclusion of the worship;
At the end of his body’s life, he rejoices in the world of Rudra together with his kinsmen,
having worshipped the devotees of Śiva according to the prescribed rite at the conclusion of the vow.
Those wearing golden garments, those who have lost their drinks, and those whose sons are destroyed by the destruction of their kin—
now, therefore, I shall duly explain the gift of Mount Meru in its proper sequence.
Beginning from the month of Kārttika, one should observe the Meru-vrata;
on the full moon day of Kārttika, a jeweled Meru must be offered before Śiva.
Now hear the measurements of all the Merus in sequence:
Vajra, Padma, Mahānīla, Sphaṭika, and the one named Nīla.
Setting aside the emerald flowers, others should be taken according to one's own means;
specifically, one *prastha* should be collected, or half a *prastha*, or even half of that.
Or else, it should be given according to one's capacity, without stinginess regarding wealth;
I shall describe the division of Mount Meru and how one should worship it before Śiva.
One should place Mount Meru, adorned by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa, within the pericarp;
then one should worship the mountain Mālyavat to its east.
To the east of that is the one named Bhadra, who shines with the appearance of a horse's chest;
further beyond Meru, in the eastern direction, lie three regions, each more eastern than the last.
Thereafter, he described in detail those three mountains to the south: Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, and Himavat.
Likewise, on the northern side, there are Nīla and Śveta from Śṛṅgavān;
and in the west, those named Gandhamālya and Ketumālya.
Thus, having fasted and become pure, one should especially worship Śiva at Meru, the lord of mountains, which is endowed with these twelve [qualities].
One should perform the great ablution (mahāsnāna) or likewise the great worship (mahāpūjā);
at the conclusion of the worship, one should fashion a Meru of jewels before the God of gods.
One should give [these] to a Śiva-brahmin while constantly recollecting the Śiva-mantra;
together with garments, one should offer Mount Meru— listen now to the fruit of that merit.
Of Mount Meru, which measures one hundred thousand yojanas, [the number] of its atoms...
For as many thousands of eons he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
indeed, he delivers the lineage of twenty-one generations from hell.
But those men who, driven by greed for immediate gain, strike down living beings—
even if they are great sinners, dogs, or even those who kill all creatures— [attain this state].

Those who have committed treachery against their guru, those who have killed an embryo, those who have killed their father, women who die during childbirth, and virgins defiled by a stake; [these are purified by the rite].
They indeed attain proximity to Rudra;
therefore, one should mentally perform the gift of Mount Meru before Śiva.
At the end of the body, with his sins washed away, he goes indeed to the world of Śiva;
now hear the fruit, which is equal in measure to Mount Meru of gold.
One should fashion Mount Meru in the center with a thousand palas,
provided with three peaks and endowed with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara.
One should construct each of its mountains with one hundred [units] each, together with Meru at the front; these are known as the sixteen lines.
In this manner, Mount Meru should be diligently offered before Śiva on all solstices, and especially during eclipses.
This should be given to the preceptor who has mastered the Saṃhitās,
as well as to the high-souled Mahāmeru together with its mountains, as previously described.
O virtuous one, you shall dwell in the world of Śiva for as many eons as there are atoms;
likewise, [you shall deliver] your fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers.
It shall deliver sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons; what could be greater than this?
Having enjoyed all the earth, he who has been instructed by Śiva enjoys [the fruits of his merit];
yet a poor man should cause Meru to be made with silver according to the measurement of gold.
Likewise, there are twelve mountains, along with the conceptualization accompanied by its arrangement;
in the northern division of the heart, that pair or the two-fold grasping exists.
The fruit previously mentioned shall indeed belong to him; there is no doubt in this matter.
Now listen as the extent of the earth, equal to Mount Meru, is described.
One should meditate upon a region, a mandala, a village, or a mountain;
however, by calculation, the remaining mountains would take ten months.
But who indeed is capable of describing the merit of the earth and its mountains?
O son, for as many particles of dust as there are in the earth,
for that many thousands of crores of years he is honored in the world of Śiva.
Having enjoyed those pleasures, the king is then born into a family of yogis;
through the attainment of knowledge, he has no further rebirth.
O son of Pārvatī, I shall describe the elephant Merumata in brief:
they are neither old nor young, and are beautifully adorned with tusks and tails.
A brave [horse], endowed with all excellent qualities, adorned with bells and chowries,
joined with a garland of stars, and decorated with a banner and a sacred text.
Adorned with divine garments and embellished with gold ornaments,
the solar eclipse should be offered to the preceptor in the presence of Śiva.
At its end, they do not bite the mountain that is one hundred thousand yojanas [in height],
which is joined with the three heavy [elements] and endowed with twelve mountains.
He is liberated from all sins and attains union with Śiva;
thereafter, his ancestors rejoice together with him in the world of Rudra.
O son, this gift of an elephant has been described by me in brief;
furthermore, Meru or whatever else was given as a gift by Raci in ancient times should also be offered.
One should not calculate the hair-tufts by number;
rather, Meru should be fashioned [with thirty-two], and the mountains with the number of the sun (twelve).
It should be given before Śiva on the full moon day of Vaiśākha or Kārttika, together with garments and seven vessels adorned with banners.
It should be given according to the prescribed rite, like Mount Meru, to that brahmin who is a devotee of Śiva and has mastered the Saṃhitās.
Having worshipped with supreme devotion with golden bracelets, earrings, a girdle,
a crown, and even two finger-rings;
Then, among all gifts whatsoever, one should adorn [the recipient] with ornaments;
indeed, a king should adorn Mount Meru with natural ornaments.
By the gift of a horse as large as Mount Meru, one is glorified in the world of Rudra for as many tens of thousands of years as there are hairs on its body.
He is glorified in the world of Rudra for thousands of great aeons;
even one who is poor due to the lack of horses may fashion [an image] out of Mount Meru.
One shall indeed obtain a fruit equal to that by the measure of a horse;
or else, Mount Meru made of cloth should be offered before Śiva.
One should fashion a mountain with various colors representing divine states of sovereignty;
Meru should be fashioned in the center with cloths, and the remaining mountains should be fashioned likewise.
According to the measurement of the cloth of existence, one should fashion each mountain with various beautiful colors, having golden peaks and made of gold.
It should be given to a Brahmin who is a devotee of Śiva in the presence of Śiva;
he attains a state of divine sovereignty for a thousand generations of his lineage.
If one should correctly perform the ritual portion as desired for a full hundred divine years,
then the state of a universal monarch (cakravartin) will manifest through the clarity of knowledge at that time.
Thereupon, he attains dissolution in Śiva and shall not undergo birth again;
or else, Mount Meru made of ghee should be given, as I shall now describe.
Meru is situated in the center, surrounded by five thousand palas;
one should arrange each of the other mountains there at intervals of five hundred palas.
One should fashion Mount Meru with three peaks, made of gold and accompanied by the deities, weighing one *pala*;
the remaining mountains should each weigh one *pala* and be adorned with garments.
Having performed a special worship, one should arrange [the offering] before Śiva;
[one should fashion] Mount Meru measuring five khāris and not imagine it as a mere abode.
One who desires Śiva’s favor should give one *khārī* to each Brahmin who is a devotee of Śiva.
He indeed uplifts his maternal and paternal lineages;
he is glorified in the world of Rudra for more than a hundred divine years.
One becomes the lord of the land-mass of Bhārata, and not otherwise;
in this manner, one should fashion Meru with three divisions using the white division.
He goes to the world of Rudra and rejoices together with his ancestors;
or else, one should fashion a mountain of grain before Śiva.
One should not conceive of Mount Meru as being measured by five *khārīs*;
rather, one should designate the remaining mountains according to each one *khārī* measure.
As before, he should fashion a golden peak and a cloth;
at the conclusion of the Śiva-worship, he should cause it to be given to a Śiva-devoted Brahmin.
For thousands of millions of eons he is honored in the world of Śiva;
likewise, his ancestors rejoice for a long time in the world of Brahmā.
One should fashion a mountain of sesame seeds measuring one-eighth of this [size];
its peaks and other features should be as previously described.
The Guru should always offer a mountain of sesame seeds before Śiva;
by doing so, that man, together with his kinsmen, attains union with Śiva.
Having enjoyed ten thousand times ten million objects of pleasure according to their desire, they enjoy the entire earth; when Śiva [manifests], they subsequently dissolve away.
Thus, twelve mountains have been described to you;
having understood the proper mantra as well as the time, one should cause Meru to be offered.
During all the solstices, and especially during an eclipse,
one who is pure should always observe a fast and perform the gift of Mount Meru.

Salutations to the one with a golden body, who is like a bull among the twice-born; salutations to the one who is the crest-jewel of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, and who is situated at the navel of the earth.
To the Lord of the twelve cities, the remover of all sins,
the pure devotee of Śiva— grant me protection in every way.
Free from sin, I go to Śiva together with my ancestors; HŪṂ, NAMAS!
You are Śiva for the sake of Śiva, and I am Śiva for the sake of Śiva.
I offer this with devotion for the sake of the liberation of my ancestors.
Thus ends the Maṃtramerudāna.
O Six-faced One, listen now briefly to the gift of earth;
earth is considered to be of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
One hundred crores of yojanas is proclaimed as the highest extent;
that which encompasses the seven islands is declared to be the middle.
One should fashion maidens with a limit of Jambūdvīpa in three ways;
the best [type] should be fashioned from five bhāras of gold.
One should likewise prescribe a tortoise made of silver half of that size, as well as a lotus;
the earth [of the mandala] is said to be excellent when it is one-third [the size], while the middling is considered to be one-fourth.
The tortoise and the lotus should be divided into three parts by means of one-third of the smallest [unit];
however, among those capable of it, one should withdraw [the division] for the sake of the devotees of Śiva.
155b) To one who has been taught the *Saṃhitā* consisting of four quarters and six categories of meaning,
a quarter [of the land] should be given, as well as among those born from the earth and tortoises.
And regarding the remaining [planets], having ascertained the knowledge according to the proper rule, one should announce it;
O child, during a solar eclipse, one should cause it to be offered before Śiva.
One should fashion Mount Meru there, along with thirteen other mountains;
one should construct Meru there using a thousand palas [of gold].
Within the two thousand [yojanas], twelve mountains are not to be conceived;
each is joined with four hundred [yojanas] and possesses one hundred caves.
In that same manner, the directions are to be conceived, and the constellations from half of that;
the continents, however, are to be conceived like the planets, while those known as Jambūdvīpa are to be understood according to reality.
What are those that are distant? Likewise, the seven [groups] beginning with the Devapitṛs, the group of eight, as well as the six beginning with Mṛga, the three beginning with Brahmā, and the Pluta.
One should conceive of the seven netherworlds (pātālas) and likewise the seven celestial worlds (lokas),
as well as the thousand-petaled tortoise and the nine-petaled lotus-born [universe].
In this manner, one should cause [the gift] to be given before Kalpaśiva to Śiva-brahmins who possess unimpaired limbs, excellent conduct, and who are knowers of the Vedic Siddhāntas.
At that time, one should offer the earth to them while remembering Smara in his many forms;
one should present it as the solar disc is being seized by Rāhu.
The gift of the earth should be performed according to the sequence of the ritual; likewise, the mountains should be properly offered starting from the east on level ground.
The planets, yakṣas, and rākṣasas, as well as the two-footed beings and the salt-ocean—
thus, according to the rules of visualization, one should cause these to be offered before Śiva.
Do we exist here as atoms, or even as the entire universe up to the realm of Brahmā?

For as many thousands of kalpas as there are years of Rudra’s lifespan, he is honored in the world of Śiva; his ancestors rejoice and go wherever they please, and they dwell in the world of water for that same duration.
At the end of that [period], those kings indeed become devotees of Śiva;
through initiation, their subjects are born with a disposition toward Śiva.
Thus has this gift of the earth been described by me to you;
he who beholds this great gift shall also dwell in heaven for a full year.
One should indeed fashion a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpapādapa) before Śiva as an offering;
one should construct that wish-fulfilling tree from one thousand palas [of gold].
Having mentally conceived the five aggregates as being complete with roots, trunk, branches, leaves, fruits, and flowers, the pure-minded one should cause these five to be given.
One should give or receive [the gift] before Śiva with the Sadyojāta mantra;
upon the fall of the body, one is glorified in the world of Śiva by means of divine celestial chariots.
He shall obtain his desired objects from the bowing Kalpavṛkṣa tree;
his ancestors rejoice at ease in Satyaloka.
For a thousand divine years, endowed with various shares,
it is for this purpose indeed that the ancestors praise the continuity of the lineage.
And there will be donors who are devotees of Śiva;
by the gift of a single leaf of the Kalpa tree, they shall deliver all their ancestors.
Those great-souled ones who behold the infinite gift of the wish-fulfilling tree obtain continuous and great enjoyments in the celestial realms.
O Mahāsena, he who gives a wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadhenu) before Śiva, weighing five hundred *tulās*, [attains] the imperishable state.
By that, everything up to the end of the world of Brahmā becomes subdued.
Now listen to how the deities reside within his body.
The gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara reside at the base of the peak; Mahādeva, accompanied by [the goddesses] Trisamā and others, resides in the middle of the head.
The goddess Jvālāmukhī shone upon the tip of his forehead;
two golden horses and two serpents were stationed within the cavities of his nostrils.
Know that the Aśvins reside in the two ears, the Moon and Sun in the two eyes;
the Vasus are in the region of the teeth, while Garuḍa is situated in the palate.
Vāgīśvarī is in the syllable *huṃ*, Yamayukra is in the two cheeks,
Oṣṭhasādhyasahasra is in the lips, and Kṣoma always resides in the neck.
The bears are situated in the region of the face, and the twilight is established upon the chest;
Dharma is stationed in the shank, accompanied by the fourfold [group].
The Gandharvas are in the middle of the hooves, the Pannagas on the tips of the hooves,
and the hosts of Apsarases are stationed in the joints of the hooves.
The eleven Rudras are on the back, and the arrow is at all the joints;
but in the womb, all... [text illegible].
Folio 157 is unclear.
But listen, O Six-faced One, to the vows for the poor according to their true nature.
Having fasted on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha while remaining firm in one's observances,
a woolen blanket smeared with ghee should be offered to Śiva on the full moon day.
Afterwards, one should offer a black bull and cow in their natural form;
such a person is honored in the world of Śiva for one hundred and fifty divine years.
In the month of Phālguna, one who is established in his observances should perform the practice of eating only once a day,
subsisting on śyāmāka grain, milk, and nīvāra rice, having conquered anger and subdued the senses.
Then, during the four-month period ending with Āṣāḍhī, one should be devoted to fasting;
having bathed Śiva with devotion according to the prescribed rite on the full moon day, one should proceed.

Having diligently worshipped according to the prescribed rite with the eight kinds of clay and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should, following the injunctions, present a pair of red cows.
A man, joined with his kinsmen, proceeds to the state of Śiva.
When the month of Caitra has arrived, he who observes a single meal,
eating flour-cakes mixed with milk while his senses are fully controlled, [attains great merit].
At the conclusion of the worship of Śambhu in all rites, one should give a pair of cows;
by those of virtuous soul, that beautiful city of Śiva becomes easily attainable.
When the month of Vaiśākha arrives, he who observes a single meal should eat only milk-rice mixed with flowers, having his senses fully subdued.
Having fully worshipped the Supreme Lord, a man should give a pair of auspicious cows;
united with his kinsmen, he goes to the state of union with Śiva.
When the month of Jyeṣṭha has arrived, he who observes the practice of eating only at night should eat food made of śāli rice, drenched in ghee and milk.
Having observed the fast on the full moon day and worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rite,
one should offer a pair of smoke-colored cows to Śiva.
One attains the world of Śiva, which is free from decay;
when the month of Āṣāḍha has arrived, one should observe the practice of eating only once a day.
One who has conquered the senses should partake of a meal of milk products;
he should give a pair of white cows dedicated to Śiva as an auspicious gift.

He who observes the practice of eating only at night (naktabhojana) when the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived is honored in the world of Śiva, endowed with divine qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
One who has conquered the senses should eat rice with milk on the sixth day;
one should offer a pair of white-footed goats to the Lord.
Manifesting seven times three lineages, he dwells in the world of Śiva;
when the month of Bhādrapada has arrived, one should observe the practice of eating only at night.
One should consume the remnants of the oblation after first performing the ritual worship of the head;
one should observe a fast on the fourteenth day and worship Śiva on the full moon day.
A pair of blue cows should be given as a gift; one shall attain union with Rudra. When the month of Āśvayuja arrives, one should observe the practice of eating only one meal a day.
One should eat rice with clarified butter and abide in celibacy;
at the conclusion of the worship on the full moon day, one should give a pair of black cattle.
One is liberated from the five sins and shall attain the world of Rudra;
when the month of Kārttika has arrived, one should observe the practice of eating only at night.
One who is firm in their vow of celibacy should eat only milk-rice;
by giving a pair of red cows, one shall attain the world of Śiva.
Indeed, he who, with his senses restrained, should observe the practice of eating only at night during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, having consumed barley-gruel mixed with milk;
One should give a pair of smoky-colored cows along with a well-adorned trident;
that man, together with his kinsmen, attains union with Śiva.
When the month of Pauṣa has arrived, one should observe the practice of eating only at night;
having mastered the senses, one should consume food that has been prepared with cow's urine and fire.
Having observed the fast on this lunar day and worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rite,
one should offer a pair of red cows adorned with ornaments to Śiva.
Having attained incomparable heavenly bliss, his prowess equal to that of Rudra,
he [should offer] to the Teacher at the conclusion of his vow, and every month before Śiva.
Earth, gold, garments, jewels, and so forth should be given with great effort;
afterwards, having restrained oneself, one should diligently ask for forgiveness as if from Śiva himself.
Whatever is performed devoid of mantras and worship, or lacking the prescribed ritual, becomes fruitless for men; therefore, one should perform it perfectly complete.
Listen briefly to the vow named Umāmaheśvara:
for women who are united with a husband, there is neither this vow nor fasting.
Questioned by Pārvatī, Śambhu said, "O Śaṅkara, tell me of the vow."
With a well-pleased mind, he proclaimed that vow to me:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall declare the supreme vow among all vows."
Women should perform this with great effort, and it should be understood that it must be done with diligence on the full moon day,
the new moon day, and on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days.
One should perform this for a year at night, not subsisting on food other than sacrificial offerings (haviṣya);
one should observe celibacy, avoiding sesame seeds and collyrium.
Likewise, it is declared that one should sleep on the ground and remain truthful;
Umā and Maheśvara should be fashioned in beautiful forms out of gold.
The two [deities] should be fashioned at the end of the absence [of the central space], measuring one span or half of that;
Śiva should be made four-armed, and the Supreme Goddess two-armed.
They should be depicted as well-formed and youthful, mounted upon bulls;
in the month of Kārtika, Gaṇeśa is on the left side and Śiva is on the right.
One should fashion [the deity] standing in the middle of a river, with a trident in hand and three eyes;
having thus worshipped him according to the prescribed rite, [one should place the image] within a copper vessel.
Having fashioned a circular image clothed in red garments and worshipped it according to the prescribed ritual,
one should observe a fast on the fourteenth day and perform worship on the full-moon day.
O son of Kṛttikā, one should keep a vigil at night during these vows,
having worshipped Śiva, the supreme cause, with the highest devotion.
Having adorned it with garlands of fragrance and beautiful red garments,
and especially with various kinds of food and drink, as well as canopies, banners, and mirrors.
Having worshipped with devotion to Śiva by means of chowries, fans, and various articles of enjoyment according to the prescribed rite, [one should do so] eleven times or in pairs.
Food should be given to you, or one should satisfy a pair;
and according to one's ability, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given, excluding the Sādhya deities.
O Lord, one should cover with cloth the vessel containing the copper bowl;
this vessel, adorned with a canopy and a parasol, should be carried upon the head.
Accompanied by the sound of conch shells and musical instruments, one should proceed to the temple of Śiva;
this is the vow that one should offer to Maheśa in the form of the Liṅga.
Having circumambulated Śiva and prostrated before him, one should undertake the vow named Umāmaheśvara; it is beneficial for women and is the best of vows.
One may undertake the commencement of this vow either on the full moon day of Vaiśākha or Kārttika;
O Mahāsena, who is capable of describing the merits of this vow?
However, I shall speak in brief; listen with a one-pointed mind, O son.
Through great austerity alone, the virtuous attain all sovereignty endowed with its qualities.
Omniscience, contentment, unmanifest awakening, sovereignty, and eternal, undiminished power—
having attained infinite power through effort, he proceeds to that state which is free from all affliction.
Now, the vow known as Liṅgavrata, which follows in sequence, is being described.
Having diligently bathed the Lord of the gods with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), [one should proceed].
Having bathed the liṅga with water scented with cool sandalwood and having anointed it,
one should worship it with white, blooming lotuses and prostrate before it.
Then one should offer the food offering (naivedya) and so forth, combined with sugar-candy, milk, and clarified butter;
likewise, *ghārika*, *kiraṇa*, *lāvaka*, and *modaka*.
One should fill it up to the top with auspicious [substances], and then perform the ritual procedure;
[this] in a stainless, pure, flawless, flower-adorned, and auspicious lotus.
Having established upon the pericarp a liṅga made of fragrant substances,
measuring the size of a thumb-joint and adorned with a pedestal and stalk;
Having established [the deity] in the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, one should worship with bilva leaves;
agallochum (aguru) is on the right side, while manasilā is situated as Brahmā.
Having placed sandalwood with the Vaiṣṇavī mantra to the east of Viṣṇukrāntā,
one should worship Śiva with various fragrant substances and saffron.
Aloe-wood, frankincense, camphor, and saffron are declared to be the incense;
one should cause to be given various fine garments that are free of loose threads.
Having offered a great wick, a set of four lamps, and likewise one with eighteen more,
while reciting the Śiva mantra, he should perform the circumambulation three times.
being disciplined, should offer the entire oblation into the *liṅga* within the *liṅga*:
"O Lord of the gods, this equal *liṅga* is offered unto you."
This vow known as Liṅgavrata is the most excellent among all vows;
by this procedure, the gods attained the state of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
By means of this vow, the state of divinity desired by the mind was attained,
having especially worshipped Maheśvara on the new moon day.
But he who, by the command of Śiva, practices the night-vow for as long as he lives,
having worshipped his guru according to the prescribed rite with garments, gold, food, and drinks;
One should diligently perform a night vigil before Śiva;
this is known as the Śitavrata, by which the state of Śiva arises for men.
One who has mastered the Vedas excels over thousands of celibate students;
indeed, one who performs the Agnihotra sacrifice excels over thousands of those who have mastered the Vedas.
One who performs the yoga of sacrifice is superior to a thousand performers of the *agnihotra*;
one who performs the yoga of mantras is superior to a thousand performers of the yoga of sacrifice.
One who is proficient in three thousand mantras is superior to one proficient in two thousand;
one who has mastered all sciences is superior to one proficient in three thousand [mantras].
Among all the millions of goals of knowledge, the devotee of Śiva is preeminent;
to him it should be given with effort, and from him it should be received according to the prescribed rite.
Therefore, with a tranquil mind, one should worship Śiva with devotion;
for on this earth, he is the source of all holy places and sacred shrines.
They dwell at the base of the *liṅga*; therefore, one should worship the *liṅga* once a day,
three times a day, or even four times a day.
He who, through negligence, eats [the food] of one who is not worthy of worship or who is a supreme lord (parameśāna), [incurs sin].
An expiation must be performed; otherwise, one will go to hell.
Worship must not be omitted during periods of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or death-impurity (*mṛtaka*).
Living beings are like bubbles in water; therefore, one should always worship the Liṅga with songs, dances, offerings, and the sounds of conchs and musical instruments.
Having shaken off all sins, he goes to the world of Śiva;
one should give a young, milk-yielding cow adorned with ornaments.
Having approached Dakṣiṇāmūrti with devotion on the full moon day of either Kārttika or Vaiśākha for the sake of a devotee of Śiva, hear now the fruit of his merit.
Indeed, the earth, along with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembled;
and the release of the bull should be performed on the full moon of Kārttika as well as at the equinox.
Having released a dark-blue bull, one attains the supreme goal;
his ancestors rejoice in the world of Brahmā—of this there is no doubt.
Now, O Six-faced One, listen here to the Liṅga-vows;
one who is firm in his vows should indeed commence this vow on the full moon day of Kārtika.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, one should worship Śiva;
a great ritual bath (mahāsnāna) should be performed, or otherwise, a great worship (mahāpūjā).
For all those observing the Liṅga-vrata, one should likewise subsist on a single meal at night after having performed worship with effort using garments, food offerings, and other such items.
One should fashion a linga made of rice-flour to the measure of one cubit;
upon the linga, one should place a prastha of sesame seeds and gold.
Incense indeed, such as kaṃduru, sandalwood, or likewise aguru, should be offered;
it should be given to the one whose form is Śiva, so that there may then be auspiciousness that is imperishable.
Having worshipped the Liṅga according to the previous procedure with the great ablution (mahāsnāna) in accordance with reality, and having smeared it with saffron, one should worship Śiva.
First, a white sandalwood linga should be fashioned according to the prescribed measurements;
then, a prastha of gold-colored rice and flowers should be offered before Śiva.
One should arrange incense made of camphor in the four directions;
eight large wicks should be offered, along with one hundred and eight [offerings] in vessels of curd.
Having performed the ritual in this manner, one should offer the *liṅga* to the *liṅgāyani*;
it should be presented to the preceptor known as Īśāna-Rudra.
O Six-faced One, by this vow one attains union with Śiva;
on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, one should worship Śiva with dūrvā grass.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should burn bright guggulu incense before Śiva,
along with milk-rice mixed with ghee and sugar-candy, measuring one prastha.
The food offering (naivedya) should be placed before [the deity], along with banners numbering as many as the Śaktis;
likewise, there should be a white flag and a linga made indeed from rice-flour.
One should place an āḍhaka of sesame seeds and gold as the sacrificial fee for the Liṅga;
one should offer this vow to the Rudra named Śaṅkara.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, having worshipped Śiva as before,
one should offer a liṅga made of boiled rice, a prastha of sesame seeds, and gold.
It should be worn with great care on the right side of Śiva.
One should burn incense consisting of a *prastha* measure each of *godana*, clarified butter,
*aguru*, *silhaka*, and camphor before Śiva in the east.
One should perform a single vow according to the prescribed rite for Ugra-Rudra;
at the conclusion of the vow, one should worship the preceptor with devotion according to one's capacity.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rite,
one should offer guggulu resin with ghee as incense and four great wicks.
One should offer various kinds of modakas soaked in ghee with milk,
according to the prescribed rite, and likewise present the liṅga.
Having thus honored the preceptor, who is worthy of worship with all his limbs and to whom abundant sacrificial fees are given,
O Mahāsena, one does not encounter misfortune anywhere.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rite,
one should smear the linga with a pala-measure of yellow pigment (rocanā).
The food offering (naivedya) should consist of one prastha of milk-rice accompanied by sugar-candies and sweets;
along with clarified butter, guggulu resin weighing a hundred palas should be offered.
One should offer a flour-liṅga together with a prastha measure of sesame seeds and gold;
it should be carefully placed in the southern direction of Śiva.
Having sent Bhavarudra away, one should then worship the preceptor;
thus should one act with diligence by one desiring imperishable liberation.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha,
having diligently worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rite, preceded by a great ceremonial bath;
Having smeared [the image] with saffron, one should worship Śiva with damana flowers.
Having fashioned a linga out of flour and adorned it with golden flowers,
one should place a prastha of sesame seeds, gold, and the linga in the southern direction as a sacrificial fee.
Two large wicks should be offered with clarified butter for the row of lamps;
likewise, two hundred palas of guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter should be offered.
One should burn one *pala* each of agallochum (*aguru*), *silphaka*, and camphor;
then, having worshipped Śiva with devotion using *damanaka* flowers.
One should offer gold and sesame-seed lingas to Bhava and Rudra; furthermore, gurus numbering as many as the Rudras should be diligently honored with gifts.
Through gifts of land and clothing, and through extensive offerings of gold and other riches,
this is known as the supreme vow (*vratottama*), to be performed every year.
Thus, he who performs this with devotion goes to the eternal state;
his ancestors rejoice in the world of Bhadra as they please.
Having spent ten thousand divine years there,
those lords of wealth attained knowledge and subsequently merged into the eternal Śiva.
O Mahāsena, he who acts like Śiva is indeed honored;
having performed [the rite] regularly on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should worship Śiva.
Having anointed [the image] with sandalwood paste, one should worship it with jasmine flowers;
saffron and *laghucandra* incense should be offered before Śiva.
There were rows of lamps, various carts, diverse kinds of food,
many wonderful paintings, and numerous spectacles accompanied by colorful displays.
There were groups of musicians and musical instruments, as well as auspicious celestial chariots;
and especially, those eight types of weapons along with their respective sheaths arrived there.
Having performed heroic wrestling matches and contests with wooden animals,
and having colored them with pigments, one should offer them before Śiva.
Two large wicks should be offered after the worship of Śiva;
one wick should be dedicated to Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and indeed one wick to Śiva.
She should indeed be given with great effort, adorned with garments and gold;
thereafter, the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga) should be performed before Śiva according to the prescribed rules.
Auspicious sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should indeed be given to a Brahmin who is a devotee of Śiva;
they yield the same auspicious fruit as that of all sacrifices and all sacred fords (tīrthas).
He who uplifts his lineage— ten ancestors and ten descendants— obtains a fruit ten million times greater than that, as well as the arising of sovereign power.
For those who are highly wise, disciplined, devoted, and of purified soul,
giving is briefly proclaimed as being endowed with the merit of all forms of giving.
Having received initiation into Śiva, one must protect it with great effort through restraints (yamas),
observances (niyamas), the practice of vows, and so forth.
Thus, she becomes fruitful when protected, just as agriculture is;
otherwise, she is uprooted by hosts of yakṣiṇīs.
164a) One who is dependent does not observe the two kinds of vows;
those free from desire lead to liberation, while those accompanied by desire lead to enjoyment.
Initiation alone is liberation for men, yet it becomes the harvest of their past actions;
its direct impeller is the Head (Śiras), which depends upon the descent of power (śaktipāta).
The descent of power (śaktipāta) is fourfold, according to the distinctions of intense, moderate, and so forth;
the sign recognized in the descent of power is unwavering devotion to Śiva.
Possessing the power of the vast scriptures and intent upon the worship of the Linga,
he maintains equanimity toward all beings and is endowed with compassion and mercy.
Forgiveness, truthfulness, purity, compassion toward all beings,
as well as existence [of virtue] and straightforwardness— these, indeed, are known as the marks [of a Brahmin].
Through initiation one becomes fit for hearing [the scriptures]; through initiation one is capable of performing worship;
and through initiation, one proceeds according to one's station, free from the burden of worldly toil.
Through initiation (dīkṣā) knowledge is attained; through initiation the supernatural powers (siddhis) arise.
Therefore, initiation indeed bestows liberation, for it is the giver of knowledge, O Naṅgiṇī.
Those who have been consecrated by the initiation of Śiva are qualified everywhere,
even in the Kaula, Pāśupata, and other systems, as well as in the doctrines known as Śaura and Sākhya.
Śiva, however, is the supreme authority; he is not to be served in any other way whatsoever.
The Śrutis, which have their root in Śiva, are especially authoritative.
In accordance with the existence of that [atom], the general view is firmly held:
everything arises from the dyad (dvyaṇuka); because of its atomicity, Śiva is the impeller.
O Six-faced One, I shall explain briefly the pervasion of the partless [reality].
One should designate the letter *u* as the principle of the Self (*ātmatattva*), while the letter *a* is the principle of ignorance (*avidyātattva*).
The essence of Śiva is indeed the letter *A*, which has been revealed as partless;
I shall now further declare the definitive teaching concerning grace (*prasāda*).
The knower of mantras should always observe the short, the long, and the protracted [vowels]:
the short burns away sins, while the long bestows liberation.
In the rite of nourishment (*āpyāyana*), the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) is indeed prolated (*pluta*), having three morae (*trimātra*).
As for the gross distinctions (*sthūlabheda*) that have been proclaimed, they are used for subduing (*vaśya*), eradication (*uccāṭana*), and destruction (*māraṇa*).

By always performing the *pluta* [prolonged] utterance and joining the syllable *hrīḥ* at the beginning and end, [the rite] is long-lasting; for the purpose of eradication (*uccāṭana*), it should be quickly marked with the syllable *phaṭ*.
At the beginning and at the end, one should employ the syllable *phaṭ* marked with the letter *repha* (r) for the purpose of killing;
joined with the syllable *vaṃ*, it draws [the target] even from a distance of hundreds of *yojanas*.
In this manner, one should apply the rites of nourishment and so forth, having first understood the names,
according to the sequence as they have been declared and in accordance with the vowels and consonants.
Having understood the distinction between the goal and the means, as well as the specific tones of the officiating priest,
practitioners will not achieve success if they perform this rite without such knowledge.
Having performed the yoga previously described, one should cause the offering (argha) for the mantra to be presented;
having offered the argha and performed the recitation (japa) of the mantra, the wise practitioner [should proceed].
One should perform the recitation for five hundred thousand times, standing on the right side of the deity;
at the conclusion of the recitation, one should arrange a ghee oblation consisting of a tenth part [of the total count].
Thus nourished, the mantra will become fit for ritual action;
consequently, whatever rites have been taught will undoubtedly attain success.
If one recites [the mantra] one million times, the people dwelling in that place will surely come under control quickly; such is the certainty of the scripture.
Having recited [the mantra] three hundred and fifty thousand times, the inhabitants of the ten villages will come together with their own bodies and through their slaughter.
One should bring the object under control with twenty-five hundred thousand recitations;
indeed, he who recites thirty hundred thousand times shall become a master of the world.
With thirty-five hundred thousand [recitations], one shall bring the earth under one's control;
and by forty thousand, one shall indeed enter the abode of Vādakeśvara.
Having recited it fifty thousand times, one becomes equal to a Vidyādhara;
there the practitioner of mantra rejoices until the dissolution of all beings at the end of the aeon.
Then, through the realization of the supported and the support, the practitioner is liberated;
[he realizes] the support as the city, the earth, and the sphere ending with Māyā.
The supreme object to be established is peaceful, beyond the reach of the means of valid cognition,
singular, eternal, unborn, all-pervading, consisting of universal bliss, and auspicious.
Through the conjunction with the city of eight, he goes upward along the path;
[namely] sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth.
Intellect, mind, and ego—this is declared to be the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka).
As long as one is not liberated from these, how can one be released from bondage?
Having joined smell with Brahmā, taste likewise with Keśava,
form with Rudra, and then touch, intellect, and ego with Īśvara;
And the dissolution of sound and mind into the fragment [of the Self] is the sixty-fold path intended by Śivā.
Thus ends the chapter on the realization of the means of accomplishment in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
167a) Īśvara said:
I shall now explain, with effort and in brief, the subtle wheel of channels (nāḍīcakra). Below the navel is the trunk (skaṃda), from which sprouts emerge.
Seventy-two thousand [channels] are situated in the center of the navel;
they pervade [the body] equally, extending horizontally, upwards, and downwards.
For these ten principal channels are arranged like a wheel;
namely, the Iḍā, the Piṅgalā, and likewise the Suṣumnā.
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Pūṣā, as well as Yasā;
Alambuṣā, and Śaṅkhinī is considered the tenth.
These ten channels are indeed proclaimed as the carriers of the vital breaths:
prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.
The Nāgas are Kurma, Udhva, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhananjaya;
Prāṇa, however, is the first wind and the lord of all ten.
Abiding in the chest of living beings, this *prāṇa*, consisting of breath, constantly fills and replenishes the exhalation and inhalation of the vital breath.
Because the vital breath (prāṇa), which is dependent upon the individual soul (jīva), departs [from the body] through the desires of inhalation and exhalation, it is therefore proclaimed as "prāṇa."
The *apāna* wind, however, carries food downward for human beings;
because it carries urine and semen, it is celebrated as *apāna*.
The wind named Samāna brings into equilibrium blood, bile, phlegm, and wind that have been drunk, eaten, or smelled, according to their respective measures.
The wind named Udāna causes the lower part of the body and the face to droop, agitates the eyes and limbs, and disturbs the vital points (marmas).
Vyāna causes the limbs to wither away; Vyāna is the agitator of diseases.
It is said that it dwells within the joints, and due to its pervasiveness (vādhikya), it is called Vyāna.
The one called Utsāra is said to reside in the closing of the eyes; Kūrma is in the knitting of the brows; Kṛkara is in the act of cutting, and Devadatta is in yawning.
O Dhanañjaya, she remains in the body-cavity (ghoṣa) and does not leave even when one is dead;
she resides in the forest of the navel-lotus, while the multitude of vital airs (vāyu-vṛnda) remains in the throat.
I shall explain to you in its entirety the wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*);
for it is by this ten-spoked wheel that the division is understood.
The living being revolves like a wheel through ten stages in their proper sequence;
that living being [is the cause] of the growth of the world of living beings, yet they are not at all deluded [by this].
The individual soul (jīva) moves through ten paths; therefore, it is proclaimed as a "wheel" (cakra).
It is called the "wheel of channels" (nāḍīcakra), by means of which he transmigrates.
In the pericarp of the heart-lotus, three channels shine forth;
they are renowned as Akṣa, Iḍā, and Piṅgalā, increasing eightfold from their own respective locations.
Therefore, indeed, their binding resides within the principle of Śakti;
by means of the other [powers] within the principle of Śakti, the vital breath moves through embodied beings.
For even in the interval of emptiness, that fruit which is destined to arise always causes its own result to fly up like a ball struck by a blow, as if it were certain to rise.
From the yoga of Īśvara, the equinox (viṣuvat) and the transition (saṃkrānti) are indeed central;
from the application of Saturn, the southern and northern solstices arise through conjunction with the Moon.
In the solstice, there are two even-folded sections on the left; they call the odd-folded section the *viṣuc*.
The transition from here and there as one moves is declared to be the solar path;
the leftward path is declared to belong to the moon.
In the case of the Sun, when there is a conjunction with Saturn, Mars, or Jupiter, it results in suffering from boils or skin diseases;
likewise, when the Moon is in conjunction with Mercury, Jupiter, or Venus, one becomes a king or a person of noble lineage, provided these planets are situated in the eastern half [of the zodiac].
The radiant one, the consumer of oblations, becomes the King (Yama) in the south-eastern quarter;
Yāmya is indicated in the south, Bhāvya in the south-west, and Nairṛta in the west.

In the western quarter (Vāruṇa) there is the state of leaves; in the northern (Saumya) that of the moon; in the northwestern (Vāyavya) that of heat; in the harsh (Pāruṣya) that of the moon’s movement; in the eastern (Saumya) that of purposeful effort; in the fierce (Raudra) that of the power of knowledge.
