Whichever direction one approaches, one attains that very state in its entirety.
Due to the conjunction with the intermediate spaces between the petals, the Self appears as if empty.

Thus, in this movement of the *puṅgala*, the secret mandala of the circulation of the channels has been described; it should be understood with effort as the cause of accomplishment for the sake of success.
Thus ends the chapter on the enumeration of the wheel of channels in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the knowledge of time, which is very difficult to perceive.
Below the navel is the bulb (kanda), which is considered the abode of the channels (nāḍīs).
O son, from there indeed the channels extend horizontally, upwards, and downwards,
numbering seventy-two thousand, like the petals of a lotus leaf.
Of those, there are ten primary ones; then follow the three beginning with *iḍā*.
Having drawn [the breath] up to twelve [finger-breadths], one should sustain it with the vital air (*jīva-vāyu*).
Thus, the movement back and forth is described as the "vehicle" (vāhana) yantra;
it extends twelve finger-breadths upward by means of the lower part.
Coming and going to his house and performing worship day and night—
such things do not exist for that great-souled one who stands in the midst of fame and infamy.
That which is my inhalation is the state of being; that which is my exhalation is the seeking of breath.
By means of that, there is the utterance of short syllables, according to the measure of its increase.
A *tuṭi* is considered to be as empty as space, and two such *tuṭis* are regarded as a pair;
the dissolution (*laya*) of those two pairs is proclaimed as the duration of a *mātrā*.
The Guru consists of two *mātṛkā*s; from those two comes the *kāṣṭhā*, and in the evening, the *guṇākalā*.
Two and a half *kalā*s constitute one *prāṇa*, which is equal in number to sixty breaths (*śvāsa*).
With thirty breaths there is his going out, and again with thirty his returning;
by that [reckoning] come days and nights, months, and twelve years.
Born from the heart, throat, palate, tip of the nose, and the space between the eyebrows up to the dvādaśānta,
the day for the prāṇa is its upward movement, while the night is its downward movement.
The rising sun is Prāṇa; residing below on the Himālaya mountain is Abhijit; the Lord is the light of that which stands eternally, the one who possesses the *sāluka* fruit.
At nightfall and at the end of the day, enjoyment and liberation are accomplished;
there is no doubt that this occurs through the worship of Śiva, recitation, meditation, and acts such as giving.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara reside respectively in the heart, the palate, and the dvādaśānta;
the time that has arisen before the junction (saṃdhyā) is proclaimed as the saṃdhyā.
Furthermore, I shall describe the day and night: outside, there are black [lines] and perpetual impurity;
where there is a pair of breaths, such is the state of the day and night.
The dark fortnight is described by the fifteen [digits] by the teachers;
likewise, the bright fortnight is established in the same manner by those very same [digits].
At the end of the lunar fortnight, from the conjunction with the moon during the waning of the lunar day,
there occurs the conjunction of the moon with Rāhu, resulting in an eclipse of the sun and the moon.
There, by means of bathing, recitation, meditation, charity, worship, and fire-rituals,
one who is free from conceptual construction attains infinite merit.
The zodiac signs, beginning with Aries, correspond respectively to five breaths each;
therein, the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) occurs during the day, and the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) during the night.
At the end of the twelve [finger-breadths] and in the heart, there are two channels, the southern and the northern;
the merit derived from these two is respectively inexhaustible in this world and the next.
Therefore, that which was previously described bears fruit; thus, the two equinoxes situated at the palate—at the beginning of Aries and in Libra—have been declared by the seers of reality.
The eight-fold *vyatīpāta* and the fortnight (*pakṣa*) are likewise established within the *prapañca* and the night;
by this very direction, they should be understood by those of their own sharp intellect.
Twelve months have been declared by me to constitute a year;
here too, the sequence of days, months, and years is to be understood as previously described.
Furthermore, sixty breaths are proclaimed to be sixty fortnights;
by means of the sequence previously described, from that [calculation], the intermediate periods and so forth are derived.
This single vital breath (prāṇa) has been declared by Śiva to be the definitive determination of the hands;
the yogi who is absorbed in that, free from conceptual construction, shall attain that very state.
He alone is worthy to know the life and death, the gain and loss, and the victory and defeat of both himself and others.
Seated in an auspicious place, composed in mind, and free from fear, the knower of reality, when questioned by men whose hands are not empty, should examine that gift.
Having first reflected upon the auspicious and inauspicious [results] according to the sequence taught in the scriptures,
one should speak likewise to another in such a way that no distress arises.
The channels known as Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā—situated on the left, right, and middle—are respectively composed of the nature of the moon, the sun, and fire; they are mixed with nectar and poison.
They possess two forms, stable and unstable, and have the natures of female, male, and neuter;
they are known as the life-force, the elements, and the roots, and consist of the essences of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara.
They bestow satisfaction, emaciation, destruction, gentleness, cruelty, fear, and wealth;
when encircled by Jupiter they are full, and when devoid of him they are empty.
For one who inquires during the *pūrṇā* [lunar day], success (*siddhi*) occurs; during the *riktā*, there will be emptiness (*riktatā*).
Regarding these two, the first mentioned should be declared for victory, and the second in due order.
In whichever direction the wind blows, there the strength shall be full;
in most cases, one should indicate the movement of the planets and so forth in the other directions in sequence.
One should cause the even syllables to meet on the left and the odd syllables on the right.
In the left and right [sides] of the lord, one should recognize the stationary and the moving;
when resting on the Sāman, there is the attainment of what was lost in the sacrifice, as well as pacifying and nourishing rites.
Furthermore, greed for satisfaction arises; life lasts until the end of the three worlds;
there is an increase in the practice of mantras and tantras, and auspiciousness such as pilgrimages to Śiva.
If one always asks gentle questions with a thick stream [of devotion], they will succeed;
[otherwise, there may be] disease, suffering, poison, enmity, loss, and fear of battle from men.
There would be no obstacle here at all; however, once bitten, one does not live.
One might live elsewhere, but for one who applies [the remedy] there, the union remains fixed in the mind.
Pure food that is wind-like, enjoyment of women, loss of wealth, gambling, eradication,
and the terrifying act of inciting enmity— these are the results.

In this world, there may arise the fear of death, diseases, and all other cruel afflictions; as well as malevolent planets, spiders, insects, and spirits such as pretas, bhūtas, vetālas, and rākṣasas.
When the sun blazes, darkness finds no peace;
therefore, for men, the moon, the sun, nectar, and poison yield results that are like fire in alternation.
Thereafter, it may yield some fruit: poison or nectar from the Sun or the Moon;
yoga, knowledge, vows, initiation, liberation, wisdom, and reverence for the guru.
Suṣumnā is that which is eternal perfection, the source of both the neuter and the couple;
what is said for the right is not on the left, and what is said for the left is certainly not on the right.
The left end and the right as described do not at all succeed in the middle;
for it is through the entry into the left, right, and middle that [the practice] becomes fruitful.
All matters such as inquiries regarding thoughts and the like are fruitless during the three [periods] of *nirgama* (exit);
one should determine both *nirgama* and *praveśa* (entry) by means of the movement of the *ghaṭī*.
When situated in the front, the Moon is on the left; when situated at the back, Yama is on the right.
Prāṇa moves through the days starting from the first day of the bright fortnight.
For three days Soma transits, and for three days the Sun transits again and again;
in this very manner, during the dark fortnight, the Sun likewise moves toward Soma for three days at a time.
From the reversal [of the sequence], one should predict quarrels and so forth after two or three days;
the wise know that the reversal of the groups of one, two, and three occurs in due order.
Disease, loss of kinsmen, death, and the loss of wealth for a year—these arise from the increase of the *yāma* and so forth; that which belongs to the southern direction is called the *mātraka*.
Likewise, there will be illness and distress for two months, as well as the loss of eyesight and wealth;
the great night [of death] lasts for three years, while the two-year period lasts for two nights.

One year [is the duration] from three days and nights; half a day from that [period]; one month from that; and beyond that, one day from half a day. One should observe these in successive order; this is the certainty.
When the moment of the equinox has arrived, if one's eyes throb, [it is a sign].
One should know that his life will not last beyond a day and night; of this there is no doubt.
Among the seasons, beginning with Śiśira, [the death] occurs at the start of the fifth day.
In the life-force (*jīva*), one should increase by three for each [element]: three horses, eight, and ten breaths respectively;
in those [periods], the wind should flow for three, two, or four days.
By giving [this] to a devotee of Bhagavān for a year, prosperity is produced here.
For one month, the wind always flows through both the night and the day;
by its movement, it indicates, in succession, the loss of wealth and other such matters throughout the day and night.

If the breath flows for ten days in both [nostrils] without a transition (saṃkrānti), then death occurs due to that lack of transition; it happens after half a day for one who follows the three paths.
If the five transits (saṃkrānti-pañcaka) do not flow at all through the mouth of one whose breath is agitated, his end is near; otherwise, there is no other [auspicious] course.
On Monday, when moving through the *suṣumnā* channel, he bestows virtue (*dharma*) and the fruits of sovereignty;
when wandering here and there, O Marut, the planet bestows worship.
One who is always absorbed in going and coming is fit to know that;
otherwise, one should know the deception of time through its three modes.
When seven equal solar days have passed, or when the sun has entered the sign of Leo or Sagittarius, accompanied by its characteristic mark; |||
If the Moon is in the natal asterism at the time of sunrise on Mount Meru,
that is the time known as Prāvṛṭ, according to those who determine death.
If, from that time onward, the wind remains in one [nostril] for half a day and is surrounded by fourteen breaths, then death occurs within a year.
If one were to carry out a sacrifice for one day and one great night at a single location,
then death would occur after twelve years and ten [years] respectively.
If [the breath] remains in one place for two days and nights, or three days and nights of the asuras,
then after eight years, one will attain the sixth [dhyāna].
May the wind carry [the breath] in one place for four days and nights.
Death is certain to be seized by means of years and seasons in succession,
just as the wind carries away days and nights that have come together.
If the wind flows through five [channels] for three years, death occurs without a doubt;
likewise, if the vital breath (*amarut*) does not remain in one place for ten or fifteen days.
When the wind [Māruta] blows for twenty days and twenty-five days respectively, there is death by rain after two years and one year, respectively.
Then, when the wind blows in one direction for six months, there is a gradual progression;
likewise, when it blows for twenty-six or twenty-seven months, there is a gradual progression of the wind.
If there is a single commonality in the [lunar] days, then death occurs within a month; likewise, if there is a single commonality in the twenty-eighth or twenty-ninth [day], death occurs in a month.
This external death occurs after fifteen days, ten days, or thirty days; or if the thirty-first breath [is absent], it occurs at that very moment.
Death occurs for men in due order over five, three, and two days;
or as stated by Atri, it may be thirty-two or thirty-three days.
Then, death occurs for two days and one day respectively on the path of the sun;
if a man who has just eaten remains healthy and cuts off his food intake, [he survives].
One who previously did not perceive fragrance, nor smells the scent of a lamp,
and who, though seeing objects, does not recognize the directions— such a person born under the [Dik] asterism shall live for four months.
Folio 172 is unclear.
173a) What is considered subtle? What indeed is considered gross and worldly? A fourth part of a *nimeṣa* (the blink of an eye) shall be a *tuṭi*.
Two *dvayas* make one *lava*;
two *lavas* constitute a *nimeṣa*; fifteen of those make a *kāṣṭhā*;
thirty *kāṣṭhās* are said to be a *kalā*; and thirty *kalās* make a *kṣaṇa*.
Two kṣaṇas are considered one muhūrta; four muhūrtas are a ghaṭikā;
eight of those are a prahara; and twelve of those are a day and night.
A fortnight consists of fifteen days, and a month arises from two fortnights. Two months are declared to be a season (ṛtu), and three of those are considered an ayana.
A year is formed from two solstices; this is considered the solar measurement. The southern course is to be known as night for the gods, and the northern course as their day.
By that measure of years, a yuga proceeds in time;
it should be known as consisting of four thousand [years] according to that reckoning.
The Kṛta age is followed by the Tretā age; there are four junctions (saṃdhi) between them.
The duration of the Tretā and Dvāpara is equal, and after the Dvāpara comes the Kali age.
This is the sequence; this sequence is designated as "one hundred thousand. One should know that there is a single division [consisting of] scent, the wave, and the group.
By those fourteen [days], a single day of Brahmā is reckoned.
During this interval, the Śakras die and are born again and again.
Three hundred days and sixty [nights] for him are thus called a year.
According to that number, as many years as there are up to a hundred are considered the lifespan of Hari;
by that measure, they remain in the boon for a full hundred years.
During this interval of time, many twice-born ones have perished; my rains shall last for that long, and then Viṣṇu goes to his imperishable state.
If for as long as a hundred years you were to rain down inexhaustible wealth, yet there were not even a single day of peace for those suffering from hunger, then what would be the point?
In the meantime, we have died again and again;
yet, by the mere blink of Sadāśiva’s eye, even that [time] comes to an end.
But when there is supreme, subtle joy, then he attains absorption into That;
that gross time is known as "sakala" (with parts), so now hear about the subtle.
When there is the practice of the vital points (marmas) through inhalation and exhalation,
that which occurs as their filling at three times is called the "threefold power" (triśakti) of the vital breath (prāṇa).
For yogis, a day and night is to be understood by means of two breaths;
the upward movement of the breath is known as the day, and when it has become one [with the downward flow], that is the night.
With those fifteen [days], it is called a fortnight;
with thirty breaths [of days], it is to be known as a month; and with twelve months, they are equal to a year.
Sixty-three hundred breaths are considered to be one ghaṭikā;
in a kalā and a prahara, the number is two thousand each.
Furthermore, seven hundred and twenty-four of these [years] are known as a *raha*;
an equal number of nights is likewise prescribed, and all this together is called an *asaṃkhyā*.
In that regard, sixty [breaths] come together; now hear the count of the vital breaths:
two tens of thousands (20,000), one thousand (1,000), and likewise six hundred (600).
And in a single day and night, the lord of yogis performs the count of the recitation.
For one who abides in the principle of Śiva, there is neither birth nor death.
Furthermore, the division [of time] is here stated again in brief:
the transits (saṃkrānti), the equinoxes (viṣuva), and the days and nights.
In this manner, the intercalary month is indeed debt, and likewise the omitted night is wealth;
the omitted night becomes flatulence, and the intercalary month becomes yawning.
Debt and desire are to be known [as the left and right]; exhalation is said to be wealth.
The upper and the lower are to be understood as designated as the left and the right.
The equinox is said to be that which has issued forth from both nostrils;
the solstice, moreover, is simply the movement from one's own position to another position.
The iḍā and the suṣumnā are located there, with the piṅgalā situated on the right;
the suṣumnā is in the middle portion, while the iḍā is established on the left.
When it moves from one channel to another, that is called a transition (saṃkrānti).
Indeed, the upward-moving prāṇa is day, and the downward-moving apāna is said to be night.
The single vital breath, which the knower of the eternal Veda knows as tenfold, is the extension residing within the fragrance of the body; this is intended as the lunar eclipse.
One should know that the day transcends the body; the wise understand it as the grasping of the sun.
Now I shall describe to you prāṇāyāma in its entirety.
The utterance of the mantra is the cause [of its efficacy], arising from the application of a single sequence of vowels;
indeed, having filled the upper [space] with the vital air (vāyu) in due order.
This is *prāṇāyāma*; it is the *pūraka*, which fills the body, having closed all the gates [of the senses] and being devoid of inhalation and exhalation.
The kumbhaka breath-retention, in which the breath remains completely full, is called kumbhavatiṣṭhet;
then the knower of yoga should release the breath upward with a single inhalation (śvāsa).
For one engaged in the yoga of exhalation, he should expel the upward-moving air;
this is known as *recaka*, which brings about the restraint (*yama*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The lotus situated at the junction of the heart stands with its face directed toward the center;
it first blossoms when filled by means of *pūraka* (inhalation).
The lotus [of the heart] becomes an upward-streaming flow when restrained by *kumbhaka*;
likewise, it is cast upward by *recaka*, which indeed carries away the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Having released the heart-lotus, it is established in the upward flow;
being exhaled, it goes to the heart in an instant, having pierced through.
Having pierced the opening of the skull, the life-force (jīva), impelled by the half-moon,
goes to the state of Sadāśiva and shall not undergo birth again.
Its length is three times that [width], and its breadth is never different;
he who knows this is declared by me to be a knower of the world in brief.
The creation is now briefly described according to its sequential order:
that which is the primordial Kuṇḍalinī is conjoined with the moon, fire, and supernatural power (ṛddhi).
She should be known as being situated in the region of the heart in the form of a sprout.
There, the placement should be performed according to the method of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa), accompanied by the emission (visarga) through the drawing-in of power;
the best of practitioners should contemplate [the deity] as flowing there, not as dead.
The world, both moving and stationary, consists of fire and barley;
thus should the supreme practitioner meditate with a steady mind.
The wise one, being captivating, should contemplate his own body as having a divine form;
thereafter, he should contemplate Śakti arising from Śiva as the entire Īśvara.
Śuddhavidyā consists of five and five; it is proclaimed as the pure reality (śuddhatattva).
Māyā, Kāla, Sakala, Niyati, and Rāga likewise [constitute the impure reality].
Therefore, through ignorance, primordial nature (prakṛti), which consists of the three qualities, binds the person;
likewise [it consists of] the mind, the intellect, the ego, and the organs of perception.
The organs of action, their objects, and the elements arise in succession;
he who practices this indeed attains the nectar that faces in all directions.
In no long time at all, she shall partake in the fruit of accomplishment.
Thus ends the chapter on the determination of time in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
The man who does not realize the fifth mantra,
which has a great body and is endowed with thirty-eight digits, is called an Ācārya.
If a guru performs initiation without correctly discerning the disciple's spiritual clarity (prasāda),
he brings neither the disciple nor himself down; of this there is no doubt.
He who, abiding in the crest-lock (śikhā) which consists of pure grace, performs initiation, that teacher,
together with his disciple, shall attain union with Śiva.
Indeed, by his grace, gods, dānavas, gandharvas, as well as yakṣas, uragas, rākṣasas, kinnaras, apsarases, and siddhas come into being.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, Candra,
Bṛhaspati, Prajāpati, as well as the Daityas, Śukra, Skanda, and Bhṛgu.
And whatever other living beings there may be, all are said to be born from the *prasāda*; these many sages of firm vows are likewise [born] from Vāmī.
They strive for the supreme Haṃsa through repeated recitation of His name;
I shall explain the division of the Vāma [path], knowing which one who has died attains liberation.
They know that Sadyojāta is produced from the syllable *A* and is endowed with eight digits (*kalā*);
one should know Vāmadeva to be born from the syllable *U*, and Aghora to be born from the syllable *Ma*.
The person born from the *bindu* is to be known as Īśāna, whose nature is the *śikhā*;
one should never conceive of any difference between the *praṇava* and its grace.
Immediately following the letter 'a', there is the cessation [of the preceding] and union with Brahman;
thus the earthly principle (pārthiva-tattva) is established in fivefold form.
The syllable *ukāra* is Vāmadeva, with Varuṇa as its deity and Viṣṇu as its presiding divinity;
one should there conceive of the *pratiṣṭhā* stage as fivefold.
One should likewise conceive of the half-moon, the Aghora, the Vidyārudra,
the Anala, and the Tattva as the letter *A* in five distinct ways.
One should conceive of the Bindu as Tatpuruṣa, Śānti, Kalā, Vāyu, and Īśvara in five ways above; the Nāda is situated between two Bindus.
The sound (nāda), the seed-syllable, and then the syllable Om arise as Īśāna;
likewise, Sadāśiva is space (kāśa), abiding in the Kalā beyond peace (śāntyatīta).
Brahmā is the heart, the location; Viṣṇu is established in the throat;
Rudra is situated in the region of the palate; and Īśvara is situated in the two nostrils.
Sadāśiva extends from the Brahma-randhra down to the range of Śakti;
above that, at the end of the twelve finger-breadths, Śiva himself is directly established.
One should know that the syllable *la*, which arises from the letter *va* and is born of the *vāmā* and *aghora* [faces], is endowed with its eight parts (*kalās*) immediately upon its manifestation.
Know that Bahurūpa consists of ten tri-kalās,
while Hara is this four-kalā Puruṣa born from the syllable *jiṃ*.
The six objects of knowledge, then Īśāna, and the group of five that has been conquered;
but the sixth is that supreme reality which stands apart from qualities such as similarity.
His body should not be described as being produced from those previously mentioned qualities;
having known the supreme ladder, which consists of five stations and is like the night.
By whomsoever the deity has been known even once, she is never forgotten.
At that very time, when that state is indeed known,
its division through *prasāda* and *praṇava* has been described by me.
One should never conceive of any difference between grace and the Praṇava;
those who understand the Praṇava in such a way wander through the cycle of existence.
Having realized the true nature of the Praṇava, who is not liberated from bondage?
Thus ends the chapter on the pervasion of the *praṇava* of grace in the *Kālottara*.
The Lord said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the knowledge of Śiva as it truly exists:
he who resides within the body is to be known as having parts (sakala), while he who is devoid of the body is partless (niṣkala).
Upon the completion of the authoritative instruction,
may that Lord Sadāśiva— who abides everywhere and who is called "Haṃsa, Haṃsa"— dwell within you.
But how can all-pervading bliss be obtained directly from the mouth of the Guru?
It is like oil residing within sesame seeds, or fragrance inherent in flowers.
Within this body of a person, he dwells both externally and internally,
just as someone with a torch in hand might go about illuminating objects.
Having illuminated the object of knowledge through knowledge, one should then abandon that [instrumental] knowledge;
one should know the flower to be the differentiated (sakala), while its fragrance is the undifferentiated (niṣkala).
One should know that the tree is with parts (sakala), while its shadow is without parts (niṣkala).
The state that is both with parts and without parts is established everywhere.
The differentiated should be known as differentiated, and likewise the undifferentiated as undifferentiated;
one should know that which transcends the body as the Supreme, located twelve finger-breadths above the navel.
One should recognize this: the Lord, while remaining there, pervades it;
even when my eye is cast elsewhere, it does not fall away from that place.
Nevertheless, for the wise, yoga proceeds without interruption;
this indeed is the supreme secret, this is the supreme syllable.
There is nothing higher than this; there is nothing more auspicious than this.
For this is the nectar of the knowledge of Śiva, taught in brief and not in detail.
The God of gods has declared this determination of the supreme syllable;
this true nature of Śiva has issued forth from the mouth of Śiva.
This secret, more secret than the secret, must be concealed with great effort;
it should never be given to one who is not a disciple, nor even to one's own son.
This scripture should be given to the teacher-god, to a devotee, and to one who is constantly devoted to devotion; it should not be given to others.
Those who give it away go to hell and never attain success;
this is known as the nectar of Śiva—this which I have told you is the truth, the absolute truth.
Having understood this, the wise man should conduct himself according to his own ease—
whether as a householder, a student, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant.
Wherever the Knower may abide, is he always the Supreme Immutable?
Is the subject capable of sacrificing the object, or Śiva [himself] within the body and so forth?
Even for a human being who has attained this state through the knowledge of the scriptures,
he is still tainted by sin and merit arising from the killing of a Brahmin or from sacrificial offerings.
Furthermore, I shall explain the direct worship in due order:
O child, during a solar eclipse, direct worship is prescribed.
Having attained the supreme state, which is peaceful, beyond the reach of speech, and transcending all objects, one should worship it directly within the lotus of the heart; such is true sacrifice.
The best of practitioners should understand that the infinite is merely a designation.
Thus ends the chapter on direct worship in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
O Six-faced One, I shall now proclaim the extraction of the *liṅga* for those who are lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika*),
as well as for those who follow the five-fold purpose (*pañcārtha*), the Time (*kāla*), and the Face (*vaktra*) systems, and for all heretics (*pāṣaṇḍika*).
Having passed three nights or five nights, one should cause [the deity] to dwell within;
this should be performed with the *hṛdayamantra* and the *vratasaṃhāra-mudrā*.
One should arrange the *mātrikās* there according to the ritual procedure prescribed by the rules;
one should draw an eight-petaled lotus, adorned with walkways and gates.
One should worship Mātṛkā there by means of the yoga of the sequence of withdrawal;
having worshipped according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) everywhere.
The wise one should offer five oblations for each caste in due order; this should be performed with the heart-mantra (hṛdayamantra) by means of the withdrawal (saṃhāra) mudrā.
Having done this, O Skanda, one should then generate the ritual of withdrawal (*saṃhāriṇī-ṛṣṭi*) there according to the previous method,
having indeed performed the final rite (*naiṣṭhika*).
By means of the yoga of creation and dissolution, those who are steadfast become purified;
unattached to sense objects, they are not tainted by the defects of karma.
Thus, for those heretical ascetics who have cultivated their selves,
the extraction of the sectarian mark (liṅgoddhāra) must be performed in order to establish them as householders.
Thus ends the chapter on the extraction of the *liṅga* in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
Thus it has been said for those whose souls delight in the practice of yoga:
"A counselor should not bring about his own death for the sake of a reward;
nor should that task be performed out of suffering, nor out of compliance with desires."
If a man, having attained worldly enjoyments, becomes disillusioned with them, he should relinquish his vital breaths into Śiva by means of the sequential practice of dhāraṇā.
Having restrained the senses from their objects such as sound with effort,
one should further restrain the group of senses along with the mind within the range of the intellect.
Having abandoned the state of egoism through the sequence beginning with the causal principle,
[one should remain] in the state of "I am Brahman" and so forth, as far as the entire range of sensory objects extends.
One should skillfully cross the bridge by means of the *vāḍa* and *karaṇa* breath-control;
likewise, having reached a hundred *mātrās*, one should indeed perform the *kuṃbhaka*.
When the breath has been exhaled through the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra),
the individual soul (jīva), having gradually caused the upper skull to burst open, ascends to the supreme state.
One who has been pierced by the essence (rasa) does not undergo birth again in the cycle of existence;
thereafter, the concluding sacrifice (udīcya-iṣṭi) should be performed according to the fourfold [requirements] beginning with the observance (samaya).
Especially for those who harbor improper doubts,
for those who have resorted to other treatises, and likewise for those engaged in [worldly] satisfactions.
The fire-sacrifice (iṣṭi) must be performed with effort; otherwise, one shall not attain the supreme [state].
It should be performed by the preceptor for four [initiates], but by the practitioner (sādhaka) for three.
However, with two [disciples], one should have [the rite] performed by the spiritual son alone among those who know the samaya within one's own lineage;
and in the absence of all such, one should not have it performed by anyone other than one who knows the samaya.
Having reached the riverbank, one should smear it with cow dung;
then, having worshipped the ritual pitcher (kalaśa) according to the prescribed rules, one should likewise worship the pitcher of the site (vāstukalaśa).
Having worshipped Śiva on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit, one should offer libations;
likewise, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed as before, preceded by the worship of Śiva.
The resident ascetic should cleanse the earth, ashes, and cow-dung by rubbing them together;
having removed all [impurities], he should place them there in the fire located in the southern direction.
Then, after sprinkling [the materials] and heating them over fire, one should contemplate the Praṇava in the heart;
having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and worshipped [the deity], one should then perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
Then, having meditated upon the auspicious Vyāna, one should offer it to the deity:
"Accept this great oblation with your own nature; may it be successful."
Having spoken thus to the god Śiva, who was situated between both [fires],
he then attempted to lead that Śiva toward the fire fueled by wood, though he was powerless to do so.
Then, one should cause Kumbha to discharge a continuous stream of weapons in the form of an unbroken circle, [saying]: "May there be auspiciousness for you now!"
Having bathed, one should then offer water; having bathed again, one should worship Śiva until the very end of the western boundary, repeating the rites in the cremation ground.
Whether through the relationship of disciple and teacher, or likewise through the relationship of those connected to the teacher,
ritual acts such as recitation (japa) and fire-oblation (homa) should be performed for one another.
A disciple should be understood as a son, while a brother is indeed considered a "little son" (putraka);
one who is constantly devoted to the observances (samaya) is likewise regarded as a putraka.
The practitioner, the spiritual son, the brother, the initiate, and the grandson—
all these are [related] to the preceptor, who is the father of all those engaged in ritual action.
For them, there is impurity for one day and a night due to the cause of a birth or death;
however, a householder should not, even in his mind, transgress the path of the world.
In the worldly view, impurity (sūtaka) is accepted as lasting until the cessation of the breath;
however, from the perspective of ultimate reality, for a person there is never any impurity whatsoever.
That Danteshṭi rite has thus been described by me here in brief.
Thus ends the chapter on the funeral rites as spoken in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
179b) Īśvara said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare [the rules] for those who are free from doubt, who practice austerity,
who are ascetics whose obstacles have been removed, and for those whose minds are not afflicted by birth-impurity (sūtaka).
The external [form] of the powers has been described as the mental sacrifice (mānasayāga).
Kārttikeya said:
O Mahādeva, how can there be birth-impurity for those who have been initiated?
If it does exist, O Lord, then what has been accomplished by their initiation?
It is not said that the initiation of the ancient Self occurs through the birth of the body;
since that [Self] is already initiated, tell me, for whom is there impurity?
The Lord said:
O Puru, the Dīpa [initiation] is proclaimed to be of two kinds: with seed (sabījā) and without seed (nirbījā).
The "with seed" bestows liberation upon the falling away of the body, while the "without seed" remains established by means of the seed.
The initiation for immediate liberation (sadyonirvāṇadīkṣā) has been previously described as resulting from the equalization of karma;
however, for children and others, it is seedless (nirbījā) and devoid of the observance of rules (samayācāra).
For those who possess the seed-syllables and are endowed with the conduct of the observance (samaya),
as well as for those initiated in both [traditions], one should offer the śikhā-oblation.
That initiation which, as before, is joined with the [cutting of] sections is for one whose nature is Śiva;
likewise, that which is without the cutting of the topknot is to be known as being for one whose nature is Mālokā.
But for those whose nature is subject to death, there is no permanent loss;
they should dwell there separately, being purified by bathing and wearing clean garments.
Since purity arises from that [inner essence] and not from anything else independently, it can never be otherwise.
One should perform the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) day after day for three days.
On the fourth day, however, it must always be performed by him as before,
O Six-faced One, for those who have received the initiation whose nature consists of worldly dharmas.
O Daughter of Śaṅkara, during their period of birth-impurity, worship is suspended;
they themselves must perform the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) as it was previously practiced.
The Supreme Lord is to be propitiated with authoritative means, songs, and hymns;
otherwise, O son of Katika, he will manifest as a Piśāca.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the mental sacrifice;
they do not remain merely absorbed in meditation, but attend upon it with these [mantras].
One should perform the mental sacrifice until the obstacle to its completion is removed,
sitting upon a pure seat measuring thirty-two finger-breadths.
In a seat that is three parts high and four parts wide, materials such as soft cloth are permitted;
among the eight types of seats, one should fasten [the cloth] upon the middle one.
The Svastika, the one known as Padma, Vīra, Ardhacandra,
the extended Yogapaṭṭa, and the Paryaṅka— these should be performed according to one's comfort.
Having led the right [foot] behind by double [the distance],
and having made the left foot’s [heel] crosswise by double [that distance], so that it touches the shank, this is the *svastika*.
One should arrange them in pairs, one after another, and likewise increase by one quarter;
know that the lotus is thus formed, and now hear briefly regarding the half-moon.
In the same way, having placed the two feet so that the soles are positioned facing each other,
this is called the half-moon posture (*ardhacandra*); now hear about the hero’s posture (*vīrāsana*).
Having placed the left foot twice as far apart and the right foot above it,
with the palms of the hands resting against each other, this is called the posture known as Vīra.
Having doubled two pairs [of syllables], one should place them respectively across and upwards;
thus, like a row resting upon a band, they form two interlocking rings.
Then, having extended both feet forward and well-bent toward each other,
one should extend both hands backward, positioned along the spine.
That is declared to be the paryaṅka posture, according to its configuration and as is comfortable;
having mastered the āsana, one should hold the head slightly bent like a peacock's.
Having placed the tongue against the surface of the palate, one should not let the teeth touch the teeth;
then, having formed the *kūrmamudrā*, or the *liṅgamudrā*, or the *dhvajamudrā*.
First, one should bring together the senses and their objects through hundreds [of repetitions];
then, having made them steady, one should contemplate the mental *praṇava*.
Then, one should gradually perform the withering and burning of the tree of the body;
likewise, by means of that very breath, one should perform its drying up through exhalation (recaka) and its leaping upward.
One should meditate on the mental ether (praṇava) beginning with the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) and ending with Śakti;
there, one should fashion a form consisting of the Self of Knowledge (vidyātman) in the shape of the Vedas.
One should mentally contemplate [the disciple] as being sprinkled from the pitcher of the nectar of the Praṇava, which consists of the five Brahmans and is filled with the water of Śiva.
The supreme external [reality] is pervasive right there, both externally and internally;
one should contemplate it there, upon the pericarp of the heart-lotus.
Resembling ten thousand suns in splendor due to its form being both with and without parts,
one performs the invocation (āvāhana), installation (sthāpana), bringing near (saṃnidhāna), and seating (niveśana).
One should worship him with water for rinsing the mouth, bathing, garments,
cakes, flowers, and so forth, as well as with divine unguents, clothes, and ornaments.
Having worshipped with canopies, banners, and parasols, with processions of men, with mirrors, and with divine offerings, and with complete and auspicious mental offerings;
The recitation should be performed mentally, as well as the rosary and the circumambulation;
having thus completed the worship, one should then proceed to the chamber for the fire-oblation (homa).
The Vṛṣavaṣka, however, is situated in the Rāla;
it is a pit with three ridges, considered to be triangular or circular, with the Moon, Fire, and Sun as its ridges.
One should perform the oblation of conceptual constructions (vikalpāhuti) with the hand of Śakti;
one should offer the five oblations of the senses, joined with all [the other elements].
Having established the sound within the minister (the mind), one should seek the stream of the mind;
having attained its state of measure, which is beyond the reach of Brahmā and the other gods.
Relying upon the arising of the vital breath (prāṇa), one should gradually proceed through the three heats;
having remained at ease wherever the moon and sun dissolve.
Then, having taken recourse to the flow of the eyebrows, one should fully master the potency of the mantra;
by thus mastering that power, the practitioner of mantra shall attain the state of universal sovereignty.
Therein, neither meditation, nor the object of meditation, nor the meditator exists;
neither the means of knowledge, nor the knower, nor the object of knowledge exists there.
However, in that state, existence arises as mere cognition;
then one should offer worship, meditation, and likewise fire-offerings (homa) to the Lord.
Thus, this mental yoga, which grants all desires for everyone and is both unartificial and preeminent— one should, by means of it, commence the internal sacrifice.
O child, the sacrifice of the arms is known as being essentially the inner sacrifice;
compared to the inner sacrifice, the [outer] sacrifices do not merit even a sixteenth part.
O Mahāsena, the external sacrifice is proclaimed as being "external"; whoever is capable and qualified should perform the external yoga.
Whoever worships Śiva with even a single correct verse according to their ability,
attains infinite existence, clearly manifest with knowledge and enjoyment.
However, he who worships with devotion the one who dwells within the body is Śiva, the creator of all; just as the individual soul is said to be within.
In whatever state one may be, whether standing, walking, sleeping, waking, eating, or engaged in sexual intercourse, one should remember Śiva in that very state.
He whose mind is fixed on Śiva is a partaker of liberation, whereas one who thinks otherwise is not;
the mudrās, maṇḍalas, and mantras have emerged from the body of Śiva.
Whatever exists, whether moving or unmoving, should be known as consisting entirely of Śiva;
yet without realizing the reality of Śiva, one [practices] mantras, vidyās, and so forth, as well as the maṇḍala.
It should be understood as being like a lump of clay, and likewise it would attain the state of a fallen [vow];
therefore, with every effort, one should fully master the potency of the mantra.
Having realized the identity of the signified and the signifier, which bestows the fruit of liberation,
one should take refuge in the Vākya, for all mantras abide within that signified meaning.
One should worship the God at night and perform the fire-oblation (homa) during the day;
likewise, meditation (dhyāna) is prescribed for the twilights, while recitation (japa) is ordained for both day and night.
Recitation performed during the day is indeed called *sāṃskārika*; that performed at night is *rājasa*;
but recitation at the twilights (*saṃdhyā*) is declared to be *sāttvika*, which accomplishes all goals.
Japa performed with loud articulation is said to be rājasa and is considered dusty;
that performed mentally is said to be sāttvika and is the accomplisher of all goals.
One should diligently apply *tāmasa* recitation for cruel rites and the like, *rājasa* for subjugation and similar acts, and *sāttvika* for divine and secret deities.
Through the cessation of the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa), that recitation is considered sattvic;
for the mind, the power of consciousness (cicchakti), the mantras, the vital breaths, and likewise Śiva [are all one].
O child, when the recitation has become effortless, that is considered supreme;
then, relying on the power of consciousness, the recitation bestows the accomplishment of all goals.
A mantra does not yield fruit when recited by a neuter person or for another; rather, it yields fruit when recited by one possessing power (śakti).
Thus ends the chapter on internal sacrifice in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
Īśvara said:
The practice of yoga should be undertaken with a good companion and in a secluded place;
however, when one is alone without a companion, one should carry a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
One should fashion a handle made of *hastotāra*, *śasta*, *śalvaja*, or *yāthāva* wood;
it should be twelve finger-breadths long, curved, and fashioned from a citron fruit.
The two regions of the base are three finger-breadths each;
from the region of the neck, the neck is considered to be four finger-breadths in height and likewise in circumference.
Three finger-breadths above that, the umbrella is considered to be half as wide [as the base], with its mouth [opening] below;
it should be very thin in both height and width, and there the stalk is fixed.
The *sāvitrī* [line] should be made three finger-breadths wide and situated above the abdomen;
one should fill it by that path as far as the throat.
Having purified it with the five waters, the five products of the cow, and ashes,
and having recited the Śiva-mantra one hundred and eight times, one should install the Liṅga upon a pure spot.
One should offer it to Aghora and then hold it firmly;
it should always be kept on the triple-junction (trikaṭikā), never on the ground, nor anywhere impure.
Just as one should not touch it there, so the sacrifice is prescribed for the sake of touching;
or else, one may drink again, consecrating it according to the previous sequence.
One should perform purification by oneself and should not cause confusion through it;
one who lacks companions must carry a water-pot according to the rule.
Householders should not perform purification themselves at any time;
thus, the rules regarding the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) have been briefly elucidated.
Thus ends the chapter on the water-pot in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
183a) Kārttikeya said:
You ought to explain specifically the consecration for householders;
likewise, how and for whom should the rite of raising the deceased and initiation be performed?
"O God, [I shall explain] in due order and in brief, out of a desire for the welfare of living beings.
Lord Īśvara said:
Having learned that the initiated one has died, the great guru should be entreated with affection or compassion, together with the high-souled disciples.
One should diligently cause her own funeral rites to be performed; then, by that very effort, she shall arise from death at the place where she died in the city.
Having bathed [the image] with water mixed with cow dung and earth consecrated by the recitation of the Astra-mantra,
and then with fragrant water containing *āmalaka* fruits and all medicinal herbs;
Having anointed it with sandalwood paste, one should surround it with various flowers;
there, one should place two well-dyed, scented garments as the lower and upper cloths.
Having put on the sacred thread (*pavīta*) and likewise a new upper garment (*sottarī*),
the Śūdras should wear an upper cloth (*uttarīya*), but it must be devoid of the sacred thread (*sūtra*).
Two purifying blades (pavitrakas) should be joined with two fingers;
having adorned them well with flowers, they are placed within the enclosure of the cloth upon the yantra.
Then, having taken [the fire] from those of his own caste who have been initiated— and not from those who are uninitiated—
he should lead it to a consecrated place that is free from charcoal and the like.
Having smeared the ground and leveled it in the two [places] according to the rule,
one should likewise prepare the alms-bowl, the *caṇḍa* vessel, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and the sacrificial thread.
The sandals, the seat, the bell, the yogapaṭṭa,
the bhadrapiṭha and so forth, as well as everything including the arghapātra and the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
All his maternal equipment, such as his share of the inheritance and so forth,
as well as gold, clothing, weapons, and likewise parasols, vehicles, and the like.
At the time of that śrāddha, it should be given by the Guru to those of purified soul;
first, water for the arghya, flowers, and so forth, should be placed before him.
Indeed, whatever materials are used for worship and in the rite of oblation,
the preceptor should place them there in the northeastern direction at the beginning of the month.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon oneself, one should perform worship such as the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) and so forth,
as well as for any other remaining person, including the preceptor (ācārya).
The initiate (samayī) and the spiritual son (putraka) should cause [the rite] to be performed for the teacher (deśika),
provided he abides by the teaching, is devoted, and the mantras are known to him.
O Lord Ṣaṇmukha, it should be performed with the *praṇava* during the propitiation (*prasāda*).
One should first place the seat (*pīṭha*) with the *praṇava*, and then deposit the mantra up to the end of the *vidyā*.
There, one should worship Maheśāna in the water-pot as well as on the sacrificial mound;
likewise, having fully worshipped him in the fire, one should then commence the ritual action.
Having performed one hundred and eight recitations of the root mantra with sesame seeds in the fire according to the prescribed method,
and having recollected the mantra through the yoga of the process of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama), he then [offered] the oblation.
O child, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti),
one should then sprinkle that corpse with arghya water, and after piercing it [with the needle] and examining it;
184a) But with the eye of the thread of knowledge, following the sequence of causes and causes-of-causes,
one should offer the water of honor and place a flower on the head, even while standing at a distance and not touching it.
O Śikhidhvaja, with two jars at the back of the Ānāyā [channel],
one should place the entire corpse upon the seat by means of whatever [method] is available.
Having observed that [the site] situated in the place of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should then sit down with concentration;
for [the ground] is not purified by prior rites and is devoid of the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) of clay.
Having brought the living soul (jīva), which has become isolated (kevalī) and has entered into proximity,
and having placed it within the hand of the mantra through instruction, one should subsequently unite it.
One should join the previous state, the body, and the jewel-lamp of blazing light;
then, at the end of the syllable *praṇava*, one should apply the crest-syllable (*śikhābīja*) followed by the name.
Then one should again place that crest-seed-syllable (*śikhā-bīja*) ending with the *praṇava*;
then, during its invocation, one should employ it for the filling.
Having thus placed the individual soul (jīva) in its own station according to the Śukra doctrine,
it is then consumed by the power of activity, just as fire consumes its own fuel.
One should initiate him according to the sequence; indeed, the guru must properly perform only the dissolution-homa for him, following the sequence beginning with earth and so forth.
Having joined [the disciple] with the supreme reality (tatva) through the full extraction (pūrṇāhuti) as before,
one should then perform the sprinkling with water from the weapon-vessel (astra-udaka) upon the right side by means of the self-mantra (ātman).
O Six-faced One, when mixed with sesame seeds, white mustard seeds, and other substances,
one should not commence the Kālacakra ritual if it is devoid of the rim.

and in the case of a ritual action (kṛtya), one should diligently place it both in front of the vessel and within it.

And when the year was completed and the thirteenth month had arrived.
One should perform the ancestral śrāddha for the purpose of pacifying the state of being a preta;
even in that regard, one who lacks the capacity for ritual action should still perform it for the sake of attaining his own welfare.
This śrāddha, consisting of initiation (dīkṣā), brings about the state of the Sugata;

One should perform the Śrāddha rite at the proper place, at the proper time, and with a worthy recipient.

a vessel of betel-nut and betel-leaf, as well as nutmegs and areca nuts.
One should offer a fragrant linga and gold to Śiva; thereafter,
the preceptor is to be honored with gold, garments, and vehicles.
O Daughter of Śaṅkara, one who performs this vow on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika attains union with Śiva along with his ancestors; now hear about this vow.
First, the great ablution (mahāsnāna) should be performed, followed by anointing with the fourfold mixture (catuḥsama).
A row of lamps numbering one hundred and four large wicks must likewise be provided.

At the door, there should indeed be Vaijayantī banners; in the center, in the cardinal directions, and in the intermediate directions, a moon-pattern should be placed upon the cloth, while incense is offered with zeal in all directions.
Or, with light incense and human ash combined with red sandalwood,
one should perform fumigation in the intermediate directions using one hundred pieces each of guggulu and clarified butter.
One should fashion a bull out of rice flour, measuring one *droṇa*, in the eastern direction;
upon its back, one should place a desired linga made of flour, twelve finger-breadths in length.
Adorned with a golden garland and decorated with strings of pearl necklaces—
for the sake of worldly enjoyment, or for the sake of liberation, or indeed for the sake of one's own self—
O Mahādeva, may this be yours; may this alone be the bestower of perfection.
Having properly and according to rule presented the offering, and having correctly observed the vow as prescribed,
one who desires it shall attain incomparable sovereignty and imperishable liberation.
Even one who has committed every sin or is a slayer of a Brahmin shall attain the state of Rudra,
provided that at the conclusion of the worship, he diligently honors his guru with supreme devotion.
With garments of gold, food, drinks, jewels, and [ornaments] such as bracelets, the gift of an elephant should be bestowed; in its absence, one made of burnt clay may be given.
When this has been done, the vow of the *liṅga* will not have been fully honored.
Now I shall fully describe the supreme vow of the image (*pratimā-vrata*).
A great ablution, a great wick, and likewise a hundred rows of lamps;
anointing with saffron and incense indeed of guggulu.
Having offered milk and ghee with one hundred and eight oblations,
[one should meditate on her] as being the size of a palm tree, four-faced, and possessing four eyes and four arms.
Her body should be formed from rice flour, adorned with various ornaments, and holding a trident, sword, bow, and arrows; a beautiful bull should also be made from flour.
One should provide Śiva there with cooling remedies for his ailments,
as well as a mirror, betel, a fan, sandals, and a seat.
One should diligently offer a Vaijayantī banner as a vehicle to the Teacher every month on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
Beginning from the month of Kārtika until the conclusion of the worship,
this is called the supreme vow, known as the Pratimā-vrata.
One who has killed a Brahmin, one who has killed his guru, one who is burdened by the five great sins, a betrayer of friends, an ungrateful person, and whoever is a violator of trust—
He too goes to the state of Rudra after twenty-one [rebirths],
and rejoices in the world of Śiva for thousands of millions upon millions of years.
At the end of that, he is born as a king, or as one who is heroic or pure;
having realized this, he attains sovereignty through the power of Śiva-initiation.
One attains step by step that state by which one is not born again;
thus should he instruct him, and one should cause the gift of land to be made for him.
He rejoices in that celestial mansion for three million divine years.
At the end of that, he shall attain the yoga by which he goes to the eternal Śiva;
this applies to one who, beginning with the month of Kārttika, subsists on the *nakta* fast.
Whether it be a great elephant, a great horse, or even a great vehicle, it should be given with diligent effort; then one shall attain that vow.
Listen briefly to the vows for those who are weary and without a protector:
beginning with the month of Kārttika, one should observe eating only once a day.
Listen now to the fruit of merit there, up until the conclusion of the horse sacrifice:
one is glorified in the world of Rudra for one hundred and fifty divine years.
Starting from the month of Kārttika until the conclusion of the Āśvina worship,
one should observe silence during the twilight hours until the appearance of the stars.
At the end of their bodies' lives, they go to the world of Rudra together with their kinsmen;
now hear the fruit of his merit until the conclusion of the worship on that very day.
There, in the world of Rudra, he dwells for sixty thousand years in truth;
at the end of that time, through the yoga of knowledge, he shall attain the state of universal sovereignty.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, one should observe the vow,
remaining without food and observing silence, continuing every month until the completion of the year.
He shall dwell in the world of Rudra as long as the four-armed Brahmā exists,
provided he observes a fast on both fourteenth lunar days.
Starting from the month of Kārtika until the end of Āśvayuja,
he shall indeed dwell in the world of Rudra for as long as a hundred lifespans of Brahmā.
Starting from the month of Kārttika until the end of the year.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who observes a fast on the eighth day of the bright fortnight:
he shall dwell in the world of Rudra for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
Such indeed is the fruit for one who performs it on the eighth day of the dark fortnight;
but by performing it with devotion during both the months of Pauṣa and Māgha, the fruit is a hundredfold greater.
Thus, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the fruit shall be like that of Śiva;
a human being obtains a fruit multiplied by two thousand.
One who desires auspiciousness should diligently observe this vow month after month,
offering either fruit, or vegetables, or even clothing, bedding, and personal ornaments.
Saffron, agallochum, betel, moon-seated vehicles, as well as beautiful ornaments, a bed, and whatever else is desired by the mind— [she gave all these].
One who desires auspiciousness should offer [this] every month before Śiva;
he obtains that which is imperishable as far as the ten directions of Brahmā extend.
Having performed the vow, one should offer the fruit to Śiva;
by this, the seeker of liberation should act so that the eternal state is attained.
Whatever substance is most delicious, whatever is beautiful to behold, whatever is difficult to obtain,
and whatever is pure— that shall be the water for the feet (pādya) for a month or for the duration of a year.

At the conclusion of the vow, one should give it to a devotee of Śiva and then eat it oneself. By that act, the person who has observed the discipline does not merely reach the end of the period of restriction;
rather, upon the completion of the vow, he attains such a state that he is not born again.
And one should instruct him in this way: "One should cause the gift of land to be made for him;
he shall rejoice in that celestial mansion for three million divine years."
At the end of that period, he shall attain the yoga by which he goes to the eternal Śiva;
this applies to one who, beginning from the month of Kārttika, subsists on the *nakta* fast.
One should diligently give a great elephant, a great horse, or even a great vehicle; then one shall attain that vow.
Listen briefly to the vows for those who are far from home and without a protector:
beginning with the month of Kārttika, one should observe eating only once a day.
Listen now to the fruit of merit for one who remains there until the horses are harnessed:
he is glorified in the world of Rudra for one hundred and fifty divine years.
Starting from the month of Kārttika until the conclusion of the Āśvina worship,
one should observe silence during the twilight hours until the appearance of the stars.
At the end of their bodies' lives, they go to the world of Rudra together with their kinsmen;
now hear the fruit of the merit of the earth as far as the limit of the horse sacrifice.
There, in the world of Rudra, he dwells for a hundred thousand years;
at the end of that time, through the yoga of knowledge, he shall attain the state of universal sovereignty.
One should observe the vow on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika; it shall consist of fasting and silence, repeated every month until the completion of the year.
He shall dwell in the world of Rudra until he reaches the four-armed Brahmā,
provided that he remains without food on both fourteenth days.
Starting from the month of Kārttika until the end of Āśvayuja,
he shall dwell in the world of Rudra for as long as a hundred lifespans of Brahmā.
Listen to the meritorious fruit of one who, beginning from the month of Kārttika until the end of the year, observes a fast on the eighth day of the bright fortnight.
He shall dwell in the world of Rudra for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras;
such indeed is the fruit for one who performs this on the eighth day of the dark fortnight.
By performing this with devotion on the two days of the month of Pauṣa, the fruit is a hundredfold;
likewise, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the fruit shall be as [great] as that of the bright fortnight.
A human being obtains a fruit multiplied by two thousand;
one who desires auspiciousness should perform this vow with diligence month after month.
Whether it be fruit, food, vegetables, clothing, bedding, or even a vehicle;
saffron, incense, betel, the moon, or a mount—none of these [are to be accepted].
Likewise, one desiring auspiciousness should, month after month, place before Śiva beautiful ornaments and a bed that is pleasing to the mind.
Having performed the vow, he who offers the fruit to Śiva attains inexhaustibility as far as the ten directions extend unto Brahman.
That which is to be practiced by one desiring liberation is thereby attained eternally:
whatever substance, whatever is delicious, whatever is visible, and whatever is difficult to obtain.
Whatever has been used as a purifier or as water for the feet should be kept until the end of the year;
at the conclusion of the vow, one should give it to a devotee of Śiva and then consume it oneself.
If one who has undertaken a religious observance does not complete it until its appointed time,
he becomes liable for penance when the violation of his vow occurs.
Having honored the teacher according to the prescribed rite with pure wealth,
one should always cause him to utter those words before Śiva in accordance with the ritual injunctions.
One should speak only after deliberation, so that there may be well-being rather than fear; he who speaks without deliberation encounters misfortune.
Neither out of affection, nor likewise out of greed, nor from hatred or delusion,
should one engage in reflection on the Dharma, but rather in accordance with the scriptures.
He who, transgressing his own treatise, proceeds according to another’s treatise, exerts himself in vain; he shall not obtain the fruit thereof.
One should diligently project oneself before Śiva within the images;
she arises from my smile, with her face turned toward him and a lamp in her hand.
A man who is devoid of wealth and well-reflective should offer [the gift] before Śiva; he shall obtain as its fruit sovereignty over the three worlds.
And various kinds of auspicious weapons made of wood,
as well as various emblems and diverse banners.
There were various birds and especially diverse flowers; there were many female and male servants, horses, and elephants adorned with colorful trappings.
All the couples, as well as the mountains and rivers,
various other Vidyādharīs, and Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara [were present].
The world-protectors, all the planets, the archways, and the celestial bodies; the temples, the trees, the groves, and the gardens.
A Liṅga made of *vacā* and ghee, when worshipped, increases the intellect;
a cloth Liṅga leads to prosperity; and a *śarṣapa* (mustard-seed) Liṅga, O Śiva, destroys evil.
Thus they speak of the momentary [forms]; one should worship them day after day.
Furthermore, O child, that which is known as the *calāvaṇa* is to be understood as manifold and wonderful.
Now hear from me concerning other mobile and immobile lingas here:
a clay linga should be made in two ways—either baked or unbaked.
The merit arising from what is cooked is ten times that of what is uncooked;
the merit arising from what is made of wood is known to be ten times that of the cooked; and the merit arising from what is made of stone is known to be ten times that of the wooden.
A stone flower is known to be ten times superior to one made of wood;
a stone made of pearl is ten times superior to that, and a fruit is traditionally held to be ten times superior to that.
Therefore, the fruit of [offering] iron is a hundredfold greater than that of tin or lead; gold bestows great prosperity, while silver increases one's progeny.
A Liṅga made of copper bestows fame and increases worship; one made of brass leads to both worldly enjoyment and liberation; and one made of lead or iron results in the destruction of enemies.
A liṅga made of clay bestows long life, while one made of clay mixed with colored powders grants all perfections;
the fruit obtained from one made of metal is a thousand times greater than that, and from one made of jewels even more so.
A linga made from jewels is considered to yield a hundred-thousandfold fruit;
among superior, inferior, and middling jewels, the fruit increases progressively for each subsequent one.
Furthermore, gems characterized by intense luster are the foremost among jewels;
likewise, the fruit obtained at a Liṅga made of such gems is ten million times greater than that at a Liṅga made of ordinary gems.
By installing a Bāṇaliṅga, one shall obtain all desires;
moreover, the fruit from a Rasaliṅga compared to a Bāṇaliṅga shall be ten million times greater.
O Śāṅkarī, who here is able to describe the qualities of that Liṅga?
The supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*, are established through the *rasaliṅga*;
likewise, liberation is attained through the *rasaliṅga*, which bestows qualities equal to those of Śiva.
Therefore, a *liṅga* consisting of nectar (*rasamaya*) should be installed with great effort;
if one should worship a *liṅga* consisting of nectar even once with devotion, [the fruit is attained].
One who goes to the station of Ananteśa shall become possessed of cattle and wealth;
indeed, when the Rasa-linga is worshipped, it brings about the fulfillment of all desires for both sides.
By bowing down, one destroys all that is ill-omened and the influence of malevolent planets;
by worshipping the Rasa-liṅga, the supreme state is attained.
One obtains all desires through the worship of the Rasaliṅga;
one should not calculate its honor, measure, or quantity.
O Commanding Lady, those who worship the Rasaliṅga with devotion even two or three times attain the supreme state, endowed with the powers of sovereignty such as the ṭeṇima and other qualities.
One should worship the *rasaliṅga* through the ritual of those struck by *ḍimba*;
thus struck by *ḍimba*, they are liberated and attain the supreme and inferior liberation (*mukti*).
Therefore, one should diligently fashion the *rasaliṅga* named Śikhidhvaja;
indeed, one should effect the fixation of mercury (*rasabandha*) according to the procedure described by Vāthala.
One should fix mercury with secondary minerals such as metals and with gems;
or else, by means of a small portion of *vali*, one should fix it with *vajralepa*.
Then, by means of a flood of the essence of blazing medicinal herbs, one should cause [the disciple] to faint and bind him;
therein the accomplishments (siddhis) abide, while the hosts of obstacles are cast outside.
Having attained the Rasaliṅga, who would not obtain their heart's desire? Or else, one should wear a ring made of mercury on the hand.
That indeed becomes inexhaustible, or it becomes imperishable,
for those men who have been consumed by fire in hell or those who are otherwise deprived of funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
Likewise, others who have been struck by lightning or those who died due to miscarriage—
by means of that very mudrā held in the hand, they declare that [the deity] is established within them.
Therefore, one who desires prosperity should fashion a linga made of mercury;
now hear from me the measurement of the site for all types of lingas.
The field of the self-arisen ones who possess passion is said to extend for one yojana in every direction; that of those exalted by jewels and gems is declared to be half of that.

Outside of that are the cities of the Kharas and the Lohas, half the size of those; and further out are the cities of the Pārthivas, as well as those requested by the Ṛṣis, Daityas, Nāgas, Gandharvas, and Vāraṇas.
And for those established by Siddhas, gods, Apsarases, and the best of men,
there is no measure of their forms, nor can they be grasped, just like an arrow [in flight].
One may have the construction of their pedestals and temples carried out according to one's own desire;
they should not be joined with defects of decay, just as a lord himself [acts] according to his will.
O son, know that their field is like that of the Self-born;
indeed, the field of the great rivers should be understood as being like the field of the Self-born.
For arrows made of wood from soft trees, the length of the shaft should be twice that of the arrowhead;
for those made of iron, it should be double that again, and each subsequent type should be double the previous.
In Ratnaja, however, it is a liṅga made of jewels; in Vāṇa, it is composed of mercury.
Thus indeed has the measurement of the field been declared for practitioners;
likewise, it has been stated regarding recitation, as well as in relation to giving and nourishing.
I shall further explain the measurement as it truly exists:
having divided the field into five parts, one should arrange them like a lotus.
The first is to be known as the pericarp (karṇikā), the second as the filaments (keśara),
the third as the petals (patrāṇi), and the fourth as the tips of the petals (dalāgra).
One should designate the outer fifth portion for the fields;
there, one should divide the previously mentioned fruit into five parts.
O son of Kṛttikā, I shall briefly describe the bases of worship:
at the commencement of worship, one should diligently perform the worship of one's own form.
For yogins, worship is always prescribed in one's own form;
at the commencement of yoga, one should always perform worship in the form of the Guru.
One should worship Śiva only once, as long as one has not yet attained liberation;
however, at the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), worship must indeed always be performed at the conclusion of the sacrifice.
One should worship ten million seats of knowledge (vidyāpīṭhas) here, or else one's own Saṃhitā;
Sadāśiva is to be worshipped in the water at the conclusion of each bath, for he is the entire [deity] in his totality.
At the conclusion of the worship in the fire, having performed the sacrifice, one should carry out the *homa*;
for the sake of removing obstacles, one should always worship Śiva upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
For even on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of mantras arises quickly;
whether Śiva is worshipped on a mound, in water, or in a ritual jar (*kalaśa*).
In the case of a permanent linga, success in one's desires should always be achieved through diligent effort.
The worship of Śiva in a mobile liṅga bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men;
one should worship Him as situated within the solar disc, reflected in a mirror.
Therefore, one should indeed worship that lunar disc for the purpose of deceiving death;
it is to be worshipped as abiding everywhere, at all times, and within all substrates.
Even there, in the *liṅga*, the Lord Dhūrjaṭi accepts worship,
even if the worship performed is incomplete in its mantras, materials, rituals, and qualities.
Nevertheless, O Six-faced One, worship performed with a *liṅga* is complete;
it must not be deficient or excessive, O Son, when the worship is performed on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
However, that worship which is deficient or excessive is proclaimed to be fruitless;
for this reason, my child, one should commence the propitiation of the Liṅga.
Thus ends the chapter on the description of the Liṅga in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
Īśvara said:
Śiva is the abode of the highest, lowest, and middling accomplishments;
by taking refuge in Dakṣiṇāmūrti, one may likewise achieve those accomplishments.
Since the supernatural powers (siddhis) reside in the *liṅga*, therefore listen now to the nature of the *liṅga*;
for it is from it that all beings dissolve and are indeed created again.
Therefore, it is called a *liṅga*; the supreme Śiva resides within it.
A *liṅga* may be made of clay, born of stone, made of wood, or consisting of the primordial waters (*sāṃbhava*).
199a) Listen now to the sequence for those made of gems, jewels, and various substances such as scents and clarified butter;
likewise, those made of oil or clay should extend up to the length of a cubit.

One should fashion a wooden vessel sixteen *aṅgulas* in length, with a girth at its base equal to that of a stone slab; it should have a middle and a top part.
The iron [measure] should be eight finger-breadths; one may further calculate other [measures] by a quarter [of a unit] for each subsequent step. Above that, those [others] follow in sequence.
Twenty-seven types of lingas have indeed been described;
O maiden, one should offer even the most formidable foot [of the deity] before these six.
And thirty-six types of lingas have been described by number;
they should be understood according to the three-fold measurement in finger-breadths, O Six-faced One.
The object of knowledge should be known as six, six, eight, and nine; it is middling, and the best is ten.
It is not threefold in finger-breadths, nor is a cubit measured by four finger-breadths.
Starting from one cubit, I have briefly described up to nine;
[the image] made of clay or stone is thus summarized, while that made of wood should be three [cubits] less.
Or, half of that measure may be made of iron;
it is proclaimed according to the dimensions of the crocodile (grāha), the interior of the temple (prāsāda-garbha), and the pedestal (pīṭha).
When the opening of the *bhūta* is divided by the *randhra*, the embryo is likewise equal;
then, according to the portion of the self that has become Brahman, [the result is] auspicious as superior, middling, or inferior.
In their midst, there are likewise two pairs of maidens, and below them another pair;
indeed, your liṅgas are present according to the measurement of the interior of the temple.
Each one, however, being multiplied threefold, becomes incalculable;
likewise, it is so by the measure of the *liṅgas* and the measure of the *pīṭhas*.
Below the hand, however, the lingas [should be made] with a reduction of four finger-breadths.
Thirty-six marks are produced by the number of fingers;
one should avoid placing a linga below the hand within the temple.
However, for the purpose of killing, one should use fierce barley-alkali from a cremation ground;
it should be sixteen finger-breadths in length and fixed upon a wooden pedestal.
Likewise, an iron [image] eight finger-breadths in size is beneficial when placed below it in the fire-chamber;
however, one should avoid using stone or wood in one's own home.
Iron bestows enjoyment and liberation when combined with mercury;
gold bestows great enjoyment; and that which originates from silver is middling.
The remaining [lengths] up to nine finger-breadths grant the highest enjoyment;
beginning from one finger-breadth, they extend up to twenty-four finger-breadths.
The characteristics have been described previously; now hear the names, O Six-faced One:
Śiva, the all-pervading, the peaceful, Dhūrjaṭi, and Nīlalohita.
To Sthāṇu, Maheśvara, the Truth, the one whose vehicle is the six-faced cloud,
the beloved of Umā, the large-eyed Śaṅkara, the Lord of Causes;
Viśara, Lakulīśa, Dravarūpa, Śapa,
likewise Bhūtanātha, Bhayamugra, Rudra, and indeed Bhairava.
It should be known [to start] from one finger-breadth up to twenty-four finger-breadths; thereafter, for hand-sized liṅgas, it extends up to the size of a man, ending at Śiva.
I have described the divisions from the hand up to the ear-cavity,
as well as the divisions and the deities within the internal liṅgas.
200a) This, being heard, is further described as the expansion (viskāra);
having taken [the measurement] from the portion of the authority over the length of the liṅga, sequentially by two and five [parts].
I have described the width of the lingas in three parts:
the first, the middle, and likewise the third.
All other types of lingas are proclaimed to be equal according to their classification;
however, the mukhalinga must be made facing upward, for one facing downward does not grant liberation to men.
All three parts indeed consist of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
[the shapes] are square, octagonal, and circular, with the latter being the lowest.
By discarding half of each corner and so forth, one obtains the eight-sided figure known as Viṣṇu;
by the same process of removing the three corners, it becomes the circle known as Rudra.
The three [sections] of the *kṣatra* are together with the half-moon; the fourth is the *kukkuṭāṇḍaka*.
The top of the umbrella is said to be fourfold according to the division of its parts.
One should cause the width of the top of the liṅga to be divided by nine auspicious parts;
the last part shall be divided into four, and this shall be the width as well as the height.
