There, O son, one should place four umbrellas, distributing them according to their respective portions; however, the *puṇḍarīka* umbrella should be placed in one portion at the corner.
Fame is proclaimed as the first bestower of radiance upon men;
from the center of the Viśāla [mandala], one should draw a line extending to the corners, measuring three parts.
By that [method], the vast and expansive station of glory for men is remembered;
it is achieved through the sequence of the corner-thread, by descending three steps above.
Then, O son of Kṛttikā, by omitting the upper corners of all four squares, there arises that which is known as Śrīvatsa, which grants all desires to everyone.
The fourth parasol is renowned by the name Śakramardana;
the parasol is said to be of four kinds, always beneficial for all seats.
And it is not otherwise;
for when the *liṅga* consists of four parts, [the image] is formed by the reduction of one-fourth part.
Furthermore, there is another characteristic mark: when the thirteen spokes meet at the junctions, by omitting two parts, the head likewise consists of three.
O Six-faced One! What should one divide threefold at the throat? [The answer is: because of the displacement of half of the lateral portions.
O Six-faced One, by rotating the corner-line in sequence, a half-moon shape must be made for the first [line] that has been divided by the subtraction.
Furthermore, the characteristics of those honored by the world-protectors are now described.

For the immobilization of enemies, one should employ the [mantra] associated with the peaceful and the auspicious; however, for killing, the southern [direction] should be employed, and the eastern [direction] for cruel rites.
For the sake of nourishment, this [mantra] of Varuṇa should be used; for expulsion, that of Vāyu is honored;
it should be employed for the attainment of desired objects, while that of Īśāna bestows both enjoyment and liberation.
For the sake of worldly enjoyment and liberation, O Prajāpati, that supreme Liṅga consisting of all the Parvas, which bestows the state of Brahman and Viṣṇu,
is proclaimed as the Aindra.
The six-cornered portion should belong to Rudra; it has the head of Indra’s subduer (Viṣṇu).
The petals are twelve, the city is surrounded by a moat, and it extends seven [units] wide.
A seven-sided [mandala] should be constructed, free from defects such as missing parts;
half of its circumference, divided by nine, is the distance for the five corners and the back.
The arm should be made with exactly three parts; that which is called Yama is intended for the destruction of Māras.
Having made it octagonal with nine parts, its length should extend toward the four directions.
When one has fashioned the head into a ten-cornered *rākṣasa* (octagon) like fire,
and made the petal devoted to the planet, the knower of the Vedas shall attain expansion.
A crescent moon should be made upon the head for the purposes of pacification (śānti), nourishment (puṣṭi), and awakening (prabodhana);
it should be gentle in appearance, like that born of the Moon, yet possessing a broad belly.

That which is marked with a mace is praised as the best; that marked with a noose is considered to belong to Varuṇa; and that which is black and elongated, worshipped by the hosts of Asuras, belongs to Vāyu.
However, for the purpose of the eradication of enemies, one should perform the Raudra rite, which is joined with a banner,
beginning from the primordial time, and which is endowed with three corners.
One should fashion a cock’s egg-shaped head as the means for attaining sovereign knowledge;
a trident-world should be made at the front, and the emblem of a ploughshare [should be placed] upon it.
As long as the linga remains perfectly symmetrical, it is marked with the face of Viṣṇu;
when it has the mark of a lotus, it is known as Brahmā, and when its top is shaped like a hen's egg, it is [Śiva].
The southern [face] should have a staff-head and be marked with the mark of a staff;
one should fashion that which was previously called Dāḍhya as having a thousand marks.
Since it bestows all desires, that [liṅga] is then considered to have a thousand rays;
one should have it constructed with a height equal to that of Rudra, and likewise for a devotee of Rudra.
One should further divide that [measurement] by the moon’s apertures (nine) for its width;
by that, one thousand and one liṅgas clearly arise.
One should avoid performing actions that involve injustice, one after another.
Then one should place the joined [syllables] devoid of written lines;
[the syllable] *payodharā* at the thousand-spoked [wheel], and the *chatra* (umbrella) upon the head, atop the head.
And another hundred and eight liṅgas, worshipped by the hosts of gods,
were fashioned with a height according to the Vedas and marked with the triṣṭubh meter and seven eyes.
Therefore, O son, one should indeed fashion eleven lingas;
made of clay, they are beneficial and are of two kinds, distinguished by being either fired or unfired.
The uncooked [liṅga] should be fashioned from vajra-stone, while the cooked one should be made of gold or copper;
likewise, the face-liṅga should be made level with the base for auspiciousness.
O son, one should not perform the rite at dawn, nor is worshiping the deity at dawn recommended;
nor is anything considered equally auspicious for all purposes, O son, except for the installation ceremony.
But what is that which is about to be described? It should indeed be fashioned so that there are three [units];
one finger-breadth (aṅgula) should be added for each cubit (pratihasta), and that [total] is conquered by eleven.
One should sequentially assign Vṛṣa, Śaṅkara, and Candra starting from Brahmā;
that measurement is the Liṅga which increases both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O child, without a measuring instrument (vimāna), this [construction] leads only to supreme suffering;
therefore, one should establish a standard measure, whether it be a linga marked with a face or otherwise.
The measurement of the face-liṅga is now briefly stated by me;
it should be made with four, three, or one face by the preceptor.
Having proclaimed the portion for worship, which is prepared according to the rules of the sacrificial fire and the officiants;
having abandoned the previous inability, one should perform the six stations.
One should first fashion the head-form, and then the forehead and the nose.
Likewise, the neck is four parts of the sandalwood [measure], and the arms are situated [therein];
having formed a bud-like gesture with both hands according to the measurement to be described.
The face should be made according to the rule, extending from the width by one-eighth part;
thus the four-faced [liṅga] has been described by me, and likewise the three-faced is now explained.
However, one should indicate his feet as being one-quarter [of the total height], and his lap and so forth; his arms must be made with four parts, and not otherwise.
One should cause the western face to be devoid [of a protrusion] and turned away;
the projection of the principal [faces] shall be one-seventh of the width.
Likewise, it should be made with one face, facing east, with gentle eyes;
one should fashion the head, the forehead, the nose, and the neck of the face.
One should rotate the portion for the base by one-fifth minus one arm-length;
the projection of the face is beneficial when made with one-sixth of the width.
Of all the face-liṅgas, the gourd or the hen is for the east-facing person,
while Aghora is the southern face.
One should fashion the faces and the liṅga according to their respective colors and natures: Uttara (the northern) as Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta as the western.
Their measurement by the hand-span (hasta) shall be as if unmanifest;
one should determine it by the measurement of the temple interior (garbha) or by the measurement of the pedestal (pīṭha).
One should indicate the manifest and unmanifest [deities] by a measure of thirty-six;
likewise for those of the self-existent ones and those made of precious jewels.
In temples, pedestals, inner sanctums, and so forth, [the installation] is prescribed as a rule;
however, one may perform it according to one's own desire for those [other objects] using one's own chosen mantra, O Śaṅkara.
In the cutting of the Vajra-liṅga, one should use ruby which bestows prosperity,
as well as puṣyanīla, nīla, and especially mahānīla.
Pearls are born from oysters and from conch shells;
likewise, coral is known to be of two kinds, as is crystal, which is of three types consisting of the nature of the sun and the moon.
One should indeed avoid a line that has been obscured by the blending of colors, or one that is marred by defects such as frost-like specks, stains, grit, or spots.
I have described the characteristics of all jewels;
indeed, O Lord, every jewel brings great prosperity when counted as half a bhāra.
Ananta and the others are remembered as joyful hosts, like lightning-flames;
they are illuminators in the night, destroyers of all poisons, and bringers of victory.

The various colors of diamonds and other gems, such as crystal and the like, should be understood according to their taste and fragrance; these jewels indeed bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Iron is to be known as fourfold in common accomplishments:
namely, the vibrating (vevaka), the cutting (kaṭṭaka), the whirling (bhrāmaka), and likewise the attracting (cuṃbaka).
Thus indeed is this known as Kāntasaṃjñā, and likewise Mahābali;
Bhīma is to be known as fourfold, and Raktākhya is exactly like that.
One should increase the contact with the peacock-neck [gem] for the sake of prosperity;
likewise, the emerald linga is of three types: the true emerald and the dust-emerald.
The Śūlajit jewel, as well as the Ārṣa, destroy disease;
the Pulaka subdues Indra, while the Vairasaṃtrāsa and Saṃbhava [jewels] likewise prevail.
O Six-faced One, having recognized such gems as these, they should be established;
specifically, that which is born of stone leads to liberation, while enjoyment follows as a secondary consequence.
The earthly [element] is recommended for enjoyment, and liberation follows as a consequence.
In this same way, the linga made of wood should be known, as well as the painted linga;
the former destroys great prosperity, while the latter increases prosperity.
Likewise, brass is desirable, while copper is common and bestows enjoyment;
an iron linga is beneficial for the destruction of enemies.
A linga made of fragrant flowers, as well as one fashioned from a reed,
is considered a temporary linga that grants all desires to men.
One should always worship with supreme devotion a stone originating from a great river or produced in a sacred site of accomplishment (*siddhakṣetra*) and the like, as if it were a *liṅga*.
Now hear the origin and the characteristics of the bāṇaliṅgas in their entirety:
those at the Narmadā and Devikā, as well as at the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
O Six-faced One, the phallic emblems (liṅgas) of the rivers Sahiṣṇu and others are indeed worshipped by Indra and the other gods, and they are marked with their respective signs.
Those yellow, six-cornered [stones] with diamond-hard points are specifically called *induligās*; they indeed bestow imperial sovereignty.
The hand-lotus is cool with its nectar yet hot to the touch;
it resembles a fiery spear or is marked by a spear.
Having installed this excellent liṅga, there shall be an outpouring of splendor;
it is considered to be shaped like a staff for the southern direction, or else in the form of a tongue.
When it is fashioned in a moment of auspicious conjunction,
then, once it has been installed, the destruction of enemies is brought about by it.
The *rākṣasa* [seal], which resembles a sword and bestows the fruit of the yoga of knowledge,
should then be brought to the state of a blade when smeared with sugar and other substances.
The [lotus] belonging to Varuṇa is circular in shape, marked with a noose, and possesses great luster;
it is characterized by growth, garlands, and clarity, while the syllables *māyā* (the seed-syllable of Māyā) reside in its center.
Black incense, belonging to the wind element, accompanied by smoke and adorned with a banner, was placed upon its head; then it began to move and fluttered about.
In a windless place, it is intended for the eradication of moving enemies;
it has the form of a mace, heavy in the middle, and situated in the center of the entire [diagram].
O Noble One, whether by day or by night, it increases the growth of the crops;
it is triangular, marked with tridents, fierce, and possesses the luster of snow, the kunda flower, and the moon.
Therein arises the equinox (viṣuva), consisting of the four castes or even composed of me;
it is marked by the numerical count of the Vaiṣṇava discus and adorned with the lotus and other [symbols].
It was marked with the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem, adorned with the lion-throne of Time (Kālasiṃhāsana),
possessed a form like that of Vainateya, and likewise reached as far as the feet of Viṣṇu.
That which is situated in Sālaprāma and other such places is called Vaiṣṇava; it bestows the fruit of all sovereignty, is numbered [among the sacred sites], and increases prosperity.
The mark of a flower, the mark of a svastika, and the mark of a śrīvatsa lead to prosperity; the mark of a horse, the mark of a black lion, and the mark of a foot increase one's kingdom.
The stated marks should be applied for the sake of prosperity; one should avoid the remainder here.
A liṅga that has the color of a lotus, or the mark of a lotus, or a water-pot—
Or, as a sign of the attainment of the knowledge of Brahman, one may bear a staff and a rosary;
Mahākāla is of uniform color, while Nandīśa has the luster of a ruby.
Resembling the hue of a ruby, it is worshipped by both gods and siddhas;
resembling the luster of a pearl or the color of a sapphire, it is highly honored by Rudras and Ādityas.
[He was] surrounded by Vasus, Daityas, Indras, Yakṣas, Guhyakas, and Yātudhānas;
[he possessed] various colors, the color of iron, and the luster of a blue lotus.
This is the definition proclaimed by those who know the reality;
for one whose [birth] day is the third or fifth, an equilibrium on the scales does not occur.
That support is declared to be made from the remaining stone;
one should not cast it back into the river again once it has been recovered.
Know that the hair-liṅga (vālaliṅga) is likewise; everything else increases suffering.
Thus has the characteristic of the arrow-liṅgas (vāṇaliṅgas) been briefly described.
A linga made of iron is beneficial in the home of those with horns (cattle), provided it measures one finger-breadth or a span; beyond that, it is not for prosperity.
There is no fixed rule regarding the jewels; one may worship whichever one is obtained.
The brilliance of the jewels and their various qualities are always praised.
This world, which is beneficial, is like a wooden structure fashioned from excellent timber,
arising from the two types of sandalwood that grow in the lovely groves of Campaka.
[The forest] produced from *sāka*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees, with *khadira*, *aśoka*, and *kiṃśuka*;
[it contained] *aśvattha*, *vaṭa*, *śrīparṇa*, *viṇdu*, *vilva*, and *gavala*.

One should avoid a tree that is decayed, one growing on a rocky precipice, one arising from an anthill, one at a triple or quadruple junction, or one that kills people, as well as one located within a village.
One should avoid a tree that is infested by insects, dried up, or similarly treated [with harmful substances], as well as one that is ulcerated, knotted, deformed, or lacking in core substance.
Stone is said to be of three kinds: masculine, feminine, and neuter;
it exists in these three forms as a child, a youth, and likewise an elder.
It has the form of a vulva and a phallus, is fearful, and likewise possesses female, male, and neuter characteristics;
it is struck by the blow of a chisel, is accompanied by old age, and is endowed with the sharp sound of a child.
Likewise, one who is excessively aged, whose milk is thin, or who is devoid of it should be avoided;
however, one who is deeply matured, possesses a deep digestive fire, has a pleasing shadow, and is charming [is to be accepted].
It remains fixed in water, heavy, even, gentle, downward-facing, free of spots,
fragrant, glossy, straight, and pleasing to the heart.
Those that are cold, discolored, deficient in lines, or of inferior quality are censured;
for the superior [line], those with deficient lines and spots (bindus) are to be avoided.
O son of Kṛttikā, the highest line is declared to be thin, as are the dots;
likewise, even if it is straight or slightly broken, it is praised.
A stone of this kind is to be accepted: it should be free from nails and fissures, devoid of cracks, with lines that are well-formed, straight, and perfectly joined.
It is characterized by bursting sounds and harsh syllables, marked by "crow's foot" (kākapada) strokes;
it resides in impure places and resembles the excrement of a monkey.
Resembling a lotus or a pigeon, with a belly like a crow's nest;
having the color of fire or madder, and resembling a snake or a frog.
Marked with footprints resembling those of lions, tigers, bears, and leopards, it appeared greyish,
like a bamboo pole smeared with mud or smoke.
One should abandon [the site] that is filled with impurities from sacrifices, as well as that which is characterized by foul odors,
and likewise that which has been struck by the rays of the sun and possesses many defects.
But that which is faultless, rich in qualities, and bestows all accomplishments is to be accepted;
this is declared regarding the male [liṅga] in the case of manifest, unmanifest, and other types of liṅgas and sacred seats (pīṭhas).
The female form of the *piṇḍas* is established upon the female stones;
with the third [stone], Gaurīśvara is placed for the sake of completing the gateway and the temple.
Furthermore, when it is cut, carved, or especially ground, that which is produced by friction (mathani) is devoid of an embryo; this is to be understood by its characteristic mark.
When anyone's complexion or voice becomes disordered at any time, then that person should be known as pregnant; one should examine this by means of an ointment applied beforehand.
Kāsī, saṃharitāla, āśvaghna, and viṣa,
combined with ṛddhi and suṣya, along with vaktrāṅga and vajrakandaka.
Through its application with *piṣṭāranāla*, it illuminates the penis at night;
it should be known as containing an embryo and characterized by a transformation, which one may observe by the falling of a stream [of fluid].
O Lord, one should diagnose a fault in that mandala by its being unevenly smeared,
or by its being soft, or by an abnormal sound.

One should indicate a frog in a madder-red color; in the color of a lizard, one should point to a lizard; in a yellowish-green color, there would be a scorpion; and in a three-spotted variegated color, it would be a scorpion.
In Aruṇa, there may be destruction; in Nistriṃśāmbha, there shall be water;
in Acāpa, there may be a royal bird; and in Kṛṣṇavarca, a serpent.
One should predict misfortune from fire-colored [omens] and loss of wealth from smoke-colored ones;
in the case of a tawny color, a rat is to be known, and two types of results may occur.
It may be of various colors, or entirely smeared with ashes and water;
such other characteristics as these should be understood in brief.
Having rubbed it with hemp and other materials, one should examine the marks;
those that are auspicious in color, auspicious in form, and well-known as such, bestow good fortune.
And with impure forms and colors, it yields contrary results;
therefore, the linga, pedestal, stone, and so forth, should be taken exactly as prescribed.
Thus ends the chapter on the Liṅga in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
Īśvara said:
O son of Kṛttikā, I shall now describe in brief the manifest signs (vyaktaliṅga) in their proper order;
that [sign] should be known as threefold, arising respectively from the finger, the door, and the hand.

Beginning from one finger-breadth up to the length of a span (vitasti), it is beneficial for domestic use; however, whether without a pedestal or with a pedestal, it should be made three kalās larger.

One should distinguish the [dimensions of] the palaces according to the measurement of the palace door. Having measured four cubits from the ground, that which is situated above the ground is considered to be outside.
That [measurement] should be divided into nine parts by subtracting one part from each of the eight directions;
in the three *tryatāla* measures, the wise practitioner should apply a reduction (*hāsa*) except for the face.
205a) One should drop [the measurement] at intervals of half a finger-breadth up to four finger-breadths;
nine manifest liṅgas are produced, of this there is no doubt.
The experts in calculation determine a threefold division for each one;
by that means, the thirty-six Liṅgas indeed become clearly manifest.
Or it should be made according to the measurement of the door, clearly endowed with its structural arrangement;
one should divide the height of the door into nine, four, or three parts.
Alternatively, the pīṭhas may be divided according to the reduction of shares into superior, middling, and inferior;
one should fashion the manifest liṅgas by means of a thirty-sixfold division.
The rule for substances within the interior of the finger-gate is thus considered;
the rule for substances regarding lingas measured by the cubit is declared.
O Six-faced One, there is no fixed rule regarding clay, stone, wood, or metal for the manifest [form]; it should be made according to the desire of the patron at the appropriate locations.
In the house, the measurement for the support of the image should be in finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
in the sanctuaries, it is considered to be in cubits (hastas); and the exterior of the house is considered according to one's own desire.
Whatever measurement has been declared for fingers, doors, and cubits, one should divide that height into nine parts and then divide those parts by twelve.
The measurement for the limbs and sub-limbs should be known as two-tenths of a finger-breadth; it must be executed with great care, and the distinction of their designations is now being stated.

Furthermore, in the consecration of images and other such objects, one should effect a distinction in nomenclature by using the titles of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), the Lords of the World (Lokeśas), and the Brahma-Ṛṣis.
One should fashion the face, heart, navel, and the opening of the belly according to the measurement of the face;
the two thighs and the two shanks are considered to be twice the measurement of the face.
The ankles, knees, and neck should each be made four finger-breadths [in length]; this is the measurement for the height,
provided it is done without detracting from the beauty of the form.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra alone are to be [worshipped], and never others at any time.
For Aṅga, Pañcamūrdhan, Bhairava, Narasiṃha, Varāha, and Vināyaka, a height of ten tālas is recommended.
One should determine the measurement for those [deities] as twice that of Rudra;
furthermore, Ananta and the others should be made in the middle, according to the measurement of the eldest.
The Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, and others, as well as the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and so forth, should be fashioned with small, medium, or large proportions; otherwise, it will not be auspicious.
Others are the principal lords of the field, the servants, and the minor grounds;
thus, according to the sequence of the principles (tattvas) and through the application of their respective dispositions.
And by means of the vision of the aesthetic flavor (rasa) of the scriptures and so forth,
one should fashion an auspicious image at Kāśī within the mandalas, for the sake of purifying the flow of the movement [of consciousness].
Her hand-gaze is permeated by the aesthetic flavor (rasa) and marked by repose; she laughs with a sense of liveliness and speaks with expressive gestures.
It flows and proceeds with ease through the placement of the body due to its purity;
such indeed is the state of yoga for those who abide in the consecration of the marks of the image.
Furthermore, those [paintings] which are devoid of aesthetic flavor (rasa), bereft of the vision of inner sentiment (bhāva),
lacking the proper placement and mandala, and executed without the movement of the brush-stroke;
An image that has been fashioned by those with elephant-like hands, using tools and ornaments made from the tusks of elephants, should be avoided, for it is presided over by cruel beings.
The forehead is prescribed to be eight finger-breadths in width;
it should have a space of two *kalās* for the hairline, where the hair meets the root.
Leaving aside the middle finger from that [measurement], it is four fingers long;
from the base, however, it is considered sharp and whetted in two parts according to the sequence.
The donor's eyes are similar to those of a staff-bearer;
the eyes are situated between the eyebrows, and the pupils are positioned at one-third of the distance between the eyes.
Five months from that, the light and the wise one (the sun) meet at the barley-mark; two barley-corns from the edge of the eye is the measure for the eye, which is beneficial when closed slightly.
An eye resembling a bow, one like a blue lotus petal,
one with the luster of a lotus, and one with beautiful pupils— these five types of eyes are beneficial.
One should determine their width as three, five, six, nine, or ten [parts], according to what is appropriate and based on the essential requirements.
The eye should take the form of a "kāpa" during observations on the ground of yoga;
however, in the state free from modification, it resembles a fish for Śiva, the Supreme Self.

His eye for sensual pleasures has the luster of a blue lotus, while his wondrous eye is like a red lotus; his third eye resembles the essence of wrath, and the remaining eyes are as wide as his own fingers.
One should arrange the glances according to the rasa and bhāva;
the nose, shoulder, and face should each occupy two beats (kalās).
One should cause the entire height of the neck to be two *yavas*, with a width equal to that; however, the middle portion should be made one *mātra* less than the root and weapon portions combined.
The root of the ear-lobe (*puṭamūla*) should not be raised at all in its lower third;
the remainder should be made fleshy and one should fashion it so that it is symmetrical with the two lobes.
The form of the Jātī flower should be fashioned with pieces of cloth.
One should cause the nostril-aperture to be made on a single line with the corner of the eye, according to the measurement of one *smarapya*.
The corners of the eyes at the ends of the ears should be two kalās;
likewise, the ears should be made elevated and broad by half a yava.
The *varti* (wax seal) should indeed be thick like the two-fold *varti*; likewise,
having fashioned a mortar-vessel (*khalvapātra*) that is auspicious and deep (*ḍuka*),
the *kakunī* (lid) should be made with a half-finger’s thickness, extending from the base along with the *saṣkulī*.
The thickness of the ear itself should be made two barley-corns on all sides.
Thus, listen now to the characteristics of the horizontal line (tiryag-gata) therein;
it is beneficial when its time is applied at the beginning, middle, and end.
The ear should be made circular and elongated, beneficial, and shaped like a noose according to one's preference;
indeed, three globes should be made, and the junction between them should be two finger-breadths wide.
Just as in the case of the jar, here the region of the *maṇḍala* should be made three finger-breadths high;
however, the eye-socket should be [only] one barley-corn [in height].
One should fashion the face of the deities as four finger-breadths (vedāṅgula) in length and two and a half finger-breadths (dvikalārddha) in width;
however, for the gentle and the deformed ones, one should prescribe a width of three finger-breadths (tryaṅgula).
The upper lip should be one finger-breadth wide, while the lower lip is set at half that measure;
the gojī (the space between the lips) should be one-quarter of that, and the mṛkkaṇī (the corners of the mouth) should be exactly the same.

O child, it is taught that there one should make the distance from the ears [to the corners of the mouth] equal to half the length of the thumb and fingers, and likewise the distance from the mouth [to the ears].
The sixty-fourth [part] is placed at the head with a measurement of thirty-six finger-breadths;
the neck is eight finger-breadths wide, and likewise both shoulder regions.
The width of the shoulders should be thus; one should gradually decrease it below the neck.
The region of the shoulders should be three units wide, and the edge of the shoulder should extend six finger-breadths forward.
The neck should be made like a bodice, with a circumference of two *śaṅkus*; the upper arms and forearms should be fashioned according to the proportions of the successive sections.
The joint at the wrist, between the elbow and the hand, is considered to be one kalā;
the palm, together with the fingers, is held to extend from the face of the hand.
The middle finger likewise measures five finger-breadths in length;
indeed, one's lifespan, knowledge, wealth, and fame are determined by the lines, while their deficiency is indicated by their absence.
The palm [is marked with] a conch, a svastika, a lotus, and so forth;
the index, ring, and middle fingers are raised by half a finger-breadth.
A maiden is considered to be half a *kalā* less [than a full measure], and the thumb is remembered as being three finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) long;
it should be placed at the root of the index finger and fashioned so that it touches the foot.

That barley grain should be made with two joints, measuring five, six, or four finger-breadths; one should make it progressively smaller from the base, through the middle and the interval, to the tip.
The joints of the middle finger [are assigned] to the lunar days (tithis), the asterisms (nakṣatras), and the Īśvarīs;
likewise for the index and ring fingers, except that they are beneficial without the [middle finger's] row.
For a girl, there should be three lunar days (parvas) in succession, each being one-quarter of a tithi less than the preceding.
The fingers, measured by half a *prādeśa*, should resemble the *khadira* or *kunduru* flower; they should be fleshy, auspicious, and free from visible veins or joints.

The measurement of the middle finger is three finger-breadths; in its middle, excluding one barley-corn (yava), and at its tip, excluding three barley-corns, the measure of the 'nāha' (circumference) is declared.
Then, one should reduce it by two rows for a girl, excluding the Veda;
likewise, the width at the middle should be equal to that at the head and the edge.
I would not be [composed] of the three qualities (guṇas) through the various elements such as taste;
therefore, one should make an opening between those two, namely the mouth and the navel.
The two wings, however, are three *yava*s each; therefore, it is endowed with two circles.
The entire *vuccaka* is five *yava*s in width, being widest at the middle.
The wings should be three times as wide in circumference as they are long, elevated by one-fourth [of that length], and composed of three and a half *kalās*; otherwise, they are not beneficial.
O Six-faced One, the region of the shoulders should be thirty-six finger-breadths in width;
the space between the armpits should be two tālas, and the region of the hips should be the same.
In the region of the two breasts, the width is sixteen finger-breadths;
at the heart it is eighteen finger-breadths, and below that it is twenty-one.
From the region of the navel, the width should be made two tālas and three aṅgulas;
its circumference should be three times that, and it should not be flattened or curved.
The two testicles should be made two finger-breadths in circumference and three parts for the welfare of progeny;
having expanded them by two finger-breadths, the upper commencement should be made at the opening.
Furthermore, one should place the weapon in front during the three periods of time, as well as the jaṅghārambha.
The knees should be seven finger-breadths; the middle of the shanks is considered to be the same;
likewise, the ends [of the shanks] are five finger-breadths, and the circumference is three times that.
The heel should be four finger-breadths in length, and the foot should be shaped like a face;
the thumb situated there should be three finger-breadths, while the forefinger should be the best of barley-grains in thickness.
One should fashion the tip of the foot with a width of five finger-breadths;
the three [other] parts of the foot are each reduced by one *pradeśinī*.
At the base, middle, and likewise at the tip of the thumb,
there are five Vedas, as well as the elements, endowed with three Kalās and half [a Kalā].
The width of the thumb should be made; there too, the nails are as before.
At the base, middle, and tip of the index finger, it is deficient and increased by a sixteenth part respectively.
The circumference should be made three barley-corns plus one barley-corn;
at the middle of the foot, there should always be a lotus, a wheel, or a kalpa-tree as a mark.
Such images have thus been described to you in brief;
moreover, images may be made of cast metal, modeled in clay, or fashioned from paint.
One should perform supernatural powers with effort, but one should avoid a crooked person with effort; likewise, one should avoid a half-starred woman, as well as a shadow that has passed away.
The *bhiṃtī*, the *gaṇḍabhitti*, and the *kṣiptikā* should be avoided;
likewise, the *īṣat*, the *arddhotthitā*, and the *parāmukhī* should also be avoided.
A horse-headed image should indeed be fashioned from clay according to its proportions;
likewise, the crown must be made, and it is now described according to its specific location.
The Svastika, the Triśikha, the Strākāra,
the Mauli, the Kirīṭin, and the Padma— these six are known as types of crowns.
The crest should be made with three, five, or one tufts;
one should fashion it as being joined with pearl strings, gems, and silk ribbons.
The crown should be indicated for the gods, and likewise the svastika for the nāgas;
for the daityas, dānavas, and yakṣas, one should fashion the form of a makara.
What indeed is the insignia of Indra and the others? It is the lotus among the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras).
Thus has this iconography been described by me to you in brief.
Now, do not even briefly attempt to determine the proportions of a woman;
her face does not truly fit within another face, nor do her other parts, except for the sphere of her breasts.
A field overrun by weeds and insects yields only two parts; the third [type] is as follows:
the ankles, knees, and necks are raised by one matya-anga.
With ninety-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas) below the neck, it bestows auspiciousness;
the region of the shoulders should be six aṅgulas, and the two parts (aṃśas) should be two kalās each.
O son, the neck is considered to be seven finger-breadths in width at the front;
however, the hands and feet should be diminished by one-seventh, as previously described.
The five-finger measurement (pañcāṅgula) applies to the three [parts] in the middle of the arm;
however, there is an increase of one finger-measure for the back of the foot and the buttocks.
The calves should be fashioned with sixteen, fifteen, and ten [units] respectively; likewise, one should fashion the middle and the ends of the shanks like an elephant's trunk.
The secret [base] is considered to be six finger-breadths in size, hairless like the back of a tortoise; and a woman, sixteen years of age, should be made very beautiful.
The region of the shoulders should be made thirty-eight finger-breadths;
the distance between the two armpits should always be made eighteen finger-breadths.
The width of the breast region should be known as eight kalās;
the two nipples, resembling bilva fruits, should each be made three kalās in size.
The face with its eyes, and below that, the space between the breasts, should be measured in width;
the face and the region of the navel likewise, while the hips are beneficial when measured by twice the length of the face.
O son of Pārvatī, the female body is enveloped by the three guṇas;
it is especially adorned with garments, garlands, excellent perfumes, and ornaments.
Likewise, forms, articles, beds, and seats [should be made accordingly];
thus is described the measurement for women, which is six and one-quarter finger-breadths in height.
O Sadāśiva, ascertain specifically the measurement:
Sadāśiva [is formed] by exactly one hundred [units] of twenty finger-breadths each.
One should determine ten *tālas* using one's own finger-breadths;
each face [of the deity] is equal, and beyond that, it is half a *kalā*.
The pair of his ankles and knees should be made with effort by means of two and one [units] respectively through the mouth; the width is considered to be as previously described.
The external [vowels] must indeed be brought inward in groups of ten, eleven, and pairs;
from that, the junctions consist of mere *kalās*, and likewise the form of the junction is as it is.
The shoulder-head should be six finger-breadths, and the hand twelve finger-breadths; its exterior should reach down to the knees—this [image] of the Supreme Lord must not be made otherwise.
When, having become firm as a vajra, one touches the knees with the hands or extends them down to the knees,
this is declared by the son of Kṛtikā to be the *vāhyā* posture.
One should fashion a five-faced [deity] surrounded by fifteen eyes;
with the upper face lacking a digit, one should rotate it all around.
The crescent moon should be three finger-breadths wide, reaching the southern end of the matted locks;
one should fashion the mass of matted hair (jaṭājūṭa) of Īśāna as five finger-breadths in length.
Having made the skull of Dakṣa his ornament,
he is fair-nosed, fair-faced, and radiant, seated upon a lion throne empowered by mantras.
He has ten arms and ten eyes, with long lotus-like eyes;
he is Īśāna with an upward-facing face, radiant as snow, and absorbed in meditation.
One should meditate upon the Lord as a person with the luster of saffron, always facing the east,
possessing a majestic form, with matted locks like serpents and eyes resembling crushed collyrium.
O Śambhu, Aghora is always situated in the southern direction;
he resembles the flower of the pomegranate tree and possesses the luster of lac and vermilion.
Adorned with many ornaments, he stands to the north,
beautiful and resembling a snow-mountain or the moon, with a smile upon his cheeks and lips.
One should always perform the rite in the west; indeed, one should always face Sadyojāta.
One should always look toward the root door by means of Īśāna.
It should always be installed facing east, or it may be installed facing west;
the lion-throne, however, shall measure eight tālas on all sides.
Half of that height, one should fashion the lotus seat consisting of six *tālas*, inlaid with the powers (*śaktis*) beginning with Vāmā; [upon this is] Sadāśiva, the God of gods.
Now the measurement of Bhairava and the others is being stated:
the face of Bhairava extends all around to the distance of two *golakas*.
The remaining height of Bhairava is as before;
its width at the base of the outer skull-cup (karpara) is seven, six, or five [units].
The chest, heart, navel, and belly, as well as the hips and so forth, in due order; likewise, the two hands, the two faces, and indeed the entire body.
Two faces and half a face, the waist consisting of three faces,
the root of the thighs, the two knees, the middle of the shanks, and their tips.
The width [of the base] should be two, four, six, or eight parts, and it should be greater by half a part;
its circumference, however, is three times the width of the previous measurement.
The sheath for the fangs should be one-sixteenth of a finger-breadth (kalā), sharp, white, and well-rounded;
the beard, however, should be made three fingers long and likewise radiant with its luster.
The beard situated on the upper lip is declared to be three finger-breadths in length;
likewise, the eyebrows are one finger-breadth in width, curved and radiant.

Its mouth is said to be three finger-breadths wide, and the measurement of its teeth is likewise declared; the tongue is shaped like a lotus petal, three finger-breadths long, and of a reddish luster.
The eye should be made with a core [of pigment], together with Bhairava and Bhairavī;
she should be made eight tālas in height, and furthermore, the forest-dwellers [should be] greater than that.
Likewise Gaurī, Lakṣmī, Durgā, and Sarasvatī;
Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and furthermore the other Mothers.
Sūkarī, Nārasiṃhī, Cāmuṇḍā, Kṛśodarī,
Ṛkṣakarṇī, Laṃpaṭākṣī, and especially Galagajī.
The Vaināyakī, the Gāruḍī, and likewise another with a deformed face—
this is declared to be the description for all of them, exceeding the three globes.
O wise one, you should prescribe the remaining tāla measures as being of the same proportions;
however, for a woman of deformed appearance, one should prescribe a height of one hundred [tālas].
The arrangement of the arms and weapons is according to the very procedure stated in the Kalpa;
likewise [are] Kārtikeya, Nandin, Gaṇeśa, and the other lords of the Gaṇas.
Furthermore, the Kiṅkaras, Kṣetrapālas, Dūtyas, and Mārikās,
as well as Sākāra and Heti, should be fashioned first according to the prescribed order.
O Six-faced One, they should be made knee-high in height;
likewise, the trident, the staff, and the umbrella should be equal in size to oneself.
A discus, a trident, a mace, a sword, and likewise a lance;
a plow, an axe, a staff, a spear, a khaṭvāṅga, and a trident.
O Daughter of Śaṅkara, the banner, the mace, the trident, the noose,
the goad, the tree, the lute, and so forth should be fashioned with four faces.
A water-pot, a rosary, books, and a bowl;
the moon and sun, an offering-vessel, a lotus, a wheel, and likewise a fruit.
The bell, the knife, Cāmuṇḍā, and so forth—these are of the nature of faces;
one should fashion them without flesh, with half the width [of the main face].
The five pretas, the piśācas, and the many beings beginning with Bhṛṅgīśa should be diligently propitiated by one who desires his own welfare.
Let them be in human form, adorned with a circle of hoods;
one should prescribe that the circle of hoods is two *tālas* in height.
Beginning from the three hoods up to the end of the thousand, one should prescribe [the marks]:
below the navel, they are like serpents, marked with lotuses and jars on their hands.
The characteristics of Gaṇeśa, Vāmana, and others— who have one hood, one face, are expanded, and possess a smoky luster— are here described briefly.
One should designate their face as three *saṃkru* (sixteen fingers) in height; the heart, navel, and abdomen should each be made eight *aṅgulas* in measure.
The thighs and shanks are two-faced and provided with knees and calves;
the neck is beneficial at two finger-breadths [in width]; thus is the height described for the dwarf type.
That image, five tālas in height, has been described by me;
its arms and forearms should be made like the face, joined at the joints.
The feet should be eight finger-breadths, and the chest should have three faces;
in this manner, Vāmana should be fashioned, and Gaṇeśa likewise with an elephant face.
One should draw his two ears measuring eight finger-breadths, with the openings of the canals clearly visible,
smooth and glossy, and adorned with bells and chowries.
The two pitchers (kuṃbha) there should have their desires [fulfilled]; having placed them together in the middle, its hand should be three-faced, and from its base it should be five finger-breadths.
A tooth four fingers long is recommended; its [width] should be six fingers.
One should have the entire auspicious [tooth] fashioned while resting upon a lotus.
Seated upon a lion or a mouse, established on a pedestal, bestowing all perfections,
holding a vessel of sweetmeats offered by himself, and endowed with an axe and bracelets.
Is it right that a hunchbacked woman, lacking a navel and intent on her own ends, should perform such an act?
Because of that, hunchbacked offspring are born; therefore, one should avoid such a woman.
In the house, a gentle [expression] should be made, and likewise in the temples;
however, in the citiśaya [hall], there should be the fierce, the laughing, and likewise the terrifying.
One should carefully avoid the *adbhuta* (wonderful) rasa;
instead, the *gaurīśvara* should be fashioned, resplendent and surpassing all in loveliness.
One should fashion Gaurī according to the proportions of Īśvara;
however, one should not fashion Śaṅkara according to the proportions of Gaurī.
In this manner, Viṣṇu, who forms half the body of Śaṅkara, should be depicted like Śaṅkara; one should likewise designate the vehicles of the world-protectors and the Mothers.
A five-tāla elephant is auspicious, while a horse is auspicious when measured at one tāla less;
a peacock is praised with three faces, and a bull is beneficial with four faces.
The buffalo should be made five tālas in height, just as the god Bhairava is;
Rudra should have three faces, be joyful, and possess a radiance equal to the sun.
He has three eyes, holds a staff in his hand, and has a tawny face like that of the Lord of Monkeys;
he who is six-faced in Kārtika has another face that possesses six streams.
In brief, these should be performed during the Ekavaktra-upavāsa;
Bhṛṅgī, Gaṅgā, and the limbs should be fashioned with great care, free from flesh.
And likewise, O Six-faced One, the Yamunā should be made black;
however, she should be ninety-six finger-breadths in length, for a woman should not be made otherwise if it is to be beneficial.

One may fashion it as being merely the size of the face, or the size of the heart, or reaching to the private parts; or it may be as far as the knees, or the ankles, or one may conceive of it as being equal in size [to the body].
The chariot forms should be constructed according to worldly convention;
having understood each case, one should employ them, ensuring they are neither too broad nor raised more than half the width.
A dome, a pinnacle, a plastered surface, or what was formerly built and so forth, may be inserted within;
or it may be fixed even in a temple or a house that is straight.
Thus ends the chapter on images in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
Now, O Śaila, I shall not describe the characteristics of the Mothers and Bhairavas;
the [mandala] should be made with the qualities of four Mothers, or else it may be omitted.
O son of Kṛttikā, I shall now declare the names and forms of the Mothers, whose effects are twofold or fourfold.
I am Brāhmī, the daughter of Daṇḍa, four-armed and four-faced, gentle in appearance, seated upon a swan, and holding a water-pot and a rosary.
Dancing along the path of the *cārī* movements, endowed with various emotions and sentiments,
the gentle Māheśvarīs were mounted upon their vehicles in vain, holding tridents in their hands.
Moving in various circles and dancing all around,
Kaumārī, seated upon a peacock and holding a spear in her hand, was endowed with great luster.
Sindūravarnā, dancing with *cārī*, *sthānaka*, and *recaka* movements, is Vaiṣṇavī; Garuḍā and Rudrā are marked with the conch, the discus, and the rosary.
She should be depicted dancing, dark blue in color and accompanied by her attendants;
she is mounted upon a buffalo devoid of stars, and holds a sword and a conch in her hands.
Smoke-colored and large-bodied, she should be made dancing;
Indrāṇī, however, is mounted upon an elephant, with her hands holding a thunderbolt and a goad.
Dancing along a graceful path, the thousand-eyed goddess,
auspicious Cāmuṇḍā, who is exceedingly full of power, stands with her sword and other weapons raised.
Svasthā-yogeśvarī should be depicted dancing, adorned with garlands of skulls, black and red in color, and standing upon a corpse.
The goddess has a scissor in her hand beginning with the letter *ka*, she causes men to flow with blood;
she holds a sword and a trident, and is adorned with arrows and a deer.
The weapon fashioned by Cakra is the destroyer of great pretas;
it is called Vikṛtāntikā, fierce, extraordinary, and terrifying.
The mistress of yoga (Yogeśī) is of such a kind: she has prominent veins and a deformed face;
alternatively, she may be one who subdues poverty and possesses an even luster.
Holding a lotus in one hand and a sword in the other, she is intent on striking with a trident;
she pierces with her trident Poverty in human form.
She should be depicted as contented, abiding in the sentiments of humor and the erotic;
she should not display desire for her own form, with both hands placed upon two lotuses.
With her hand grasping a lotus-banner, dancing on all sides and accompanied by various *lūṣapa* dancers, the master of the dance (*padācārya*) should arrange [the formation].
She is beautiful, with a gentle form like that of the moon, devoted to dance,
marked by a blue garment and a water-pot, fair and white-complexioned, and accompanied by horses.
Associated with the lunar mansions and the stars, filled with the conjunctions of the zodiac signs,
and provided with various musical instruments and bridges, they should be made endowed with beauty.
The goddess of the southeast has a red body;
she holds a sword in her hand, stands upon a ram, dances, and is accompanied by nāgas and gandharvas.
Vāruṇī, holding a noose in her hand and possessing the form of a young woman,
should be depicted dancing, endowed with the dancing gesture (nṛtyahasta).
Vāyavyā has kusha grass in her hand; Rūpiṇī has a turned-away face; Bhaumacārī is thrice-blessed; and Viṣṭapasthā is adorned.
She should be depicted as dancing, endowed with divine garments and hands;
she is Nābhasvatī, black in color, moving through the sky, and firmly established.
Padmahastā, Sunayanā, Kāntā, Dṛṣṭi,
Vināyikā, Cāmuṇḍā, and the one named Laṃpaṭā— these should be fashioned as those who are greedy for raw flesh.
Dancing, greatly intoxicated, with eyes squinting at the edge of the circle;
having the form of Gaṇeśa, with the shape of an elephant, [holding] a ladle-vessel, an axe, and a tree.
One should have Lambodarā depicted dancing while seated upon a mouse;
Gāruḍī, having the form of Garuḍa, holds a staff and a water-pot in her hands.
Lambodarī, with a serpent in her hand, adorned with a snake-bracelet,
dancing, most terrifying, and perspiring from her long arms.
Four-armed and four-faced, resembling the hibiscus, the kunda flower, and the moon,
she is equipped with an arrow and a bow, stands upon a corpse, and is intent on dancing.
Thus Vijayā, who is to be worshipped, is red and stands upon a horse;
likewise Jayantī, being of a loathsome form, stands upon the Sun and Bhīma.
Aparājitā should be fashioned as standing upon delusion (moha), with her banner raised, dancing, possessing a dark luster, and accompanied by various musical instruments.
And she set forth, fleshless, perfected, resembling the moon in a lunar mansion;
the goddess held a sword and a shield, and was adorned with a garland of skulls.
Thus, though red, when consumed it dries up the complexion;
she is white with the luster of a blue lotus, possessing limbs like a blue lotus, and abiding within a blue lotus.
Resembling a *malinī* leaf, with a beautiful body and fresh youth,
she has either four or six arms, and is adorned with serpents.
She set forth, mounted upon a bull, adorned with eighteen arms;
she was either white or red-bodied, intent upon our own *tāṇḍava* dance.
Smoke-colored and of beautiful form, one should direct [the visualization] toward the potter;
she is dancing, large-eyed, and adorned with blossoming eyes.
Having ascended her divine bed, she should contemplate thus during the night:
"The dark night of Time (Kālarātri) has arrived, bearing many forms."
But when she stands in the *ātma-dvīsthānaka* posture, moving with the *vratyālīḍha* gait,
overcome by the sentiment of terror (*bhayānaka-rasa*), and agitated in her gaze as she looks at what is seen and unseen;
The very beautiful Asurātrī should be depicted with a garland in her hand;
she should be fashioned with a smiling face and adorned with a gentle gaze.
Endowed with various offerings, serene, and possessing a reddish luster,
one should make the "Happy Night" (Sukharātri) ritual, since from it happiness is attained.
With a face as beautiful as a copper-crested cock, endowed with a circular gaze,
the goddess holds a sword and a bowl, dancing on all sides.
In this manner, the horse-faced [mudrā] is adorned with two vaiśākha postures,
concealed by the hands on the cheeks, and released by the vardhamāna [gesture].

Seated upon a lion-throne, with a lion’s face, possessing a massive form and the brilliant luster of gold, she delights in the *pratyālīḍha* posture; she is devoted to Viṣṇu and established in the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
And those [goddesses] are endowed with laps, with gaping mouths, bearing wheels, conchs, and swords; they are goddesses who are intensely greedy for human flesh.
Likewise, Vyāghramukhī should be fashioned holding a noose, a spear, and a mace; she may be mounted upon a tiger skin or seated upon a copper-colored elephant with her hand placed upon it.
She was dark, formidable, with eyes like arrows, adorned with a dagger and a vessel;
thus she had a jackal’s face and a protruding belly.
Holding a *vardhamānaka* in her hand, adorned with a sword and a shaven head,
she has the face of an owl, is like a flickering lightning bolt, and is all-pervading.
The goddess Karkaṭā, dancing with a terrifying gait, holds a sword and a severed head; her breasts are swollen from drinking wine.
Thus, Bhīmānūpuravāṭikā had the face of a cat, eyes like bees, and hands bearing arrows; she was intent on striking with swords and scimitars.
And eat the terrifying *dṛkṣakarṇī*, which has a luster like black collyrium;
it shines with the flickering movement of a snake's head, appearing as if fashioned from a *kṛkara* [cricket].
The goddess, holding a staff and meat in her hands, performs a dance;
she has the faces of five monkeys and is solely intent upon the staff and the proclamation.
With hands like the wings of a swan, she is momentarily darkened by fierce dogs;
with the face of a camel, she is highly deformed and adorned with swords and bells.
The movement resembling a serpent is performed externally with the exhalation;
it should be executed like a dog's snout, intent upon the two types of movement.
Kartarīmukhahastā holds a knife in her hand, while Kartarīmukhadhāriṇī bears a knife in her mouth;
Gomukhī is deformed and terrifying, and Samopaditamartalī is likewise formidable.
The goddess should be depicted with a sword at her waist and a pair of scissors poised in her mouth;
she has a most terrifying face, stands with feet together, and is in a dancing posture.
The goddess holds a sacrificial hook and a curved knife;
she is fierce and radiant, auspicious with an aged face, and her hands are placed upon a sword and a noose.
Her eyes are joined with a sidelong glance, adorned with squinting looks;
she is mounted upon a lion, has the face of a serpent, and is adorned with eighteen arms.
She should be joined with ten attendants, swift by name and in deed;
she should have the face of a ruddy sheldrake and be accompanied by a ruddy sheldrake.
The goddess holds a sword and a bowl; she is devoted to the great sage’s water.
She has a beautiful face and a gentle countenance; she is fair-faced and of lovely disposition.
She is joined with actions that are difficult to perform and unpleasant; she is unskilled from time immemorial,
exceedingly emaciated, loathsome, and devoid of flesh.
With a razor-edged blade in her hand, she is likewise joined with an upper garment;
holding a maternal uncle’s staff and accompanied by enemies, she is then possessed of [such] power.
This night is exceedingly dark and most terrifying, bringing on the Kali age;
it stands with its whirlpools of calamity, intent on devouring men as its prey.
By means of the four crossings,

[she is] joined with various *huṃ* sounds and adorned with various instruments; she is unrestrained, having stepped upon those who are established in their positions, and is accompanied by ten thousand leaders.
The goddess Khaḍgakumbhavatī should be depicted as having transferred [her essence] into the form of Kāryā;
she, the sovereign of Laṅkā, should always be portrayed with many faces and many arms.
She has ten arms, she is gentle, and she is seated upon a lotus;
such indeed is Bhadrakālī, yet she is black and should be visualized as such.
Standing in the ālīḍha posture, she who resembles the sun, the crusher of the Daityas,
bearing a vessel of blood, is Siddhi, endowed with a divine jar.
She should be depicted seated in the lotus posture, gentle and beautifully adorned;
he who installs her with diligence shall likewise obtain sons.
The goddess named Araṇī has five hair-tufts on her head;
she possesses ten arms and holds various musical instruments raised aloft.
She whose urine is unperforated, who is endowed with [auspicious] qualities, who shines with a gentle gaze,
and who stands in the midst of a herd of cows— she is indeed the "cow's urine" (gomūtrikā) and not the "non-increasing" (navardhanī).
The goddess has five faces and ten arms, is armed with various weapons, possesses a gracious countenance, and is adorned with serpent-locks.
One should fashion its eastern face as fearsome, resembling Garuḍa;
the remaining hundreds of faces should be gentle and beautiful in form.
Śrīghāṇārdvānau is the foremost among the Mothers (Mātṛs), the increaser of happiness;
she should be depicted with ten arms, possessing a beautiful form and in the prime of youth.
In the assembly of various musical instruments, she is not indeed manifold, though she has spread herself through various parts;
yet, as the instrumental music of the seven notes, she consists of eightfold arms.
One should cause the eighteen-fold musical instrument of Koṇāraka to resound with its accompaniment;
then, through the threefold division, one attains dissolution by means of the delay in the midst of the elements.
Having assumed the forms of cow-urine and so forth, as well as the *dupuṭa* and *aṃcupuṭa* gestures,
he manifested in the form of musical instruments and the *naṃdī* drum, roaring away the fever born of obstacles.
The *sāmyatāla* is fourfold, as are the *vikāras*, the *paṭaha*, the *mārga*, the *deśī*, and the *krama*; furthermore, one should distinguish the *antadvardhadhāna*.

Endowed with sixty-four gestures, adorned with thirty-two graces, possessed of a beautiful gait and a pleasing gaze, she is established in the nine dramatic sentiments and filled with aesthetic flavor.
Equal to various states of being, adorned with various name-mandalas,
she possesses various great flavors; the Kula is characterized by fifty common gestures (abhinaya).
Her movement through the realms is perceived by the four [senses] and so forth;
she is the object of various immeasurable perceptions, yet her singular characteristic is that she abides in her own state.
But the movement of weapons occurs through the sequence beginning with *sarat* and so forth, from the fourfold [state].
In all rites for averting misfortune, one should establish merit and the two [deities] upon the seat;
[this concerns] sleep, lying down, and sitting...
Thus ends the chapter on the Face of the Mother-Bhairava in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
Now I shall duly explain [the sequence] in order:
the seat (sīṭha) is to be known as consisting of action (kriyā), while the Linga is considered to consist of knowledge (jñāna).
Therefore, in this very way, Umā the Goddess is the great seat (mahāpīṭha) of Śiva, who is the Self, and Sadāśiva is the liṅga.
I shall now describe, in brief, the characteristics of lingas and images.
The length of the pedestal (pīṭha) should be equal to the measurement of the height of the liṅga;
its height should extend up to Viṣṇu, and it may be either manifest (vyakta) or unmanifest (avyakta).
One should fashion the image so that it is elongated relative to its pedestal; in terms of length, the image should be equal to the pedestal, while its width and height should be half of that.
Alternatively, she grants success through the measure of her shoulder, not through pride;
her calves are covered with fat, long in length, and raised to half the width [of the hips].
Once seated, she should be made square and not elongated;
at the beginning, she is considered to be like a mass of milk, pure and extending for a thousand [yojanas].
One should always perform [the practice] equally for all, with particular attention to the face and the *liṅga*;
likewise, the Vajrā and the Moon-digit (Candrakalā) are established as beginningless.
On the lap of Surā, Amṛtā should be fashioned; she is considered to be Padmāsaṃvartakā.
Furthermore, Nandāvartā should be fashioned; O son of Pārvatī, [these rules] do not apply to others.
For all [other parts], one may fashion either a single section or many sections;
however, for the face-liṅga, one should fashion two sections or many sections.
One should bind [the deity] with copper wires, or else with golden ones;
the binding of the pedestal should not be done with iron wires for the sake of attaining minor accomplishments.
A long pond is proclaimed as the *pratimā* among the recollections;
likewise, I shall describe the removal of obstacles for others in brief.
A square [altar] should be made for Indra for the attainment of sovereignty;
that called the "womb" (yoni) is beneficial for heating weapons upon the fire-linga.
The *nālaka* (tube) of the left [nostril] should shine forth, situated within the interval of the wandering [wind];
that of the right is a half-moon, and its posterior part is a semicircle.
In the middle of that [pedestal], there should be a tube like an arrow, unattached to the wood;
the Rākṣasa pedestal is triangular, and the channel is located in the left corner.
The pedestal (pīṭha) should belong to Varuṇa, resembling the full moon and having five girdles;
likewise, the stalk (nāla) should be fashioned with a neck and provided with feet.

Alternatively, one may draw a hexagon upon the praliṅga; the stalk (nālaka) is in the northern direction, while at the back and front there is a connection of edges, with a pair of edges near the two arms.
For the eradication of enemies, one should fashion a hexagon;
for the side of the linga, an octagon, with its channel facing the eastern direction.
In the Raudra [liṅga], the base is circular and marked with tridents; in the Pūrva [liṅga], it is tubular;
in the Brahma-liṅga, it is considered to be lotus-shaped; and in that of Viṣṇu, it is considered to be the form of a digit of the moon.
One thousand and eight hundred [lines] are beneficial for the Sahasrāṅka;
likewise, I shall describe the characteristics of the Padma and other [yantras] according to their divisions.
And for all the pīṭhas, there may be a form even without reliance on a liṅga;
listen now to the characteristics regarding its height and breadth.

The pedestal (pīṭha) that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation should be made such that its height is one-sixteenth part [of the temple], and its width is likewise. It should extend from the water-level downwards.
An expert in the scriptures should fashion the girdle (*mekhalā*) in the same manner as the stalk (*nālaka*);
having left a space for the support of the *liṅga* in the middle, one should divide the pedestal (*pīṭha*) by fifteen parts.
They call the abode of the moon the pericarp of the lotus of the heart;
in the supreme Śiva at the throat, there is no entry by means of the two-footed [mantras] in succession.
By dividing [the circumference] by parts equal to the number of the infinite-faced moon (one hundred and twenty-five), the whirling lotus with its pericarp is formed;
this is known as the Padma [mandala], which leads likewise to both liberation and worldly enjoyment.
The neck [of the jar] consists of the Vikāra, Rākā, Anta, Varma, Agni, Indu, and Śikhā; and the Jagatī foot likewise constitutes the neck of the altar on the jar, in due order.
One should rotate it by means of each individual point through which the exit occurs;
this is declared to be the *payodharā* [line], four-cornered, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
On the face and the lingas, they should be made on the thousandth and the fifty-first marks;
for the elongated form of the manifest linga, a tank (vāpī) should be made, or otherwise not.
When the number of seats is divided by twelve, the entry of the *pada*s for *ka-ga-kha* and likewise for *ka-kha* should be performed according to the *Nigama*, *Ananta*, and *Sūkṣma* systems.
The son of Kṛttikā should fashion Ananteśa as being crushed;
the six-cornered Vajrā is said to bestow the sovereignty of liberation and the accomplishment of success.

On a pedestal fashioned with eight lotuses, one should effect the exit from each of the individual locations of *ka*, *kha*, *ka*, and *kha*; furthermore, it should be done again at the end of the ocean-like words.
Then, the crescent moon, adorned with the glory of the eastern half of the infinite Lord,
became the immortal crown-ribbon of his circle.
Because she bestows good fortune and liberation, she is therefore known as Candrakalā;
she is nectar for the sake of all accomplishments and is especially the giver of liberation.
The wise one should cause it to enter the six-fold girdle and fashion half of the pedestal;
the neck is formed by Śrīkaṇṭha, and that which is above it is proclaimed as the great upper portion.
In brief, the exit of Saṃvartā should be performed with three steps;
the neck in the field of Vikārabhakta is marked by Tatpuruṣa.
The triple-form [mantra] below the girdle and likewise above the neck is indeed known as Nandāvartī,
which accomplishes all desires.
Alternatively, the triple-belted [mandala] may be established with its upper and lower parts aligned;
it should be fashioned as a Nandāvarta, or as a four-cornered square, or perfectly circular.
The image should be elongated; one should avoid the three-angled and eight-angled forms, excluding the *jīvi*.
Furthermore, one should arrange the various parts according to their mutual distinctions.
Due to the arrangement of its configuration, no specific numerical limit exists;
from the eastern and western liṅgas, the channel extends toward the north.
For those whose faces are turned northward or southward, the stalk is beneficial when placed on the eastern side;
this is specifically taught for those honored by the world-protectors (Lokapālas).
I have described the construction of all the lingas;
the stalk (nālaka) is at the front, occupying one-third of the width, extending upward.
It is stated that for images of the highest class, the proportions are three, five, two, and three cubits, according to the portion of the Vedas, the elements, or the flavors.
It is always praised when measured by eight, nine, and twelve finger-breadths, and it is considered excellent when measured by ten;
furthermore, a hollow is prescribed in the neck for the purpose of water exiting.
O Six-faced One, one should designate a trench at the base of the root with five rows of fine lime-plaster extending for half the width in front.
Thus is the water-channel described; its depth at the front is double [the width].
And for all pedestals, the height is one-sixteenth part [of the total measurement].
From the base upwards, the width should be double at the root;
the excavation should be equal in width [to the base], and one should lead the elevation up to the top of the wall.

For an image made of clay, a pedestal made of clay is beneficial; for one made of wood, one made of wood; for one made of metal, one made of metal should be used; and likewise for one made of gems, one made of gems.
A jewel is praised when it is strung upon a thread; everything is established within the arrow.
With diligent effort, one should worship the arrow alone as being without support, and not anything else.
On a throne of fine cloth, on a seat made of silk, or on a pedestal of flowers—or indeed on any such support—one should perform worship; one should not worship that which is without a support.
A gem originating from its own source, such as gold or silver, is more auspicious than one from a different source; furthermore, for gems and jewels, a pedestal made of gold is beneficial.
One should know that for those made of silver, the pedestal is made of gold; for those made of silver, however, it is brass.
For a crystal [image], there should be a copper pedestal, and the binding should be produced from silver.

For jewels, there should be a pedestal made of gold; for those made of precious gems, it may also be made of silver. Furthermore, the fastening for all of them should be made of either silver or gold.
One should fashion the lingas, such as those made of jewels and arrows, in five ways;
one should place two parts in the excavation, or even five parts.
For as many atoms as there are in the linga, the temple, and the pedestal,
for that many great kalpas shall the creator enjoy his rewards.
The merit from [an image with] the signs of being baked, as opposed to unbaked, shall be tenfold;
the merit from one made of wood compared to one made of clay shall be tenfold greater than that.

Just as that [merit] from one made of stone is ten times greater than that from one made of wood, so too is that from one made of metal; and from one made of metal, that from one made of gems is ten times more meritorious; and from that, merit from one made of precious jewels is remembered as being tenfold.
Through the conceptualization of the *vāṇaliṅga*, there is the attainment of immeasurable fruit;
likewise, O Śikhidhvaja, the thousand-marked [liṅga] bestows all desires.
There is no fixed enumeration of lingas by way of substance;
a linga may consist of four types of material: stone, clay, wood, or metal.

In its measurement, there are three kinds of finger-breadths (aṅgula): seven, eight, and nine barley-corns; [the first] by the movement of the little finger, and the other two respectively by one-third and one-quarter of that movement.
From that threefold cessation of the *viddhi-rāma* (the third note),
six notes are to be known as the *ṣaḍja-śruti* occurring behind the *ṣaḍja*, starting from the lowest limit of the *kanyasa* (lowest) scale.
The Vedas are the Viṣkambhas of the Sāman; the first [Viṣkambha] is all the Samādhis.
The Guardians of the Directions are the Liṅgas and Viṣkambhas; thus there are ten, making fourteen in total.
O-faced one, there are three types: one hundred and eight, one hundred and one, and one thousand;
that which is unmanifest has a single abode, while its divisions are said to be six.
Thus, the height of the material *aṅgula* for the various types of *liṅgas*, distinguished by their width and configuration,
consists of one hundred and eighty-eight *hasta*s in number.
The number should be thirty-six thousand, perfectly measured;
at the beginning and at the end, one should decrease the portion of Rudra and increase the portion of Brahmā.
Therefore, by the reverse of this, one should effect increase or decrease in what is honored with the sacrificial thread (*śūlārcita*).
Thus, the extent of the wings and the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) is equal to that [of the central body].
Due to the equality of their proportions, there should be a mutual overlapping of their shadows;
indeed, the number of liṅgas is determined in this very way by the measurement of the interior of the temple.
Just as the number of liṅgas was previously determined according to the measure of the pedestals,
one should likewise determine the specific number of pedestals here in this same manner.
In the first case, a thousand lingas should be fashioned, but not in the other;
one should likewise fashion one hundred and eight lingas marked with the image of a deity.
Since that which is a portion of the Veda grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation from beginningless time,
one should always fashion the Mukhaliṅga, for it is entirely equal to everything.
Having first established the measurement, one should then worship the Mukhaliṅga;
O Śāṅkarī, then the six types of coughs, which consist of the faults of the vital breath (āyu-doṣa), shall not occur.
One should determine the characteristics within the *liṅga* composed of the manifest and the unmanifest;
there, one should effect the emergence by means of the diagonal lines from the corners.
At the base, there are two parts, and the junction occurs with the two lines;
this first set of four lingas bestows liberation solely upon men.
Indeed, according to the very sequence previously described, they bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
as well as longevity, prosperity, beauty, sovereignty, intelligence, and fame.
If one who knows the proper application should nevertheless construct a linga with a different characteristic,
that which is undesirable arises for him; therefore, having understood this correctly, one should fashion it accordingly.
Thus ends the chapter on the sacred seats (pīṭha) in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
The examination of the ground and the Vāstu sacrifice for the protector of the field are now described.
A field measuring one, two, or three hundred [units] is considered inferior, middling, or superior, respectively.
O Śikhidhvaja, purification should be performed according to the measure of the bows;
white, red, yellow, and black [threads] are established for the Brahmins and the other castes respectively.
The waters flow clockwise and are auspicious; they are adorned with flowering trees, delightful, fragrant, sweet, and devoid of inferior beings.
A lineage that has abandoned its elders should be forsaken; likewise, a family that is full of sand and pebbles, overrun by wicked creatures, or situated near impure water should be avoided.
Just as a quiver is prepared for shooting, being well-fitted and free of splinters, so too should the enema-bag be made;
one should crush it with the feet.
A site that slopes toward the east and north is praised; likewise, it should be provided with flowers and water, and made as smooth as the surface of a mirror by the artisan.
221b) In that regard, when undertaking the acquisition of a field, one should first perform a sacrifice to the non-gaṇas and the guests;
having offered bali to the lords of the directions, one should then perform the fire oblation (homa).
At the conclusion of the oblation, having recognized the signs, one should extract the splinter;
having correctly understood the celestial and atmospheric signs according to the prescribed ritual.
One should recognize it as a wicked thorn when the Hora has entered a malefic sign;
the Sun, as the Banner (Dhvaja), is situated upon the head of embodied beings.
From contact, the auspicious thorn [is found] among the master builder, the teacher, and the craftsmen;
the two mouths are considered to be smoke, while the thorn belonging to the Earth element should be declared as residing in the bones.
The planet Venus (Bhārgava) is to be known as a lion, situated on the chest with both arms;
Mercury (Budha) is a dog, residing in the belly; and Jupiter (Liṅgajīva), whose nature is Taurus, is meritorious.
Khara and Śani are to be known as situated in the two knees;
Gaja, whose presiding deity is Candra, is situated in the two shanks.
Rāhu is assigned to the vulture; he stands upon three feet.
One should declare that there is a splinter in whichever limb he touches.
One should indicate a bone-thorn in the presence of a crow, a donkey, or smoke;
a thorn that is auspicious in a banner or an elephant, middling in a lion, and auspicious in a bull.
The lowest is Mercury. 222a) [The text is not clear.]
The glorious one holds a vajra-banner and likewise holds a shield and a noose;
he has two eyes and one face, and his radiance is like molten gold.
Assuming the pratyālīḍha posture, adorned with various ornaments,
Vivasvat, whose body is the sacrificial site (vāstu), stands upon the right foot.
He has one face and three eyes, possesses a luster like crushed collyrium,
has two arms, is mounted upon a buffalo, and holds a staff in his outstretched hand.
In the western site is the deity Deha, with Mitra as the leader;
he resembles snow, the kunda flower, and the moon, and possesses three eyes and four arms.
Holding a noose and a goad, fierce, with a spear in hand and possessing great strength,
he stands in the ālīḍha posture, surrounded by ten million servants.
The deity named Pṛthivīdhara resides in the northern direction of the site;
he has four arms, one face, three eyes, and is adorned with a crown.
White as the moon, possessing great vital strength, he holds a Vaiṣṇava seat and a lotus;
his hands bear an arrow and a deer, and he is likewise adorned with a mace.
O Bhīma, that army was always endowed with various ornaments;
it consisted of those who were slightly hunchbacked, dwarfs, three-faced, and likewise six-armed.
223a) With eyes like lotuses at their corners, bearing a discus, spear,
and mace, equipped with arrows and a quiver, he is joined by ten million Pramathas.
Likewise, Āpavatsa should be known as situated in the direction opposite to that of Tadiga;
however, he is white like the moon and stands within the circle of the mandala.

Likewise, according to the *Dṛṣṭāntasāra*, it is endowed with the power of evoking aesthetic sentiment (*sarasabhāva*), and it possesses the qualities of being faultless (*apavada*) and like a calf (*apavatsa*), as well as the imaginative arrangement of the "weapon of the mouth" (*vaktrāyudha*).
Savitṛ is to be known as being on the foot, and Sāvitrī likewise;
similarly, Indra and Indrajaya are situated in the direction of the Rākṣasas (the southwest).
In the northwest are Rudradāsa and Rudrapādika;
likewise, Śarva and Pādika are the lords of the directions; and Khakṛśānu and Agnikoṣṭaka [are located there].
Mṛga and Patīna are located in the southwest; Rogavāyu and Padārddha are situated in the west.
I shall now describe Parjanya and the others, each occupying one square, in their proper order.
Marjani, Yajñiyā, Māhendrī, Sūryā, Satyā, and Tṛṣā—these are situated in the east; now those in the south are being described.
Pūṣan, Vitatha, Saṃjña, as well as Gṛhakṣata,
Yama, Gandharva, and Bhṛṅga are stationed in the southern direction.
Dauvārika, Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, Pracetas,
and the Asura named Śoṣa are stationed in the western direction.
Then there are Nāgamukhya, Bhalvāḍha, Somā, and likewise Ṛgādiṣṭi;
these are to be known as the Padikās, and their meditation is now described.
Savitṛ has the luster of a red color and holds a sword and a noose in his hands;
Sāvitrī, likewise named, is similarly endowed with a bundle of kuśa grass.
Indu has the luster of the color of gold, possesses three eyes, and is equipped with a thunderbolt;
he holds a blue lotus in his hand and is accompanied by ten million warriors.
In the same manner, Indrajaya should be depicted with a sword and a noose held in his hands;
O Śikhidhvaja, I shall now describe their placement in the outer enclosure.
