Rudra is like black collyrium, bearing a trident and a sword, and possessing three eyes;
likewise, Rudrajaya should always be depicted holding an arrow and a staff in his hands.
And those situated in the middle enclosure have been described by you as equal;
now, O Śikhidhvaja, I shall describe those situated in the outer enclosure.
One should meditate upon the Lord, three-eyed, bearing a trident, a sword, a shield, and a lotus;
he has one face and three eyes, and his complexion is white as a spear and a sword.
Nānācārī, Kṛtābhyāsa, Parjanya, Meghavāhana, Jaya— who is radiant like a lotus— and Dhanurvāṇāsicarmadhṛk.
Indra has a thousand eyes and is adorned with the thunderbolt and the goad; Sūrya has the luster of the color of vermilion and holds rays and a lotus in his hands.
One should know that Truth (Satya) has four faces, possesses a luster equal to a ruby, stands upon a lotus banner, and holds a spear and a goat in his hands.
The fifth [face] is that of a bull, beautiful and endowed with youth;
it is the god holding a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), equipped with a staff, rosary beads, and bracelets.
Not abiding even for a moment like a lotus,
fashioned by the rays of the sun, resembling the flower of the pomegranate tree, she possessed a form of extreme wonder.
The deity should be fashioned with twenty-one faces and fifty hands;
his faces should be directed toward the cardinal directions, one above the other.
One should prescribe a decrease by one digit for each successive upper face;
the eastern face is considered that of Puruṣa, while the southern is regarded as Bhairava.
Uttara and Vāmadeva are in the north, while Sadyojāta is in the west;
these are declared to be the directional forms and the faces of Bhṛśa.
The Atharvaveda is in the east, the Sāmaveda in the south,
the Yajurveda in the north, and the Ṛgveda is considered the face in the west.
The previously mentioned measurements for the faces are indeed variable;
Vaikuṇṭha is the eastern face, while Narasiṃha is the southern.
The northern face is indeed Vārāha, and Kāpī is situated in the west;
thus, by the reduction of faces, all eight finger-breadths are indeed diminished in pairs.
Indra, Yama, Kuvera, and Varuṇa as the western face—
here too, a reduction by one digit (kalā) must be made for the son of Kṛttikā.
The eastern face is like the sun, the southern face is like fire;
the northern face is like the moon, and the western face is like the earth.
The measurements indeed decrease by one sixteenth part (kalā) at each stage, starting from four finger-breadths;
the "face of space" (vyomavaktra), measuring one sixteenth part, stands above all of them.
O Six-faced One, in this manner, the reduction of the red [color] should be performed for the others:
the sword, spear, arrow, javelin, bow, discus, mace, and shield.
A lotus-leaf eye, a rosary, a citron fruit, and a water-pot; a plow, a spear, a mace, a noose, a staff, and likewise an axe.
A lute, a vallakī, a flute, a tree, the moon, the sun, a sword, a book, the śruk and śruva ladles, a vessel, a ḍamaru drum, and a banner.
The Kaṅkāla weapon, the great weapon, the Brahmāstra, and likewise the Picchikā;
the Khādaka weapon, the Aghorā, together with the conch and the drum.
One should likewise fashion other such ornaments for Bhṛṅgin;
furthermore, the Supreme Lord should be depicted as dancing.
Hara was endowed with dancing hand-gestures, possessed of aesthetic sentiments and emotional expressions,
perfected in his movements and gaits, and occupied the mandala through his various postures.
Endowed with various bodily movements and various modes of performance,
it is manifested through the distinctions of *lāsya* and *tāṇḍava*, accompanied by various musical instruments.
The world, established in cotton cloth and other materials, resounds with the emergence of various sounds;
furthermore, it is composed of words such as "Indra" and "cloth."
It is marked with signs and covered by various arrangements,
resounding with the notes Ṣaḍja, Madhyama, Gāndhāra, and Ṛṣabha.
Through the meditations on one's own limbs, according to the sequence of dissolution and breaking [of bonds],
this universal form, called Bhṛśa, has been revealed to you.
One should visualize in the intermediate space a form resembling crushed collyrium,
holding a trident, a sword, and an excellent mallet, and fond of the excellent skin of a venomous serpent.
Agni should have a spear in his hand and be seated upon a parrot;
Pūṣan, white as a cow, should be seated upon the moon with a bow and arrow placed in his hands.
Vivasvān should always be depicted as smoke-colored, possessing a splendor equal to that of Kṛtānta (Yama), mounted upon a corpse, bearing a staff, and clothed only by the directions.
Vikarāla is of massive body; likewise is Gṛhakṣata.
But what should be done for Sahasraṅkin? [One should visualize] Yama as having the luster of crushed collyrium.
Clad in white garments, with staff and noose held in his hands,
accompanied by ten million diseases, and surrounded by terrifying and fierce hells.
The Gandharva, possessing the luster of a conch shell, is equipped with a sharp-edged spear and a goad;
accompanied by ten million Gandharvas, he resembles a black bee and a white lotus.
On the fourth day, he has one face and holds an arrow, a thread, and a bow;
he is dark-complexioned like a deer or a blade of dūrvā grass, with a shield and sword fashioned in his hands.
He should be made with a hundred eyes, adorned with the expanse of his staff,
known as Pitṛ, and surrounded by deities numbering in the tens of millions.
The gatekeeper has a staff in his hand, is formidable with a flat face,
holds a noose, and may be dark-complexioned like a lotus leaf or a black antelope.
Hemābha is golden-hued, while Sugrīva has a beautiful form and holds a brick-staff; Puṣpadaṇḍa is rich with splendor and is endowed with a hand bearing a *bhuśuṇḍi* weapon.
Pracetā should be depicted with a complexion like molten gold, holding a noose and a goad in his hands,
seated upon a serpent, and surrounded by ten million serpents.
The Asura should have a sword in hand, be dark-complexioned, and adorned with a shield;
the remaining [deities] should be made extremely emaciated— this is the rule for the Rājāvarta [mandala].
Likewise, Ulkāhasta and Daṇḍin, accompanied by ten million diseases,
as well as Roga with a thunderbolt-like face, should be fashioned holding sixty parasols in their hands.
Filled with various diseases and enveloped by manifold ailments,
the wind blew with a dark hue, adorned with a mass of smoke.
The hawk should be made resembling a lotus, equipped with various weapons,
joined by ten million serpents, and its face indeed like that of a lion.
The glorious one, bearing a bow and a trident, intent on threatening with his index finger,
resembling the color of a partridge, [carries] a staff and a rosary.
Bhalvāṭa is like snow and is endowed with a spear and a bell.
O Six-faced One, know him who has twelve arms, whose vehicle is the peacock, who consists of the nectar of the moon, and who is endowed with a water-pot.
The wise one, appearing like a tittiri bird, wears a staff and a rosary; he holds a preeminent bunch of *darbha* grass and carries a water-pot placed in his hand.
Know that Lambakrūra is marked with a garland and a lotus;
and Diti is always of a reddish-white luster, bearing a conch and a discus.
In the center is Brahmā with four feet; his meditation is revealed [therein]:
Samarīci, Vivaśvān, Mitraghna, and Pṛthivīdhara.
Six steps are fully enumerated, and their meditation has been declared:
Āpa, and Āpavatsa, Padika, and Padika-sthita.
Sāvitra, Savitṛ, likewise Indri and Indrajaya,
Rudra and Rudradaśa— these are proclaimed as the Padikas.
The deities situated within the eight corners should be known as occupying squares;
the remaining ones should be known as occupying single squares—this is the summary of the house-vāstu.
Skandha, Yāma, Jambhaka, and Pilipiccha are in the east;
Carantī, Vidārī, Pūtanā, and the evil Rākṣasī [are in the other directions].
Starting from the northeast corner and situated outside the Rakshasi,
Skanda and the others have distorted faces and are white, red, yellow, and black in color.
The vajra, sword, staff, trident, noose, and so forth, as well as the mace and skull;
Skanda and the others have been correctly described—now listen to [the description of] Rakta and the others.
A sword, a dagger, a knife, a razor, a shaven-headed bell, a scimitar, and a pair of shears—
these should be fashioned in sequence, and furthermore, they should be made deformed and cruel.
O sinless one, I have thus described to you the deities residing within the body of the site (vāstu);
if one acts without meditation, O moon-like one, it shall result in the ruin of the kingdom.
In the case of a deficiency in strength there is famine; if the auspicious fire-oblation is deficient, there is ruin.
Therefore, one should diligently perform [the rites] accompanied by meditation, substances, and ritual action.
Thus, the procedure for all yogas has been fully proclaimed.
The eighty-one-square site-plan for houses,
known as "The Delighter of the Gods," is formed by an arrangement of eight times eight squares.
Know that the *śatapada* (one hundred squares) is eternal, named "the Steadfast," and bestows excellent accomplishment;
[it applies] to monasteries, forts, cities, towers, towns, villages, and market towns.
One should likewise arrange beds, seats, celestial palaces, as well as leaf-huts,
places of accomplishment, and temples for sacrifice.
In ponds, wells, tanks, and the like, in forests and groves,
and everywhere else— whether specifically mentioned or not— one should thereafter perform the hundred-step rite.
The leaf known as Vetāla is considered to consist of twenty-five squares on the ground;
one should arrange it in five ways within the station of the immortals.
Likewise, when observing the conduct [of the preceptor], when honoring him, when sitting on the same seat,
as well as during the installation of the Brahma-stone and the entry into the doorway.
O Six-faced One, having worshipped the Vāstu deity who is established in the form of the Sūtra,
one should lead it forward upon the surface of the earth, firmly established in its place.
One should mark it with that measurement; then, by means of those three names,
the triangular field arises with its sevenfold measurement.
This [fire-pit] should be constructed as a domestic pit or a pavilion in the temple;
that site of the deity must be made complete with mantras and a girdle.
Having divided the field into six parts, one should cast half a part forward; by that measure, one should mark [the boundary] from the midpoint of the field toward the north.
By extending six lines from the six [original] lines, there shall be a field consisting of eight [squares] and six lines;
from the eastern half, excluding one-twelfth [of the side], they are raised up at the fire-quarters.
That which is known as the half-moon is produced by rotating it upwards;
the yoni should be made as before, arising according to the measurement of the field.
One should fashion a square by setting aside one-eighth of half a corner;
from the midpoint of the eastern side, an octagon arises through the placement [of lines] in the cardinal directions.
In this manner, O child, one should likewise fashion a sixteen-sided and even a thirty-two-sided figure in sequence, so that it becomes circular.
Just as a field is produced according to the measurement of its four sides, so too here the [mandalas] beginning with the triangle should be calculated; otherwise, it is not beneficial.
One should fashion the body of the Vāstu deity according to the dimensions of each individual house.
228b) Not clear 229a)
The worship should be performed according to the procedure declared in the Siddhānta by those learned in the Siddhānta;
the worship must be carried out in due order with one's own materials and according to the conduct of Rāma.
That which is stated in the Siddhānta is not found in the Vāma, nor is the Vāma practice in the Dakṣiṇa;
whatever rule is proclaimed in a particular system, it yields fruit only therein.
But even if she has attained perfection, if she forcibly devours raw flesh, she shall go to hell;
therefore, one should conduct oneself with every effort according to the method taught by Svāyambhuva.
Thus ends the chapter on the Vāstu-sacrifice in the Kālottara Mahātantra.
The Lord said:
Now I shall fully describe the sequential installation of the pitchers;
one should always perform the Vāstuyāga on level ground as it has been eternally taught.
Once the Vāstu deity has been worshipped and gratified, the placement of the water-pots (kumbha) should then take place;
these pots should be made of gold, silver, or clay, or, in their absence, of copper.
For a hand-sized [vessel], eight finger-breadths are recommended, with a weight of three or five *palas*;
for each subsequent hand-size, there is an increase of one finger-breadth and likewise five *palas* in weight.
The world-protectors (Lokapālas) should be fashioned with variegated designs and their respective emblems;
the stone slabs should be one cubit in length, and half of that in width and height.
One should likewise fashion the parts called the base (ādhāra) and the head (mūrdhan) upon the pitchers;
however, in the middle region between the two stones, it is beneficial to have a cavity half the size of the pitcher.
The artisan should fashion auspicious insignia, such as a vajra and so forth, there;
having made the city square in accordance with the dimensions of the temple.
One should purify the collection of stone jars with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
having cleansed them with the eight types of earth, decoctions, and scented water.
There, one should worship the eight Vidyeśvaras in their proper sequence;
having performed the fire oblation according to the rules, one should commence the installation of the stone.

One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the stones starting from the southeast and ending with the northeast; one should place the central stone, which has the form of Ādhāraśakti, upon the Brahma-stone.
One should conceive of the *ātmatattva* as extending up to the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the *vidyātattva* as ending with the mind (*manas*),
and the *śivatattva* as reaching up to the intellect (*buddhi*) and the ego (*ahaṃkāra*).
Just as it is for the central jar, so it is for those in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with that mantra a hundred thousand times, or half of that.
Having fashioned this [image] with nine [parts] by means of the Guru, one should indeed cause it to be suppressed;
thereafter, a stone slab should be placed upon the pitcher, and one should likewise worship it.
Having dissolved [the deity] according to the rule and worshipped it, one should afterwards cast the *bhūtabali* offering;
then, having sipped water and touched the limbs, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as before.
Then one should worship the preceptors with garments of gold, drink, and other offerings; subsequently,
a fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed for the sake of purifying any deficiencies or excesses, beginning with Śiva.
Having done this according to the rule, one should then construct the temple;
the elder of the Vedas [the first] consists of four [units], while the last [the sixth] consists of six and three [units].
Or, starting from five and increasing by five, the last [term] is the fifth object;
or, starting from a row and increasing by five, the limit is the hand, reaching as far as the *vipaṅkti*.
One should never construct a temple for Śambhu less than four cubits in height;
anything less than twenty-five cubits is considered a mere dwelling for worldly beings.

O Six-faced One, there is indeed no fixed rule for fish, stone, wood, and metal when they are clearly defined; however, having taken the temple door as the standard, these [proportions] must be applied.
O son of a carpenter, one should not construct a temple that is shared by both manifest and unmanifest beings, nor by those who are fearful and those whose nature is earthy.
And for those made of gold and jewels, no such restriction exists here;
this is indeed the case for arrows and especially for self-manifested (*svayambhū*) liṅgas.
Listen to the characteristics of the pedestals and sanctums according to the dimensions of the palaces;
their specific features regarding the doors will be described by me in brief.
When the site is divided into eight parts, the pedestal (pīṭha) shall consist of four parts;
the inner sanctum (garbha) shall be made with twelve parts, and the wall (bhitti) with two parts.
The width of the door should be equal to that of the pedestal (pīṭha), and its height should be twice that;
the height of the pillar-shaft (jaṅghā) is declared to be according to the measurement of the width of the shaft.
One should fashion the peak (śikhara) as twice that [height] and beautiful with its moving parts;
likewise, when the field is divided into nine parts, the pedestal (pīṭha) shall consist of one part.
The inner sanctum (garbha) should be made with one square unit (pada), while the inner wall (garbhabhitti) should likewise be one square unit;
the hollow space (śuṣira) shall measure one part, and the outer wall (bāhyabhitti) shall consist of the same measurement.
The four doors of the *dindu* should be equal in width to the *pīṭha*, or they may be double that size; O Moon, the outer wall should be one and a half parts.
The height should be twice the width, or indeed one and a half times the width; the measurement of the plinth and the spire should be executed as previously described.
For those whose growth follows the sequence of the pentads and so forth, there should be two elephants for each hand;
the pedestal (pīṭha) should have the same length as the linga, and likewise the three enclosures (āvaraṇas).
One should fashion the external portion as a share equal to the liṅga;
the width and height of the gateway (dvāra) should then be twice that [liṅga].
The height of the shank (jaṅghā) should be made equal to its own width;
the nose-projection (nāsāya) and the inner recess (nāmyagarbha) should be according to the measurement of the interior chamber (garbha), and not otherwise.
The nose-ornament (*nāsāmañjarī*) is auspicious when it reaches halfway up the pinnacle (*śikhara*);
however, the nose that has issued from the womb (*garbhādhāna-sṛtā-nāsā*) is not auspicious without the pavilion of the womb-path (*garbhavartma-maṇḍapa*).
"Having emerged from the portion of the essence of the Vedas within the pavilion—
this, O son of Kṛtikā, is declared to be the general characteristic."
231a) I shall now declare the specific characteristics of the palaces:
the Meru [type] is considered to be fifty cubits, minus five.
O beloved, the work that brings about the destruction of calamities is the Kailāsa-Śaṅkara;
it is beneficial when thirty-five cubits in size, auspicious on all four sides.
The thirty-fold [measure] consists of two horns; indeed, it is exactly like that.
The Śrīvatsa, Bhadra, and Praśrata are considered to be twenty-five cubits in length.
One should fashion it like an elephant or Mount Kailāsa, but one should not conceive of it as being upward-facing;
[it may also be shaped like] a swan, a Garuḍa, a lotus, an octagon, a hexagon, or a sixteen-sided figure.
One desiring prosperity should construct [the temple] at most in two rows;
the king's palace should be constructed measuring fifteen cubits.

Water is not recommended as it causes obstruction; likewise, [the shapes] having eight, six, or five corners, as well as the *valabhī* (pavilion) shape with nine cubits, and so on up to the *paṅkti* (row) shape, are not advised.
Temples should be constructed according to the measurement of the *liṅga* and their proper proportions;
they must never be made smaller than four cubits.
However, for rites such as killing (māraṇa) and expulsion (uccāṭana), [the distance] should be less than four cubits;
rather, it is declared that a "haunted house" (bhūtagṛha) should be used, and the rite performed within the range of spirits.
The modification consists of one-twelfth part of the solar dimension; it is applied to the best, mediocre, and lowest [structures].
Having given the width on both sides, the height is equal to the width.
One should construct the *talacchanda* (the ground plan) right there and proceed according to the prescribed rules;
following the sequence of the *talacchanda*, one should fashion the upper structure (*ūrdhvakṣatra*).
One should lead the upper chanda as far as the limit of the altar;
having excluded one-fourth of the measure of the crest (śikhā), one should proceed with the drawing.
One should arrange the neck, the pitcher-base (*kumbha*), and so forth there in the fourth part.
Three parts [are for] the flower-cluster (*mañjarī*). Having divided the shank (*jaṅghā*) into seven parts, one should determine the divisions.
The *masūraka* should be one part, while the shank (*jaṅghā*) should consist of five parts.
One should fashion the *kapota* (dove-shaped molding) as merely one-third of the sacrifice;
one should arrange the *masūraka* and the neck (*grīvā*) there, and that [neck] should enter into the middle portion.
From that, one should turn back a portion measuring three units from the previous turn;
this is declared to be the *masūraka*, which is defined as the characteristic of the shank.
Nāgarī, as well as Lāḍhī, Rāḍhī, and Drāviḍī;
however, the pure Nāgarī is devoid of the embellishments of the legs.

The *lāḍhī* and *vairūḍhī* should be joined with pairs of male and female [notes], while the *patra* should be crowded; the *mañjarī* should be made abundant, and the *jaṅghā* and *vajra* should always consist of thirty [beats].
The Nāgarī script is used in the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa), while the Lāḍhī is proclaimed for the Lāḍha region;
the Drāviḍī is in the southern part, and the Vairāḍhī is found throughout all countries.
Thus, I have described the general classification of the shanks.
Understand briefly the form of the *kapotapālī* (dovecot):
one should divide the incoming portion of the *kapotapālī* into ten strips (*daśapaṭṭa*).
The leaf, the lotuses, the lotus-pond, the empty space, the leaves, the lotus-pond, the swan, the radiance, likewise the female swan, and the lotus-pond joined with its arrangement.
Thus, O hero, the stages ending with the pigeon have been briefly described to you;
the decrease and increase of these stages are said to be common to all.
One should divide the field of the ground according to its unevenness; then, having passed over the middle ground, one should count the ground above.
One should collect [the earth] in such a way that the same number is produced;
having taken [earth] from another site, one should apply it beneath the ground.
The decrease and increase of all the stages have been revealed;
one should conceive of the stage as being endowed with eight characteristics.
Having divided the height of the base into three parts, one should construct the plinth;
in one part, the shank should be fashioned, along with the *samasūra* and the *kapotikā*.
The pinnacle, together with its crest and amalasaraka, should consist of two parts;
one should fashion the projections of the storeys according to the pinnacles.
Mallakakosala, Pañcaśṛṅkhalaka,
Ṣaṭviṃdu, Auṣadhalekhya, Puṣkara, and Candrasālaka.
One should draw the ear with a half-lotus design and a crest;
having understood them as either pure or mixed, one should apply them accordingly after repeated consideration.
The characteristics of the ground have been explained; now listen again to those of the boundary-marks (āghāṭas).
One should delineate the boundary-marks in the form of roots and blossoms.
This [which follows] is generally beneficial for all types of palaces;
I shall now describe their specific characteristics based on the distinctions of their names.
The eye, divided into eight parts, surrounds the Meru field;
it should be threefold in width, consisting of eight, twelve, and sixteen [parts] respectively.
With the remainder, one should then rotate the middle of the shanks;
from the corner, displaced by nine parts, one forms the corner-binding marked with the bull-emblem.
One should effect the exit through the aperture (randhra), the bull-bannered one (vṛṣāṅka), and the fire (dahana);
therein, at the junction of the stars (tārāji), there is the fire, and from that, the entry and the exit.
The entry into the center of Meru occurs through the successive swallowing of the sun and other [planets];
thus, from the *talacchanda* (ground-pattern) up to the *mūrdhacchanda* (head-pattern), it should be so.
Indeed, up to the altar (vedikā), the cause (hetu) and then the design (chaṇda) are completed;
it has four gates, four names, and is of wonderful structure and lineage.
The five-fold flood is known as Meru, which likewise has sixteen stages;
it is characterized by the nails, the modifications, the vowels, and the Vasus.
Thus, sixty-four petals are proclaimed for the five obstacles;
by the measurement of the five grounds, they are likewise four, three, and two.
O Six-faced One, one should diligently arrange two by two in each direction;
one should designate Meru as the beginning of the one hundred and four meters.
For unmanifest [liṅgas] and likewise for those whose nature is both manifest and unmanifest,
a square [pedestal] measuring one and a half parts grants success when used with manifest liṅgas.
O son of Kṛttikā, I shall explain Mandara in brief:
having first divided the area of the ocean into equal portions, one should then establish the field.
Its corner should consist of the Guṇakoṇa type, and the binding of the corner should be accompanied by a fillet;
the entrance and the exit should likewise be made with six and four [units].
With eight *rasas* (sixteen) in the middle, the *nirgama* (projection) is beneficial for the *mandara*;
as the *talacchanda* has been described, so too should the *mūrdhacchanda* be.
A fourfold enclosure (ghāṭaka) should be constructed, provided with a ground-level platform (yugeṃdra-bhūmikā),
consisting of two pairs of peaks (kṣukūṭa) each measuring one unit (ādyāṅga-parimāṇa).
In this manner, eighty-eight petals are formed from the transformation of the root and the nose;
thus, one hundred petals arise, minus the row of the central filaments.
I shall describe in brief and in due order the temple of Kailāsa, which has four names, four gates, and bestows all accomplishments.
One should divide the length by six and the width by three;
the central chariot (madhyarathaka) should be fashioned with eight [parts] protruding from it.
The Tricaturtha-ṣṛhi is joined with the Vedas, while the Padika is beneficial; the Kailāsa is square, joined with separate chariot-like structures.

At the edge of the Vedas (the boundary), one should prepare a foundation (bhūmikā) endowed with twelve [parts]; and one should duly arrange foundations numbering fifty-four (five elements, four Vedas, two eyes, and one moon).
The roof-coverings are made of *nakha*, *ṛk*, *kāra*, *vasu*, and *veda*;
according to the previously stated sequence, there are two peaks (*kūṭa*) in each of the directions.
By that, thirty-two peaks arise; of this there is no doubt.
From the point of impact, the peak is the form of the primary abode.
One should arrange the meters here according to the measure of three padas;
the temple of Śaṅkara should be made on Kailāsa, but not that of anyone else.
I shall explain the layout of the celestial palace (vimāna), O destroyer of Krauñca;
when the field has been divided into twenty-one parts, the middle exit of the ground [is determined].
The entrance should be constructed with the Vedas [four parts]; one should fashion the pillar with one part (Bhaga).
Then, leaving two parts from the pillar, the corner is formed.
The vimāna is thus described as having a single door and being dear to Śiva;
likewise, a great vimāna, which is the abode of Śiva, should be constructed in this very manner.
One should arrange the middle chariot-structure with five parts and the entrance with four;
the placement of the pillars is by one part, while the corner region is by three.
O Śivā, a great celestial mansion (mahāvimāna) should be constructed, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it should be adorned with three stories, a pinnacle (tirāghājya), and embellished with the levels of the Śakti.
The foundation-stones should be laid with four, three, and two [units] respectively;
one should draw the coverings in sequence with six, twelve, and twelve [units].
As before, twenty-six [syllables] are determined as the peak-essences (kūṭasāra);
however, the central peak among them is now stated according to its numerical value.
Thus, O Śikhidhvaja, the meters of the Śrīvatsas, the Bhadras, and likewise others, have been described as having twenty-one morae.
The measurement of the *cchaṃdas* belonging to the *āghāṭa* stage has been declared;
I shall now describe their division, beginning with the *talacchaṃda* and proceeding upwards in combination.
In the city-site, which is square and well-proportioned with doors and windows,
one should omit the three regions of the corners and avoid constructing them with corner-junctions.
One should not conceive of its exit at two, three, or six steps;
thus is the Bhadra [mandala] fully described, which is beneficial for the retention of all [mantras].
It should be constructed with four doors, provided with a common foundation, and bestowing all accomplishments;
likewise, the characteristics of the enclosures and the ground-levels should be established.
O auspicious lady, it is known as Vimāna-vat, which always bestows auspicious success;
indeed, it is Sarvatobhadra, surrounded on all sides by many peaks.
In the eastern field divided into eight parts, the corner [of the mandala] is formed by two parts;
that which is known as Bhadra is called Nali when it is bent.
The foundation of the *āghāṭa* stage should be conceived as being like a celestial palace (*vimāna*);
however, one should construct the palace there using *āghāṭas* and celestial palaces.
Furthermore, the division of the Śrīvatsa of Vardhamāna is described:
it is considered to be three [units] in the middle of the chariot, within a field of five rows divided by arrows.
And with two [units] plus a half, there is likewise the Śrīvatsa and the Bhūmivardhana;
I shall now describe the Saṃpūrṇaśāla temple, divided by the sun [twelve].
Likewise, there is no [projection] at the two corners; with three [parts], there is no exit for the middle; and with one and a half parts each, there is the *kapola* (cheek) between those two.
A complete *sāla* (enclosure) has been described for the purpose of crushing enemies;
however, in a sacred field (*purākṣetra*) dedicated to a devotee of Rudra, one should construct a *khaṇḍaśāla* (partial enclosure).
The corner in the middle should be like a Śrīvatsa, and likewise the chariot-arches;
the cheek is made with one and a half parts, and the water-channel from half a square.
He who is known as Khaṇḍaśāla is the supreme shatterer of enemies;
he should cause that which exists in the field of Vikārabhakta to revolve.
One should construct a middle chariot with four [parts] and its exit;
from that, one should fashion the water-interval with a half-and-a-quarter part.
Likewise, with half [of that measure] and similarly with three parts of the corner-section,
one should fashion the cheeks there for those [faces] devoid of the inner water-channel.
The Nandivardhana [mandala] should be made with four corners and four protrusions;
because it increases joy through its fullness, it bestows all desires.

Furthermore, the characteristic of the *chanda* (desires) belonging to the level of the boundary (*āghāṭabhūmikā*) should be fashioned like a celestial palace (*vimāna*), either for the sake of beauty or otherwise.
Thus, these four types of lotuses are endowed with many petals;
the *gavākṣa* tree should indeed be circular, while the *garuḍa* is known to have six corners.
The *kumbha* (pitcher) and *kumbhaka* (pitcher-like) forms are praised; they are joined with the face of a half-elephant.
Having made the four-sided [area] double, one should know that it is divided into rows accordingly.
Its width, however, is four [units], and its middle chest is circular;
its interior (garbha) consists of four parts, and likewise its wings and interior again.
The wall should be one *padika*; its name is Haṃsa, and it has six faces.
Having established Brahmā in the center, Śiva and Keśava are placed on the two wings.
The Supreme Lord, possessing form, should be fashioned facing eastward, adorned with a *śrīvatsa* mark and the *bhadra* [curl], and having a *haṃsa* with distinct blossoms.
One should avoid [the two] deities facing each other, as well as behind one another;
likewise, I shall describe [the positions] with thirty bows in front and at the chest.
It is taught that one should diligently place the Prāṇī in front;
having established it in a location free from defects and devoid of piercing, what [benefit] will arise?
Having abandoned the boundary that is twice as large for both sides and measuring up to the height [of the structure],
those wise ones who build palaces and such [elsewhere] clearly cause suffering.
Otherwise, for whom would suffering arise from the act of doing?
Great roads, crossroads, wheels, wells, and the like would come into existence;
likewise, cow-paths, triple junctions, or great boulders and such would be perceived [without cause].
Since death makes one its prey, therefore one should renounce all variety.
In a sacrificial ground, village, market town, or similar location, one should install [the deity] facing forward;
situated facing east, it bestows auspiciousness.
Therefore, facing forward is praised, not sideways or with the back turned;
the central deity of the region brings fear of an enemy army.
Therefore, one should not place it in the middle, nor should it be to the south;
rather, it should be in the north-western part of the site, and thus the western direction is recommended.
Sovereignty in the eastern quarter, distress in the south-eastern region;
pestilence in the southern quarter, and suffering in the south-western region.
Prosperity is found in the western direction; it resides in the northwest for eradication.
In the north there shall be the attainment of wealth, and in the northeast for the accomplishment of all goals.
One should worship Mahādeva and Viśākha, and indeed Viṣṇu, who is beneficial, in the east;
likewise, Brahmā and Kroñcasūdana, the consumer of oblations, in the southeast.
The Mothers, beginning with Bhairavī, are beneficial in the south; likewise, the Guhyakas, Kṣetrapālas, Kiṅkaras, and the Vikṛtas are beneficial in the Rākṣasī direction.
Hita is in the western direction for the entire village and city;
Kṣetrapāla is in the northwestern direction, and the Mothers are in the northern direction.
In the northeast, one should worship the deity Yogin, as well as Mṛtyujihva, Aṭaṅkin, and Vināyaka; and furthermore, Vāyu in the region of the wind.
Having established Gaṇeśa in the southwest and Durgā in the northwest,
one should diligently construct temples for the gods and houses for those possessing virtuous qualities.
In cities, villages, market towns, and so forth, it is not thus, nor otherwise;
[it is likewise] in palaces, trees, wells, and the like.
A house overtaken by shadow must be abandoned, for it certainly brings death;
it should be enclosed by a wall so that the shadow does not cause harm.
O Śikhidhvaja, this characteristic has been declared according to the sequence;
the *āyatavalabhī* should be made twice or three times [the size] of that.
Its width is five [units], and its length is measured by five rows;
its wall is one square (pādika), but it does not include a portion for a door.
Its width should be one pada, and its breadth two padas;
it should be made twice as high as the elevation of the *valabhī*.
O Goddess, one should perform the *saṃbharaṇa* rite and then proceed with the *sakhya* [rite];
now hear briefly the characteristics of the eight-sided and sixteen-sided [yantras].

By joining the field-axle (kṣetrākṣa) with the corners, one should lead it to the intermediate directions. Having thus marked the base (vailā), one should mark the shank (jaṅghā) with those known as lotuses.
Just as a lotus called Padma should be fashioned by the skill of an artisan,
I shall now fully describe the Śrīkaṇṭha temple, which exists in many forms.

Auspicious works should be undertaken in the cardinal directions as well as in the intermediate directions; these should be fashioned with one, two, or three facets, arranged according to their design.
In the interval between the cheeks, one should move it so as to have a support;
likewise, the supports should be made similar in shape to a chariot-crow (rathakāka).
One should compose [verses] possessing metrical feet, known by the name Śrīkaṇṭha;
thus has the definition of the Dodhaka meter been briefly stated.
Describe the formation of the *mañjarī* and the characteristics of the neck and the *ālaka*.
Having fashioned the pinnacle (*śikhara*) like a *veda*, it should be four-cornered and likewise like a *veda*.
The neck should be made with one part, and its shaft (sāraka) should be twice that height;
the top knob (cūlaka), measuring one part, should be fashioned in the shape of a liṅga.
The top-knot should resemble a water-pot, marked with a lotus and shaped like a citron;
it should be made with a cord four times [the length of] the hair-locks, while the wick itself is threefold.
The circumference is three times the body which is one and a half times [the diameter];
the circumference of that which is double [the diameter] is by a thread of one and a half times [the diameter].
Having relied upon the bodies of Śrī, the manifestation is exactly like this:
whether the trunk is divided tenfold, or again into five parts.
One should indicate the width of the *skandha* by decreasing it by two parts; then,
having multiplied [the base] by five, the width of the *vedī* is declared.
One should divide that into nine parts, either two parts for one part or one part for one part;
then, by such division, the height of the *jaṅghā* (the plinth) extends from the *kapota* (eaves) up to the *vedikā* (railing).
One should discard a portion by portion according to the width and height;
or else, the reduction is calculated by means of the rule of three (trairāśika).
Or one may arrange uneven seats by means of a division into parts;
one should determine this through the skillful intellect of the artisan by means of the relinquishment of various portions.
A trident-point must never be fashioned; a trident-point causes destruction.
O Six-faced One, it should be made with a parrot [beak] and an enclosure, even without a shaft.
The formation of the nose is known to resemble the petal of a blue lotus;
the neck should be made from half a vedī, and the *sāraka* should consist of five parts.
The height of the cūlaka from the neck should be made with two and a half parts;
its width should be made with one-third [of that], or according to the measurement of the liṅga.
Similarly, its two parts—the Viṣṇu and Brahma [sections]—should be equal.
The Viṣṇu [section] should be placed on the Dvāsāraka, and its height shall be one and a half parts.
Thus has the characteristic of space been described by the son of Kṛtikā;
it should be fashioned even without a [specific] mark, and it is to be installed just like a [conventional] liṅga.
In Valabhī, Keśarī is to be made, as well as the bull of Śaṅkara;
the elephant of Śrī is to be fashioned, and likewise the lotus of Sūrya.
With effort, using the upper part of the nose, one's own weapon should be made upon the shaft;
it should be made according to the measurement of the shaft, consisting of three parts.
One should assign the trident to Śaṅkara, especially among the deities;
the discus to Hari; and the world-protectors should likewise imagine their own respective weapons.
The mañjarī should extend from the width by a portion equal to the height of the netra-mountain;
however, a candraśālā should be constructed for the sake of stabilizing it.
And so that the palaces do not collapse due to earthquakes or great winds,
a flagstaff-support must be constructed according to the measurement of the altar-pole.
For the smallest [temples], one should construct a wall devoid of a pond;
the inner sanctum (garbha) should be made larger, and one should not reduce the size of the linga due to parsimony.
The pedestal should be equal in measurement to the door-pedestal according to the dimensions of the liṅga;
if the shadow of the liṅga falls upon the pedestal by even a single foot, then a defect occurs.
Likewise, when the shadow of the pedestal falls upon the linga, it brings death to men;
therefore, with every effort, one should ensure they are level.
In the first and the non-first [breaths], one should respectively decrease and increase the portion of Rudra;
therefore, one should effect the increase and decrease of the objects of sense in the worship of the gods.
Thus, by the reduction of the image, the width of the pedestal (piṇḍikā) remains equal in proportion; because of this equality of measurement, there shall be no overlapping of the shadow in front.
From the wall, a hollow space should be made extending one hundred [units] and twice as wide;
rising twice that height, there should be a temple for the deities in all directions.

O Six-faced One, the width of the door-panels is considered to be one-quarter of the total width of the doorway; their height above and below should be made with half of that [panel-width] as the interval.
One should determine the lords of the door by means of the branch-base and the height;
in the east is Mahākāla, and Nandin is the lord of the eastern branch.
Bhṛṅgī should be placed on the southern right door-post, and Darbha likewise on the northern one;
on the southern branch of the western door, one should lead Vṛṣan.
Ṣaṇmukha is in the north, while Svadhunī is always further to the north;
Yamunā is on the left branch, situated at the northern gate.
Men should be depicted there holding garlands of lotuses and carrying water-pots in their hands,
and women should be adorned with ornaments.
The Gandharvas have lutes in their hands, and likewise the Vidyādharas have garlands; there is also a pair consisting of a cow and an elephant, as well as a pair beginning with a horse.

A door with nine branches is for the superior [caste], one with seven branches for the middling, and one with five or three branches for the inferior; such a door should be constructed as it bestows prosperity.
One should fashion the door-jamb with svastika creepers; the width of the jamb should be made according to the span of the doorway, while its thickness should be half of that.
At the front of the door, there should be a crescent moon, and its width should be half of that; this is declared to be the *iridvāra*. Now hear [the description] of the *sāṃdhāra* or otherwise.
The width of the door is best when it is sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas), middling at fifteen, and lowest at seven; this range is indeed beneficial for the subject.
O Six-faced One, it should be made twice as high as its width;
the placement of the *śākhā* and *udumbara* should be performed according to their own measurements.
Gaṇeśa is at Duṃbarikā, and likewise the eight planets and Umā;
similarly, Nāṭyeśvara should be fashioned together with Vālmīki and Vyāsa.
In front of the door, a half-moon (ardhacandra) is beneficial, with a width equal to that of the door;
beyond that, the pillars known as kapicchas should be made, measuring one-sixth [of the door's width].
The neck and the heart should be made at the half-point of the branch; furthermore,
there is the enumeration of the pedestals (pīṭhas), the abodes (dhāmas), and the banners (dhvajas).
The purification of other doors is performed with effort by means of vowels;
the preparation of beds, seats, and vehicles is accomplished by those known as the *bhūtas*.
The purification of ponds, wells, and tanks is performed by means of fire;
it brings stability, burning away [impurities], great fortitude, and the destruction of demonic hoards.
Affliction, the attainment of all goals, disease, and likewise the hoisting of banners and so forth;
certain death from burning, and subjugation—these occur in sequence for the [planets] beginning with Mars.
The qualities of those born of the elements have been declared; now the qualities of those beginning with fire are being described.
Knowledge and its destruction are recorded as the qualities of those who are to be spoken of.
Women, wealth, prosperity, and likewise the state of being a husband;
poison, punishment, great power, the seven fruits, and one's own origin.
Having thus understood each respective division, one should act accordingly;
for the linga, the door, and the pedestal, there may even be an additional portion within the houses.
One should perform the gift of longevity, or one may arrange for its reduction;
one should practice purification in such a way that the purification of life may arise.
One should avoid a door that is either too large or too small;
at the beginning of the construction, one should carefully employ heartwood and timber produced from such [proper] sources.

Likewise, the two door-panels, which should be raised by themselves, must be made with great effort so that they produce the sounds "kūjan" and "vītkāra," and likewise have many sections within the house.
The pedestal for the banner should be constructed in accordance with the dimensions of the primary sanctuary;
one should fashion the flagstaff as a bull or as a trident.
One should design its circumambulatory path from one-fourth of the height of the spire;
alternatively, it may be half, one-third, or one-quarter of the main temple's dimensions.
O Six-faced One, thereafter, according to the divisions of the smallest and so forth, the temples and palaces must be constructed facing toward the main sanctuary.
Starting from five pillars up to a hundred,
the arrangement of the Gaṇa-shrine is conceived in the form of a principal temple.
Listen briefly to the classification of pavilions at the top of a temple:
pavilions are prescribed when placed at the four gates of a temple.
Only a single pavilion should be constructed with a single entrance;
however, it is beneficial for a four-faced house to have sanctums (garbhas) on both sides.
In this manner, one should diligently construct four-faced pavilions;
one may fashion them from the interior of the womb-chamber, up to the edge of the wall, or from the entire hollow space.
Having added together the lengths of both sides, one should determine the length of the pavilion;
the width beneficial for the pavilion is that length diminished by one-third.
The arrangement for the single-faced [temple] has been explained first;
now, the distinction in the nomenclature of the pavilions (maṇḍapa) starting from the pillar is being described.
Hara, Śiva, Ananta, Padma, Deva, Śikhī, Śaśin, Priya,
and Mahāpriya— these are declared to be the nine pavilions (maṇḍapas).
The younger sons are to be appointed from twelve years onwards;
furthermore, I shall describe the auspicious age for the middle sons as being above eighteen years.
Sunanda and Nandana, Variṣṭha and Varada,
Viśāla and Suśīla, as well as Śrutīśi and Haritadaka.
But for those of medium stature, there are forty-six teeth due to their increase;
they are Jaya, Jayabhadra, Buddhi, and Buddhivara.
Ānanda, Nandana, Puṣpa, Bhadra, and Puṣpaka,
as well as Rudra— these extend up to the sixty-fourth [tattva] by way of increase.
The pavilions (maṇḍapas) are of eight, six, and four pillars, with the Miśraka being the lowest;
the deity is at the front of the Śukanāsā, and there are two pillars and a maiden (kumārikā).
I shall once again proclaim the characteristics of houses for men:
for kings, the house should be one hundred and eight cubits in length.
There is a reduction of one-quarter from the width, and there are five central houses;
each [side] consists of eight [units], arranged beneficially starting from the east.
One should arrange houses in the corners by extending half a unit from each direction;
one may obtain either four-winged, five-winged, or two- or three-winged structures.
Thus, twenty-five pure houses have been described;
by subtracting seven from seventy-two, the five roots are proclaimed.
Likewise, other [buildings] should be constructed in the cardinal and intermediate directions for the protection of the treasury;
however, the houses should be located in the fifth middle [direction], at a distance of six, six, and six [units] from the edge.
In the cardinal directions, there are two [types] for each over seven days, or nine starting from the corners as before;
they are not shown here because of their great number due to the various divisions beginning with the single-hall (ekaśālā) design.
Regarding the previous [method of] royal houses, it is said that this specific distinction is now declared:
by reducing four [houses] at each step, one should rotate sixty-four houses in five turns.
O Six-faced One, one should arrange for the sacrificial priests and the twice-born the most excellent dwelling,
consisting of four halls all provided with porticos.
O twice-born one, twenty-one houses are reduced by four for the Kṣatriyas and the other two [castes], resulting in seventeen and fifteen houses respectively.
For the three starting with the Kṣatriya, there are two, three, and four houses.
By subtracting three, one, or none [of the degrees], the five root houses are obtained;
then, by subtracting one-eighth of that from the beginning, it shall be from the corner at half of that.
He should place the temple in the northeast, the assembly hall in the east,
the kitchen in the southeast, and the bedchamber in the southern direction.
Likewise, one should fill the interior there; otherwise, it is not beneficial. For the removal of impurities, however, one should perform the *teṣkāgāra* rite in the western *rākṣasī* direction.
In the northwest is the place for threshing, likewise filled with household utensils;
in the north is the treasury—this has been described by me in brief.
In the center of that [city], the king’s palace stands;
it may have four wings, or three wings, or two wings, but never just one wing.
In a stable Nandyāvarta [mandala],
the ninth [part] and the pathways (vīthikā) should be made both inside and outside, and likewise above.
The structure known as Hiraṇyanābha,
which is devoid of the eastern wing and the Mūtraśāla, is an excellent field that bestows prosperity upon men.
A house with a kitchen in the south always brings suffering from the hearth;
a house deficient in the west brings death to men through Yakṣas.
For those who are endowed with meditative concentration, the goal is accomplished and the hall of spiritual powers is perfected;
through the application of the preliminary practices such as water-offering, great sovereignty is established.
The direction known as Daṇḍa, situated between the east and south, is equal to a staff for men;
the direction known as Vāta, joined with the north and west, is fond of quarrels.
With the eastern and western [halls] and the northern and southern halls, what indeed is called the *kadā* that has been constructed?
One should cause the heap of signs arising from the house to be divided by eight;
when the asterism is extracted, it becomes the asterism, and from the asterism arises the rising of the sign and its degrees.
Starting from one hundred cubits, the temple of the twice-born (Brahmins) should be seven and a half stories high; for the others, it should be five stories high, following the respective order.
For those of the lowest class, the house shall be devoid of a foundation and free from measurement;
its extent in length or breadth shall be according to the [prescribed] number.
The height of the door shall be seventy-nine finger-breadths,
and its width shall be half of that.
One should determine the thickness of the walls of houses according to the width of the door,
using multiples of one, three, eleven, twenty-seven, fifteen, and eight [units].
For the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, the height is twice the width;
[the altars] are as long as the Vasus (eight) in their respective quarters, and equal in width.
To the left of the altar, starting from the ninth part of the length, one should provide steps for the path; the base of the altar should always be level with the ground.
By those very means of movement, one should indeed proceed further upward;
likewise, outside, inside, and in the middle of the stages (bhūmikās).
The porticos (alindas) should be fashioned from wood above the floor level;
they should be joined with rows of pillars whose tops point upward and likewise with northern doors.
Those lacking an *alinda* (porch), pillars, or a *pratihāra* (side-wing) are declared to be the lowest;
they are proclaimed among those who are censured like dogs.
I shall again explain, in due order, the characteristics of the doors:
[the first] causes fear from lords, the second [causes] instability for women, and the third produces the glory of victory and majesty.
Dharma, quarrel, and the sun are in the east; hear now that in the south are burning, pleasure, pain, death, decay, and virtuous conduct.
In the south there is wretchedness and lack of prosperity; likewise in the west,
there is the binding of vows without flowers, yet there is happiness from agriculture and the increase of crops.
The loss of wealth, emaciation, disease, and likewise exorcism are declared for the western direction; hereafter, those for the northern direction are stated.
And what is seen regarding protection?
It is the accumulation of wealth, as well as misery, wind, destruction, and decline; these are declared to arise from the northern direction.
In the east, there are those known as Jaya and Mahendra;
in the west, there is likewise a triad belonging to Pūṣan, Gandharva, and Dakṣa.
Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, and the third named Varuṇa,
along with Mukhya, Bhalvāṭa, and Soma— this triad in the north is auspicious.
One should designate Kṛttikā as belonging to Īśa, Pūrvaphalgunī to Parjanya, Viśākhā to Jaya, and Jyeṣṭhā to Mahendra.
Likewise, one should assign Punarvasu to the Sun; and for these [other planets],
one should assign Hasta, Abhijit, Śikhī (Jyeṣṭhā),
and Āndrā (Mṛgaśiras) as they are situated.
Anurādhā is established in Saṃsthā; Viśākhā is situated in Pūṣan;
Revatī is to be known as being in Vitattha; and Mūla is indeed in Gṛhakṣata.
Know that Bharaṇī belongs to Yama, while Gandharva is in Pūrvāṣāḍhā;
Aśvinī is in Bhṛṅgadeva, and one should assign Citrā to Mṛga.
Maghā should be known for Pitṛ, Auśanasa and Pūrvabhadraka for Jyeṣṭha;
Pūrvāṣāḍhā for Sugrīva, and Phālgunī for Puṣpadantaka.
Rohiṇī is recommended for Varuṇa; Śatabhiṣaj is considered for Vāsara;
Aśvinī for Śoṣa; Tiṣya for Roga; and Āṣāḍhā, whose deity is Vāyu, [is prescribed].
Know that Svāti, Nāga, and likewise Mukhya are always associated with Mūla;
Bhalvāḍa, Āśleṣā, and Abhijit are [associated with] the Rākṣasa group; and Śravaṇa and Dhaniṣṭhā are established as belonging to Vāyu.
O son of Kṛttikā, Uttara and Bhadrā have thus been described.
One should perform the Jvara [rite] in accordance with the moon and stars;
the sacrificial hall in the northeast should be beneficial, provided with four doors,
joined with scales and incomparable [materials], and free from intoxicated celestial musicians.
One should not prescribe a pillar-width that exceeds one-sixteenth of the total width; rather,
the height of the pillar should be increased by two parts,
and the pillar-base (stambha-śāpaka) should likewise be made, along with its support and its projection on both sides.
Thus has the characteristic of temples been correctly described.
Thus ends the chapter on the characteristics of temples in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
244a) Īśvara said:
The consecration pavilion (adhivāsanamaṇḍapa) should be at the top of the palace, neither too far away nor to the side,
nor behind, nor in a corner.
For an elephant, a four-faced pavilion with a width of two cubits should be constructed;
for others—whether manifest, unmanifest, or of a dual nature—the measurement increases by two cubits each.
Half of that measure, however, should be for the pavilion for the ritual site in the east and the northeast;
that same dimension applies to the arrangement for the purpose of the mandala.
One should have four pavilions constructed there together with the central hall;
at the base, there should be an altar measuring four cubits in extent and eight finger-breadths in height.
A canopy of that same size, adorned with a network of small bells, [was placed] there;
a *nāgropama* tree was to its east, and a *mudumvara* tree to its south.
One should arrange the Aśvaccha tree to the north, the Plakṣa tree at the western gateway,
and the Dhārika tree as the food for the gods of the pavilion.
For a one-cubit [temple], the door should be five cubits; for two- and three-cubit [temples], it should be six and seven [cubits] respectively.
For the medium-sized [temples], the arrangement of the doors is by an increase of one-third of a cubit.
For the elder [deities], a gateway (toraṇa) of one cubit increased by one cubit at a time is beneficial;
the ground-level gateway may range from one cubit up to three cubits in height.
The width should be measured by one-third, half,
or a quarter of the height; otherwise, it is not beneficial.
The shaft is considered to be eight finger-breadths long, up to a maximum of sixteen;
its width is likewise, and it should be made of *dumbara* wood at the branch-end.
One should fashion the root-lobes with an extension of five finger-breadths;
the svastika should be placed in the center when [the base] is oriented to the east, and when it is situated to the south.
An *utpala* lotus should be placed on the left, and a *padma* lotus on the west;
thereafter, the door-keepers beneath the branches should be fashioned as before.
Its banners are seven cubits long and one-seventh as wide;
they are the color of the world-protectors, while the ninth is snow-white in luster.
The subjects are known to have five cubits in height, with complexions such as white and red;
they are moreover endowed with bamboo-made poles measuring three or five cubits.
In the ritual placement (nyāsa) consisting of the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti), one should arrange nine sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa);
however, for a [mandala] measuring one cubit, one should arrange a pit of only one cubit.
Thereafter, for the remaining [dimensions], there should be an increase of one finger-breadth (aṅgula) in successive order.
One should cause the ninth pit to be made as the central pit of the altar.

The sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*) made of *palāśa*, *arka*, *atthaka*, and *pippala* wood are recommended; they should be twenty-seven *darbha* blades in width, measuring only the length of the hand, and half a cubit (*hastārddha*) in size.
One should diligently prepare one hundred and eight stalks each of Apāmārga, Khadira, Śamī, Dūrvā, and Daṇḍarā grasses.
The enclosing sticks (paridhis) are merely external, or circular, as are the Kṛttikās;
likewise are the seat, the fan, the large and small sacrificial ladles (śruk-śruva), and the fire-vessel.
Two argha vessels, a bell, water for washing the feet (pādya),
incense, ghee, sesame seeds, wood for the fire, rice grains, and a collection of flowers.

Incense, ointment, and the cleansing agent, as well as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the eight-limbed prostration, should be offered into each pit; likewise, many lamps should be provided.
For the purpose of bathing, one should take earth from a collection of water containing astringent decoctions produced from the Udumbara,
Vaṭa, Aśvattha, Āmra, and Jālbūlaka trees.
Rocanā, aloe-wood, and Himalayan sandalwood originate from sacred fords, anthills, and reeds, from the midst of sacred fields, from Gajāhvaya (Hastināpura), and from rivers and mountains.
There were many diverse and perfectly pure food offerings,
as well as delightful drinks consisting of sugar and milk.
A noble throne (bhadrapīṭha) should be constructed from solid wood;
it should be twice the width of the Brahma-portion and marked with lotuses.
He should not, however, use a four-legged couch adorned with a girdle-base,
nor likewise a bedstead or a mattress that is half a cubit in width.
He likewise [offered] a couch provided with a cloth head-rest and pillows,
a pavilion, a mirror, a battle-axe, an umbrella, a fan, and sandals.
A sword and a dagger, a shield and a javelin, a bow,
a camphor vessel, gold, and likewise two golden rods.
A wooden vessel, a broom, a tripod, a grinding stone,
as well as a mortar and pestle, and likewise ornaments.
Others [should provide] household utensils made of gold and silver;
and three offering vessels (arghapātra) made of gold, silver, and copper.
The vessel for water for the feet should likewise be made of gold, silver, or copper, being of the highest, middling, or lowest quality, and twelve finger-breadths in width.
Likewise, there should be a vessel for the golden unguent and one for the honey-mixture (madhuparka);
furthermore, there should be a golden Śiva-pitcher and a Śiva-weapon pitcher.
One should not prepare ten jars for those made of copper or brass;
rather, two should be placed at each door, covered with cloth and joined with flowers.
Likewise, eight *śānti*-vases should be placed upon the edge of the altar;
for the purpose of bathing, twenty-seven *paḷa* jars should be prepared.
For daily or occasional rites, eight hundred [beads] are recommended;
or else, for all medicinal herbs, turmeric, fragrant substances, and mustard seeds [are used].
Various types of bathing materials, such as parched grain, water from sacred fords (tīrtha), and so forth;
and for the sake of the mandala, a compass, chalk, and colored powders.
There, the Kūrmaśilā (Tortoise Stone) should be grasped; it is two kalās greater than Brahmā, square on all sides, and provided with nine wells.
The small pit should be made two finger-breadths wide and half that depth;
one should deposit the Brahma-portion, which is one-eighth of a quarter [of the area] and octagonal in shape.
O Six-faced One, in that regard, by whatever means the state of being established in the center of the Brahma-stone arises, by those same means the efforts must be diligently applied to the wells.
Then, as before, there is a diamond; an indranīla gem on the south;
a blue pearl and a topaz in the northwest.
One should place ruby and lapis lazuli in the east in sequence;
likewise, gold, copper, iron, tin, lead, and brass.
And one should place eight metals to the east,
including iron, as well as mica, bitumen, gold, pyrites, and copper.
Gold, red ochre, sulphur, mica, uśīra, atyūta, ākrāntā, śoṇa, and sandalwood as well.
Agarūmāri, kuṣṭha, and likewise śaṅkhapuṣpaka;
rice, wheat, māyī, sesame seeds, and indeed lotus.
One should place barley, millet, and rice to the east;
likewise, one should place a tortoise, the earth, and a golden lotus situated in the middle of the semen.
In the absence of gems, one should place a vajra; in the absence of metals, gold; in the absence of seeds, barley is recommended; and in the absence of minerals, realgar.
In the absence of medicinal herbs, however, one should place sahadevā;
but in the absence of all these substances, one should pour liquid into the wells.
The six-part milk-rice (*pāyasa*) is intensely desired;
O God, for those who recite [the mantra], that indeed appears as a pair in the mouth of the embodied one.
A pair of garments made of silk, cotton, or similar materials should be given to the Guru;
one should cause these to be presented to the two attendants of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍabha) and to the guardians of the images (mūrtipa).
At the time of the southern door, two golden vessels are prepared;
two auspicious golden rods, measuring four finger-breadths in length, are also provided.
A crown, two armlets, two earrings, two bracelets,
a pearl necklace, and a girdle should be offered with great care to the Guru.
One should examine a single cow along with its calf and its ornaments for the sake of the Guru;
as for the characteristics of the linga, the pedestal, and the stone, there are three ages [of measurement].
At the conclusion of the ritual acceptance, there should be two [images] adorned with golden ornaments;
for the chariot procession, however, there should be a chariot decorated with various garments.
Adorned with a garland of small bells and joined by Buddhas and gods,
having commenced the chariot procession, [one should perform it] briefly until the end of the consecration.
One should cause garments, gold, jewels, land, and female elephants to be given to the Guru;
one should likewise cause them to be given to the victorious Mūrtipās and the Sādhakas.
According to one's capacity, one should avoid stinginess regarding wealth;
one should offer garments, gold, vessels, and food consisting of rice and milk-pudding.
During the time of the chariot’s circumambulation, one should play various musical instruments;
likewise, one should honor the fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers.
May they rescue sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons from the roar of the horse;
may medicinal herbs, grains, trees, minerals, and fruits [do the same].
"One who has employed these [mantras] for the God of gods attains the state free from affliction.
Thus ends the chapter on consecration (*adhivāsana*) in the *Kālottara-mahātantra*.
247b) Īśvara said:
Having bathed well, with a purified soul and free from anger and harshness,
the preceptor together with the image-keepers should gradually perform the purification of the temple from its sins.
One should first worship the preceptor, and thereafter worship him as if he were Śiva; likewise, one should worship the guardians of the images in due order, as well as those who recite the mantras.
Then the Nāndī-śrāddha should be performed by the preceptors who have been initiated;
having thus performed it according to the rule, one should bind the bracelet upon him.
The Guru should then perform the binding of the turban for him with a golden one, over which the Mahāpāśupatāstra mantra has been recited one hundred times.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the pure and venerable body as before,
one should worship the gatekeepers in the sequence starting from the east.
Having thus fashioned arches over the water-jars with the mantras beginning with Tatpuruṣa and others,
one should enter by the western door and thereby dispel all obstacles.
Having sat upon a pure seat, one should perform the cremation of the funeral cake (piṇḍa);
thereafter, one should perform the ritual of integration (sakalīkaraṇa) and likewise the mental sacrifice (manasayāga).
The son of Kṛtikā should fashion his hand as consisting of all the principles (tattvas);
the son should perform the purification of the site through burning and nourishing.

One should sprinkle [the site] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and likewise with water for the *argha* offering; then, using the weapon mantra (*astra-mantra*), one should perform the ritual projection of rays (*vikara-kṣepa*) against the demons, ending with Varuṇa.
The collection of the casting [of the thread] should be performed with the sword of Śiva at the time of death;
one should worship the Śiva-kumbha on the altar in the northeast corner.
To its right, one should place the weapon-vessel facing the door; then, having worshipped the world-protectors residing within the jars along with their weapons and vehicles.
The banners [should be worshipped] with the Śakti-mantras, and the flagstaffs likewise with the faces [of the deities];
then the quiver for arrows should be offered, and thereafter one should worship the two jars.
As before, one should perform the worship of Gaṇeśa and the Guru with the yoga-paṭṭa;
one should install the seat up to Śuddhavidyā, and the forms up to the end of Mūrti.
O Six-faced One, one should perform the mounting of the pervasive deity,
as well as the forms of the binding of mudrās, the water for the feet (pādya), and the water for sipping (ācamanīya).
The offering of water for honor (argha) should be performed, as well as bathing and anointing;
worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as the face, limbs, and feet.
A garland of lamps should be offered, as well as food offerings and drinks;
then, having performed the ritual rinsing (ācamana), one should worship and likewise perform the recitation (japa).
Then, having worshipped with devotion, one should proceed to the fire-chamber;
there, the drawing [of the mandala] should be performed with the Astra-mantra, and then the sprinkling with the Varma-mantra.
One should place there the fire of gnosis, possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand suns,
within the center of the heart-lotus, as it were, once more in the *sūṣumṇā*.
By the mere act of placing that [mantra], one becomes fit for all rites,
beginning with the ceremony of conception (garbhādhāna) and ending with the final rite of liberation (niṣkṛti).
In the presence of the wind and fire of knowledge, the sixteen digits do not hold value;
in rites that are obligatory, occasional, or for specific desires, one must perform the worship of the fire of knowledge.
By a single sprinkling alone, the consecration of the *śruk* ladle is accomplished;
in the same manner, this should be done for the clarified butter using the water from the *argha* vessel.
Endowed with all ritual preparations, one should perform every rite;
the offering of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) must also be performed while maintaining meditative concentration (dhāraṇā).
For what purpose [is this]? For the sake of incense and lamps; one should protect the food with the *mudrā*.
Having worshipped Śiva with devotion according to the previously mentioned procedure, [one should proceed].
One should worship with flowers, water-offerings, perfumes, and incense, together with the appropriate mudrās;
and one should satisfy [the deity], who is joined with the faces and limbs of Śiva, with clarified butter.
Then, the image-keepers (mūrtipās) should perform the fire-oblation (homa) while seated upon their respective seats;
having offered the oblation, they should indeed proceed from the [offering area] to the bathing pavilion (snānamaṇḍapa).
Two altars should be constructed with effort in the bathing pavilion:
the first is for the bath, and thereafter, the other is for the application of the marks.
O Six-faced One, for the purpose of removing the defects of craftsmanship, one should perform a bath with earth, ashes, cow dung, decoctions, and fragrant waters, using the Śiva-weapon mantra.
Having worshipped with various kinds of perfumes, garments, and flowers,
he should then extract [the image] according to the prescribed rite and place it upon the altar.
Having placed [the stone] face up upon a wooden plank (tūlikā), one should extract the characteristic marks;
the height of the linga, including its modifications, is divided into three parts by means of proportional measurement.
Furthermore, the interval between the lines is considered common to all liṅgas;
the width of the liṅga should be one-fourth or one-eighth of its height.
When the liṅga is eight barley-corns in height, the line should be deep and wide;
its width, characterized by that line, measures one aṅgula according to the Jyeṣṭha-Rudra measurement.
The Lakṣma-rekhā should be drawn out, and likewise the Pakṣa-rekhā;
furthermore, the Kanyasa-saya-rekhā is established at nine māṃsas.
The five parts, including the portion of Rudra and the modification, are to be abandoned;
having bound the portion of Rudra within the portion of Rudra, one should divide by the eyes (two).
Its height is said to be three parts, one quarter, and a half part of its width;
this characteristic has been correctly described, beginningless and honored by the Asuras.
From half of that, it would otherwise emerge from two side-lines;
when divided by eight, nine, and three, the vertical and the *uṣaṭṭa* [are determined] by the serpents (*nāgas*) in sequence.
It does not grant success in those [signs] beginning with Aries when increased by two and a half parts;
or else, having subtracted two parts from the sign divided by nine, [the remainder is auspicious].
The two fortnights [of the month] are determined by the numbers nine, twelve, and eleven respectively; this triad is common to all.
A junction should be made by means of two lines, or alternatively, it may be a serpent-noose (nāgapāśa).

In the sixth [house], the measure of the portion is shaped like a barley grain, or sometimes it is considered to have two wings; or, with one wing diminished, it is beneficial in the seventh house when known as the elephant shape.
A single line, perfectly complete and ending at the portion of Viṣṇu, should be drawn;
then three vertical lines are to be made, either on the first or the second [square].
The *liṅga* worshipped by the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) is said to have a width of one thousand units;
it is described as having equal proportions, with its dimensions measured in *yava*s or *aṅga*s according to the prescribed characteristics.
The opening of the eyes for images that are of a fearless nature is auspicious when performed upon a linga made of nine gems, but not so for one made of metal or earth.
However, it should be fashioned on one side, but it must not arise from the fragrant water (gandhodaka);
on the pedestal (piṇḍikā), it should have the shape of a vulva (bhaga) situated in the middle of the characteristic opening.
Once it has been previously marked by the Guru, the artisan should then extract [the image].
When the door has been made with the proper characteristics, it should be filled with the Mṛtyujaya mantra.
Since [the deity] seated upon the auspicious throne is to be bathed with ghee and honey,
as well as with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), decoctions, earths, and collections of fragrant substances;

One should surround it with fruits, flowers, and the like, as well as with eight jars containing [substances from] the Vakṣārā mountain; then, having applied the ointment called Raktacandra, one should wrap it with a red cloth.
Having bathed the pedestal and the stone there, and having smeared them with unguents,
one should offer the *arghya* and apply a forehead mark (*tilaka*) using yellow pigment (*rocanā*).
Sprouts of dūrvā grass and white mustard seeds, having been made cool, should be placed upon the head;
then, having yoked [the horse] to chariots, one should perform a circumambulation of the city.
The sacrificer, together with his wife and all his kinsmen, should cast a mixture of flowers, gold, and jewels; he shall proceed unhindered.
At every step, one shall obtain the fruit of ten million sacrifices;
and those who suffer from the five winds (pañcavāta) attain the supreme goal.
One should cause [the disciple] to enter through the eastern door of the sacrificial pavilion;
he should then be placed upon an auspicious throne and provided with a bed to lie upon.
One should arrange his head toward the east or the south;
a vessel containing equal parts of ghee and honey should be placed at his feet, and a water-pot at his head.
One should arrange the household utensils as previously described;
having offered the enjoyments and given them away, one should then install the image.
From Brahmā, one should perform the placement of the forms (mūrtinyāsa) for the portion belonging to Rudra;
therein, the earth-form (kṣmāmūrti) is proclaimed as the presiding deity in every respect.
Mantreśvara and Śikhaṇḍin are the two by whom one should place the first three forms;
Rudreśāna and Śrīkaṇṭha are to be placed by the one whose form is Vahni.
The preceptor should place the sacrificer, the supporter of cattle, and the three forms;
he should then join the tip of the sun, the one Rudra, and the one situated in the southwest.
One should join the water-born single eye with me [the Self] in one place;
the Lord Vāyu, O Śivottama, the Guru should install [him] as residing in Vāyu.
Indra and Mahādeva are there, as is Maheśvara in his subtle form.
When Jupiter is situated in the northern quarter, one should not place the triad;
rather, one should place the triad in the northeast, beginning with Kha, Bhīma, and likewise Ananta.
The support of the principle of the Self (ātmatattva) should be placed in the portion belonging to Brahmā;
likewise, in the portion belonging to Viṣṇu, [it should extend] up to the limit of the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva).
Having joined the sequence upon the seat, one should then [apply] the self-knowledge and its sphere of experience.
Or the form (mūrti) may be joined fivefold as Saṃkṣobha and the others, together with Fire, Wind, and Space; and Brahmā and the rest are the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās).
There are other forms of the Lord, such as Mūrti and Mṛtti, as well as Sadyojāta and the others in sequence;
I shall describe these eight types of installation in due order.
Dhārikā, Dīptimatī, Ugrā, Jyotsnā, and these others—
[along with] Dhātrī and the rest, beginning with Vāmā— are established as the embodiments of the Śaktis.
The fivefold [powers] beginning with Vāmā are to be applied; I shall describe them briefly:
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Kriyā, Jñānī, and Icchā as the fifth.
Without [the aforementioned], five [deities] are said to abide in the partless state. Now I shall explain, in due order, the ritual placement of the forms (*mūrtinyāsa*) for those who are fierce.
Tamākhyā, Ghorasaṃjñā, Mohākhyā, Ratisaṃjñakā,
and Apajvarā as the fifth— these are the [five]...?
Saṃveśa, Antaka, Mohakṛt, Ravināyaka,
and Dipti Ugra as the fifth— these are remembered as the five Lords of the Mūrtis.
And as for the eightfold sin and purification: one should cause it to be performed by means of a form (mūrti).
[This should be done] with a common mantra, or with the *praṇava*, or with the *śiva* [mantra].
Having done this according to the rule, one should worship with the Kṣayamā and other [mantras];
and one should perform the cessation with the Nirāyinī.
One should perform the visualization of the three channels and install the three deities within them;
in this sequence, one should offer libations together with the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās).
In the cardinal and intermediate directions, in due order, one should perform the recitation of the Brahmāṅgas,
the Samaya, or the Nigarbha, as well as other [mantras].
He should recite the *garbha* mantra together with the *dhyāna*, and the *nigarbha* alone;
first the *Mahāpāśupata*, and the *Aghorāstra* on the right.
In the western direction;
in this manner, one should proceed in sequence, with the recitation of the weapon-mantra being the most excellent.
With earth and sesame seeds, one should likewise construct the enclosure wall;
having [invoked] the world-protectors according to the scripture, one should cause them to be sprinkled.
Having performed this according to the prescribed placement, one should then carry out the fire offering (homa) to the form (mūrti),
to the lords of the forms (mūrtīśvara), and likewise to the Great Lord of the forms (mūrtimaheśvara).
