For each [deity], one hundred oblations are to be offered with sesame seeds smeared with clarified butter; likewise,
[one should offer for] the principle of the self (*ātmatattva*), up to the end of the self, and within the sphere of knowledge and ignorance (*vidyā-avidyā*).
One should assign the Śiva-tattva, which extends to the end of rāga, to Brahmā;
the Ātma-tattva, ending with niyati, and the Vidyā-tattva, ending with kalā.
The principle called Śiva, ending with Śuddhavidyā, resides in the portion of Viṣṇu and consists of three principles;
likewise, the principle of Ātman ends with Īśvara, while the one called Vidyā extends up to Sakala.
The Śiva-tattva extends as far as Śakti, while within the [tattva] called Rudra there are three tattvas;
in this manner, one should indeed conceive of these three tattvas within the image.

One should conceive of the image as consisting of three parts: that called *ātman* extending to the navel, that called *vidyā* situated at the palate, and that called *śiva* reaching to the top of the head.
One should likewise purify the two types of self-knowledge at the sacred seat (pīṭha),
and one should also purify that which is the foundation, known as Kūrma, situated above it.
The ritual of installation, the fire sacrifice, and other rites must be performed for seven nights or even five nights by the image-makers who are experts in the principles of reality.
One should not perform it for less than three nights or one night;
rather, a great festival should be held, along with fire-offerings, worship, and recitation at that time.
"An offering of fermented grain and curd should be given to the lords of the world with extensive [accompaniments].
Thus ends the chapter on the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) in the *Kālottara Mahātantra*.
The Lord said:
Now, the foundation for both the manifest and the unmanifest is being described;
likewise, the installation and the stability of the doors, the lamps, and so forth, as well as the stationary objects.
The *utthāpana* (raising) is especially for those [images] that have become worn out, such as those with missing limbs;
furthermore, their *sthāpana* (installation) and *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration) are considered to be fivefold.
O Destroyer of Krauñca, I shall describe the installation of the mobile and immobile [deities].
Having performed the daily rites, one should not depart while reciting the mantra of the temple.
The expulsion of obstacles should be performed there with the Pāśupata [mantra];
having abandoned the Brahma-sthāna, one proceeds by degrees at intervals of a barley-corn and half a barley-corn.
Relying on the northern direction, one should place the tortoise-stone there;
one must not place it in the center, for in this way the form becomes both manifest and unmanifest.
One does not attain happiness in the three [stages] by abandoning the middle and remaining fixed;
rather, one experiences happiness here through movement even by the measure of a barley grain.
Having uttered the *pārthiva* seed-syllable, one should place the tortoise-stone (*kūrmaśilā*) there;
thereafter, the placement of jewels (*ratnanyāsa*) should be performed after smearing the site with milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Having bound [the disciple] with a cloth over the eyes, one should perform protection with the sword of Śiva;
then, having gone near the liṅga, one should awaken Maheśvara.
Having received permission from the preceptor,
he should have it moved by artisans amidst the sound of musical instruments and auspicious songs, and the resonance of various hymns of praise.
Without securing the door, the Liṅga— whether manifest, unmanifest, or of both forms—
should be carefully brought inside, or else once the door has been secured.
One should enter through the door, but one should cause [the deity] to enter with the *ākāśa* [mantra];
indeed, in the case of a worn-out *liṅga*, entry from above is prescribed.
If a fool should cause the Supreme Lord to enter through the wrong door,
there will be death for the patron and the abandonment of the officiating priests and others.
Having rested at the location of the natural pit, one who has mastered his hand should cause [the image] to enter;
having placed it upon the frame and fixed it with hanging strings, it is made perfectly clear.
Then, one should perform the binding of the upper seat by way of emanation;
having recollected the foundational mantra, one should install the power of action (kriyā-śakti).
In this case, however, pacification (śānti) should be performed with ghee and guggulu;
that joint should be diligently filled with adamantine cement (vajralepa).

One should bathe [the image] with the peace-pitchers (śāntikumbha) containing ghee, honey, and other waters; having performed the cleansing, one should carry out the appropriate mantra-installation (mantranyāsa) for oneself.
One should place the seat there, extending down to the feet upon the pedestal;
one should assign the root mantra to the portion of Brahmā and the portion of Rudra.
The display of mudrās should be performed, and one should offer the water of cessation (nirodhārgha);
having arranged [the mantras] beginning with Ananta, otherwise according to the location of the seat (pīṭha).
O Śikhidhvaja, one should place Lokeśānī and the other weapons at the base [of the central deity],
and arrange the assembly of Gaṇas in the portion belonging to Viṣṇu.
Then, one should perform the ritual bath with extensive displays according to one's means;
various kinds of worship should be performed, along with many food offerings.
In this manner, one should remain awake for four days;
one should provide the preceptors with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), food, and vehicles.
In eating, leaping, and giving, there is no fault or the like, nor the three [restrictions];
on the fourth day, having bathed it, it should be worshipped according to the prescribed rite.
There, one should perform the ritual bath, and likewise sometimes the common bath;
the preceptor must perform the hundred-fold bathing ceremony there.
Having offered the full [oblation], one should designate Caṇḍīśa as the restrainer;
he should be established in the northeastern direction, or he may be placed upon the top of the liṅga.
Whether the linga be fixed or mobile, made of gems, clay, wood, stone, metal, or fashioned from variegated materials, Caṇḍa remains within it as its controller.
In the Siddhānta, and not in other tantras— neither in the Vāma nor in the Dakṣiṇa—
there is [prohibition against] the substance of Caṇḍa, the substance of the Guru, and likewise the substance of the Deity.
"He who eats [forbidden food] even in his mind is cooked in the Raurava hell";
thus should the installation be performed by both householders and those committed to lifelong celibacy.
It should always be avoided by the Pāśupatas established in the Soma-siddhānta,
and likewise by the Kālāmukhas established in the fourth refuge.
One should neither worship nor consecrate a *liṅga* established by these [persons];
they are declared to have renounced [their vows] and are censured for performing installations and other such rites.
Thus, for that which is mobile, a two-fold installation must always be performed:
the placement of the jewels on a separate pedestal, or, if without such a pedestal, it is beneficial to place them directly upon that [mobile] base.

One should perform the placement of the forms and the formless, the collection of the principles (tattvas) of the embodied deities, as well as Caṇḍa and the others; now listen further regarding the doors and so forth.
In this matter, the placement (nyāsa) of the Embodiment and the Lord of the Embodiments should be performed as before;
or else, having performed the fire-oblation (homa) together with the Śrīkhaṇḍa, one should perform the subsequent rite.
Having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) as before for those whose images have been manifested,
one should perform the ritual placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa) through the yoga of pervasive connection (vyāptisandhāna).
O child, the installation of the manifest and unmanifest linga is declared to consist of the manifest and unmanifest, with the fierce placement (caṇḍanyāsa) performed as before.
The installation of the doors and so forth should be performed afterwards; listen briefly [to this].
Indeed, on the door-panels, it should be done first, just like the [installation of the] *liṅga*.
One should worship Vāstu at the entrance and then place an udumbara branch above it;
having placed the jewel-pitcher in the middle portion, listen now to the sequence for what follows.
Or else, one should prepare a jar made of copper or gold, containing precious gems within; [and place therein] barley, white mustard seeds, *krānta*, sesame, *aramba*, and yellow orpiment.
Likewise, Sahadevā and Lakṣmaṇā,
having placed [the vessel] filled with mercury upon an inverted udumbara fruit, [should do so] with the *praṇava* or with the *śiva-mantra*.
One should place the Māyā-tattva at the threshold and the Ātma-tattva [within];
and one should place the Vidyā-tattva, consisting of Śiva’s knowledge and action, upon the two door-posts.
One should place [the deity] situated upon the *udumbara* tree above by means of pervasion;
all rites such as ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and fire-oblation (*homa*) should be performed as previously described.
Thus, the consecration of the gateway has been described to you in brief;
the consecration of the temple, however, should be performed near the nose [the pinnacle].
One should place there the jar containing the five gems, which has become the embodiment [of the deity];
the jar should be eight finger-breadths high, or one cubit, and made of gold.
One should contemplate the mantra of self-knowledge as having a single form with the mind; then,
by means of the exhalation (*recaka*), one should place there the jar whose nature is that of the Lord (*īśvara*).
One should fashion its body up to the limit of the Māyā-tattva;
having performed the placement of its limbs in direct order, one should install the Lord (Īśvara).
The ten channels beginning with Prāṇa, such as Iḍā and the others, should be joined;
one should then install the Form (Mūrti) and the Lord of the Form (Mūrtīśvara) according to the very sequence previously stated.
Having performed one hundred oblations for each reality, one should effect the suppression;
thereafter, one should perform the suppression and scatter the offering of the world-ant.

Then the altar-base (vedībandha) should be fashioned, followed by the neck (kaṇṭha) with its leftward spiral (vāmala) and crest-ornament (sālaka); having thus completed these with effort, one should then install the pinnacle (cūlaka).
According to the procedure stated for the *liṅga*, without the extraction of the characteristic marks,
one should establish the Śiva-principle in the crest and the Vidyā-principle residing within the pitcher.
Having placed [the deity] upon the upper part of Brahmā for the sake of stabilization,
one should then install the Mūrti-mantra there, accompanied by the Brahmā-aṅgas.
When this has been done, one should thereafter arrange the vehicle of the ritual action and so forth;
the *ātmatattva* extends to the knees, while the *vidyā* is within the range of the *vidyā*.
Then, one should contemplate the Śiva-tattva above that and the triad [of principles] in sequence;
the homa should be performed with the appropriate materials, and at its conclusion, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa).
255b) I have explained to you in brief the consecration of the crest-lock (cūḍā). O destroyer of Krauñca, I shall now describe in summary the consecration of the banner (dhvaja).

The staff reaching up to the shanks is known as the best; that reaching to the middle of the thighs is the middling; and that reaching to the feet is the lowest. One should fashion the banner in the same manner.
White is always best for bestowing peace; red is for the accomplishment of power;
yellow should be employed for paralyzing, and black is beneficial for paralyzing.
A staff made of bamboo is prescribed, which is free from knots and blemishes,
devoid of defects such as crookedness, or one made of strong wood that is likewise considered fit.
The staff and the banner should be diligently sprinkled with the Śiva-weapon mantra;
having worshipped them with the Śiva-weapon mantra, one should place them above the deity.

One should especially cover the mattress with a cloth; likewise, one should diligently place the knowledge of the Self (Ātmavidyā), Śiva, and the three sections (Trikhaṇḍā) and so forth in their proper sequence.
The Mūrtis, the Mūrtīśvaras, and likewise the Mūrtimaheśvaras;
thereafter, all the rites such as the ritual placement (nyāsa) and the fire-oblation (homa) must be performed there.
O Śikhidhvaja, it must be performed with the weapon-mantra and not with any other;
one should install the banner, which has become the embodied form, upon the stalk of the supporting lotus.
One should always install the six-faced [deity] with its limbs using the Pāśupata weapon and the [Pāśupata] face-mantra;
however, one should not install the banner with the Pāśupata weapon, but rather with the Aghora weapon.

One should offer flowers, water for honor, incense, lamps, and especially food offerings according to the prescribed ritual; one should meditate upon him as possessing the splendor of ten thousand suns.
He has a distorted, protruding, black, and tawny beard, mustache, and hair;
he is four-armed and three-eyed, with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
Having circumambulated him while wearing the sacred thread, he beheld the one who holds a trident, a sword, and the gesture of granting boons with his staff,
the destroyer of the fear of gods, asuras, and nāgas who had witnessed him.
The hoisting of the banner is declared to be meritorious and bestowing the fruit of auspiciousness;
by seeing the hoisting of the banner, the destruction of all sins occurs.
The fruit of all sacrifices and the fruit of all sacred fords and austerities belong to him;
by seeing the hoisting of the banner, the destruction of all sins occurs.
Upon seeing the hoisting of the banner, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices and the fruit of all sacred fords and austerities; this is no false word.
One is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Śiva;
thus, there is benefit in the installation of both earthen and painted liṅgas.
However, one should perform the entire sequence beginning with the ritual bath upon the mirror;
the rites of ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and fire oblation (*homa*), etc., should be performed [therein], as merely offering incense involves no fault.
O son of Kṛttikā, the installation of the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) must be performed;
all rites such as the ritual depositions (nyāsa) and fire offerings (homa) should always be conducted just as for a liṅga.
When the scripture is thus established, the fruit is a hundredfold by virtue of the indicative mark;
therefore, this scripture should be explained day after day to practitioners and others.
One should also establish a temple or a monastery as a seat of learning (vidyāpīṭha). Thus has the installation been described in brief, along with its specific details.
Thus ends the chapter on installation in the *Kālottara-mahātantra*. The Lord said:
I shall explain the restoration of the dilapidated in its entirety, concisely and in due order;
when the restoration of the dilapidated has been performed, the original fruit is once again obtained.
One should guard against indigestion with great effort, but one must never retain what has been digested.
If one should, out of delusion or ignorance, extract [the mantra] while it is undigested, [he incurs a fault].
In the terrible Raurava hell, one lives for three great kalpas;
therefore, with every effort, one should always protect against indigestion.
If it has become worn out, one should diligently replace it with another;
one should not wear it, as that would bring about the suffering of injustice, like a king or a thief.
There is no contradiction among the signs; one is purified by knowing half of the *lakṣa*.
Their installation and elsewhere should be performed in the same sequence as before.
Whether it be being installed or already established, if one should worship it as a limbless [form],
or sometimes as the portion of Brahmā, or even as the portion of Viṣṇu or Rudra.
The focal point may be the side-line, the head, the creeper-like eyebrows, the chest, the back, or likewise the sides; or it may be the upward-bending crest of the head.
Whether it be the pedestal (pīṭha), the girdle (mekhalā), the stalk (nālaka), or the space between stalks;
or whether it be the tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā), the door, or even the temple itself.
If a water-pot or a jar is broken or even worn out,
one should give [the equivalent value] in silver by the month, whether it be one finger-breadth, half a finger-breadth, or half of that again.
The crown of the head, the nose, the mouth, the ears, the chin, the cheeks, the earrings,
the shoulders, the arms, the forearms, and the collection of hands and fingers.
The bracelets, the limbs, the weapons, and the seats;
the heart, the chest, the waist, the back, the shanks, the thighs, and the toes.
In the same way, the halo of light, the hair, and so forth—
whether already present or being established— are broken apart when [the mirror] is shattered.
Having withdrawn each respective [element], he should likewise establish another quality;
he should establish that other form as consisting of that [quality], for Śiva is not otherwise.
Setting aside that which is made from unrefined materials, one should prefer that which is made from refined ones;
wood is beneficial compared to clay, stone is praised over wood, and metal is beneficial over stone.
An image made of iron is recommended for one born under a metal [sign], while one made of gems is beneficial for one born under a gem [sign];
having understood this, one should diligently extract a worn-out image and replace it with a new one.
Likewise, one should extract a jewel that has lost its luster from the back of a fire,
even if it has been handled by outcasts or worshipped for a very long time.
Having likewise extracted one that is deficient in ritual procedure, and especially one that contains an embryo;
as well as one that is slightly deformed, burnt, or lacking the proper measurements—one should remove it.
He should extract that wound with a measure equal to its size, or slightly less than its measure;
then, by that same measurement, he should determine both its width and its circumference.
A linga that is deficient in its ritual requirements, whose form is manifest yet unmanifest due to fear,
or one established by heretics or ascetics, should not be worshipped.
Having removed [the old image], one should install a new one under the asterism Kṛttikā;
for a shrine that is dilapidated or corrupted by defects is considered a dwelling place for malevolent spirits.
Depending upon that [element], there arise the great elements, piśācas, brahmarākṣasas,
as well as diseases that are difficult to ward off, such as epilepsy and possession by spirits.
There shall be famine as well as pestilence, evil dreams, and ill omens;
there shall be affliction of the people, affliction of the womb, and affliction of the king upon the twice-born.
In that region, fear arises from thunderclaps, the touch of wind, and other such portents;
likewise, the falling of meteors and the crashing of thunder in all directions shall occur.
And other such faults as these arise;
therefore, with every effort, one should remove a worn-out linga.
O Mahāsena, when the *liṅga* has been extracted while it is still unripe [or undigested], no fault arises in that case regarding the pedestal, the temple, the pinnacle, or the pavilion.
Therefore, with every effort, one should never disturb that which is well-established;
one should not even attempt to complete that which is poorly established, but rather, having understood each case, one should extract it [from difficulty].
I shall explain its extraction in due order:
first, one should feed the preceptors with milk-rice and ghee.
Gold, gems, and so forth, as well as vehicles and the like, should be given to them;
one should worship the water-pot there on the right side of the deity.
In that very manner, worship should be performed daily upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Having diligently performed the fire-oblation (homa), one should offer the external and internal oblations (bali).
In each portion, one should offer a thousand oblations with the *astra* mantra;
having touched the ointment with *kuśa* grass, one should again recite the *astra* mantra.
"One thousand or half of that," and so forth, was taught regarding the Kṛttikās;
just as it is beneficial in the Brahmabhāga, in the Haraga, and in the Rudra,
so too [it is beneficial] in the stone of the Pīṭha and likewise in the door-frames.
The dismissal (visarjana) should be performed either in the temple or in the small pavilion (cūlaka);
then, one should effect the dissolution (saṃhāra) of all [deities] into the Praṇava alone.
One should dismiss Śiva— the three-part form, the Lord of forms, together with his limbs—
as well as the god Caṇḍeśvara, who is both manifest and unmanifest and the restrainer.
One should bind it with gold on the fruit, having gone to the shoulder of the bull;
and having raised it at the sides, one should lead it outward.
The artisans should carry the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) on a chariot and deliver it behind;
having cast the stone image into water, one should burn the wooden image with fire.
Having cast iron into water, one should then dissolve it again;
likewise, O King, having cast even that which is produced from jewels and destroyed into water.
But having cast the image made of cloth into water, one should burn it in the Śiva-fire;
this is the limit for its installation.
One should install another [liṅga] again according to the previously stated procedure;
however, if the liṅga is defective, then one should purify that liṅga.
If the pedestal is devoid of qualities, or likewise [if] the pedestal is defective,
one should abandon that which is deficient and preserve that which possesses qualities. One should always worship Maheśvara with effort in the center of the site.
Furthermore, one who desires prosperity should quickly establish a deity endowed with attributes; for by protecting even those that are worn out, one attains the supreme state.
Thus ends the chapter on the restoration of the dilapidated [temple] in the Kālottara Mahātantra.
The Lord said:
O King, when the signs are common [to both], no other action should be performed;
its installation is like that of a linga, and its ritual activity is within the scope of one who possesses power.
From the three parts of the liṅga, the length should be two hundred [parts];
likewise, the thread should be equal, and the pedestal (pīṭha) should be equal as well.

O Six-faced One, the bull should be made with its head raised high; its length, measured from the base of the phallus to the top of its head, should be six times the height of the phallus, O Six-faced One.
Then, that [measurement] is one finger-breadth; its double, however, becomes a *kalā*.
[The rest is] sufficient... the *tāraka* [is] auspicious.
It is renowned as Khaṇḍadvibhāra and is considered to consist of two complete ālas.
The face of the bull should be sixteen aṅgulas in measure;
likewise, one should determine its width at the region of the horns.
In the middle of the two corners, however, the width should be six kalās.
The placement (*nyāsa*) of the ten [syllables] on the region of the cheeks consists of three parts; the worship of the eyes is performed sequentially.
The two eyes should be treated as equal, yet according to the view of Tārādika and others, they are distinct.
Likewise, it is endowed with three [lines];
in this auspicious [form], the crescent moon is indeed one finger-breadth in width.
The pinnacle-mass (*śṛṅgapiṇḍī*) is half a *kalā* in height; on the pinnacle, the two eyes are two *kalās* high.
The pinnacle at the edge [is] ...
the interval between the pinnacles is two *kalās*, or three *kalās* when accompanied by the mass.
The two [ears], five fingers long and one kalā wide at their base, are circular.
One should prescribe a width of five finger-breadths (pañcāṅgula) for the middle of the ear;
beyond that, the two ears should be made with a thickness of three barley-corns (triyava).
But I am not endowed with three times the root, nor joined with a straight line.
The region of the crest should have three folds, while the rounded upper portion has two lines;
the neck is considered to have eight eyes, and likewise, Hara is on both the left and the right.
Then, five *netras* (twelve finger-breadths) for the shanks, with the joint-line measuring one *aṅgula*;
the two joints [of the knees] are eight *aṅgulas*, and the two ankles are beneficially measured at three *aṅgulas*.
Furthermore, the height of the *khara* is said to be four finger-breadths (*vedāṅgula*) for each tooth;
from the *khara* up to the *āphara*, it is raised by three and a half faces.
The head has eight eyes, and the neck is likewise broad;
the hump has three eyes, the base has one eye, and there should be three eyes on the back.
The back [of the altar] is eighteen kalās in width, excluding the three kalās at the corners;
from there, up to the limit of the *pracchā*, its length shall be twelve kalās.

"From the crown of the head down to the base of the secret organ, the width should be double [the height]"; having been stated by way of this general instruction, it is now being explained by me once again.
At the commencement of the shank, the circumference is sixteen finger-breadths;
at the base it is fourteen finger-breadths, and the joint is fifteen finger-breadths.
Then, the circumference of the upper leg (ūru) should be seven finger-breadths;
listen now to the sequence for the ankle (gulpha), which measures eleven finger-breadths at the back of the foot.
The base of the trunk has two eyes, and its tip is one finger-breadth wide;
the trunk is shaped like a crow's beak and has three hanging faces.
Now hear concerning the width of the back region from its base to the middle:
the extent at the base, the middle, and the end is ten, eight, and seven [units] respectively.
O Six-faced One, the circumference at the base is four times the width;
however, it is proclaimed that the circumference at both ends is three times the width.

In the middle part, the navel should be two *kalās* long, and likewise the *kaṃvala*; at the end of the navel, the testicles should be made, and the two hanging [scrotum] parts should be two *kalās* each.
The lower leg (parājaghā) is ten finger-breadths (aṅgulas), while the upper leg (upajaghā) is half of that;
the joint between them is two [finger-breadths], the two eyes [of the foot] are [two], and the ankle (gulpha) should be four finger-breadths.
The blade should be five finger-breadths long and one and a half finger-breadths wide;
at the tip of the finger, it should be fashioned with the shape of a knife.
The circumference at the base of the shanks is twenty-two finger-breadths;
at their ends, the girth is eight finger-breadths, and at the joint, it is exactly nine finger-breadths.
The shank, however, is produced from fifteen fingers; the two ankles are twenty fingers in length according to the great [proportion].
The arrangement of the limbs and sub-limbs should be carried out in accordance with what is beautiful.
Having thus prepared the bull and invested it according to the prescribed ritual,
and having established it during a royal conjunction (rājayoga), one shall obtain the fundamental fruit.
Untimely death is pacified, and one is not oppressed by calamities;
the king attains victory, and the social classes rejoice constantly.
The characteristics of the bull's son have been briefly described;
endowed with the fivefold installation, they have been told to you in summary.
Thus ends the chapter on the characteristics of the bull in the *Kālottara Mahātantra*.
The Lord said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain, in due order according to the rules:
withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), meditation (dhyāna), breath control (prāṇāyāma), and concentration (dhāraṇā).
Reasoning and meditative concentration—these six limbs are called yoga;
yet yoga is also described as that which transcends its own limbs.
The energetic one, possessing the adjuncts of means for the sake of attaining the goal, [should practice];
now, the limbs of yoga of immeasurable splendor are the most excellent.
I shall explain this in brief; listen with a one-pointed mind, my son:
the sense-faculties are necessarily engaged in their respective objects even during dreams.
Having drawn back those [senses] that were seated [upon their objects] through the force of their respective bases by means of speech and so forth, [he restrains them] each by its own path.
The mind is thoroughly bound by the thread, resting upon the hand;
this garland of innumerable objects is [held] by the one whose form is the lotus of the heart.
Having withdrawn the mind from each sense-object, one should cause it to rest upon a friend; since this is a correct and thorough resting, it is called *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal).
Food, nourishment, joy, and clarity arise;
yet, for the sake of contentment among the virtuous, it is shattered by its opposite.
Then the restraint of the senses and the withdrawal [of the mind] are called the ten [limbs];
meditation and concentration are attained through the secondary eye, which possesses a divine form.
Just as one who possesses a hundred thousand [in wealth] gains joy through service,
so too does one with the power of wisdom, though restrained by his strength, draw others in through his good fortune.
One is not able to prevent that which is irresistible and falls upon those who are powerless;
that meditation is declared for meditators as the bestower of the fruits of the path of meditation.
The vital breath is indeed known as *vāyu*,
and it is perceived through its various divisions within the pathways of movement and consciousness.
When that [mind] has attained complete cessation, it is called *prāṇāyāma*.
Indeed, it is declared to be of three kinds in this scripture, which is preeminent in its excellence of color and power.
Having first secured the paryanka, kamala, bhadra, or svastika posture— whether mobile or firm—
according to the prescribed method and according to the specific way in which it was bound; 262a)
Then, having formed the tortoise-mudrā and gazing at the tip of the nose,
the body, the head, and the back should be made straight like a staff.
One should hold the neck very firm, neither too extended nor bent;
one should support the neck with effort so that the head is held level.
Facing heaven and earth, with his gaze fixed on the tip of the nose,
he should slightly close his eyes and keep his teeth from touching one another.
O Six-faced One, when [the breath] has reached the middle of the palate, one should properly perform the practice situated on the path of yoga with the tip of the tongue.
In this manner and others like it, one should cause [the practitioner] to act with complete steadiness by means of the instrument itself;
for one who is thus established, breath control (prāṇāyāma) is described according to the rule.
Filling [the breath] is called *pūraṇa*; retention (*dhāraṇā*) is considered *kumbhaka*.
Having exhaled through the nostrils, O one-eyed one, that is *prāṇāyāma* known as *recaka*.
The Āgneyī, Vāruṇī, Aiśānī, and Amṛtā—
these four meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās) are established, O Six-faced One, according to the differentiation of their functions.
The preceptor should indeed establish the mouth of Rāhu at the tip of the axle today;
he should then direct the auspicious, divine, and manifold radiance toward the tip of the trident.
From the big toe to the edge of the skull, it is enveloped in a circle of rays; through its intense brilliance, it extends across the horizontal, downward, and upward directions.
O Six-faced One, the supreme practitioner should contemplate until everything residing within the body has been reduced to ashes, and then he should likewise withdraw it.
By this [practice], the yogi’s wind, phlegm, and other [imbalances] are instantly pacified;
likewise, obstacles and whatever other malevolent beings there may be are likewise subdued.
One should maintain this for the sake of conviction, even in the rite of seedless fire,
during the subduing or burning of an enemy, for one's own constant welfare.
Or, at the Tulā and Havirdhāna [conjunctions], one should remember the Vāruṇī dhāraṇā. I shall describe the Vāruṇī dhāraṇā briefly, exactly as it exists.
One should remember the seed-syllable *śiras*, the letter *va*, and the lotus-born [Brahmā] at the throat;
the one whose self is to be meditated upon should contemplate with the path consisting of the element of water.
One should contemplate that the entire universe is being filled with streams of water that have issued forth from the contact of the vibrating *śītkāra* sound and so forth.
Having entered into the *suṣumnā*, from the agitation of the lotus at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) down to the circle of the foundation (*ādhāramaṇḍala*),
one becomes the abode of all accumulated merit.
Having been immersed in water that was like nectar in form, yet possessing the touch of snow, he was tormented by the heat of his body,
which was largely afflicted by hunger, thirst, and exhaustion.
The practitioner of mantra should maintain concentration (dhāraṇā) for the sake of nourishment, remaining free from sloth.
O son, I shall now explain the concentration pertaining to Īśānī in brief.
When the prāṇa and apāna have ceased in the lotus within the ether that is Brahman,
one should contemplate serenity there until the heart-center has also dissolved.
From that great state of being, there arises that which is all-pervasive in nature—
the supreme half, utterly peaceful, devoid of appearance, and stainless.
All that moves and is unmoving appears as real though it is unreal,
so long as its true nature of subtle vibration has not been perceived from the mouth of the Guru.
When that supreme reality is seen, the moving and unmoving world,
as well as the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge— all these are merely mental constructs within the heart of meditation.
The ownership of the mother, the maternal uncle, and the calf, as well as recitation, fire-oblation, worship, and so forth—
these have been correctly explained to you in brief as the concentration on Īśāna.
One should meditate in succession on that which is called Amṛta, a concentration (dhāraṇā) comparable to nectar;
one should meditate upon a lotus resembling the full moon, situated within the three Muṣṇis.
One should diligently contemplate [the deity] situated in the sky, possessing a splendor equal to ten thousand moons,
as a full orb in the firmament, surging with the waves of Śiva’s bliss.
Likewise, one should meditate upon the heart-lotus; in its center, one should recollect one's own body.
Filled with this, the supreme practitioner becomes free from all opposing afflictions.
"O Yoginī, four dhāraṇās have been proclaimed, which always shine forth for one who has attained the stages and is dispassionate; their mastery arises, my son."
"Uha" is the expression of reasoning, which consists of investigation;
"uha" is said to be reasoning (*vitarka*), and its definition regarding the object to be reasoned about (*ūhya*) is now stated.
May that power of yours, which always manifests as ignorance,
[reveal] the supreme non-duality, the peaceful, the logical, and the universal form.
O Lord, the supreme nectar is said to be obtained through reflection;
by performing worship to the deity, Brahman is thereby attained.
O Six-faced One, this conclusion has been approved since its very inception;
an illustration of this has been declared here in the scripture known as the Āgneya.
O Mahāsena, I shall now tell you that which is called Vāthula;
it exists as it truly is, for its reality is not scattered by the six [categories].
Even the fluid [semen] moves the mass of body hair, yet the hair itself has no mind nor does it have such a desire;
surely Śiva makes this quiver in such and such a manner.

264a) O Blessed One, is this half of the body, or is it the vital breaths; is it the entirety of the body hairs, or is it the semen; is it the purpose of action, or is this entire universe a mere expansion of activity, utterly devoid of intrinsic reality?
"Why is it that you are here with such a manifold arrangement of perceptions?"—
thus, in these two sūtras, right reflection has been explained by me.
Thus ends the chapter on yoga in the *Kālottara-mahātantra*.
The Lord said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the forms and colors of the elements;
the earth, together with its presiding deities, consists primarily of lamps, oceans, and mountains.
For the sake of attaining yogic perfection, one should meditate upon the golden-hued deity Brahmā;
having fully realized the principle of the body, one should indeed fix the mind upon Māra.
Having withdrawn his limbs like those of a tortoise, with his mind dissolved therein and intent upon that alone,
as he practices the form, his own true nature shall manifest.
Because there is no doubt regarding the manifestation of individuality, that [consciousness] too is endowed with divinity;
it is yellow, or rather, enveloped by the quality of the subtle element of smell.
The Yoginī, who has been brought face-to-face through yoga with joy,
manifests her form for the sake of one who has attained virility through the application of the fivefold blows.
When he should also approach that earthly deity,
even then this same initial procedure applies; however, he should practice its specific [mantra].
Joined with the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra) and marked by the half-moon and lotus,
he melts the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, by means of his meditative absorptions.
Having conquered, one should enter the fire; by that victory, it blazes up in an instant.
Forms attain the state of being formed, and those who go attain the state of being forms.
Then, having conquered the fire, the wind— possessing its own brilliance— ascends upwards, carrying various wonderful drops that move according to its will.
With abundant strength and vigor, with a steady staff, and being virtuous,
one should be endowed with concentration of mind and a non-conceptual consciousness.
Free from diversity and endowed with all virtues, it arises without obstruction;
by its mere will, it effortlessly withdraws the entire universe along with all its constituent elements.
If the mind, having been projected into space, dissolves perfectly,
then the yogi becomes of the nature of space— in which [space] the world is seen by one who is free from mental constructs.
Then, by means of the method of *udghāta*, the knots must be pierced with effort;
at that time, O son, the truly manifold form (*viśvarūpa*) is attained, and not otherwise.
The upward strike is clearly manifested; by that, it is called *udghāta*.
The untying of the knots of the channels (*nāḍī*) is considered its essential nature.
For one who is thus engaged in yoga performs all actions indeed by means of the vigor exerted through that mastery, practicing them again and again.
"By which one who is not under his own control does not obtain the desired fruit.
Thus ends the chapter on the Opening of the Secret in the *Kālottara Mahātantra*.
The Lord said:
Now, therefore, the characteristics of recitation (japa) are briefly stated:
one should perform the threefold recitation while holding the rosary in one's hand.

One should employ vocal recitation for minor rites, whispered recitation for rites of accomplishment, and mental recitation for the sake of enjoyment and liberation; indeed, one should practice these at all times.
One should take up an auspicious rosary and fashion it with one's own hand;
thereafter, one should begin the recitation while remaining invisible to other people.
The instrument is indeed speech and mind, along with the mantra as the Supreme Self; whatever has ascended into the consciousness, when recited, that shall become the recipient of the fruit.
But he who possesses appropriate consciousness, O Six-faced One, may gradually ascend to the state of action within the sphere of transformation, just as one passes through the past.
For the practitioner of mantra proceeds in this way:
he should join together that auspicious mantra, beginning with Brahmā and extending down to the knees, once again right here.
That which is the all-pervading Supreme Brahman is indeed the supreme power (śakti); by means of transformation, that very power becomes the supreme branch.
The fourth state (turya) becomes deep sleep; deep sleep goes to the state of dreaming;
and the waking state comes to the state of dreaming—thus it is again from this waking state.
O Blessed One, up to the limit of power, what is that?
It is the expressed and the expresser, as well as power, the self, and the mind.
Having performed the conjunction of mantras, one should again begin the recitation,
[visualizing] that supreme Lord in the form [of the deity] situated within the lotus of the heart.
Stainless, resembling crystal, throbbing with its own radiance—
his power consisting of sound issued forth as great flames.
From that pure one, who possesses those qualities, the lineage of the *varṇin*s emerged; from her was born the Mother of Mantras, and from her very summit arose the King of Mantras.
Just as a creeper clings to its beloved flower that has emerged,
even so one should contemplate the rosary and the thread as being like a wheel.
One should effect that dissolution into the heart-made [deity], and likewise for that which consists of the heart;
thus, one should worship the single Lord of Mantras with the inner grain.
When one contemplates that which is known as the recitation (japa), it becomes characterized by a count of one hundred thousand;
by resorting to the yoga of the equinox (viṣuvadyoga), one attains imperishability.
Indeed, the Great Breath (mahāprāṇa), through compassion alone, reaches the ultimate goal;
thereafter, one should perform circumambulation of that which is situated upon the summit of Meru.
O Six-faced One, one must diligently avoid stepping over the back of the pervasive, stainless, and great-souled Lord, who exists in the form of a knot.
In rites for pacification (*śāntika*), one should meditate on [the deity] with the luster of crystal; likewise in rites for enrichment (*pauṣṭika*).
In subjugation (*vaśya*), he has the hue of the *kiṃśuka* flower; in attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), he is like a mountain of gold.

One should always meditate upon and recite the mantra of Śiva while visualizing him as having the luster of collyrium for killing, the luster of a wing for causing enmity, and the luster of smoke for driving away.
Recitation is traditionally held to be threefold according to the form of the higher and the lower;
it is intended to be accomplished by means of the eight locations, manifesting sound.
Whether with a core (sagarbha) or without a core (nirgarbha), the sacrifice of fortune is revealed;
that which is with a core is accompanied by meditation, while that which is without a core is devoid of meditation.
If it is without a core, yet possesses a core within, the fruit shall be a hundredfold;
this should be performed by one desiring to ascend, as it bestows success in all accomplishments.
Relying upon the mobile Śākta power, one should begin the whispered recitation (upāṃśujapa).
O son of Sūryasomāmaya, Śakti is declared to be of two kinds.
Moving within the heart and extending to the three *ṣuṣṭha*s, she dwells in the wings;
at sunrise on the day, it should be recited by one desiring liberation while the breath is present.
At moonrise during the night, however, one who desires worldly enjoyment should perform the recitation;
having understood the coming and going [of the breath], the recitation should be performed, and not otherwise.
When the sun has set in the sky and the moon’s rays have not yet arisen, the recitation performed by Marut, who is ever-moving, bestows the accomplishment of all aims.
That state should be known as consciousness-only, devoid of rejection and grasping;
the wise know it to be free from all means of valid cognition and consisting of the cessation of conceptualization.
This knowledge of the Kālottara has been told to you in brief;
likewise, in the heart-lotus, knowledge arises as pure existence alone.
This supreme secret must not be told to just anyone;
this knowledge, which resides in the oral instruction of the Guru, is exceedingly difficult to obtain.
O son, it should be given when the impurities are fully ripened, and not otherwise;
when the flow of the vital breath (prāṇa) occurs while situated in the movement of the iḍā for a day and night.
In that regard, having attained contact with that [mantra], one should always recite it for the sake of enjoyment;
O Daughter of Śaṅkara, for both enjoyment and liberation, recite whatever desire you have, for these are indeed sacrifices.
When the vital breath (jīva) has come to rest in Piṅgalā, those desiring liberation should then recite [the mantra];
it should be recited while situated within Suṣumṇā for the sake of both enjoyment and liberation.
The iḍā is praised for rites of pacification (śāntika) as well as for those of nourishment (pauṣṭika) and attraction (ākarṣaṇa);
likewise, the piṅgalā is for battle, as well as for eating and sexual union.
O son of Kṛttikā, Suṣumnā is to be understood as being present in all ritual actions;
the practitioner of mantra should recite the name of the fetus and perform the rite after having ascertained its name.
And here, O Destroyer of Krauñca, I shall explain the pervasion (vyāpti) in brief:
the position of the sun is in the midst of fire, and the moon is in the midst of the sun.
Through the burning of the three fists, the solar power (*sūrya-śakti*) goes to dissolution;
the station of the sun is the region of the heart, where it attains dissolution into the moon (*soma*).
The lunar power (cāndrī-śakti) is declared to be the form of the syllable *tat* among the *tattvas*.
Having understood this with effort, the wise practitioner should perform the recitation (*japa*).
Or else, for the sake of attaining perfection in the practice of the path, one should remember the dhāraṇā;
having understood this, whoever should recite [the mantra] shall become a partaker of the fruit of perfect success.
This must not be disclosed, my child; it should always be guarded like one's own life.
It must never be given to one who is not a disciple, nor ever to one who lacks devotion.
This recitation is specifically remembered as being of three kinds;
and by filling the principles (tattvas), O son, there occurs the entry into another body.
For the sake of accomplishing cruel rites, the recitation is said to consist of light;
therein, one should contemplate the pure milk-like sound within.
For the sake of attaining enjoyment and liberation, for the destruction of faults and suffering,
and for the purpose of accomplishing all undertakings through tranquility, one should practice without hesitation.

While performing the rite, meditating thus upon bliss, good fortune, and the fulfillment of goals, the recitation becomes what is called "sound"; one should then contemplate that which is situated therein.
Having abandoned that which is composed of the self, which is all-pervading and resembles a drop of dew at night,
one should meditate upon the heart-lotus with one's own mantra as an exalted sound.
It is eternally risen, indeed devoid of effort,
situated in the state of prāṇa and apāna, and infused with meditative cultivation (bhāvanā).
O Six-faced One, one should indeed mutter the mantra that grants the fruits of all desires,
or else, O Six-faced One, uttering a sound produced with effort.
But solely by means of one's own mantra, that [recitation] should be white like before;
the succession of syllable after syllable should be neither hurried nor delayed.
With a mind free from distraction, intent on the welfare of others, and endowed with that which is truly excellent;
during the forenoon, the midday, and the afternoon of the day.
Furthermore, for practitioners and others, the wearing of rags has been prescribed here;
likewise, one should diligently avoid bathing, worship, and fire-offerings at night.
Is there worship for killing and expulsion? Indeed, it is beneficial for causing enmity;
however, meditation must always be performed by all virtuous people.
"Mental recitation, likewise, should be performed by those free from doubt.
Thus ends the chapter on recitation in the *Kālottara-mahātantra*.
Īśvara said:
The measurement of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is stated by me in brief:
it is shaped like a kadamba flower bud, being equal in its extent and height.
Know that the shell is measured at one hundred crores and three times that in circumference; it is the place of compression for ten million kalpas and likewise the abode of Kālarudra.
Dhūmra measures ten koṭis, and after that, the last one measures five koṭis;
thirty-two hells are situated there, one above the other.
The height of each is measured at ninety-nine lakhs;
O Śikhidhvaja, the interval between each is exactly one lakh.
The hells, together with the intermediate spaces, are considered to be thirty-two crores;
the height of the world of the Kūṣmāṇḍas is ninety-nine lakhs.
Beyond that, the height of the seven netherworlds (pātālas) is described there as being [each] thousands of yojanas in number, corresponding to the count of the openings.
O Six-faced One, there is one thousand intermediate spaces for each;
O Six-faced One, its height upon the earth-element is three hundred thousand [yojanas].
The surface of the earth extends fifty koṭis upward from the cauldron;
the cauldron, Kālarudra, smoke, and likewise darkness [occupy the space below].
The hells, the intermediate spaces, as well as the realm of the Kūṣmāṇḍas,
the seven netherworlds (pātālas), and the entire range extending up to the protective crust of the earth (bhūvarma).
I have described the Kaṭāha and Kālarudra as being fifty million [yojanas] in height;
from the Svarloka up to Maharloka, they extend for ten million [yojanas].
In that [region], the distance should be calculated as eight million five hundred thousand [yojanas];
the number of people is said to be eighty million, and for those two [regions], it is twelve crores.
The truth is that there are ten crores of Śrīkaṇṭhas for every crore of transformations;
the density of the upper part of the shell is established at a measure of one crore.
Beyond that, the Brahmāṇḍa is fifty crores in height;
from the Kālāgni up to the Egg (Aṇḍa), it is one hundred crores in height.
Furthermore, the extent of the cosmic egg from the surface of the earth is described:
Meru is to be known as the center of the earth, rising one hundred thousand [yojanas] high.
But having entered into its various transformations, it rises eighty-four thousand yojanas high,
while its base is spread out for a thousand yojanas.
Know that above it is double [in size], triangular and circular in shape;
the region of Ilāvṛta, however, is situated to the north of the square Meru.
The number of thousands of yojanas is nine in sequence;
all of them, extending for one thousand [yojanas], stand surrounding Mount Meru.
The Rudra and Aśva regions are each two thousand three hundred leagues in extent;
Mālāvat is eighty-four [thousand], with two rows of cities on both sides.
Its width is one thousand and a quarter yojanas;
on the western side of Meru lies Gandhamādana, extending for a thousand [yojanas].
Ketumāla and Ketumālā are two thousand [yojanas] in extent;
their length, height, and width are the same as those of the eastern continents.
Likewise, for those mountains situated to the west, [the same applies] to the left and right sides;
and thus, it is said that the southern side of Meru belongs to the western direction.
Ilāvṛta measures nine thousand yojanas;
beyond that, one should know the mountain named Niṣadha by its name.
Beyond that is Harivarṣa, situated at nine thousand [yojanas];
Hemakūṭa is said by me to have an extent of two thousand [yojanas].
Beyond that is the region marked by thousands of yojanas, which consists of the Puruṣa;
beyond that is the one named Himavat, extending for two thousand [yojanas].
The land known as Bhārata consists of nine divisions and is established at nine thousand yojanas in extent.
The new continent is bow-shaped, joined by nine oceans;
it measures five hundred [yojanas] in land and five hundred in water.
On a region of the Himalayan slopes, there stands a lake named Vindusaras;
there resides Kumārī, whose form is composed of virtues, appearing like a rainbow.
Indraka, Kaseru, Tāmra, Gabhastimat, Mārgya, Saumyaka, Gandharva, Varuṇa, and Kumārī is considered the ninth.
Kumārī is situated on the Himavat mountain as the first and foremost;
these seven mountains are joined with the island of Kumārī.
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Suktimat, Dakṣaparvata, Vindhya, and Pāriyātra— these are the seven principal mountains.
Just as with Kumārī, so too should one know that the five hundred [leagues] of water have entered Kṣāradvīpa,
which consists of the ocean.
Kumāryā [is situated in] Malayadvīpa; after that come Varāha and the others.
Kumuda and Svākhavalaya are joined at the edge of Vāgauprānta.
Malaya is situated on the island of Malaya, or it is located on Trikūṭa;
indeed, Laṅkā, the abode of the Rākṣasas, lies at the foot of Trikūṭa.
Furthermore, to the north of Meru, as before, is Ilāvṛta;
there is the mountain Nīla, whose delightful ridges consist of nine parts.
The mountain Śṛṅgavān stands beyond, extending for nine thousand yojanas and two thousand white golden peaks.
After that, Kuruvarṣa is to the west, equal in measurement to Śveta;
thus indeed has Uttarakuru been described with effort from Meru.
O Mahāsena, situated within the salt ocean are ten mountains; I shall describe to you two more than those, starting from the east.
The three eastern divisions are remembered as Ṛṣi, Dundubhi, and Dhūmra;
and Candra, Kaṅka, and Prāṇa are the three in the northern direction.
Aśoka, Varāha, and his own son Svanandana are in the west;
Cakra, Maināka, and Valiha are in the south—thus in three directions.
The submarine fire (Vaḍavānala) is situated between Cakra and Maināka;
it is revealed as being one hundred thousand yojanas in extent, [surrounding] Jambūṣaḍaṃ.
Jambū, Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śālmali, Gomeda, and Puṣkara— O observer of good vows, this is considered the group of the seven islands.
One, two, four, eight, sixteen, and doubling again;
established in magnitude, it stands at sixty-four lakhs.
The salt sea, the milk sea, the curd sea, the ghee sea, the sugarcane sea, the wine sea, and the sweet-water sea as the seventh— these oceans are situated there in their respective order.
The wise one should conceive of the extent of the oceans as being like that of the continents;
beyond them, the golden ground extends for ten koṭis.
The Lokāloka mountain extends for ten thousand yojanas;
however, the measure of the king of oceans from the inner rim is one crore yojanas.
Twenty-seven lakhs are established in the state of Vṛtta;
thereafter, the number of Koṭis should be known as thirty-five.
O Mahāsena, its circumference is nineteen lakṣas [of yojanas],
and the thickness of the cauldron is measured at one koṭi yojanas.
Thus, this authoritative knowledge concerning the Brahmāṇḍa, together with its secret, has been revealed to you in brief. What more do you wish to ask?
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Dancing of the Egg of Brahmā" in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
The validity [of the means of knowledge] and so forth will be stated by me once again;
the principle of water is said to possess ten times the qualities of the principle of earth.
From that, there is a tenfold increase up to the level of *tattva* consisting of *kalā*;
from that, it is increased a hundredfold by *kāla*, and from that, multiplied a thousandfold.
O Mahāsena, from that [Māyātattva] arise the qualities of Vidyā multiplied by a hundred thousand;
Aiśvara is multiplied by ten million, and Kāla is an arbudāvuda-fold.
O Śikhidhvaja, the number of the *vudā* principles is infinite;
the principle of Śiva, however, is beyond numbering, devoid of qualities, and characterized by the absence of action.
Know it to be beyond comparison, devoid of appearance, transcending the means of valid cognition, consisting of the nature of pure awareness, and free from action and time.
Neither non-existent, nor existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor something that is not anything at all—such is the deity.
That which does not exist in such a way, yet exists, exists as the ultimate truth.
That which is the essence of all, formless yet appearing as form, omnipresent and all-pervading—
neither "this" nor "not this"— is the remaining reality, the eternally imperishable.
O one of great austerity, know that this discourse is for the sake of fulfillment;
by means of the instruction of the Vedic doctrine, the supreme reality is revealed within this established conclusion.
Neither worship, nor likewise bathing, nor recitation, nor concentration;
neither meditation is the cause, nor indeed the binding of mudrās.
O son of Kṛtikā, one should know that before the Supreme Reality (prodatattva),
there are no gifts, no sacrifices, and likewise no vows, O Śivā.
272a) The "Mother's Sweetmeat" (mātṛmodaka) should be understood as being foremost among the realities of gnosis;
just as it is devoid of fruit, O child, it cannot be described.
In that same way, one will not be able to express the true nature of the senses through speech;
for one who has lost what was gained and whose circle of kinsmen has perished, there arises no further appearance of [worldly] connection.
And even for the Lord of Speech himself, it cannot truly be expressed in words.
Thus indeed has the Śiva-tattva been described and maintained;
yet as it truly is, it is not grasped with joy like a wild elephant.
By some a foot is seized, while by others the tail is pulled.
Some [seized him] by the hand, others by the teeth, and still others by the back of the ear.
Each individual limb of those elephants exists in the mud;
one does not find an elephant consisting of all its limbs [there]. In that same way, one should point out the ultimate reality (tattva).
United with all limbs yet devoid of all limbs,
formless, free from qualities, peaceful, the essential nature is Śiva in his entirety.
Just as there is a diverse manifestation of intoxication from drinks and the like,
so too does the entire sound abide within the essence of the peacock's egg.
Likewise, it is established within all things like oil in sesame seeds; by means of its division into shadows and lights, it is considered to be every form of manifestation.
It is situated everywhere without division, like oil in a sesame seed.
Know that the sesame seed is the manifest (sakala), while the oil is said to be the unmanifest (niṣkala);
yet for Śiva, there is no conceptualization of the relationship between the support and the supported.
That which is the support of all, the supreme Śiva—
such as this, the supreme doctrine is to be understood through its own constituent parts.
This, along with its secret, must not be told to just anyone.
Īśvara said:
At the time of taking a vow, as well as at the conclusion of the vow,
and likewise at the commencement of the supreme accomplishments (*siddhis*),
one attains the success of the ritual action, especially if one begins it with [the appropriate] intent.
From among the previously mentioned maṇḍalas, one should evolve a single one;
it should be made great, [measuring] a thousand [units], and not otherwise.
With curd, milk, clarified butter, and honey, as well as with scented water,
saffron, sandalwood, and camphor, one should perform the anointing.
Combined with pieces of sugar, milk, and clarified butter, and accompanied by the drinking of milk;
furthermore, there should be a row of lamps before it, provided with large wicks.
It should indeed be given with effort; one should perform the recitation (japa) twice as much.
And according to one's capacity, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed until the conclusion of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
O son, the preceptors beginning with Sāyaka, as well as others initiated by Śiva,
should be worshipped with great effort and without stinginess regarding wealth.
O Mahāsena, indeed, the breaking of a vow arises from stinginess regarding wealth;
therefore, one should avoid stinginess regarding wealth with every effort.
Afterwards, one should offer all the vows and other rites to Śiva;
having grasped flowers in both hands, one should place the divine knees upon the ground.
Having mentally performed one’s own mantra, one should offer it into the hand of Śiva;
one seeking enjoyment, for the sake of attaining enjoyment, and one seeking liberation, for the sake of attaining liberation.
Having remembered [the deity] with the left hand, one should offer the excrement into the left [hand];
then, having prostrated like a staff, one should cast a handful of flowers.
Thereafter, one should always offer gifts of food to the devotees of Śiva;
by abandoning anger, greed, and the like, the attainment of all perfections will come to pass.
Thus, in brief, the dedication of the vow has been proclaimed;
O child, this is the supreme procedure for the accomplishment of the siddhis.
O son, the offering of *argha* and the sprinkling [of water] should be performed according to the ritual procedure;
having truly received the command, one will then become worthy of attaining *siddhi*.
O son, that teacher who performs initiation without knowing the supreme reality is cooked in the Raurava hell, together with his disciple.
Therefore, O Six-faced One, the reality should be understood through the successive lineage; having received the command from the Supreme Lord, the remainder of the elements [is established].
O observer of excellent vows, having brought about the emergence of the mantra and its dissolution,
and having realized the non-difference between Śiva and Śakti, then success rests in the palm of one's hand.
Mantras received by oneself never attain success;
however, one who has slain a guru, a father, or even a mother may sometimes achieve it.
O Six-faced One, mantras taken up on one's own initiative do not bring success;
knowing this, one should with effort seek out the lineage that bestows Śiva.
Devoid of lineage succession, she is grasped in all ritual acts;
the single Śakti exists as threefold in the form of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire.
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā possess the splendor of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire;
they are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, whose essence is the Self, Knowledge, and Śiva.
Relying upon the signifier (vādaka), a clear expression arises;
another form is the signified (vācaka), while the supreme is established as the signified object (vācya).
O Six-faced One, having joined the mantra with the mind, the power, and the principle (tattva),
for it is by Śiva that the devotee of Śiva indeed attains the state of the mantra.
Abiding in the temple of consciousness, which is devoid of sound, free from taking and giving,
liberated from existence and non-existence, and devoid of meditation and the object of meditation;
Thus has this supreme knowledge been revealed to you as a secret. Thus ends the chapter on the Transmission of Mantras in the great tantra, the Kālottara.
Īśvara said:
One who desires accomplishment should perform the consecration of the site according to the prescribed rite;
it should be auspicious, provided with flowers and water, and free from harmful creatures.
Especially a single liṅga mixed with sandalwood paste and water,
or a bāṇaliṅga or a self-manifested (svayaṃbhū) liṅga, which has been sprinkled by kinnaras and apsarases.
O great king, whether it be the one resorted to by the Nāmadaityas or that which is constantly worshipped,
the dualistic liṅga (dvaitaliṅga) is always praised in this Pārameśvara scripture.
One should worship the Linga that possesses both duality and non-duality for the sake of attaining perfection;
however, a mantra of either non-duality or duality alone never bestows fruit when worshipped.

Therefore, with every effort, one should realize both duality and non-duality, which bestow auspiciousness; yet in non-duality that is free from ritual conduct, non-duality alone becomes the bestower of the fruit.
In the place of the Mother, there is a bull with many lingas, filled with human blood;
it is joined by many practitioners, and the field-protectors are secured.
In a sacred field filled with singing and dancing, crowded with wicked women, and frequented by yoginīs, spiritual accomplishment never arises.
One should avoid the gates in the southern and northern directions for the accomplishment of siddhi;
the western gate is for those with arms [the practitioner], and the western son bestows liberation.
For causing enmity and eradication, the south or the north is recommended;
for victory, the east is beneficial when the sun is in Mahendra or Sūrya.
One should cause the western gate to be made at Puṣpadanta and Pracetas;
the southern gate is situated at Bhṛṅga, and Soma is desired in the north.
One should construct the temple of the Siddhas with four faces or one face, excluding two or three faces; it should have five mouths and one chest.
They are skillful, bold, free from [worldly] qualities, learned in the scriptures, intent on spiritual success, steadfast, devoted to the vow of truth, pure, and endowed with tenfold courtesy.
Companions should always be engaged— seven, five, or three;
one should not perform the middling or supreme accomplishment without a companion.
The wise one should drive eight stakes made of *khadira* wood into the cardinal and intermediate directions; having recited the *Pāśupata-astra* mantra, he should clearly plant them with his hand.
Then worship should be performed, and especially the fire-oblation (homa);
likewise, one should offer the sacrificial food (bali) to the other worldly spirits in due order.
The worship of the triad of Kṣetrapālas is performed in the southern direction (the direction of the Rākṣasīs),
following the sequence of the Mātṛkās, accompanied by the six musical instruments and the description of the field.
Therefore, one should worship there equally that very Lord of the group (vargīśvara),
as well as Ananta, Ādara, Indu, Īśvara, Ugra, and Ūṣara.
Ṛddhi, ṛśo, ḷ; gu, ḹ, kau; ekāsyā, airaḍhi, and likewise;
uja, ṣadha, ambu, and askāra; [these are] Parameśvara.
Karaṅka, Khaga, Galā,
Mardhara, Uḍu, Caṇḍī, Cchaṭī, Jaṭī, and likewise Ṛ, Ṝ, and Ra.
And he is known as Kākāṭakīṭha, the son of Ḍāmaroḍhaṭṭa;
he is Nāgastha, Chchasthaṭī, Dakṣa, Dhanada, and Nandivardhana.
Paṅkavṛka, Phalaphala, Valabha, Smīmara-priya, Yakṣa, Uroga, Alaya, Anta, Varvara, and the one known as Śakti.
Maṭha, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Haṃsa, and Kṛpaṇa are recorded as the last;
that which is named Anta is situated in the eastern direction within the group of vowels (avarga).
In this way, the subtle letter *ka* is situated in the southeastern direction;
likewise, the supreme Śivas are stationed in the sequence beginning with the *ca*-group.
O Mahādeva, one should know that these fourteen [sites] are lost by name even with effort; [they are]:
Ekaliṅga, Mahādeva, Śmaśāna, and Bhṛṅgināyaka.
One should worship Mahāsena on a riverbank, Nandikeśvara at a confluence,
Mahākāla in a cow-pen, and Brahmā at a crossroads.
One should place Daṇḍa on a single tree, Vināyaka at the site of a treasure,
Piṅgala at the site of the Mothers, and Jambhala at the abode of the nectar.
Vīrabhadra was worshipped in battle, Vṛṣabha while stationed on the mountain,
and Kāmadeva, accompanied by Rati and Prīti, in the forest.
In the garden, one should worship the one named Vasanta, who holds a staff in his hand and possesses great strength;
he should satisfy him with curd, milk, clarified butter, sugar, and indeed with milk alone.
With white flowers, auspicious incense, and [offerings] devoid of living beings or bodily parts, O son;
beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, using the words of their respective names, [one should worship] the flute and so forth.
"O Six-faced One, the word 'svāhā' should be employed during the fire-oblation (homa) for the lords of the fields;
thus has this secret concerning the seizing of the field been declared to you."
Thus ends the chapter on the acquisition of sacred sites in the *Kālottara-mahātantra*.
The Lord said:
Hereafter, I shall explain the threefold accomplishments (siddhis) in their proper order:
the superior ones beginning with *aṇimā*, the middling ones consisting of liberation (*mokṣa*), and the lower ones consisting of worldly waters (*carāpa*).

The inferior accomplishments (siddhis), such as subjugation and the like, which involve atheism, have been described; having resorted to the southern form, one should mutter the Pāśupata mantra one hundred thousand times.
Having performed the fire sacrifice (homa) ten times the number of recitations, one becomes capable of attaining all perfections;
this is the method for dispelling obstacles, for the practitioner is not otherwise able [to succeed].

O Six-faced One, the wise practitioner, using his own mantra, should drive in eight stakes made from the wood of milk-exuding trees according to the *Ṣaḍāvarta* rite in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Following the sequence starting from the east and extending as far as the domain of the northeast,
the mantra-practitioner should drive stakes into the directions for as long as he wanders about.
When this has been done, having offered the oblation (bali) to the lords of the directions as before,
the arghya for the mantra should be presented, along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) based on the specific form [of the deity].

Whether it be a self-manifested (svayambhū) or a stone liṅga (vāṇaliṅga), or one established by men for the sake of spiritual attainment (siddhi), protection must first be performed; thereafter, the protection of the mantra follows.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the hands and the placement upon the body in due order;
one should contemplate one's own body with effort between the two moons.
By that [mantra], one's body becomes composed of nectar and invulnerable even to the gods;
this is declared to be the protection of oneself. Now, the protection of the mantra is being described.
One should place the mantra within the womb of Śakti; from that, success is born. Mantras should not be applied to a person by Śiva in such a way as to [seek] fruit.
Those who are powerless, those who abide in the individual soul (puruṣa), and those who abide in Śiva have peaceful minds;
therefore, the claim that mantras reside in Śakti is a false statement according to the established conclusion (siddhānta).
The primordial power is Parā, the supreme Śaiva energy that bestows the fruit of Śiva;
she should be known as non-different from Śiva himself, just as radiance is non-different from the sun.
The Supreme Power (Parāśakti) spoke the mantra; she is indeed the primordial Kuṇḍalinī.
Residing in the region of the heart, she possesses the splendor of the sun and fire.
However, it should be understood as threefold here, according to the divisions of *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and so forth;
having learned from the mouth of the Guru that [the central channel] is firmly established within the *suṣumnā*.
Pervading up to the limit of the twelve finger-breadths within all living beings, it exists in the heart;
by means of the path of the trident, yogis proceed to the limit of the twelve.
Through the distinction of going and coming, she proceeds to the state of Śaṅkara;
having resorted to the supreme reality, she attains perfect bliss.
Thus, having understood the arising of Śakra, one becomes capable of protecting the mantra;
striking at the end of the river and inflaming delusion are of no use.
"Established in Śakti, one should accomplish various kinds of siddhis through power.
Thus ends the chapter on the description of Śakti in the *Kālottara-mahātantra*.
The Lord said:
Having taken refuge in Dakṣiṇāmūrti, one should mutter [the mantra] five crores of times;
having performed the fire-oblation (homa) with cow's ghee and sesame seeds for one-tenth that number.
Indeed, the supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā* are accomplished for him, and not otherwise;
through ten million recitations, the middling powers are attained, and one should offer oblations of guggulu resin smeared with ghee.
One attains the state of moving through the air (khecaratva) by performing oblations ten times the number [of recitations];
however, the fruit is bestowed solely by the single hair of Kapila (ekāpila), which grants invisibility.
And specifically for the purpose of rendering seedless, for the agitation of the bonds,
for the destruction of the great fever, and likewise for the attainment of the Tree.
Furthermore, O child, there is the *dhaṭa* ordeal for proving innocence; again, the ordeal of fire that blazes without fuel;
as well as the ordeal of the transmission of poison and the neutralization of poison itself.
First, the preliminary rites must be performed; only then should one commence the ritual action.
For him, the accomplishments (*siddhis*) are attained; without that, one does not possess accomplishment at all.
Therefore, one should perform the preliminary service with every effort.
Thus ends the chapter on preliminary service in the *Kālottara Mahātantra*.
The Lord said:
In the forenoon, one should perform rites of pacification (śāntika) and likewise those of nourishment (pauṣṭika);
the wise practitioner should accomplish the rites of subjugation (vaśya) and attraction (ākarṣaṇa) at midday.

One should accomplish the rites of immobilization (stambhana) and delusion (mohana) while the sun is stationary; at night, the rite of subduing enemies (māraṇa) should be performed during its setting, and never otherwise.
When the practitioner's breath is devoid of the breath of the one to be accomplished,
then, having ascertained the name with effort, he should accomplish the siddhi.
With *vaṣaṭ*, *auṣaṭ*, *jñaṃ*, and *saḥ*, one should perform the encapsulation (*saṃpuṭa*) known as the *sādhya*.
[One should worship] with white flowers, food offerings (*naivedya*), and white perfumes and ointments.
One should worship Śiva together with the Brahma-mantras and the limbs (aṅgas) on the sacrificial ground with diligence;
one should assign the limbs to the Brahma-mantras using the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* along with its constituent parts.
The Brahmā-mantras are short, while the long ones are the limbs of another caste;
the pedestal is by means of the *jyaṃ* syllable mantra, and the form (*mūrti*) is by means of the three-syllable mantra.
One should place the supreme [syllable] at the end of "vaṣaṭ" using the auspicious three-syllabled mantra;
for rites of pacification, one should offer oblations of *dūrvā* grass moistened with the three sweets.
O Six-faced One, one should accomplish pacification and nourishment through the ritual application of one hundred thousand oblations;
this may be done either with the *praṇava* or with the *māyā* syllable.
Or, O observer of excellent vows, through the previously mentioned root mantras, eternal peace is attained even amidst great portents of celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial origin.
By that, O son, peace (śānti) is produced through the Rudra-śānti;
furthermore, that which was previously mentioned in five ways should be applied in the rite of nourishment (pauṣṭika) by means of the "encasement" (sampuṭa).
In rites for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), one should employ [the mantra] three times—at the beginning, middle, and end.
For nourishment, one should perform a *homa* with *dūrvā* grass smeared with the three sweets; from two such nourishing oblations, [nourishment results].
I shall tell you the secret of cutting through the mantras of others;
having received the command, one must perform this most wonderful cutting of the mantra.
One should write the *putraka* [mantra] using the *mātṛkā* letters in reverse order with fierce embers;
one should place the seed-syllable of dissolution (*saṃhārabīja*), namely the syllable *haṃ*, upon the head, and assign it to the face.
One should know that the two eyes of the serpent are situated at the corners of the mouth;
its nostrils are at the base of the ears, and they understand its two lips to be the letters Ya and Ma.
One should place the syllable *ra* on the two cheeks of the trembling one who possesses the taste of passion;
and one should place the four Vedas on the pair of eyebrows and the right shoulder of the one purified by the river.
In this manner, one should employ the letters beginning with *ḍa* and ending with *ṛ* for the purpose of speech and so forth.

Having performed the sequential placement (nyāsa) starting from the letter *ja* up to the letter *ga* on the thighs, knees, shanks, ankles, and toes, one should then place the letter *va* on the west.
The letter *ai* should be applied to the right side, while *ḷ* is on the left;
*ḷ* is at the chest and *ṛ* likewise in the flesh; one should place *ṛ* in the bone and *ṅ* in the marrow.
The syllable *u* is in the region of the knee, likewise *ī* in the semen (*śukra*) and *i* in the heart;
O son of Kṛttikā, the previous mantra is not to be recited here.
Having thus drawn the Putraka in a terrifying empty house,
or in the house of a mother, or with fruits that cause fear;
Having written [the mantra] on a sacrificial board (phalaka), one should likewise draw it as if it were a corpse;
at the three junctions of the day, one should worship each one in sequence according to the ritual procedure for worship.
O Destroyer of Krauñca, for up to seven days, one should employ the weapon-mantra,
the sword-mantra, as well as the command, meditation, the vidyā, or the mantra.
One should cause [the victim] to be decapitated; of this there is no doubt, one should strike him down upon the ground of the stake. This is the supreme secret; it must not be told to just anyone.
One should perform this illusion for all [beings]; therefore, one should protect it with effort.
Alternatively, one should place a weapon upon the three channels at the path of the throat.
Engaged in meditation, one should contemplate [the deity] with the luster of fire for three days;
then, through this knowledge of the command, the meditation, and the mantra, one should indeed sever [the bonds] within the sphere of gnosis.
Thus, this secret of the interruption of the mantra has been revealed;
now the Vidyā that effects internal meditation, attained through the sequential transmission, is being described.
One should join the Tāraka mantra with "namo 'ntam" (ending in "namaḥ") for the Blessed One; at the end of that,
one should place the word "Gāṅgam."
After that, one should place the eight-syllable mantra: "O Mahākālī, O Goddess who feeds on flesh and blood, O Goddess with a red and black face."
At its conclusion, one should see me, as well as the footprints of humans;
